additional_notes: Somewhat formal/literary synonym of „manchmal“. Often used in writing or more elevated speech. Typical placement is like other adverbs of frequency (e.g., after the verb in main clauses).
target_language_example: Bisweilen gehe ich nach der Arbeit noch spazieren.
native_language_example: Occasionally I go for a walk after work.

additional_notes: Common polite phrase used when you want someone to pause and wait (in shops, on the phone, at an office, etc.). Often expanded to “Bitte warten Sie (einen Moment).” (formal) or “Bitte warte (kurz).” (informal, to someone you address with “du”). You may also hear it on hold messages: “Bitte warten.”
target_language_example: Einen Moment bitte, bitte warten Sie kurz.
native_language_example: One moment, please—please wait a moment.

additional_notes: Used in the pattern „jemanden (Akk.) um etwas (Akk.) bitten“ = to ask someone for something. Common in polite requests, often with „bitte“: „Ich bitte Sie um …“ (formal) / „Ich bitte dich um …“ (informal).
target_language_example: Ich bitte Sie um Hilfe.
native_language_example: I’m asking you for help.

additional_notes: Common, informal everyday expression meaning someone has had too much alcohol. Used with "sein": "Ich bin blau" (I’m drunk). You can also hear "blau werden" (to get drunk) and "sich blau trinken" (to drink oneself drunk). Not used for being literally blue—use "blau" as an adjective for color ("Der Himmel ist blau").
target_language_example: Ich war gestern Abend total blau.
native_language_example: I was totally drunk last night.

additional_notes: Common everyday term for a bruise (an area of skin that turns blue/purple after a bump or injury). Often used with the verb „haben“ (to have): „Ich habe einen blauen Fleck.“ Plural: „blaue Flecken“.
target_language_example: Ich habe einen blauen Fleck am Arm.
native_language_example: I have a bruise on my arm.

meaning: a black eye; (figuratively) a close call (getting off lightly).
additional_notes: Literally “blue eye.” Most commonly used for an injury: „ein blaues Auge haben“ = to have a black eye. Also used figuratively in the phrase „mit einem blauen Auge davonkommen“ (“to get away with it with just a scare / minor consequences”).
target_language_example: Zum Glück sind wir mit einem blauen Auge davongekommen.
native_language_example: Luckily, we got away with it with only minor consequences.

additional_notes: "chinesisch" is the language (not capitalized in German), and "sprechen" means "to speak." You can swap in other languages: "Englisch sprechen" (to speak English), "Deutsch sprechen" (to speak German). Often used in questions like "Sprechen Sie Chinesisch?" (formal) or "Sprichst du Chinesisch?" (informal).
target_language_example: Sprichst du chinesisch?
native_language_example: Do you speak Chinese?

additional_notes: Common abbreviation of **das heißt**. Used to clarify, rephrase, or specify what you just said (like English **i.e.** / **that is to say**). Often written as **d. h.** or **d.h.** in texts.
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns um 18 Uhr, d. h. nach der Arbeit.
native_language_example: We’re meeting at 6 p.m., that is, after work.

additional_notes: Used mainly in formal writing to clarify or specify something (similar to English “i.e.”). It’s uncommon in spoken German; in speech you’d usually say “das ist …”, “das heißt …” (often abbreviated “d. h.” in writing), or “also …”.
target_language_example: Du brauchst ein Ausweisdokument, d. i. einen Personalausweis oder Reisepass.
native_language_example: You need an ID document, i.e. an ID card or passport.

additional_notes: Used to point to something/someone at a distance, often with a gesture. “Da” = there, “drüben” emphasizes “on the other side/over there.” Common in spoken German; also appears as “da drüben” vs. “dort drüben” (a bit more explicit).
target_language_example: Die Toilette ist da drüben, neben der Tür.
native_language_example: The restroom is over there, next to the door.

additional_notes: Used to point out a location that is farther away and toward the back of a room/area (opposite of "da vorne" = up front). Common in spoken directions: "Da hinten ist die Toilette." You can also use it without a verb when pointing: "Da hinten!"
target_language_example: Die Toiletten sind da hinten links.
native_language_example: The restrooms are back there on the left.

additional_notes: Used to point out a place or object located higher than the speaker (on a shelf, upstairs, on a hill, in the sky). Often paired with a gesture. Contrast: „da unten“ = down there. You can also say „dort oben“ (a bit more specific/less immediate) or „hier oben“ = up here.
target_language_example: Der Schlüssel liegt da oben auf dem Regal.
native_language_example: The key is up there on the shelf.

meaning: to be there; to be present; to exist (depending on context).
additional_notes: Most commonly means “to be there / present,” often about attending or being available: „Ich bin um 8 Uhr da.“ = “I’ll be there at 8.” It can also mean “to exist” in a more general sense: „Gibt es das noch?“ – „Ja, das ist noch da.“ = “Does that still exist?” – “Yes, it’s still there.” Distinct from „dasein“ (one word), which is a noun meaning “existence.”
target_language_example: Bist du morgen bei der Besprechung da?
native_language_example: Will you be there at the meeting tomorrow?

additional_notes: "Da" means "there" (or "here" depending on context), and "sind" is "are" (3rd person plural of "sein"). You’ll most often see it in sentences like "Da sind ..." to point out that something/someone is present or exists in a place: "Da sind zwei Stühle" (There are two chairs). In questions, word order changes: "Sind da noch Tickets?" (Are there still tickets?).
target_language_example: Da sind noch zwei Plätze frei.
native_language_example: There are still two free seats.

additional_notes: Used to point out a place that is lower than where the speaker is (or lower on a map/screen). Often used with pointing: „Da unten ist der Eingang.“ Can refer to a general area rather than a precise spot. Related: „hier unten“ = down here; „da oben“ = up there.
target_language_example: Der Eingang ist da unten, neben dem Aufzug.
native_language_example: The entrance is down there, next to the elevator.

meaning: up there / over there in front.
additional_notes: Points to a location that is some distance away and ahead (in front of the speaker). Often used with a gesture, and commonly paired with verbs like „sein“ or „stehen“ (e.g., „Da vorne ist…“ / „Da vorne steht…“). Contrast: „hier vorne“ = up here in front (near the speaker); „da hinten“ = back there (behind).
target_language_example: Da vorne ist die Bushaltestelle.
native_language_example: The bus stop is up there (in front).

additional_notes: "Da" means "there" (often pointing to a place or situation), and "war" is the past tense of "sein" (to be): "was". Used to say that something existed/was present at a certain time, or to point back to something that was there. Often appears with an object: "Da war ein Problem." (There was a problem.)
target_language_example: Da war gestern ein Fehler im Formular.
native_language_example: There was a mistake in the form yesterday.

additional_notes: Uses the simple past (Präteritum) of **sein**: **waren** = “were.” **da** means “there” (at that place). Common in descriptions of a past situation: **Da waren viele Leute.** It can also be used to point out something you noticed in the past context (“There were … right there.”).
target_language_example: Gestern da waren viele Leute im Park.
native_language_example: Yesterday there were a lot of people in the park.

meaning: to have (something) with you; to have on you.
additional_notes: Used when you’re carrying something or have it available (in your bag, pocket, etc.). Often appears in questions like „Hast du deinen Ausweis dabei?“ (= Do you have your ID with you?). Word order: „Ich habe … dabei.“ In the past: „Ich hatte … dabei.“
target_language_example: Hast du dein Ticket dabei?
native_language_example: Do you have your ticket with you?

meaning: to be there; to take part (to join in).
additional_notes: Commonly used to say someone is present or participating: "Bist du dabei?" = "Are you in?/Are you coming?" It can also mean being in the middle of doing something with a comma + "zu" + infinitive: "Ich bin dabei, meine Wohnung aufzuräumen." = "I’m in the process of cleaning my apartment."
target_language_example: Bist du heute Abend dabei?
native_language_example: Are you coming / Will you be there tonight?

meaning: to be in favor of (something); to support it.
additional_notes: Used to express agreement/support for an idea, plan, or proposal. Often contrasted with „dagegen sein“ (to be against it). The „dafür“ refers back to something already mentioned (e.g., a suggestion), and you commonly use it with nouns or „dass“-clauses: „Ich bin dafür, dass …“.
target_language_example: Ich bin dafür, dass wir früher anfangen.
native_language_example: I’m in favor of us starting earlier.

meaning: against it/that; however/on the other hand.
additional_notes: A common pronominal adverb: **da-** refers to something already mentioned, and **-gegen** means “against.” Use it instead of *gegen es/das* (which is usually not natural): *Ich bin dagegen.* = “I’m against it.” It can also introduce a contrast, like “however/on the other hand”: *Ich mag Tee. Dagegen mag ich keinen Kaffee.*
target_language_example: Ich bin dagegen, dass wir so spät losfahren.
native_language_example: I’m against us leaving so late.

additional_notes: Common in everyday speech and often more southern/colloquial than "zu Hause" (which is standard and used everywhere). Used to say where you are ("Ich bin daheim") or that you’re going home/going back home ("Ich gehe daheim" is regional; standard is "Ich gehe nach Hause" or "Ich gehe heim").
target_language_example: Ich bleibe heute daheim.
native_language_example: I’m staying home today.

additional_notes: Most commonly used as a connector meaning “therefore/so” to introduce a conclusion: „Es regnet, daher bleiben wir zu Hause.“ It can also mean “from there” in a more literal sense, especially with verbs of coming/knowing: „Ich komme daher.“ In everyday speech, „deshalb/darum“ are often used similarly to the “therefore” meaning.
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Zeit, daher komme ich später.
native_language_example: I don't have time, so I'll come later.

additional_notes: “dahin” expresses direction (movement toward a place or endpoint). Often used with motion verbs like gehen/fahren/bringen: “Ich gehe dahin.” It can also mean “until then / up to that point” in phrases like “bis dahin” (= until then) or “von da an bis dahin” (= from then until then). Contrast: “da” = there (location), “dahin” = to there (direction).
target_language_example: Wir fahren morgen dahin.
native_language_example: We’re driving there tomorrow.

meaning: “in that respect / in that regard”; “to that effect.”
additional_notes: Formal phrasing used to specify what something relates to (a statement, instruction, question, change, etc.). Often appears as **dahingehend** (one word) and is common in written German and official contexts. Typical patterns: **eine Frage/Bitte/Änderung dahingehend, dass …** (“a question/request/change to the effect that …”).
target_language_example: Wir haben eine Änderung dahingehend vorgenommen, dass die Öffnungszeiten länger sind.
native_language_example: We made a change so that the opening hours are longer.

additional_notes: A polite, formal way to address an audience (e.g., announcements, speeches, presentations). Often used as the opening of a public address: “Meine Damen und Herren, …” Capitalized because both nouns are plural forms of "die Dame" (lady) and "der Herr" (gentleman).
target_language_example: Meine Damen und Herren, der Zug nach Berlin fährt von Gleis 3.
native_language_example: Ladies and gentlemen, the train to Berlin departs from platform 3.

meaning: to start (with it/that); to begin doing that.
additional_notes: Used when the object/thing you’re starting with is referred to as “it/that.” “Damit” points back to something already mentioned or obvious in context. Common in instructions and planning. Word order can change: in a main clause you’ll often see the split verb (“Ich fange damit an …”), while in subordinate clauses it stays together (“…, weil ich damit anfange”).
target_language_example: Ich fange damit an, die Küche aufzuräumen.
native_language_example: I’m starting by tidying up the kitchen.

meaning: to stop (doing) that; to quit it.
additional_notes: Used when you refer back to an action or behavior with **damit** (“with that / that”). Often said as an instruction or request: **Hör damit auf!** (“Stop it!”). Grammar: **aufhören** is separable, so in the imperative you say **Hör ... auf**; in a statement: **Ich höre damit auf.** You can add the thing you’re stopping: **Ich höre damit auf, zu rauchen.**
target_language_example: Hör bitte damit auf, so laut zu sein.
native_language_example: Please stop being so loud.

meaning: to mean (by that); to be referring to that.
additional_notes: Used when clarifying what someone intends with a statement, often in questions or explanations. It commonly appears as "Was meinst du damit?" (What do you mean by that?) or "Ich meine damit …" (What I mean by that is …). "damit" refers back to something previously said or implied.
target_language_example: Was meinst du damit?
native_language_example: What do you mean by that?

meaning: to expect it; to count on that (happening).
additional_notes: Used when you anticipate something (often something likely or possible). Common patterns: „Ich rechne damit, dass …“ (I expect that …) and „Damit musst du rechnen.“ (You have to expect that / you have to be prepared for that). „damit“ refers back to something (a situation, consequence, event).
target_language_example: Ich rechne damit, dass der Zug Verspätung hat.
native_language_example: I expect the train to be delayed.

meaning: to let off steam; to vent (anger/frustration).
additional_notes: Used when someone releases built-up stress or frustration, often by complaining, talking it out, or doing something physical. Can be used with "bei jemandem" (to vent to someone) or "über etwas" (to vent about something).
target_language_example: Nach dem stressigen Tag muss ich einfach mal Dampf ablassen.
native_language_example: After the stressful day, I just need to let off some steam.

additional_notes: Most commonly used to talk about the next event in time: something happens, and *danach* something else happens. It can also mean “about it/for it” with certain verbs that take **nach** (e.g., *danach fragen* = to ask about it), but beginners will most often meet it in the time sense (“afterwards”).
target_language_example: Wir essen, und danach gehen wir spazieren.
native_language_example: We eat, and afterwards we go for a walk.

additional_notes: Common, neutral phrase for something that happens from time to time (not regularly). Often used with the present tense. Similar to "ab und zu" or "hin und wieder."
target_language_example: Ich gehe dann und wann ins Kino.
native_language_example: I go to the cinema every now and then.

meaning: to work on it; to work toward improving something.
additional_notes: Used with "an" + pronoun: "daran" = "an + das" (on it/at it). It can refer to a task (working on something) or self-improvement (working on a problem, habit, or relationship). Common variants: "an etwas arbeiten" (to work on something), "daran arbeiten, dass ..." (to work on it so that ...).
target_language_example: Ich arbeite daran, mein Deutsch zu verbessern.
native_language_example: I’m working on improving my German.

meaning: to remember (to do something); to think of it.
additional_notes: Often used with an infinitive clause: „Denk daran, + zu …“ = “Remember to …”. It refers back to something previously mentioned (“that/it”), like “think about it/remember it.” In speech you may also hear „dran denken“ (colloquial shortening).
target_language_example: Denk bitte daran, den Termin abzusagen.
native_language_example: Please remember to cancel the appointment.

meaning: to remind (someone) of it / to remember it (by prompting).
additional_notes: Commonly used as "jemanden daran erinnern, (dass ...)" = "to remind someone (that ...)". The pronoun "daran" refers back to something previously mentioned ("of it/about it"). You’ll also see related forms like "sich daran erinnern" (to remember it) and "dich daran erinnern" (remind you / remember it).
target_language_example: Kannst du mich bitte daran erinnern, den Termin zu bestätigen?
native_language_example: Can you please remind me to confirm the appointment?

meaning: to believe in it / believe that (it will happen).
additional_notes: "daran" means "in it" / "in that" (referring back to something already mentioned). Common patterns: "Ich glaube daran" (I believe in it), "Glaubst du daran, dass …?" (Do you believe that …?). With "müssen" it can become an idiom: "daran glauben müssen" = "to have to die / be the one who gets it" (e.g., in movies or jokingly about being fired), which is much stronger than the literal meaning.
target_language_example: Ich glaube daran, dass wir das schaffen.
native_language_example: I believe that we can do it.

meaning: to be to blame for it; to be responsible for it (negatively).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is at fault for a situation. The pronoun "daran" refers back to something previously mentioned ("for that/for it"). Common patterns: "Wer ist daran schuld?" (Who is to blame?), "Ich bin nicht daran schuld." (It’s not my fault.), "Er ist daran schuld, dass …" (He’s to blame that …). Often used with "nicht" to deny blame.
target_language_example: Ich bin nicht daran schuld, dass der Bus zu spät ist.
native_language_example: It’s not my fault that the bus is late.

meaning: to doubt it / to have doubts about it.
additional_notes: "daran" means "about it/that" and refers back to something already mentioned. The verb is "zweifeln" and it’s used with the preposition "an" + dative: "an etwas (Dat.) zweifeln". In conversation you’ll often see it as "daran zweifeln" (= doubt that), or "daran zweifeln, dass …" (= doubt that …).
target_language_example: Ich zweifle daran, dass er heute kommt.
native_language_example: I doubt that he’s coming today.

meaning: on it; to it; about that (depends on the verb/preposition).
additional_notes: "Darauf" is a pronominal adverb: da- + auf. It often replaces "auf + [thing]" (e.g., "auf den Termin" → "darauf"). Common with verbs/adjectives that take "auf" such as "sich freuen auf" (look forward to) or "warten auf" (wait for). It can also mean "after that/then" in a sequence ("Darauf sagte er ..." = "Then he said ...").
target_language_example: Ich freue mich darauf.
native_language_example: I’m looking forward to it.

meaning: to pay attention to (that); to make sure (that).
additional_notes: Common with a "dass"-clause or with "auf + Akkusativ" (e.g., "auf die Aussprache"). "Darauf" refers back to what follows (or to something already mentioned): "Achte darauf, dass ..." = "Make sure that ..." / "Be careful to ...". The verb is separable in many forms: "Ich achte darauf" / "Ich habe darauf geachtet".
target_language_example: Achte bitte darauf, dass du die Tür abschließt.
native_language_example: Please make sure you lock the door.

additional_notes: Used to say that the result or answer depends on a condition or detail. Very common in the phrase "Es kommt darauf an" (“It depends”). The word "darauf" refers back to something (often followed by "ob" + clause, or "worauf" in questions).
target_language_example: Ob wir pünktlich ankommen, kommt darauf an, wie viel Verkehr ist.
native_language_example: Whether we arrive on time depends on how much traffic there is.

meaning: to answer (to it / to that); to reply to that.
additional_notes: Used with the pronoun-adverb "darauf" (= on it/to it) to refer back to something already mentioned (a question, email, request, comment). Often paired with "auf + accusative": "auf die Frage/E-Mail antworten". Word order: "Ich antworte darauf." / "Darauf antworte ich nicht."
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte darauf antworten?
native_language_example: Can you please reply to that?

meaning: to insist on it; to insist that (something happens/is true).
additional_notes: Used when someone strongly demands something or won’t change their position. Often followed by "dass" + clause ("bestehen darauf, dass...") or by a noun/infinitive with "darauf" referring back to what’s being insisted on. Note: "bestehen" also means "to pass" (an exam), but "darauf bestehen" means "to insist".
target_language_example: Ich bestehe darauf, dass wir pünktlich losfahren.
native_language_example: I insist that we leave on time.

meaning: to point out; to draw attention to (something).
additional_notes: Often used in formal or neutral contexts to highlight an important detail or to inform someone about a fact. It can take an object clause with „dass …“ (e.g., „Ich möchte darauf hinweisen, dass …“) or a noun phrase with „auf + Akkusativ“ (e.g., „jemanden auf etwas hinweisen“).
target_language_example: Ich möchte darauf hinweisen, dass der Zug heute später kommt.
native_language_example: I’d like to point out that the train is arriving later today.

meaning: to wait for it/that; to wait (for something mentioned).
additional_notes: Used when the thing you’re waiting for is referred to with a pronoun (darauf = “on it/for it/for that”), often pointing back to something already known from context (e.g., an answer, a bus, permission). With a specific noun, you usually say „auf + Akkusativ warten“: „Ich warte auf den Bus.“
target_language_example: Ich warte darauf, dass du mir antwortest.
native_language_example: I’m waiting for you to answer me.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to something already mentioned (a place, object, person, goal). Very common with movement verbs like gehen/laufen/rennen: „auf etwas zugehen“ = to walk toward something. In a sentence it’s often split: „Er ging darauf zu.“ = „He walked toward it.“
target_language_example: Sie ging auf die Tür zu und klopfte.
native_language_example: She walked toward the door and knocked.

meaning: therefore; that’s why; about it/that (in set phrases).
additional_notes: Commonly used to give a reason or conclusion: „Ich habe keine Zeit, darum komme ich nicht.“ (= therefore/that’s why). Also appears in fixed expressions like „Es geht darum, …“ meaning “it’s about … / the point is …”. Related to other “da-” words like „damit“ (with it/so that) and „daran“ (on it/about it).
target_language_example: Ich bin müde, darum gehe ich früh ins Bett.
native_language_example: I’m tired, so I’m going to bed early.

meaning: to ask for it; to request it.
additional_notes: "darum" refers back to something already mentioned ("for that/about that"). Common with prepositions like "um" (to ask someone for something): "jemanden darum bitten" = to ask someone for it/for that. More formal/polite than just "fragen"; often used in requests and emails.
target_language_example: Ich möchte Sie darum bitten, mir die Unterlagen bis Freitag zu schicken.
native_language_example: I would like to ask you to send me the documents by Friday.

additional_notes: Used to highlight the main point or what really matters in a situation (“That’s the whole idea”). Very common in spoken German. Often appears as a response to clarify or emphasize the key issue: “Genau darum geht es!” You’ll also see variations like “darum geht’s” (more colloquial) or “Darum geht es nicht” (“That’s not the point”).
target_language_example: Genau darum geht es: Wir müssen Zeit sparen.
native_language_example: That’s exactly the point: We need to save time.

meaning: to take care of it; to deal with it.
additional_notes: Used with a pronoun or object to mean you handle a task/problem: „Ich kümmere mich darum.“ (= I’ll take care of it.) The full verb is „sich um (etw./jdn.) kümmern“ (to take care of something/someone). Conjugation: ich kümmere mich, du kümmerst dich, er/sie kümmert sich; past: „hat sich (darum) gekümmert“.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich kümmere mich darum.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll take care of it.

additional_notes: Common in writing and formal speech to add extra information or go beyond what was just mentioned. It can refer to an abstract point ("beyond that") or simply add another point ("furthermore"). Similar in meaning to "außerdem" and "zusätzlich", but "darüber hinaus" often sounds a bit more formal.
target_language_example: Das ist schon teuer; darüber hinaus dauert die Lieferung sehr lange.
native_language_example: That’s already expensive; furthermore, the delivery takes a very long time.

meaning: to think about it; to consider it.
additional_notes: Used when you want to say you’re considering something or will reflect on it. Often refers back to something already mentioned (darüber = “about that/it”). Common patterns: „Ich denke darüber nach.“ (I’ll think about it.) / „Denk darüber nach!“ (Think about it!) / „Ich muss darüber nachdenken.“ (I need to think about it.).
target_language_example: Ich muss darüber nachdenken, ob ich morgen Zeit habe.
native_language_example: I need to think about whether I have time tomorrow.

meaning: to talk about it/that; to discuss it.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "reden" (to talk) with the adverb "darüber" (about it/that). Common for suggesting or agreeing to discuss a topic: "Wir müssen darüber reden" (We need to talk about it). Often used when the topic is already known from context; for a specific noun you can also say "über + Akkusativ" (e.g., "über das Problem reden").
target_language_example: Können wir später darüber reden?
native_language_example: Can we talk about it later?

meaning: to talk about it/that; to discuss it.
additional_notes: Used when the topic has already been mentioned or is clear from context. It uses the preposition-like part "darüber" (= "about it/that") and the verb "sprechen" (= "to talk/speak"). Very common in everyday speech; you can also say "darüber reden" (more casual) or "darüber sprechen" (slightly more formal).
target_language_example: Können wir später darüber sprechen?
native_language_example: Can we talk about it later?

meaning: the realm; the empire (also: “the Reich,” especially in historical contexts).
additional_notes: "Reich" refers to a state or political realm/empire. It’s common in historical terms like "das Deutsche Reich" (the German Empire/state) or "das Heilige Römische Reich" (the Holy Roman Empire). In modern contexts, it can strongly evoke Nazi Germany ("das Dritte Reich" = the Third Reich), so use it carefully and usually in historical discussion.
target_language_example: Im Heiligen Römischen Reich gab es viele Fürstentümer.
native_language_example: In the Holy Roman Empire there were many principalities.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the first occurrence/experience of doing something. Often followed by a clause with **dass** or **als** (past): *Das erste Mal, dass/als ich in Berlin war…* Also common with **zum**: *zum ersten Mal* = “for the first time.”
target_language_example: Ich bin das erste Mal in Deutschland.
native_language_example: It’s my first time in Germany.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase meaning something functions properly or a plan/method is successful. "Das" refers to something specific (an idea, device, method) and is often stressed to mean “that (one) works.” You can also answer a suggestion with it: "Ja, das funktioniert."
target_language_example: Wenn du die App neu startest, funktioniert das wieder – ja, das funktioniert.
native_language_example: If you restart the app, it works again—yes, that works.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken German. Used to say something is possible or acceptable (e.g., a time, price, plan). With intonation it can also mean “That’s fine/OK.” For “That’s not possible,” you’ll often hear “Das geht nicht.”
target_language_example: Können wir uns um fünf treffen? – Ja, das geht.
native_language_example: Can we meet at five? – Yes, that works.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase meaning something cannot be done or won’t work (a rule, a plan, a machine, a request). Often used to refuse or point out a problem. Similar alternatives: "Das funktioniert nicht" (That doesn’t work), "Das ist nicht möglich" (That’s not possible).
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, das geht nicht.
native_language_example: Sorry, that’s not possible.

additional_notes: Used to say something is sufficient, often to stop an action (e.g., adding more, explaining more). Common in everyday speech; can sound firm depending on tone. Literally “that suffices.”
target_language_example: Danke, das genügt – ich brauche keine weiteren Informationen.
native_language_example: Thanks, that’s enough—I don’t need any more information.

additional_notes: Common in everyday conversations when confirming availability (in a shop/restaurant) or confirming something is already done/handled. It can stand alone as a short answer, or be extended, e.g. “Das haben wir (leider) nicht” (“We don’t have that (unfortunately)”) or “Das haben wir schon” (“We already have that”).
target_language_example: — Haben Sie Hafermilch? — Ja, das haben wir.
native_language_example: — Do you have oat milk? — Yes, we have that.

additional_notes: Used to clarify, explain, or restate what you just said (often like English “that is,” “meaning,” “i.e.”). In conversation it can also introduce an implication: “Das heißt, du kommst nicht?” = “So that means you’re not coming?” Commonly followed by a comma when it introduces a clause: “Das heißt, …”
target_language_example: Ich bin Vegetarier, das heißt, ich esse kein Fleisch.
native_language_example: I’m vegetarian, that means I don’t eat meat.

additional_notes: Common in shops and service situations as an elliptical, friendly way to say something is available, often completed with “da” (“right here”): “Das hätten wir (da).” Grammatically it uses Konjunktiv II (“hätten”), but it usually refers to present availability, not the past. If stressed differently or in a longer sentence, it can also literally mean “we would have had that,” but that’s less common as a standalone phrase.
target_language_example: Ja, das hätten wir da – in Blau oder in Schwarz.
native_language_example: Yes, we have that right here—in blue or in black.

additional_notes: A common sentence fragment used to point out location (“It’s here.”) or to introduce a statement about the current place (“Here, it is …”). Very often followed by an adjective or rule: “Das ist hier verboten/normal/anders.” If it starts a sentence, it’s capitalized (“Das”); in the middle of a sentence it’s usually “das” (e.g., “Ich finde, dass das hier …”).
target_language_example: Das ist hier verboten.
native_language_example: That’s forbidden here.

additional_notes: Used to agree cautiously or acknowledge that something is possible without fully committing. Common in conversation as a neutral response (similar to “could be” or “maybe”). Often said on its own, or followed by a contrasting point: “Das kann sein, aber …”
target_language_example: Das kann sein, aber ich bin mir nicht sicher.
native_language_example: That could be, but I’m not sure.

meaning: the last time; (sometimes) for the last time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a previous occasion: "das letzte Mal" = "last time". Often appears with the preposition "beim" (="when" in a specific situation): "beim letzten Mal" = "last time (when we did this)". With "zum" it can mean "for the last time" (often as a warning): "zum letzten Mal!".
target_language_example: Das letzte Mal habe ich den Bus verpasst.
native_language_example: Last time I missed the bus.

additional_notes: Used when someone has the authority to make the final decision in a discussion (at home, at work, etc.). Often used with a person as the subject (e.g., "Meine Chefin hat ..."). Literal meaning is "to have the last word," which matches the idiomatic English meaning.
target_language_example: Am Ende hat der Chef das letzte Wort.
native_language_example: In the end, the boss has the final say.

additional_notes: Used to say that an activity is enjoyable. Literally “that makes fun,” but in English you normally say “That’s fun” or “I’m having fun.” You can also specify what is fun: “Das macht Spaß, Fußball zu spielen.”
target_language_example: Das macht Spaß!
native_language_example: This is fun!

meaning: “That has to be.” / “It has to be done.”
additional_notes: Used to say something is necessary or unavoidable (“it has to be this way”). Often said when you accept an unpleasant necessity (e.g., rules, repairs, expenses): “Das muss sein.” Can also emphasize that something is required: “Das muss sein, sonst …”
target_language_example: Ich weiß, es ist teuer, aber das muss sein.
native_language_example: I know it’s expensive, but it has to be done.

additional_notes: Used to say something is suitable or acceptable (a time, plan, size, etc.). Often followed by a detail: “Das passt mir (gut).” = “That works for me.” Also common in shops about clothing sizes: “Das passt.” = “It fits.”
target_language_example: Um 15 Uhr? Ja, das passt (mir).
native_language_example: At 3 p.m.? Yes, that works (for me).

additional_notes: Used to say something is sufficient, or to tell someone to stop (e.g., too much noise, too many questions). Tone depends on context: it can be neutral (“that’s enough money”) or annoyed/firm (“Stop it, that’s enough.”). Often used alone as an exclamation: “Das reicht!”
target_language_example: Das reicht, hör bitte auf.
native_language_example: That’s enough, please stop.

meaning: "that’s supposed to be (it)" / "this is meant to be…" (often showing doubt or surprise).
additional_notes: Literally "that should be." In everyday speech it’s often used to question or criticize something, implying it doesn’t meet expectations: "Und das soll alles sein?" = "And that’s supposed to be all?" You’ll also commonly see it with a noun: "Das soll ein Witz sein" (That’s supposed to be a joke).
target_language_example: Und das soll alles sein?
native_language_example: And that’s supposed to be all?

additional_notes: Used to agree with someone or confirm that something is correct. Very common in everyday speech. You can also use it to confirm information (like a date, a price, or a fact). A close opposite is “Das stimmt nicht.” (“That’s not true / That’s not right.”).
target_language_example: A: Du kommst aus England, oder? B: Ja, das stimmt.
native_language_example: A: You’re from England, right? B: Yes, that’s right.

additional_notes: Used to disagree or correct someone’s statement. Common in everyday speech and can be neutral or firm depending on tone. Often used as a full sentence; you can also say “Das stimmt.” (“That’s true/correct.”).
target_language_example: Nein, das stimmt nicht. Ich habe das nicht gesagt.
native_language_example: No, that’s not true. I didn’t say that.

additional_notes: Contraction of "das war es". Common in spoken German to say something is finished, to wrap up an explanation, or to end a conversation or task. Can sound a bit abrupt depending on tone; you can soften it with "Das war's dann" or "Das war's für heute."
target_language_example: So, das war's für heute. Danke fürs Zuhören!
native_language_example: So, that's it for today. Thanks for listening!

meaning: “That would be it.” / “That’s all.” (often: “That would be great.”)
additional_notes: Colloquial contraction of „das wäre es“ (= „das wäre es“ / „das wäre’s“). Used to wrap up a request or confirm the last thing mentioned: „…und das wär’s.“ Also used to say something would be ideal/sufficient: „Ein Kaffee, das wär’s.“ Common in spoken German; in writing you may also see „das wär’s“ or the more formal „das wäre es“.
target_language_example: Ein Wasser, bitte – das wär’s.
native_language_example: A water, please—that’s all.

meaning: to depend on that / to depend on it.
additional_notes: Used to say that the result or decision depends on something previously mentioned ("davon" = "on that/about that"). Very common in answers: "Das hängt davon ab" (“That depends”). Often followed by a clause with "ob" (whether) or a question word: "Es hängt davon ab, ob ..." / "Es hängt davon ab, wie/was/wann ...".
target_language_example: Es hängt davon ab, ob du morgen Zeit hast.
native_language_example: It depends on whether you have time tomorrow.

meaning: to assume; to proceed on the basis of (something).
additional_notes: Common in both spoken and written German to express an assumption or starting point: "Ich gehe davon aus, dass ..." = "I assume that ...". "Davon" refers back to an idea/fact already mentioned or understood, and "ausgehen" here means "to start from" (not "to go out"). Often used in formal or neutral contexts (emails, work, school).
target_language_example: Ich gehe davon aus, dass du morgen Zeit hast.
native_language_example: I assume you’ll have time tomorrow.

meaning: to tell (someone) about it/that; to talk about it.
additional_notes: "davon" refers back to something already known from context (a topic/event/experience). It’s often used with a dative object for the listener: "jemandem davon erzählen" (to tell someone about it). In conversation, "davon" can mean "about it" or "about that" depending on what was mentioned before.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir davon erzählen?
native_language_example: Can you tell me about it?

meaning: to benefit from it; to get something out of it.
additional_notes: Often used to talk about what advantage (or lack of advantage) someone gets from something. Very common in the negative: „nichts davon haben“ = „not get anything out of it / not benefit from it.“ You can add what the benefit is with an object: „Was habe ich davon?“ = „What’s in it for me?“
target_language_example: Was habe ich davon, wenn ich früher komme?
native_language_example: What’s in it for me if I come earlier?

meaning: to think of it/that; to have an opinion about it.
additional_notes: Used with the pattern „etwas von etwas halten“ (= to think of something). „davon“ refers back to something already mentioned. Very common in questions like „Was hältst du davon?“ (What do you think of it?). In answers you often use: „Ich halte viel davon“ (I think highly of it) / „Ich halte nichts davon“ (I’m not a fan of it).
target_language_example: Was hältst du davon, heute zu Hause zu bleiben?
native_language_example: What do you think about staying at home today?

meaning: to hear about it / to hear of it.
additional_notes: Used when you’ve heard information about something (news, a rumor, a topic, a person) but not necessarily experienced it yourself. Often appears with questions like „Hast du davon gehört?“ (= Have you heard about it?). „Davon“ refers back to something already mentioned or understood from context.
target_language_example: Hast du davon gehört, dass der Zug heute ausfällt?
native_language_example: Have you heard that the train is cancelled today?

additional_notes: Used when you mean you literally dream about something while sleeping or you strongly wish for something. "Davon" refers back to the thing ("of it/that"). Often followed by "dass" + clause ("Ich träume davon, dass …"). You can also say "von etwas träumen"; "davon träumen" is used when the thing is already known from context.
target_language_example: Ich träume davon, einmal nach Japan zu reisen.
native_language_example: I dream of traveling to Japan one day.

meaning: to know about it; to be aware of it.
additional_notes: “Davon” means “of it/about it” and refers back to something previously mentioned. Very common in negatives: “nichts davon wissen” = “to know nothing about it / to have no idea about it.” You can also say “etwas davon wissen” = “to know something about it.”
target_language_example: Ich wusste nichts davon.
native_language_example: I didn’t know anything about it.

meaning: to get someone to do something; to persuade someone to do something.
additional_notes: Used when someone causes or persuades another person to take an action. Often appears with an object + “dazu” + infinitive clause: “jdn. dazu bringen, etw. zu tun” (to get someone to do something). Example structure: “Er hat mich dazu gebracht, es zu versuchen.”
target_language_example: Wie hast du ihn dazu gebracht, zu kommen?
native_language_example: How did you get him to come?

meaning: to be part of it; to be included (in that).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something belongs to a group, category, or list that has just been mentioned. Often followed by a noun in the nominative: "Dazu gehören A, B und C." ("A, B, and C are included.") You’ll also see it with a dative group: "X gehört dazu" (X belongs to it), or "X gehört zu Y" (X belongs to Y).
target_language_example: Zu den Kosten gehören auch Steuern und Gebühren dazu.
native_language_example: Taxes and fees are also included in the costs.

meaning: to be added (on top of that); to come in addition.
additional_notes: Used to add extra information, costs, work, problems, etc. Often with a clause introduced by „dass“: „Dazu kommt, dass …“ = “On top of that, …”. Also common with „noch“ for emphasis: „Dann kommt noch … dazu.“ In separable-verb word order, „dazu“ often appears at the end: „Es kommt noch Geld dazu.“
target_language_example: Dazu kommt, dass wir morgen früh aufstehen müssen.
native_language_example: On top of that, we have to get up early tomorrow.

meaning: to tend to (do something); to be inclined to.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a general tendency or habit. It’s typically followed by an infinitive with „zu“: „dazu neigen, etwas zu tun“. „Dazu“ refers back to the action just mentioned or understood from context (similar to “to do that / to do so”). Common in neutral, everyday and written German.
target_language_example: Ich neige dazu, zu spät ins Bett zu gehen.
native_language_example: I tend to go to bed too late.

meaning: to say/add something about it; to comment on it.
additional_notes: Used when you want to add a remark or give your opinion about something that was just mentioned. Often appears with questions like “Was kannst du dazu sagen?” (“What can you say about that?”). The “dazu” refers back to a topic/statement (about that / on that).
target_language_example: Was kannst du dazu sagen?
native_language_example: What can you say about that?

meaning: to be the case; to be so.
additional_notes: Often used after a statement to confirm that something is true or as things are: "So ist es" / "Wenn dem so ist..." (= "If that’s the case..."). It’s somewhat formal and fixed in wording; you’ll also see it with "wenn": "Wenn dem so ist, ...".
target_language_example: Wenn dem so ist, müssen wir früher gehen.
native_language_example: If that’s the case, we have to leave earlier.

meaning: to shake your head (to show “no” or disagreement).
additional_notes: Common gesture meaning you disagree, refuse, or don’t understand. You can also use it to express disapproval or disbelief: „Er schüttelte den Kopf“ = “He shook his head.” Often used with verbs like „(mit dem Kopf) schütteln“ or in the fixed phrase „den Kopf schütteln über + Akk.“ (“to shake your head about/at …”).
target_language_example: Sie schüttelt den Kopf und sagt: „Nein, danke.“
native_language_example: She shakes her head and says, “No, thanks.”

meaning: to keep your mouth shut; to be quiet.
additional_notes: Literally “to hold the mouth.” Used to tell someone to stop talking or to keep a secret. Often sounds rude/harsh, especially as an order (“Halt den Mund!”). A more polite alternative is “Sei bitte leise” (please be quiet) or “Nichts sagen” (don’t say anything).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte den Mund halten? Ich versuche zu telefonieren.
native_language_example: Can you please keep your mouth shut? I’m trying to make a phone call.

meaning: to have the courage (to do something).
additional_notes: Commonly used with an infinitive + „zu“: „den Mut haben, etwas zu tun“ = “to have the courage to do something.” Also often appears in the negative: „nicht den Mut haben“ = “not have the courage.” Related noun: „Mut“ = courage.
target_language_example: Ich habe den Mut, meinen Chef um Hilfe zu bitten.
native_language_example: I have the courage to ask my boss for help.

den Nagel auf den Kopf treffen

target_language_multi_word_term: den Nagel auf den Kopf treffen
meaning: to hit the nail on the head; to be exactly right.
additional_notes: An idiom used when someone expresses something perfectly or identifies the real problem/point. Common in spoken and written German. Grammar tip: you’ll often see it with a subject + trifft, e.g., „Du triffst den Nagel auf den Kopf.“
target_language_example: Mit deiner Analyse triffst du den Nagel auf den Kopf.
native_language_example: With your analysis, you’re hitting the nail on the head.

meaning: the right way; the correct path (accusative).
additional_notes: Most commonly used after verbs that take the accusative object, especially: „den richtigen Weg finden“ (to find the right way), „den richtigen Weg einschlagen“ (to choose the right path), „den richtigen Weg zeigen“ (to show the right way). Can be literal (finding your way somewhere) or figurative (making the right choice in life/work). „Weg“ = way/path; „richtig“ = right/correct; „den“ shows it’s masculine accusative.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, wir finden schon den richtigen Weg.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, we’ll find the right way.

additional_notes: Used in comparisons with a comparative form (e.g., besser, schneller, wichtiger) to mean “more … than ever.” Most often appears as “mehr + comparative + denn je” or “so + adjective + wie nie zuvor / denn je” in written or formal speech.
target_language_example: Die Preise sind höher denn je.
native_language_example: Prices are higher than ever.

additional_notes: Used to contrast with what was just said: something is true or happens even though there is a reason it might not. Common in both spoken and written German; often placed after a comma or at the start of a sentence. Similar in meaning to "trotzdem" (often a bit more formal).
target_language_example: Es regnet, aber wir gehen dennoch spazieren.
native_language_example: It’s raining, but we’re still going for a walk.

additional_notes: This is the genitive plural form of “die Herzen” (“the hearts”). It’s used to show possession/association, often in fixed phrases or titles, e.g. “die Königin der Herzen” (“the Queen of Hearts”). On its own, “der Herzen” usually sounds incomplete without a noun before it.
target_language_example: Die Königin der Herzen ist eine Figur aus „Alice im Wunderland“.
native_language_example: The Queen of Hearts is a character from “Alice in Wonderland”.

additional_notes: Used when counting or ranking people/things and referring to a masculine noun or a person understood as male (or a group member referred to with a masculine form). It’s the nominative masculine form of the ordinal number: der erste (the first), der zweite (the second), der dritte (the third). Often used with an implied noun: „Wer ist der dritte?“ = “Who is the third (person)?” For other genders/cases: die dritte, das dritte; den dritten, dem dritten, etc.
target_language_example: Er ist der dritte in der Reihe.
native_language_example: He is the third in the line.

meaning: the first (male person/thing); the one who comes first.
additional_notes: "Der Erste" is the masculine nominative form of the ordinal number "erste" and is often used as a noun (meaning "the first one"), especially when referring to people (e.g., in a line, a ranking, a competition). For other genders/cases you’ll see forms like "die Erste" (female), "das Erste" (neuter), or accusative "den Ersten". As an adjective before a noun: "der erste Tag" = "the first day".
target_language_example: Wer ist der Erste in der Schlange?
native_language_example: Who is the first in line?

additional_notes: Used when the adjective *letzte* is treated like a noun (a “nominalized” adjective). Refers to the last person/thing in an order or sequence. Form changes with gender/case/number, e.g. *die Letzte* (feminine), *das Letzte* (neuter), *die Letzten* (plural). Often used about people: *der Letzte in der Schlange* (“the last in line”).
target_language_example: Ich war der Letzte in der Schlange.
native_language_example: I was the last one in line.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the next person/thing in a sequence. In queues or at service counters, "Der Nächste!" means "Next!" or "Next, please!". As an adjective it’s usually followed by a noun ("der nächste Zug" = "the next train"), but as a standalone noun it means "the next (person/one)".
target_language_example: Der Nächste, bitte!
native_language_example: Next, please!

additional_notes: Used with masculine nouns to indicate the 2nd item/person in a sequence or ranking (e.g., der zweite Mann = the second man). As a standalone phrase, it can mean “the second one (male)” when the noun is understood from context. Declension depends on the article/case: der zweite (nom.), den zweiten (acc.), dem zweiten (dat.).
target_language_example: Er ist der zweite in der Schlange.
native_language_example: He is the second in line.

meaning: in the evening (at some point in the evening).
additional_notes: Genitive form of "der Abend" used mainly in fixed time expressions (e.g., "eines Abends" = one evening, "des Abends" = in the evening). It’s somewhat formal/literary and less common in everyday spoken German than "am Abend" or "abends".
target_language_example: Des Abends saßen wir noch lange auf dem Balkon.
native_language_example: In the evening, we sat on the balcony for a long time.

meaning: in the morning (at some point in the morning).
additional_notes: A somewhat formal/time-of-day expression using the genitive case: "des" + "Morgens". It means "(some time) in the morning" and is often used in narratives, news, or more formal speech. In everyday conversation, learners more often hear "morgens" (in the mornings) or "am Morgen" (in the morning).
target_language_example: Des Morgens war es noch sehr kalt.
native_language_example: In the morning it was still very cold.

additional_notes: Somewhat formal/written way to say something happens regularly. It’s used as an adverbial phrase (like „oft“) and can go at the beginning of a sentence for emphasis or later in the sentence. Common variant: „des Öfteren mal“ (more casual).
target_language_example: Ich bin des Öfteren in Berlin.
native_language_example: I’m in Berlin quite often.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens repeatedly or regularly. It’s common in speech, but in standard written German the preferred form is usually "des Öfteren" (capital Ö) or simply "oft" / "öfter". Often placed with a time adverb in the sentence (e.g., "Ich bin des Öfteren dort.").
target_language_example: Ich bin des Öfteren in Berlin.
native_language_example: I’m in Berlin fairly often.

additional_notes: Used to give a reason/result: statement A, deshalb statement B. When it starts a main clause, it counts as the first element, so the verb comes next (inversion): „Ich bin müde. Deshalb gehe ich ins Bett.“ It’s close in meaning to „darum“ and „deswegen“.
target_language_example: Ich habe morgen früh einen Termin, deshalb gehe ich jetzt nach Hause.
native_language_example: I have an appointment early tomorrow, so I’m going home now.

meaning: “all the better” (in a comparison: “the …, the better”).
additional_notes: Used in paired comparative structures: je + comparative … desto + comparative. It expresses that one thing increases as the other increases (often translated as “the more…, the better…”). You can also hear umso instead of desto: „je mehr…, umso besser“.
target_language_example: Je früher wir losfahren, desto besser.
native_language_example: The earlier we leave, the better.

additional_notes: Used in a correlative comparison, typically after a clause with "je" (or also "desto"): "Je X, desto mehr Y" = "The more X, the more Y". Common with adjectives/adverbs and comparatives. In writing you may also see "umso mehr" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Je mehr ich lerne, desto mehr verstehe ich.
native_language_example: The more I learn, the more I understand.

additional_notes: Used with a comparative clause introduced by „je“ or „umso/desto“ to form a proportional comparison: „Je mehr …, desto weniger …“ (“The more …, the less …”). „Desto weniger“ typically introduces the second clause and is followed by the rest of the sentence (often verb-second).
target_language_example: Je länger ich warte, desto weniger habe ich Lust.
native_language_example: The longer I wait, the less I feel like it.

additional_notes: Very common connector that refers back to a reason just mentioned. Often used to explain a consequence or conclusion: statement/reason + „Deswegen …“. Similar to „darum“ and „deshalb“. Can also start a sentence. In speech, it can imply “that’s why” more than a formal “therefore.”
target_language_example: Ich bin krank, deswegen bleibe ich heute zu Hause.
native_language_example: I’m sick, so/that’s why I’m staying home today.

meaning: to intend to; to plan to (have the intention).
additional_notes: Used to say what you intend/plan to do. Very common with an infinitive clause introduced by „zu“: „Ich habe die Absicht, … zu …“. In everyday speech, people often use „vorhaben“ or „beabsichtigen“ instead. Grammar: „Absicht“ is feminine („die Absicht“); with a specific intention, use „die Absicht haben, etwas zu tun“.
target_language_example: Ich habe die Absicht, nächstes Jahr nach Deutschland zu reisen.
native_language_example: I intend to travel to Germany next year.

meaning: “the elderly / older people” (or “the old ones,” depending on context).
additional_notes: Plural noun phrase: **die Alten**. Often refers to older people as a group (similar to “the elderly”). It can also mean “the old ones” in contrast to something newer (e.g., old buildings, old rules), but for people it usually means older people. It can sound a bit blunt; in polite contexts you may also hear **ältere Menschen** (“older people”) or **Seniorinnen und Senioren**.
target_language_example: Viele Angebote in der Stadt sind speziell für die Alten.
native_language_example: Many offers in the city are specifically for the elderly.

meaning: (Keep your) eyes open; watch out; pay attention.
additional_notes: Most commonly used as an imperative: "Augen auf!" = "Watch out! / Pay attention!" You’ll also hear it with a verb, e.g. "Halt/Behalt die Augen auf" (keep your eyes open) or "Mach die Augen auf" (open your eyes; also can mean ‘wake up to reality’ depending on context).
target_language_example: Augen auf! Da kommt ein Fahrrad.
native_language_example: Watch out! A bicycle is coming.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase (also used figuratively). Literally “to close the eyes.” You can also hear it in instructions (e.g., relaxation, photos, medical exams). Figurative use: to ignore something on purpose (“to turn a blind eye”).
target_language_example: Schließ bitte die Augen.
native_language_example: Please close your eyes.

additional_notes: Commonly used with the verb "machen" ("Mach die Augen zu!" = "Close your eyes!") or "haben" ("Ich habe die Augen zu." = "My eyes are closed."). You can also say "die Augen zumachen" as one word (very common in speech).
target_language_example: Mach bitte die Augen zu.
native_language_example: Please close your eyes.

meaning: to open your eyes; (figuratively) to become aware / realize something.
additional_notes: Literally means “to open the eyes.” Often used figuratively with “für” + accusative (“die Augen für etwas öffnen”) meaning “to make someone aware of something.” You can use it with a person as the object: “jemandem die Augen öffnen” = “to open someone’s eyes (to something).”
target_language_example: Dieser Bericht hat mir die Augen geöffnet.
native_language_example: This report opened my eyes.

meaning: to lose control (of oneself); to lose one’s temper.
additional_notes: Used when someone can no longer control their emotions or actions (often anger). Common with contexts like arguments, stress, or provocation. You can also specify what kind of control with "die Beherrschung über etw. verlieren" (less common) or use the pronoun: "Er verliert die Beherrschung" = he loses his self-control.
target_language_example: Als er das hörte, verlor er die Beherrschung und schrie sie an.
native_language_example: When he heard that, he lost control and shouted at her.

meaning: corner; (also) a street corner/turn; a small area/part (of a room).
additional_notes: Most commonly means a physical corner (of a room, table, building) or a street corner. It’s also used for directions and proximity: „um die Ecke“ = just around the corner/nearby. In some contexts it can mean a cozy little spot/area, e.g. „eine gemütliche Ecke“ (a cozy corner).
target_language_example: Der Supermarkt ist gleich um die Ecke.
native_language_example: The supermarket is just around the corner.

additional_notes: Used when someone can’t wait calmly anymore and starts to get irritated or impatient. Often said with verbs like „nicht“ (Ich verliere die Geduld) or in the past tense (Ich habe die Geduld verloren).
target_language_example: Ich verliere die Geduld, wenn der Bus immer zu spät kommt.
native_language_example: I lose patience when the bus is always late.

meaning: to give (someone) your hand; to shake hands.
additional_notes: Used for greeting, saying goodbye, or introducing yourself. Common patterns: „Jemandem die Hand geben“ (to offer/extend your hand) and „Jemandem die Hand schütteln“ (to shake someone’s hand). In German you typically say what you do *to someone* in the dative: „Ich gebe Ihnen die Hand.“
target_language_example: Zur Begrüßung gebe ich Ihnen die Hand.
native_language_example: To greet you, I shake your hand.

meaning: to offer/extend a hand; to help (someone).
additional_notes: Usually used as "jemandem die Hand reichen" (to offer someone your hand), literally for helping someone up or guiding them, and figuratively for offering help/support or reconciliation (a friendly gesture after a conflict). Not the most common phrase for a handshake; for that you’ll often hear "jemandem die Hand geben".
target_language_example: Kann ich dir die Hand reichen?
native_language_example: Can I give you a hand (help you)?

additional_notes: Common greeting or farewell in more formal or professional situations. Often used with the dative: „jemandem die Hand schütteln“ (to shake someone’s hand). Also: „Händeschütteln“ = handshaking.
target_language_example: Ich möchte Ihnen die Hand schütteln.
native_language_example: I’d like to shake your hand.

additional_notes: Used when someone stops believing that something good will happen or that a situation will improve. Often used with a direct object or clause: „die Hoffnung auf etwas aufgeben“ (give up hope for something) or „die Hoffnung aufgeben, dass …“ (give up hope that …).
target_language_example: Ich will die Hoffnung nicht aufgeben, dass wir eine Lösung finden.
native_language_example: I don’t want to give up hope that we’ll find a solution.

additional_notes: Common in everyday and formal German for giving up or no longer believing something will get better. Used with a person as the subject (often "ich/er/sie/wir"). In a full sentence it typically appears as "(die) Hoffnung verlieren" or "keine Hoffnung mehr haben" (a close alternative).
target_language_example: Bitte verliere nicht die Hoffnung.
native_language_example: Please don’t lose hope.

additional_notes: A common greeting/farewell in formal or business contexts. Usually used as "jemandem die Hand schütteln" (to shake someone’s hand). Also appears as "Wir schütteln uns die Hände" (we shake hands with each other).
target_language_example: Ich habe dem Chef die Hand geschüttelt.
native_language_example: I shook the boss’s hand.

meaning: to shut up; to keep quiet.
additional_notes: Common, rather rude way to tell someone to be quiet. Often used as an imperative: „Halt die Klappe!“ You can soften it with „Bitte“ or use a more polite alternative like „Sei bitte leise“ / „Bitte sei still“. Literally refers to a “flap/lid” (Klappe), but the phrase means keeping your mouth shut.
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte die Klappe halten? Ich telefoniere gerade.
native_language_example: Can you please shut up? I’m on the phone right now.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is responsible for a problem or mistake. Often appears as: „jemandem die Schuld geben“ (to blame someone) or „jemandem die Schuld an etwas geben“ (to blame someone for something). Common with the verb „geben“: „Gib mir nicht die Schuld!“
target_language_example: Gib ihm nicht die Schuld an dem Unfall.
native_language_example: Don’t blame him for the accident.

meaning: the sun rises / is coming up.
additional_notes: Used to talk about sunrise or when it’s getting light in the morning. The verb is "aufgehen" (to rise/come up), but in the present tense you often split it: "geht ... auf". You can also use it figuratively for a new beginning (less common for beginners).
target_language_example: Steh auf, die Sonne geht auf!
native_language_example: Get up, the sun is rising!

additional_notes: Common in everyday speech to refer to an unspecific time period around now. With past context it often means "recently" (e.g., what happened the last few days/weeks). With a future context it can mean "in the next few days". Often used without a preposition: "Ich war die Tage krank."
target_language_example: Ich habe dich die Tage angerufen.
native_language_example: I called you the other day / recently.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase meaning to be honest. You can also say "die Wahrheit gesagt" (told the truth) and the opposite is "lügen" (to lie). Often used with "Ich muss dir die Wahrheit sagen" (I have to tell you the truth).
target_language_example: Ich muss dir die Wahrheit sagen: Ich habe das vergessen.
native_language_example: I have to tell you the truth: I forgot that.

meaning: to kill time; to pass the time (when you have nothing to do).
additional_notes: Used when you’re waiting or bored and do something just to make time go by. Very common in spoken German. Grammatically, it’s a separable verb: *totschlagen* → *schlägt ... tot* (e.g., *Ich schlage die Zeit tot*).
target_language_example: Wir müssen noch eine Stunde warten—wollen wir in der Stadt die Zeit totschlagen?
native_language_example: We still have to wait another hour—do you want to kill time in town?

additional_notes: Literally “the whole world.” Used both in a literal sense (the planet) and more often hyperbolically to mean “everyone” or “all of it.” Common in phrases like „Die ganze Welt weiß das.“ (Everyone knows that.) or „für die ganze Welt“ (for the whole world).
target_language_example: Die ganze Welt schaut das Finale.
native_language_example: The whole world is watching the final.

meaning: the whole time; all the time; constantly.
additional_notes: Common time expression meaning something happens continuously or throughout a period. Often used with the present tense for habits (Ich bin die ganze Zeit müde.) or with the past for a specific period (Ich habe die ganze Zeit gewartet.). Also used to reassure someone that something stayed the same: Die ganze Zeit war ich zu Hause. Word order: it can go at the beginning (Die ganze Zeit habe ich...) or in the middle like other time adverbs (Ich habe die ganze Zeit...).
target_language_example: Ich habe die ganze Zeit auf dich gewartet.
native_language_example: I waited for you the whole time.

meaning: recently; in the last little while.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a period leading up to now (days/weeks/months depending on context). Often appears with phrases like „in letzter Zeit“ (recently) or „in der letzten Zeit“ (in recent times). Don’t confuse it with „die letzte Zeit“ meaning “the final time” — here „letzte“ means “recent/most recent.”
target_language_example: Ich war die letzte Zeit viel beschäftigt.
native_language_example: I’ve been very busy lately.

meaning: most of the time; the majority of the time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about what usually happens or is true in general. Often paired with verbs like „sein“, „arbeiten“, „bleiben“, etc. Word order: it can be moved to the front for emphasis (e.g., „Die meiste Zeit bin ich …“).
target_language_example: Die meiste Zeit arbeite ich von zu Hause.
native_language_example: Most of the time I work from home.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the current/next occasion, often contrasting with another time (e.g., last time). Common with verbs like „klappen“ (work out) or „besser machen“ (do better). It’s usually two words: „dieses Mal“ (not *diesmal* in standard writing).
target_language_example: Dieses Mal komme ich pünktlich.
native_language_example: This time I’ll be on time.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the present/next attempt or occasion, often contrasted with other times (e.g., "last time"). Also common with promises or expectations: "Diesmal klappt es." = "This time it’ll work."
target_language_example: Diesmal komme ich pünktlich.
native_language_example: This time I’ll be on time.

meaning: 'but/though' (contradiction), or 'actually/after all'; also 'yes' in reply to a negative statement/question.
additional_notes: Very common German particle with several uses. (1) As a conjunction, it contrasts with what came before (similar to “but/however”): „Ich bin müde, doch ich gehe.“ (2) As a modal particle, it adds emphasis or a friendly push, often hard to translate directly: „Komm doch rein!“ ≈ “Do come in.” (3) As an answer word, it contradicts a negative question/statement: „Du hast keine Zeit.“ — „Doch!“ = “Yes, I do.”
target_language_example: Du hast keine Zeit? – Doch, ich habe Zeit.
native_language_example: You don’t have time? – Yes, I do have time.

additional_notes: Used to point to a place that’s not near the speaker, often across from you or on the other side (e.g., across the street, in the corner). Common in spoken directions. Often paired with a pointing gesture. Similar to plain "dort" (there), but "drüben" adds the idea of "over on the other side/over yonder."
target_language_example: Die Bushaltestelle ist dort drüben, neben dem Supermarkt.
native_language_example: The bus stop is over there, next to the supermarket.

additional_notes: Used with movement/direction (answering “Wohin?” = “Where to?”). In standard spelling it’s often written as one word: “dorthin”. Similar forms: “da hin” (more conversational) and “hierhin” (to here).
target_language_example: Wie komme ich dort hin?
native_language_example: How do I get there?

additional_notes: Used to indicate movement toward a place that is away from both the speaker and listener (or already known from context). Often answers “Wohin?” (Where to?). Contrast: „hierhin“ = to here; „dahin“ is similar to „dorthin“ and is very common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Wir fahren morgen dorthin.
native_language_example: We’re going there tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used when someone should stay outside (often before entering a room/building). "Draußen" = outside (often outdoors, not inside). Word order can change depending on the sentence: "Warte draußen!" (Wait outside!) / "Ich warte draußen." (I’m waiting outside.) / "Kannst du draußen warten?" (Can you wait outside?).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte draußen warten?
native_language_example: Could you please wait outside?

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens after a period of three days (relative to a time just mentioned). Common in stories, narration, and everyday speech. Word order stays as shown: number + time unit + später.
target_language_example: Wir haben uns am Montag getroffen, und drei Tage später habe ich ihn wieder gesehen.
native_language_example: We met on Monday, and three days later I saw him again.

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens. Often followed by a time period: „dreimal pro Woche“ (three times per week) or „dreimal am Tag“ (three times a day). Can also be used for repetition: „Sag es dreimal“ (say it three times).
target_language_example: Ich gehe dreimal pro Woche ins Fitnessstudio.
native_language_example: I go to the gym three times a week.

meaning: You can do it / You’ll manage it.
additional_notes: An encouraging phrase used to motivate someone. Literally “you manage that,” from *schaffen* = “to manage/achieve.” Often said to cheer someone up before a test, task, or difficult situation. In more formal situations you might say *Sie schaffen das* (to one person, formal) or *Ihr schafft das* (to a group).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, du schaffst das!
native_language_example: Don’t worry, you can do it!

additional_notes: Means something is true in every part/way: totally, thoroughly. Often used for personality/character or for being soaked/dirty: "ein Deutscher durch und durch" (German through and through), "durch und durch nass" (soaking wet). It can also appear with adjectives: "durch und durch ehrlich" (completely honest).
target_language_example: Er ist ein Musiker durch und durch.
native_language_example: He’s a musician through and through.

meaning: in a mess; mixed up; confused/chaotic.
additional_notes: Used to describe disorder (things not tidy) or confusion (people/situations). Often with verbs like „sein“ (to be) and „bringen“ (to throw into confusion): „Alles ist durcheinander.“ / „Das bringt mich durcheinander.“ Also common as an adjective-like form: „ein durcheinanderes Zimmer“ is possible but less common than „ein Zimmer im Durcheinander“ or „ein unordentliches Zimmer“.
target_language_example: Nach dem Umzug war alles durcheinander.
native_language_example: After the move, everything was a mess.

meaning: since forever; always (for a very long time).
additional_notes: Used to say something has been true for as long as anyone can remember (a long-standing situation or tradition). Often used with past tense: „Das war/ist hier eh und je so.“ A very common longer variant is „eh und jeher“, with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Das war hier eh und je so.
native_language_example: That’s always been the case here.

additional_notes: Used as a sentence adverb to introduce a frank opinion, confession, or slight criticism. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence ("Ehrlich gesagt, ..."), but it can also appear mid-sentence. Slightly more formal than "ehrlich gesagt" in tone is "ehrlich gesagt" is neutral; very common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ehrlich gesagt, habe ich keine Lust heute auszugehen.
native_language_example: To be honest, I don’t feel like going out today.

meaning: 'an eye on' (keep an eye on / have your eye on).
additional_notes:
Used with a verb, most commonly: 
- **ein Auge auf etw./jdn. haben** = to keep an eye on something/someone; also can mean to want something or be interested in someone ("have your eye on").
- **ein Auge auf etw./jdn. werfen** = to take a look at; also can mean to take an interest in someone.
Takes **auf + accusative** (auf wen? auf was?).
target_language_example: Kannst du ein Auge auf meine Tasche haben?
native_language_example: Can you keep an eye on my bag?

additional_notes: Common, neutral way to express a small amount or degree. Often used with adjectives/adverbs ("ein bisschen müde" = "a bit tired") or with verbs in the sense of doing something a little ("ein bisschen warten" = "wait a bit"). In speech it’s frequently shortened to "’n bisschen".
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte ein bisschen langsamer sprechen?
native_language_example: Can you please speak a little more slowly?

meaning: once and for all; for good.
additional_notes: Used to say something will be decided, done, or stopped permanently, with no more discussion or repetition. Often appears with verbs like „klären“ (clear up), „entscheiden“ (decide), „beenden“ (end), or „aufhören“ (stop). Sometimes written as „ein für allemal“.
target_language_example: Wir müssen das ein für alle Mal klären.
native_language_example: We need to clear this up once and for all.

additional_notes: A formal, somewhat old-fashioned way to say "jeder". You’ll see it in literature, proverbs, official or solemn language. It behaves like the pronoun/adjective "jeder" and is inflected: ein jeder Mann, eine jede Frau, ein jedes Kind; also: einem jeden, eines jeden, etc.
target_language_example: Ein jeder ist für sein eigenes Glück verantwortlich.
native_language_example: Each and every person is responsible for their own happiness.

additional_notes: Used before plural nouns to mean a small number (often 2–4, sometimes just “some”): ein paar Tage (a few days), ein paar Leute (a few people). With time/amounts, it often means “a couple”: ein paar Minuten (a couple of minutes). Don’t confuse with das Paar (“the pair/couple”), which is a noun meaning exactly two.
target_language_example: Ich bleibe noch ein paar Minuten.
native_language_example: I’ll stay a couple more minutes.

additional_notes: Common, neutral way to say a small amount or degree. Often used before adjectives/adverbs ("ein wenig müde" = "a bit tired") or with verbs to mean "a little" ("Warte ein wenig" = "Wait a bit"). Also used with nouns: "ein wenig Wasser" = "a little water". Similar to "ein bisschen" (very common, slightly more casual).
target_language_example: Können Sie ein wenig langsamer sprechen?
native_language_example: Can you speak a little more slowly?

additional_notes: Used in fairly formal/literary language to mean when it starts getting dark (toward evening). Often appears with prepositions like „bei“, „mit“, or „nach“: „bei Einbruch der Dunkelheit“ = “at nightfall.”
target_language_example: Bei Einbruch der Dunkelheit sind wir nach Hause gegangen.
native_language_example: At nightfall, we went home.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase meaning you’ve thought of something or have a suggestion/plan. Often used with a clause introduced by „wie/was/wo…“ (e.g., „Hast du eine Idee, wie…?“) or with „für“ + accusative to mean “an idea for” something (e.g., „eine Idee für ein Geschenk“). You can also say „Ich habe eine Idee!“ when you suddenly think of a solution.
target_language_example: Ich habe eine Idee: Wir treffen uns morgen früher.
native_language_example: I have an idea: Let’s meet earlier tomorrow.

additional_notes: Most often used with nouns: **eine Reihe von + dative** = “a number of / a series of” (e.g., *eine Reihe von Problemen*). It can also mean a physical row/line (like seats): *in der ersten Reihe* = “in the front row.”
target_language_example: Ich habe eine Reihe von Fragen.
native_language_example: I have a series of questions.

meaning: to play a role; to matter (be important).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is important or has an influence in a situation: „X spielt (eine) Rolle“ = X matters. Often appears with negation: „Das spielt keine Rolle“ = That doesn’t matter. Common patterns: „eine große/wichtige Rolle spielen“ (to play a big/important role), „bei etwas eine Rolle spielen“ (to matter in something), „für jemanden eine Rolle spielen“ (to matter to someone).
target_language_example: Ob du pünktlich bist, spielt eine große Rolle.
native_language_example: Whether you are on time plays a big role / really matters.

meaning: to take a look; to have a quick glance.
additional_notes: Very common phrase meaning to look at something briefly. Often used with prepositions like „auf“ (at/on) or „in“ (into): „einen Blick auf … werfen“, „einen Blick in … werfen“. In everyday speech you’ll also hear „mal“ to soften it: „Kannst du mal einen Blick drauf werfen?“
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte einen Blick auf meinen Lebenslauf werfen?
native_language_example: Could you please take a look at my résumé?

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase. It conjugates as machen: ich mache einen Fehler, du machst einen Fehler, er/sie/es macht einen Fehler; Perfekt: ich habe einen Fehler gemacht. Often also used with an object: einen Fehler in etwas machen (e.g., in der Rechnung). Similar meaning: sich irren (to be mistaken).
target_language_example: Ich habe einen Fehler gemacht.
native_language_example: I made a mistake.

meaning: to have a boyfriend; to have a (male) friend.
additional_notes: Often means “to have a boyfriend” in everyday conversation, especially when talking about relationship status (e.g., "Hast du einen Freund?"). It can also mean “to have a (male) friend,” but if you mean a platonic friend in general, Germans often say "einen Freund/eine Freundin" (depending on gender) or more clearly "einen guten Freund" / "einen Kumpel" (informal). For a girlfriend (romantic), say "eine Freundin haben"—but note "Freundin" can also mean a female friend, so context matters.
target_language_example: Sie hat einen Freund und ist sehr glücklich.
native_language_example: She has a boyfriend and is very happy.

meaning: to have a plan; to know what you’re going to do.
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase for having an idea/strategy, often about what to do next. You can use it in questions: „Hast du einen Plan?“ = “Do you have a plan?” In context it can also mean “to have a clue/know what’s going on,” especially with words like „schon“ or „überhaupt“: „Hast du überhaupt einen Plan?“
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich habe einen Plan.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I have a plan.

additional_notes: Used to say you already have a scheduled meeting/doctor’s visit/time slot and therefore may be unavailable. Common with a time and/or place: „Ich habe um 10 Uhr einen Termin.“ You’ll also hear related phrases like „einen Termin machen/vereinbaren“ (to make/schedule an appointment) and „einen Termin absagen“ (to cancel an appointment).
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, ich kann nicht kommen — ich habe um 15 Uhr einen Termin beim Arzt.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come — I have a doctor’s appointment at 3 p.m.

meaning: one after the other; one by one.
additional_notes: Used to say people or things happen in sequence, not at the same time. Often used with actions like coming, leaving, speaking, or being called. Variations: „eine nach der anderen“ (all/mostly female things/people), „eins nach dem anderen“ (things/neutral), and plural „einer nach dem anderen“ can also refer to a group of people one by one.
target_language_example: Bitte kommt einer nach dem anderen ins Büro.
native_language_example: Please come into the office one by one.

meaning: one night; during the night (on an unspecified night).
additional_notes: Used to set the scene for a story or past event when the exact date isn’t important. It’s the genitive form of „eine Nacht“ and often appears with past tense narration (Präteritum/Perfekt). Similar in meaning to „in einer Nacht“ but „eines Nachts“ sounds more like “one night” in storytelling.
target_language_example: Eines Nachts habe ich ein lautes Geräusch gehört.
native_language_example: One night I heard a loud noise.

meaning: one day; someday (at some point in the future or past).
additional_notes: Common in storytelling and everyday speech to mean an unspecified day. Often refers to a future hope/plan ("Someday...") or to a past event ("One day, ..."). Similar to "eines Morgens/Abends" (one morning/evening).
target_language_example: Eines Tages möchte ich nach Berlin fahren.
native_language_example: Someday I’d like to go to Berlin.
