meaning: just because; just like that; simply (for no special reason).
additional_notes: Used when something happens without a specific reason, plan, or effort: "Warum? – Einfach so." It can also mean “just/any old” in the sense of “without preparation or planning” (e.g., dropping by unannounced). Tone is neutral and very common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ich bin einfach so vorbeigekommen.
native_language_example: I just stopped by (for no particular reason).

meaning: once; one time (also used like “just” to soften a request).
additional_notes: Most commonly an adverb meaning “once”/“one time”: *Ich war einmal in Berlin* (“I was in Berlin once”). In everyday spoken German it can also act as a softener similar to “just” in English, especially in requests/suggestions: *Komm einmal her* (“Just come here a moment”).
target_language_example: Kannst du das bitte einmal wiederholen?
native_language_example: Can you please repeat that once (just repeat that, please)?

meaning: to realize; to understand (and accept) / to inspect (e.g., documents).
additional_notes: Often used as a separable verb meaning “to realize/accept”: *Ich sehe ein, dass …* (“I realize/accept that …”). In this sense it frequently implies admitting something (often after disagreement). It can also mean “to inspect/consult” in formal contexts: *Unterlagen/ Akten/ Dokumente einsehen* (“to look at/inspect files/documents”).
target_language_example: Ich sehe ein, dass du recht hast.
native_language_example: I realize (and accept) that you’re right.

meaning: to hire; to set/adjust (a device or setting); to stop/cease (an activity).
additional_notes: Most common everyday use is "to hire" (e.g., a company hiring employees). It’s a separable verb: *ich stelle (jemanden) ein*, *wir stellen ein*, past participle *eingestellt*. It can also mean adjusting settings (e.g., a thermostat, a radio) or discontinuing something (*den Betrieb einstellen* = to cease operations). Often confused with English *install*—but *installieren* is “to install.”
target_language_example: Die Firma stellt nächste Woche zwei neue Mitarbeiter ein.
native_language_example: The company is hiring two new employees next week.

meaning: to move in (into a home); also: to pull/bring in (e.g., curtains)
additional_notes: Most common everyday meaning is "to move in" with **in + accusative**: *in eine Wohnung / in ein Haus einziehen* (to move into an apartment/house). In other contexts it can mean "to pull in" (*die Vorhänge einziehen* = pull the curtains) or "to collect" money (*eine Gebühr einziehen* = collect a fee).
target_language_example: Wir ziehen nächsten Monat in die neue Wohnung ein.
native_language_example: We’re moving into the new apartment next month.

additional_notes: A common saying used when a situation had problems at first but turned out fine in the end. You can say it as a comment after things work out. Often written with a comma: “Ende gut, alles gut.”
target_language_example: Der Flug hatte Verspätung, aber wir sind trotzdem rechtzeitig angekommen – Ende gut, alles gut.
native_language_example: The flight was delayed, but we still arrived on time — all’s well that ends well.

additional_notes: Used when something happens after a delay or long wait, often showing relief, impatience, or satisfaction. Common in everyday speech and can also mean “eventually” depending on context.
target_language_example: Endlich bist du da!
native_language_example: Finally you’re here!

additional_notes: Used to say that someone can speak English, or to ask if someone speaks English. You’ll often hear it as a question: „Sprechen Sie Englisch?“ (formal) or „Sprichst du Englisch?“ (informal).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, sprechen Sie Englisch?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you speak English?

additional_notes: Used as an adjective/adverb meaning "appropriate" or "corresponding" (e.g., entsprechend reagieren = react accordingly). It can also be used like a preposition meaning "according to / in accordance with" and then it usually takes the dative: entsprechend den Regeln = according to the rules. Often translates as "accordingly" when referring back to what was said or decided.
target_language_example: Wir handeln entsprechend den Regeln.
native_language_example: We act according to the rules.

meaning: to be successful; to have success.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something succeeds (often after effort). Common in formal or neutral contexts. Conjugate the verb “haben” (ich habe, du hast, er/sie/es hat, wir haben…). You can also add “mit” to specify what you succeed with: “Er hat Erfolg mit seinem Projekt.”
target_language_example: Mit dieser Methode wirst du Erfolg haben.
native_language_example: With this method, you will be successful.

meaning: to have a cold; to be (slightly) ill with a cold.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "sein" to describe your condition: "Ich bin erkältet" (I have a cold). You can intensify it with "stark" (badly): "Ich bin stark erkältet." Common in everyday conversation for mild respiratory illnesses (runny nose, sore throat).
target_language_example: Ich bin erkältet und bleibe heute zu Hause.
native_language_example: I have a cold and I’m staying home today.

meaning: to mean it; to be serious (about something).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone is not joking and truly intends what they say. Often appears in questions or with an object: „Meinst du das ernst?“ (Are you serious?) / „Ich meine es ernst.“ (I mean it.) / „Er meint es ernst mit ihr.“ (He’s serious about her.)
target_language_example: Meinst du das ernst, oder machst du nur Spaß?
native_language_example: Are you serious, or are you just joking?

additional_notes: Common in everyday German. Often used with an object in the accusative (e.g., jemanden/etwas ernst nehmen). You can also negate it: „nicht ernst nehmen“ = “not take seriously” / “not take to heart.” Similar in meaning to „für voll nehmen“ (more informal) or „seriös behandeln“ (more formal).
target_language_example: Du musst das ernst nehmen.
native_language_example: You have to take that seriously.

additional_notes: Common in spoken German to mean “let’s do this first” or “for the moment.” It can soften what you say and buy time (like “well, first…”). Often shortened to “erst mal.” Word order is flexible depending on emphasis: “Erst einmal…” at the start of a sentence is very common.
target_language_example: Ich muss erst einmal einkaufen, dann kann ich vorbeikommen.
native_language_example: I have to go shopping first, then I can come by.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken German. Used to say you’ll do something first, or to pause/soften a plan or request: "Ich muss erst mal ..." = "I first need to ..." / "Let me ... first." Often written as two words (erst mal); in informal writing you may also see "erstmal". Similar to "zuerst" but usually more casual and conversational.
target_language_example: Ich muss erst mal einen Kaffee trinken.
native_language_example: First I need to have a coffee.

meaning: all the more; even more so (especially).
additional_notes: Used to strengthen a statement, often meaning “even less/ more likely in that case.” Common in comparisons and reasoning: if something is true in one situation, it’s even truer in a stronger situation. Often appears with negatives: „Ich habe keine Zeit, erst recht nicht heute.“ = “I don’t have time—certainly not today.”
target_language_example: Wenn du schon müde bist, bist du nach der Reise erst recht müde.
native_language_example: If you’re already tired, you’ll be even more tired after the trip.

meaning: first class (ticket/travel class); also: first grade (school).
additional_notes: Most commonly used for travel: "erste Klasse" = the highest class on trains/planes, often with more comfort. With school, it means first grade and is usually used with an article: "in der ersten Klasse" (in first grade). Note the adjective ending: "erste" changes with case/gender, e.g. "die erste Klasse" (nom.), "in der ersten Klasse" (dat.).
target_language_example: Wir fahren heute in der ersten Klasse.
native_language_example: We’re traveling first class today.

additional_notes: Often used with a possessive pronoun: „mein/dein/sein/ihr erstes Mal“. It can be neutral (first time doing an activity) but in context it can also be a euphemism for someone’s first time having sex, so the topic depends on the situation. Also common: „zum ersten Mal“ = “for the first time.”
target_language_example: Das ist mein erstes Mal in Berlin.
native_language_example: This is my first time in Berlin.

additional_notes: Used to explain the meaning of a word, phrase, sign, or situation. Often followed by a noun, an infinitive clause (e.g., „… zu + Infinitiv“), or a full clause introduced by „dass“. In speech it’s also common to use it like “I mean/that is” when clarifying what you just said.
target_language_example: Was bedeutet „Entschuldigung“? – Es bedeutet „sorry“.
native_language_example: What does “Entschuldigung” mean? – It means “sorry”.

meaning: to be serious (about something); to mean it seriously.
additional_notes: Used when you want to say someone is not joking and truly intends what they say or do. Often appears as: „Meinst du das ernst?“ (Are you serious?), „Ich meine es ernst.“ (I mean it.), or with a preposition: „Er meint es ernst mit ihr/seinem Job.“ (He’s serious about her/his job.).
target_language_example: Ich meine es ernst mit dem Deutschlernen.
native_language_example: I’m serious about learning German.

meaning: “it feels (like…)” / “it seems (like…)” (about a sensation or impression).
additional_notes: Used to describe how something feels physically or emotionally, often followed by „wie …“ (“like …”): „Es fühlt sich an wie …“. Common in the phrase „Es fühlt sich an, als ob …“ (“It feels as if …”). In German you’ll also hear the full verb form: „Es fühlt sich gut/schlecht an“ (“It feels good/bad”).
target_language_example: Es fühlt sich an, als ob ich Fieber hätte.
native_language_example: It feels like I have a fever.

additional_notes: Used to say that something existed or happened in the past, especially in stories, reports, or written German. It’s the Präteritum (simple past) form of *es gibt*. Typically followed by an accusative noun: *Es gab einen Fehler / viele Probleme.*
target_language_example: Es gab gestern einen Unfall.
native_language_example: There was an accident yesterday.

meaning: 'there is/there are' (to exist; to be available).
additional_notes: Most commonly used as the fixed phrase **es gibt** + noun (in the accusative) to say that something exists or is available: **Es gibt einen Park** (There is a park). It stays **es gibt** even with plural nouns: **Es gibt viele Leute** (There are many people). In questions the word order flips: **Gibt es ...?** (Is there/Are there ...?). Past: **es gab**; perfect: **es hat ... gegeben**.
target_language_example: Es gibt hier einen Supermarkt.
native_language_example: There is a supermarket here.

additional_notes: Used with a dative person (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen): the thing is the subject and the person is in dative. Commonly used as “Es gefällt mir …” (“I like …”), or with plural things: “Es gefallen mir die Schuhe.” (“I like the shoes.”).
target_language_example: Es gefällt mir sehr.
native_language_example: I like it a lot.

meaning: it's about; it's about (the topic is).
additional_notes: Used to introduce or clarify the topic/subject of a conversation, meeting, email, etc. Usually followed by a noun or noun phrase: „Es geht um das Problem / um Geld / um deine Frage.“ Not the same as physical movement: „Es geht“ can mean “it’s going/it works,” but „es geht um …“ means “it’s about …”.
target_language_example: Es geht um deinen Termin morgen.
native_language_example: It’s about your appointment tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say that something exists or is available. The thing that exists comes in the accusative case (e.g., "Es gibt einen Park" = "There is a park"). Not the same as the literal-looking "it gives" in English.
target_language_example: Es gibt hier ein gutes Restaurant.
native_language_example: There is a good restaurant here.

meaning: it applies; it is valid; the rule is.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is true/valid or that a rule applies in a situation. Common in written/formal contexts (rules, signs, contracts). Often followed by a clause with „dass…“ or used with „für…“ (for) to specify where it applies: „Es gilt für Kinder…“. Related: „Es gilt: …“ introduces a rule; „Es gilt, … zu …“ can mean “it is necessary to / one must …” in a formal style.
target_language_example: Diese Regel gilt nur für Erwachsene.
native_language_example: This rule applies only to adults.

meaning: “it’s about / it’s a matter of; it is (in the sense of identifying what something is).”
additional_notes: Used to clarify or identify what someone is talking about, often in formal or neutral contexts (emails, announcements, explanations). It’s commonly followed by a noun phrase: “Es handelt sich um + noun” (e.g., “einen Fehler”, “eine Anfrage”). Similar in meaning to “Es geht um…”, but a bit more formal and often implies “to be”/“to concern” rather than “to go”.
target_language_example: Es handelt sich um einen Druckfehler im Vertrag.
native_language_example: It’s a printing error in the contract.

meaning: “there has been / there was” (perfect tense of “es gibt”).
additional_notes: Used to say that something existed or happened. It’s the perfect tense form of **es gibt** (“there is/are”). In everyday speech, German often prefers the simple past **es gab** (“there was/were”), but **es hat … gegeben** is also common, especially when referring to a past event with a result or in some regions. The thing that existed/occurred is usually in the accusative: **Es hat einen Fehler gegeben** (“There was a mistake”).
target_language_example: Es hat gestern einen Unfall gegeben.
native_language_example: There was an accident yesterday.

additional_notes: Past perfect (Plusquamperfekt) form used mostly in written stories or when talking about an earlier past time: *Es hatte (etwas) gegeben* = "There had been (something)." Often appears with time words like *zuvor* (before), *früher* (earlier), or another past event: *Es hatte vorher viel Regen gegeben.* In everyday speech, Germans often prefer *Es gab ...* unless they need the 'earlier past' meaning.
target_language_example: Es hatte gestern Abend einen Unfall gegeben, deshalb war die Straße gesperrt.
native_language_example: There had been an accident last night, so the road was closed.

additional_notes: Used with *heißen* (to be called / to mean). Common for explaining the meaning of a word or phrase (*Es heißt …* = “It means …”), and for giving a name (*Er heißt …* = “His name is …”). With a name, German often uses a person/thing as the subject rather than *es* (e.g., *Der Film heißt …* = “The movie is called …”).
target_language_example: „Guten Appetit“ – es heißt „enjoy your meal“.
native_language_example: “Guten Appetit” means “enjoy your meal.”

additional_notes: Used to say that the right moment has come to do something. Very often followed by an infinitive with “zu” (e.g., „Es ist Zeit, zu gehen.“). You can also add “für” + noun: „Es ist Zeit für eine Pause.“
target_language_example: Es ist Zeit, nach Hause zu gehen.
native_language_example: It’s time to go home.

additional_notes: Used to say that one option is better than another. Often followed by a comparison: “als …” (than …) or “wenn …” (if …). You can also use it to give advice: “Es ist besser, … zu …” (It’s better to …).
target_language_example: Es ist besser, heute zu Hause zu bleiben.
native_language_example: It’s better to stay at home today.

additional_notes: Used to say something is unimportant or you have no preference. Common in everyday speech. You can add what it doesn’t matter to you: "Es ist mir egal" (It’s all the same to me / I don’t care). Note: "Mir ist egal" is also very common and can sound a bit blunt depending on tone.
target_language_example: Es ist egal, welchen Film wir anschauen.
native_language_example: It doesn’t matter which movie we watch.

meaning: it’s the same; it doesn’t matter.
additional_notes: Common in spoken German. "Es ist gleich" can mean (1) two things are identical/equivalent (often expanded to "Es ist das Gleiche"), or (2) you don’t care which option happens (“either way is fine”), similar to "It’s all the same to me." For “it doesn’t matter” you’ll also hear "egal" or "das ist egal".
target_language_example: Mir ist es gleich, ob wir heute oder morgen gehen.
native_language_example: It doesn’t matter to me whether we go today or tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say something is clear/understood, or to emphasize that something is obvious (“of course”). Often used as a standalone reply. For “Sure, no problem,” Germans more often say “klar!” or “alles klar.”
target_language_example: —Kommst du morgen? —Ja, es ist klar.
native_language_example: —Are you coming tomorrow? —Yes, of course.

additional_notes: Used to say that something can happen or can be done. Common in neutral/formal situations; in everyday speech you also hear “das geht” (“that works/that’s possible”). Often followed by “dass …” (“that …”) or an infinitive with “zu” (e.g., “Es ist möglich, das zu machen.”).
target_language_example: Es ist möglich, morgen früher zu kommen.
native_language_example: It’s possible to come earlier tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is required/essential (often in formal or neutral contexts). Common patterns: „Es ist notwendig, dass …“ (It’s necessary that …) and „Es ist notwendig, zu + infinitive“ (It’s necessary to …). Similar everyday alternatives: „man muss …“ (you have to …) or „es ist wichtig“ (it’s important).
target_language_example: Es ist notwendig, dass du deinen Pass mitbringst.
native_language_example: It’s necessary that you bring your passport.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is required. Often followed by a subordinate clause with „dass“ (e.g., „Es ist nötig, dass …“), or with an infinitive clause using „zu“ (e.g., „Es ist nötig, das zu machen.“). In everyday speech, Germans often also say „Es ist notwendig“ or „Das muss sein.“
target_language_example: Es ist nötig, dass wir heute früher gehen.
native_language_example: It’s necessary that we leave earlier today.

additional_notes: Used to say that a situation has gotten worse or is worse than expected/than something else. Often followed by a comparison: „Es ist schlimmer als …“ (“It’s worse than …”). You may also hear: „Es wird schlimmer“ (“It’s getting worse”) or „Es ist noch schlimmer“ (“It’s even worse”).
target_language_example: Ich dachte, es wird besser, aber es ist schlimmer.
native_language_example: I thought it would get better, but it’s worse.

additional_notes: Meaning depends on context: **sicher** can describe safety/security (e.g., a place or method is safe) or certainty (similar to “sure/certain”). In conversation, you’ll also hear **sicher!** as “sure!/of course!”, but **es ist sicher** is a full sentence meaning “it’s safe/secure” or “it’s certain.”
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, es ist sicher, hier zu warten.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s safe to wait here.

additional_notes: Used to say that something cannot be done or cannot happen. Often followed by an infinitive clause with „zu“ (e.g., „Es ist unmöglich, das zu machen.“). More casual alternatives include „Das geht nicht.“ (“That won’t work / That’s not possible.”).
target_language_example: Es ist unmöglich, heute noch einen Termin zu bekommen.
native_language_example: It’s impossible to get an appointment today.

additional_notes: Used to express that something probably won’t happen or isn’t true. Often followed by a clause with "dass" ("Es ist unwahrscheinlich, dass …") or used alone as a reply. You can also use "sehr" to strengthen it: "Es ist sehr unwahrscheinlich."
target_language_example: Es ist unwahrscheinlich, dass der Zug pünktlich kommt.
native_language_example: It’s unlikely that the train will arrive on time.

additional_notes: Often used as **es ist es wert** (“it’s worth it”) or with **zu + infinitive**: **Es ist wert, (etwas) zu tun** (“It’s worth doing (something)”). Also common: **Das ist es wert** (“That’s worth it”).
target_language_example: Es ist es wert, Deutsch zu lernen.
native_language_example: It’s worth learning German.

additional_notes: Used to say that something matters or should be taken seriously. Often followed by a clause with „dass …“ (that …) or by „zu“ + infinitive (to …): „Es ist wichtig, dass du pünktlich bist.“ / „Es ist wichtig, genug zu schlafen.“ You can emphasize with „sehr“ (very): „Es ist sehr wichtig …“.
target_language_example: Es ist wichtig, dass du heute kommst.
native_language_example: It’s important that you come today.

additional_notes: Used to say the answer isn’t fixed and depends on the situation or conditions. Often followed by “auf + accusative” to name what it depends on, e.g. “Es kommt auf das Wetter an.” In conversation you can also hear the shorter “Kommt drauf an.”
target_language_example: Es kommt darauf an, wie viel Zeit wir haben.
native_language_example: It depends on how much time we have.

additional_notes: Used as a fixed, somewhat formal-sounding exclamation to express support, celebration, or a toast. It’s followed by the person/thing you’re cheering for (often with an article), e.g. “Es lebe der König!” The verb form “lebe” is a special subjunctive form used for wishes/cheers, not ordinary everyday speech.
target_language_example: Es lebe die Freundschaft!
native_language_example: Long live friendship!

additional_notes: Used to say that an effort, cost, or wait is worthwhile. Often followed by an infinitive with “zu” (e.g., “Es lohnt sich, … zu …”) or a clause with “wenn” (“Es lohnt sich, wenn …”). Common variants: “Es lohnt sich nicht” (it’s not worth it), “Das lohnt sich” (that’s worth it).
target_language_example: Es lohnt sich, früh aufzustehen.
native_language_example: It’s worth getting up early.

additional_notes: Used to say that an activity is fun. Often paired with an infinitive: „Es macht Spaß, Deutsch zu lernen.“ You can also specify who is having fun with a dative pronoun: „Es macht mir Spaß.“ (It’s fun for me / I enjoy it.)
target_language_example: Es macht Spaß, mit Freunden zu spielen.
native_language_example: It’s fun to play with friends.

additional_notes: Used to express an impression or assumption rather than a sure fact. Very common with an infinitive clause: “Es scheint zu regnen.” (It seems to be raining.) Also used with “als ob/als wenn” (as if) or a “dass” clause (that…). Don’t confuse with “Es scheint.” meaning “The sun is shining.” in the literal sense (from “scheinen” = to shine).
target_language_example: Es scheint, als ob der Zug Verspätung hat.
native_language_example: It seems like the train is delayed.

meaning: “it is said/supposed to be …” (subjunctive, used in reported speech).
additional_notes: "Es sei" uses Konjunktiv I of "sein" (to be). It’s common in formal writing and news to report what someone claims without confirming it: "Er sagt, es sei …" / "Es heißt, es sei …". In everyday spoken German, people often use the indicative instead ("… es ist …").
target_language_example: Er behauptet, es sei zu spät.
native_language_example: He claims (that) it’s too late.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an exception/condition: something is true or will happen, except if the following clause applies. Commonly followed by a clause with verb at the end (subordinate clause): “..., es sei denn, du kommst morgen.” It can also be used at the start: “Es sei denn, du kommst morgen, ...”.
target_language_example: Ich komme heute nicht, es sei denn, du brauchst dringend Hilfe.
native_language_example: I’m not coming today unless you urgently need help.

additional_notes: Means handling a task on your own instead of paying/asking someone else. Very common in DIY or everyday situations. Often used with “lieber” (preferably) or “einfach” (just): “Ich mache es lieber selber.” Also common: “selbst” instead of “selber” (same meaning). Word order can vary depending on the sentence: “Ich mache es selber.” / “Ich will es selber machen.”
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich mache es selber.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll do it myself.

additional_notes: Used to say how something appears (often visually) or to introduce what you think is happening. Very commonly followed by: (1) “wie …” = “it looks like …” (Es sieht aus wie ein Hund.) (2) “als ob …” = “it looks as if …” (Es sieht aus, als ob es regnet.) In speech you’ll often hear the longer phrase “Es sieht so aus, als ob …” = “It looks like …”.
target_language_example: Es sieht aus, als ob es gleich regnet.
native_language_example: It looks like it’s going to rain soon.

additional_notes: Used to say something appears to be true based on what you can see or what you know so far. Often followed by a clause with „dass“ (es sieht so aus, dass …) or by „als ob“ (es sieht so aus, als ob …). In conversation it can also stand alone as a reaction: „Es sieht so aus.“ = “Looks like it / Seems so.”
target_language_example: Es sieht so aus, dass wir heute Regen bekommen.
native_language_example: It looks like we’re going to get rain today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce information you found out later, often unexpectedly. Very common in spoken and written German. Often followed by a clause with „dass“ (e.g., „Es stellt sich heraus, dass…“) or by a direct statement. Related phrasing: „Es hat sich herausgestellt, dass…“ (present perfect: “it turned out that…”).
target_language_example: Es stellt sich heraus, dass der Zug heute ausfällt.
native_language_example: It turns out that the train is canceled today.

additional_notes: "es" is a pronoun meaning "it" and refers to something already mentioned or clear from context: "Kannst du es tun?" = "Can you do it?" In everyday German, "tun" often sounds a bit more formal or emphatic than "machen" (which is more common for many “do/make” situations). Depending on context, "es tun" can also be used as a euphemism for having sex (similar to English "do it").
target_language_example: Ich kann es nicht tun.
native_language_example: I can’t do it.

additional_notes: A common way to apologize or express regret. Often used as “Es tut mir leid” (more complete/most common) = “I’m sorry,” where “mir” = “to me.” You can strengthen it with “sehr”: “Es tut mir sehr leid.” Also used to politely decline or give bad news: “Es tut mir leid, aber …” = “I’m sorry, but …”.
target_language_example: Es tut mir leid, ich habe keine Zeit.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I don’t have time.

additional_notes: Common, polite way to apologize or express sympathy. Used for both minor mistakes (bumping into someone) and serious situations (bad news). Often followed by a reason with "dass" (e.g., "Es tut mir leid, dass …"). You can soften it with "wirklich" (really) or "sehr" (very): "Es tut mir wirklich/sehr leid."
target_language_example: Es tut mir leid, ich habe keine Zeit.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I don’t have time.

additional_notes: Common way to say you feel pain. Used for physical pain (a body part) and sometimes emotional pain. You can add what hurts with a dative pronoun/body part: „Mir tut der Rücken weh.“ (My back hurts.) Also common: „Tut es weh?“ (Does it hurt?)
target_language_example: Mein Bauch tut weh.
native_language_example: My stomach hurts.

additional_notes: Set phrase used at the beginning of fairy tales and stories. Literally 'it was once' (es = it, war = was, einmal = once). In everyday conversation you might say "früher" (back then) or "einmal" (once) instead.
target_language_example: Es war einmal ein König, der in einem großen Schloss lebte.
native_language_example: Once upon a time there was a king who lived in a big castle.

additional_notes: Used to say that the right time has come to do something, often as a prompt or gentle pressure. Commonly followed by “zu” + infinitive: “Es wird Zeit, zu gehen.” It can sound more impatient depending on tone/context (similar to “It’s about time!”).
target_language_example: Es wird Zeit, dass wir losfahren.
native_language_example: It’s time for us to leave.

additional_notes: Used to say that something will exist/occur or be available later. Very common with a noun phrase as the thing that will be available: “Es wird + (Akkusativ) + geben.” You can also see it without “es” in more casual speech (“Wird heute Pizza geben.”), but the full form with “es” is standard.
target_language_example: Es wird heute Abend Pizza geben.
native_language_example: There will be pizza this evening.

meaning: "it would be better" (suggesting a preferable option).
additional_notes: Used to give polite advice or a recommendation, often followed by "wenn..." ("if...") or an infinitive clause (e.g., "..., früher zu gehen"). It’s the subjunctive (Konjunktiv II) of "es ist besser" and sounds softer than a direct command.
target_language_example: Es wäre besser, wenn du jetzt gehst.
native_language_example: It would be better if you left now.

additional_notes: Often used to make polite requests or suggest what you would like to happen. Common patterns: “Es wäre schön, wenn …” (“It would be nice if …”) and “Es wäre schön, … zu …” (“It would be nice to …”). It uses Konjunktiv II (wäre = would be) to sound softer and less direct.
target_language_example: Es wäre schön, wenn du morgen Zeit hättest.
native_language_example: It would be nice if you had time tomorrow.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase for going somewhere (often a restaurant) to eat. Literally “go eat,” and it often implies leaving home/your current place to eat. Can be used with places (z.B. im Restaurant) or with people (mit Freunden).
target_language_example: Wollen wir heute Abend essen gehen?
native_language_example: Do we want to go out to eat tonight?

additional_notes: Used when you want a different thing/option than the one mentioned. Often contrasts with what you currently have or are talking about. Grammar note: it’s the neuter form (etwas), so the adjective takes neuter endings: e.g., „etwas anderes“, „mit etwas anderem“ (dative).
target_language_example: Ich möchte etwas anderes bestellen.
native_language_example: I’d like to order something else.

meaning: something completely different; something else entirely.
additional_notes: Used to correct a misunderstanding, change the topic, or emphasize that the thing being discussed is not the same at all. Often appears after a verb like „sein“ (to be): „Das ist etwas ganz anderes.“
target_language_example: Nein, das ist etwas ganz anderes.
native_language_example: No, that’s something completely different.

meaning: "Your Majesty." (a very formal way to address a king or queen)
additional_notes: Used as a direct form of address, often set off by commas: „Eure Majestät, …“. The possessive is usually „Eure“ (not *euer*) in this fixed address. When talking about a monarch (not addressing them), German typically uses „Ihre Majestät“ = “Her/His Majesty.” In traditional/formal usage, verbs often appear in the plural of respect: „Eure Majestät haben …“.
target_language_example: Eure Majestät, darf ich Ihnen etwas zeigen?
native_language_example: Your Majesty, may I show you something?

meaning: Your Majesty (a royal form of address).
additional_notes: A very formal, respectful way to address a king or queen directly. Usually used with the pronoun “Sie” and in formal speech; in modern everyday German you’ll mostly see it in historical contexts, films, ceremonies, or when talking about royalty.
target_language_example: Eure Majestät, darf ich Ihnen etwas anbieten?
native_language_example: Your Majesty, may I offer you something?

meaning: to have someone/something driven; to get a ride (have someone drive you).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "lassen" to mean "to have/let someone do something" + "fahren" (to drive/travel). Often used when you are not driving yourself: "Ich lasse mich fahren" = someone drives me. In a sentence, "lassen" is conjugated and "fahren" stays in the infinitive at the end: "Ich lasse mich nach Hause fahren."
target_language_example: Ich lasse mich morgen zum Flughafen fahren.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m getting a ride to the airport (I’m having someone drive me).

meaning: to ride a bike; to go cycling.
additional_notes: Common verb phrase. Usually written as two words: „Fahrrad fahren“. In the present tense: „Ich fahre Fahrrad“, „Du fährst Fahrrad“. You can also say „Rad fahren“ (same meaning, a bit shorter).
target_language_example: Am Wochenende fahre ich oft Fahrrad.
native_language_example: On the weekend, I often ride my bike.

meaning: to drop; to let fall; (also) to ditch/abandon (a plan, topic, etc.).
additional_notes: Literally means “let fall.” Common for physically dropping something: “Ich habe mein Handy fallen lassen.” It’s also used figuratively to mean stopping or giving up on something (a plan, idea, topic): “Lass das Thema fallen.” In separable verb forms, the parts split: “Ich lasse es fallen” (I drop it) / Perfekt: “Ich habe es fallen lassen” (I dropped it).
target_language_example: Ich habe mein Glas fallen lassen.
native_language_example: I dropped my glass.

additional_notes: A subordinating conjunction used for hypothetical or precautionary conditions (often in instructions, emails, official language). It sends the verb to the end of the clause: "falls + ... + Verb". Often similar to "wenn", but "falls" tends to sound a bit more formal and closer to "in case".
target_language_example: Ruf mich an, falls du Hilfe brauchst.
native_language_example: Call me if you need help.

meaning: to be wrong; to be mistaken.
additional_notes: Used to say that a guess, assumption, or opinion is incorrect. Very common in spoken German. Often appears as: „Ich liege falsch.“ (I’m wrong) or „Du liegst falsch.“ (You’re wrong). The opposite is „richtig liegen“ (to be right).
target_language_example: Ich dachte, der Zug kommt um acht, aber ich lag falsch.
native_language_example: I thought the train would come at eight, but I was wrong.

additional_notes: Used when something is written with the wrong letters/spelling (often names, addresses, words). Common pattern: „etwas falsch schreiben“ / „einen Namen falsch schreiben“.
target_language_example: Ich habe deinen Namen falsch geschrieben.
native_language_example: I misspelled your name.

additional_notes: Used to say that nearly all items/people/things in a group are included, but not 100%. Often answers “What did you do/buy/pack?” or describes a situation. Note the difference: “fast alles” (almost everything) vs. “fast alle” (almost all [people/plural nouns], e.g., fast alle Freunde).
target_language_example: Ich habe fast alles für die Reise gepackt.
native_language_example: I packed almost everything for the trip.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re very close to a destination or nearly ready/finished. Common in texting or when someone is waiting for you: "Ich bin fast da" = "I’m almost there." Note that German "fast" means "almost" (not English "fast").
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich bin fast da.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m almost there.

additional_notes: Used with nouns to say that the amount/number is nearly zero. It behaves like a negating determiner: **fast kein** + noun (e.g., *fast keine Zeit*, *fast kein Geld*). With plural nouns you usually use **fast keine** (*fast keine Freunde*). Note: **fast** here means “almost,” not “quick/fast.”
target_language_example: Ich habe fast kein Geld mehr.
native_language_example: I have hardly any money left.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens very rarely. Often placed near the verb: "Ich gehe fast nie ..." (= I almost never go ...). Similar to "kaum jemals" (more formal).
target_language_example: Ich trinke fast nie Kaffee.
native_language_example: I almost never drink coffee.

meaning: out of place; inappropriate (in this situation).
additional_notes: Used to say that something doesn’t belong in a certain context, is unsuitable, or is inappropriate. Commonly appears with "sein": "Das ist hier fehl am Platz." You can also use it about behavior, comments, or objects.
target_language_example: Dein Kommentar ist hier völlig fehl am Platz.
native_language_example: Your comment is completely out of place here.

meaning: out of place; inappropriate (not suitable in this situation).
additional_notes: Usually used with „sein“ to say that something doesn’t belong or isn’t appropriate in a given context: „Das ist hier fehl am Platz.“ The form „am Platze“ is a slightly older/more formal variant of „am Platz“; both are common in fixed expressions.
target_language_example: Dieser Witz ist bei der Beerdigung völlig fehl am Platze.
native_language_example: This joke is completely inappropriate at the funeral.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase. Conjugate the verb "machen" (ich mache, du machst, er/sie/es macht, wir machen, ihr macht, sie/Sie machen). Often used with "einen" in the singular: "einen Fehler machen" = "to make a mistake"; plural: "Fehler machen" = "to make mistakes."
target_language_example: Ich habe einen Fehler gemacht.
native_language_example: I made a mistake.

additional_notes: Used when something starts burning (often suddenly). Can be literal (a building catches fire) or figurative (enthusiasm “catches fire,” i.e., spreads quickly). Often used with "hat Feuer gefangen" in the past tense.
target_language_example: Die Pfanne hat Feuer gefangen.
native_language_example: The pan caught fire.

additional_notes: Common colloquial phrase used to say you’re totally tired or drained (physically or mentally), often after work, stress, travel, etc. Can also mean “completely done/finished” in some contexts, but most often refers to being exhausted.
target_language_example: Nach der Arbeit bin ich fix und fertig.
native_language_example: After work, I’m completely exhausted.

additional_notes: Literally means “flying saucer.” Used for a classic disc-shaped UFO. Grammar: feminine noun phrase; usually used with an article (eine/die fliegende Untertasse). Plural: fliegende Untertassen.
target_language_example: Am Himmel haben wir eine fliegende Untertasse gesehen.
native_language_example: We saw a flying saucer in the sky.

additional_notes: Common in school, work, and customer service contexts. Often used with a conditional: „Wenn Sie Fragen haben, …“ (“If you have questions, …”). You can add a person: „Ich habe noch Fragen an dich/Sie.“
target_language_example: Wenn Sie noch Fragen haben, können Sie mich jederzeit anrufen.
native_language_example: If you still have questions, you can call me anytime.

additional_notes: Common verb phrase meaning to ask one or more questions. You can also say "eine Frage stellen" (to ask a question). Often used with a person in the dative: "jemandem Fragen stellen" (to ask someone questions).
target_language_example: Darf ich Ihnen ein paar Fragen stellen?
native_language_example: May I ask you a few questions?

meaning: to be able to speak French / to know French.
additional_notes: Uses the modal verb "können" (can, be able to) with a language to say you can speak/understand it. Often you’ll use it with a subject: "Ich kann Französisch." Capitalize the language name ("Französisch").
target_language_example: Kannst du Französisch?
native_language_example: Can you speak French?

additional_notes: Used to say that someone can speak French or is speaking French. The adjective is usually lowercase here (französisch) because it names a language. Common patterns: „Ich spreche Französisch.“ (I speak French.), „Sprichst du Französisch?“ (Do you speak French?), „Kannst du Französisch sprechen?“ (Can you speak French?).
target_language_example: Sprichst du französisch?
native_language_example: Do you speak French?

additional_notes: Used for people/things from another country ("ein fremdes Land" = a foreign country) and for things you don’t know or that feel strange/unfamiliar ("Das ist mir fremd" = That’s unfamiliar to me). Common opposites: "bekannt" (familiar/known), "vertraut" (familiar).
target_language_example: In dieser Stadt ist mir alles fremd.
native_language_example: In this city, everything is unfamiliar to me.

additional_notes: A common Christmas greeting in German, used in person, in cards, emails, and messages. Often said in December, especially on or around December 24–26. You’ll also hear variations like "Frohe Weihnachten und ein gutes neues Jahr!" (Merry Christmas and a happy new year!).
target_language_example: Frohe Weihnachten! Ich wünsche dir schöne Feiertage.
native_language_example: Merry Christmas! I wish you happy holidays.

additional_notes: A common New Year’s greeting in German. You’ll hear and say it around New Year’s Eve and on New Year’s Day. Often used with wishes: “Ich wünsche dir/euch ein frohes neues Jahr!” (I wish you a happy new year!). Also commonly written as “Frohes neues Jahr!” and sometimes with the article: “ein frohes neues Jahr”.
target_language_example: Frohes neues Jahr! Ich wünsche dir viel Glück und Gesundheit.
native_language_example: Happy New Year! I wish you lots of luck and health.

meaning: to bear fruit; to pay off (bring results).
additional_notes: Used both literally (plants/trees producing fruit) and very often figuratively for efforts, plans, or investments that finally show results. Common in perfect tense: „hat Früchte getragen“.
target_language_example: Die harte Arbeit hat endlich Früchte getragen.
native_language_example: The hard work finally paid off.

additional_notes: Used to say that something will happen at some point in the future, even if you don’t know exactly when. Often followed by a statement about an unavoidable result or realization. Literal meaning is “earlier or later,” but the natural English equivalent is “sooner or later.”
target_language_example: Früher oder später musst du dich entscheiden.
native_language_example: Sooner or later you have to decide.

meaning: to have breakfast; to eat breakfast.
additional_notes: Verb used for the activity of eating breakfast. Commonly used with a time or place ("Wir frühstücken um acht" / "Ich frühstücke zu Hause") or with "mit" for company ("mit meiner Familie"). You can also use it without an object, but you may add what you’re eating ("Ich frühstücke Müsli").
target_language_example: Ich frühstücke jeden Morgen um sieben.
native_language_example: I have breakfast every morning at seven.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a precaution/backup scenario. It’s a conjunction that typically starts a subordinate clause, so the conjugated verb goes to the end of that clause: „… für den Fall, dass es regnet.“ Often used with preparations (taking something, planning something) and can be similar to „falls“ (more common/shorter).
target_language_example: Ich nehme einen Regenschirm mit, für den Fall, dass es regnet.
native_language_example: I’ll take an umbrella with me, in case it rains.

additional_notes: Used to talk about future time or as advice/decisions that should apply from now on. Often follows verbs like planen (to plan), hoffen (to hope), wünschen (to wish), sich merken (to remember), or as a general statement: „Für die Zukunft …“. Also common in the phrase „Alles Gute für die Zukunft!“ (All the best for the future!).
target_language_example: Für die Zukunft möchte ich besser Deutsch lernen.
native_language_example: For the future, I want to learn German better.

additional_notes: Means something lasts permanently, with no end. Common in emotional statements (love, promises), but also in everyday contexts (moving away, quitting a habit). Often used with the present tense or future meaning: „Ich bleibe für immer hier.“
target_language_example: Ich werde dich für immer lieben.
native_language_example: I will love you forever.

meaning: for oneself; on its own / separately.
additional_notes: Often used with reflexive pronouns to mean doing something for your own benefit or alone (e.g., „Ich brauche Zeit für mich.“ = I need time for myself). It can also mean something stands by itself, separate from others (e.g., „Jeder zahlt für sich.“ = Each person pays separately). In some contexts it implies being “by itself” or “in itself,” as in „für sich genommen“ (taken on its own).
target_language_example: Ich brauche heute Abend etwas Zeit für mich.
native_language_example: I need some time for myself this evening.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re fully focused and ready to listen. Often appears as “Ich bin ganz Ohr.” It’s an idiomatic expression: the literal words mean “completely ear,” but the meaning is “I’m listening closely.”
target_language_example: Erzähl ruhig weiter — ich bin ganz Ohr.
native_language_example: Go on—I'm all ears.

additional_notes: Emphasizes being alone with no one else present or helping. Often used with verbs like sein (to be), bleiben (to remain), or lassen (to leave): „Ich bin ganz allein.“ / „Lass mich ganz allein.“ Similar to „völlig allein“ (more formal) and stronger than just „allein“.
target_language_example: Ich bin heute Abend ganz allein zu Hause.
native_language_example: I’m completely alone at home this evening.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone is alone, without any help or company. Common in everyday speech; often stronger than just "alleine". Can describe being physically alone (no other people) or having to do something without assistance.
target_language_example: Ich bin heute Abend ganz alleine zu Hause.
native_language_example: I’m all alone at home tonight.

additional_notes: Often used to emphasize a strong contrast with what you expected or with something mentioned before. Common in comparisons ("als" = than) and corrections (e.g., "nicht ..., sondern ..."). Word order is flexible in sentences, but the phrase stays together as an intensifier + adjective.
target_language_example: Das ist ganz anders als ich gedacht habe.
native_language_example: That’s completely different from what I thought.

additional_notes: Often used to intensify an adjective/adverb: "ganz schön teuer" = "pretty expensive." Depending on tone/context it can sound like mild surprise, admiration, or complaint. Literally "completely beautiful," but in everyday speech it usually means "quite/pretty" rather than "beautiful."
target_language_example: Das ist ganz schön teuer!
native_language_example: That’s pretty expensive!

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that something is total/absolute. Very common with negation (e.g., "ganz und gar nicht" = "not at all") and with adjectives like "falsch" (wrong) or "unverständlich" (incomprehensible).
target_language_example: Das ist ganz und gar nicht wahr.
native_language_example: That is not true at all.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize zero/none, usually before a noun with an indefinite article/number word: "gar kein(e)". It declines like "kein" (e.g., gar keine Zeit, gar keinen Hunger, gar kein Problem). Often appears in negatives to intensify: "Ich habe gar keine Zeit" = "I have no time at all".
target_language_example: Ich habe gar keine Zeit.
native_language_example: I have no time at all.

meaning: not at all; not (in the slightest).
additional_notes: Used to strongly negate something. Often answers a yes/no question or contradicts a statement: „Gar nicht!“ = „Not at all!“ It commonly appears with verbs: „Ich verstehe gar nicht.“ (I don’t understand at all.) In everyday speech, it can also intensify a negative statement: „Das ist gar nicht so schwer.“ (That’s not so hard at all / actually not that hard).
target_language_example: Ich habe gar keine Zeit.
native_language_example: I have no time at all.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that there is zero of something. Common in answers and in negations with verbs like haben/sehen/wissen/tun (e.g., „Ich habe gar nichts.“). Often sounds stronger than plain „nichts“.
target_language_example: Ich habe gar nichts gesehen.
native_language_example: I didn’t see anything at all.

meaning: to be patient; to have patience.
additional_notes: Used when asking someone to wait calmly or saying you will wait calmly. Often used with the imperative: „Hab(e) Geduld!“ (Be patient!). You can also say: „Haben Sie bitte Geduld.“ (Please be patient.)
target_language_example: Bitte haben Sie Geduld, der Arzt kommt gleich.
native_language_example: Please be patient, the doctor will be here in a moment.

additional_notes: Often used with **für** + accusative to say something is suitable for a purpose or person: **für Kinder geeignet** (suitable for children). You’ll also see it in set phrases like **geeignet sein** (to be suitable) and in ads/instructions: **Nicht für … geeignet** (not suitable for …).
target_language_example: Dieses Programm ist für Anfänger geeignet.
native_language_example: This program is suitable for beginners.

additional_notes: Passive voice of **finden** (“to find”). Often used when talking about lost items, missing people, search results, or something being discovered. Common with a place or context: **in/bei/auf … gefunden werden** (“to be found in/at/on …”). Past participle is **gefunden**; auxiliary is **werden** (present) or **wurde/ist … worden** (past passive).
target_language_example: Der Schlüssel wurde in der Tasche gefunden.
native_language_example: The key was found in the bag.

additional_notes: Used to express an opinion opposing a plan, idea, or action. Usually followed by a noun in the accusative or a da-compound (e.g., „dagegen sein“ = to be against it). Common in discussions, votes, and giving your stance: „Ich bin gegen den Vorschlag.“ / „Bist du dafür oder dagegen?“
target_language_example: Ich bin gegen diesen Plan.
native_language_example: I’m against this plan.

additional_notes: Used as an exclamation (often with an eye-roll tone) when you think what someone said is nonsense, exaggerated, or unacceptable. Usually written/spoken as "Geh bitte!" It’s informal/colloquial and doesn’t mean "go, please" in this context.
target_language_example: Geh bitte! Das glaubst du doch selbst nicht.
native_language_example: Oh please! You don’t even believe that yourself.

additional_notes: Imperative (du-form) of **gehen** + **nur** (“just/only”). Used to tell one person to go, often either as encouragement (“Go ahead, don’t worry”) or as dismissal (“Just go then”). Tone depends on context and intonation. For more polite forms: **Gehen Sie nur** (formal) or **Geh ruhig** (“go ahead / feel free to go”).
target_language_example: Wenn du keine Zeit hast, geh nur—ich schaffe das allein.
native_language_example: If you don’t have time, just go—I can manage on my own.

meaning: to go to work (to go and work).
additional_notes: Colloquial word order; more common is "arbeiten gehen" or the more standard "zur Arbeit gehen". Used when you mean you’re leaving somewhere in order to work (often as part of your daily routine).
target_language_example: Ich muss gleich gehen arbeiten.
native_language_example: I have to go to work soon.

meaning: to let (something) go; to drop it / stop holding on to it.
additional_notes: Often used with an object or a pronoun: „Ich muss das gehen lassen.“ = “I have to let it go.” It can mean letting go emotionally (stop worrying/stop being upset) or literally releasing/allowing something to move. In some contexts it can also mean “to let something run” (e.g., a machine/engine): „den Motor laufen/gehen lassen“.
target_language_example: Ich muss das jetzt einfach gehen lassen.
native_language_example: I just have to let it go now.

meaning: to have to go; to need to leave.
additional_notes: Used to say you must leave (often because of time, an appointment, tiredness, etc.). In conversation it’s commonly used with a subject: „Ich muss gehen.“ (I have to go / I need to leave). It can also mean needing to go to the bathroom, especially with context like „Ich muss mal gehen.“ or „Ich muss dringend.“
target_language_example: Sorry, ich muss jetzt gehen.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go now.

meaning: to go to bed; to go to sleep.
additional_notes: In normal German, the more common (and more natural) word order is **schlafen gehen**: *Ich gehe schlafen.* / *Wir gehen schlafen.* It’s used for the action of going to bed (and usually implies you’ll sleep), similar to “I’m going to bed.”
target_language_example: Ich bin müde. Ich gehe schlafen.
native_language_example: I’m tired. I’m going to bed.

additional_notes: Very common verb used with the dative to say who something belongs to: „Das gehört mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen.“ You’ll also see „gehören zu“ meaning “to be part of / to belong to (a group/category)”: „Das gehört zur Familie.“ Present tense: ich gehöre, du gehörst, er/sie/es gehört.
target_language_example: Wem gehört dieses Buch? – Es gehört mir.
native_language_example: Who does this book belong to? – It’s mine.

meaning: to belong to; to be part of.
additional_notes: Used to show membership/ownership or that something is included in a group/category. Often followed by a dative noun/pronoun (e.g., zu mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen). In the sense of “be part of,” it can also be used with things/ideas: “Das gehört zur Aufgabe” = “That’s part of the task.”
target_language_example: Dieses Buch gehört zu mir.
native_language_example: This book belongs to me.

additional_notes: Common in shopping/returns contexts (e.g., on signs or in ads: „Geld zurück!“). Often used with verbs like „bekommen“ (to get) or „geben“ (to give): „Ich bekomme mein Geld zurück.“ / „Sie geben mir mein Geld zurück.“
target_language_example: Ich möchte mein Geld zurück, bitte.
native_language_example: I’d like my money back, please.

additional_notes: Used to confirm or agree with what someone said (“Exactly.”). It can also mean “exactly/precisely” in descriptions of time, numbers, or details (e.g., “exactly at 3 o’clock”).
target_language_example: Genau! Das meine ich.
native_language_example: Exactly! That’s what I mean.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is equal in quality/degree to something else. Often followed by a comparison with „wie“ (e.g., „genauso gut wie …“ = “just as good as …”). Can also stand alone to mean “equally well / just as good.”
target_language_example: Dieses Restaurant ist genauso gut wie das andere.
native_language_example: This restaurant is just as good as the other one.

additional_notes: Used with **haben** to form the perfect tense of *nehmen*: **ich habe … genommen** = “I took / have taken …”. Also appears in passive constructions: **… wird genommen** = “... is taken.” Common in everyday phrases like **den Bus / den Zug / ein Taxi genommen** (“took the bus/train/a taxi”).
target_language_example: Ich habe den Bus genommen.
native_language_example: I took the bus.

meaning: just barely; only just (in time / still).
additional_notes: Used to say something happened at the very last moment or was only barely true/possible. Often implies it was close to failing or being too late. Common with past tense for last-minute success ("Ich habe den Zug gerade noch erwischt.") and with "noch" meaning "still" in the sense of "only just" ("Es ist gerade noch warm genug."). Word order can vary, but "gerade noch" usually stays together.
target_language_example: Ich habe den Bus gerade noch erwischt.
native_language_example: I just barely caught the bus.

additional_notes: Common in directions and instructions. Often used with verbs like „gehen/fahren“ (to go/drive): „Gehen/Fahren Sie geradeaus.“ It can also describe doing something in a direct way, e.g. „geradeaus sagen“ (to say something plainly/directly).
target_language_example: Gehen Sie an der Ampel geradeaus.
native_language_example: Go straight ahead at the traffic light.

meaning: to like working; to enjoy working.
additional_notes: "Gern" means "gladly / with pleasure" and is commonly used to express that you like doing something. You’ll often hear it with a modal verb: "Ich arbeite gern" (I like working) or "Ich würde gern arbeiten" (I’d like to work). To say you don’t like working: "Ich arbeite nicht gern."
target_language_example: Ich arbeite gern im Team.
native_language_example: I like working in a team.

meaning: to like (someone/something); to be fond of.
additional_notes: Used to express liking or fondness. With a person, it often implies warmth/affection (sometimes close to “care about”), but it can also be used neutrally. Commonly used in the present tense (e.g., „Ich habe dich gern.“). Note the difference: „gern haben“ = like/be fond of, while „gern + Verb“ (e.g., „Ich schwimme gern.“) = like doing something.
target_language_example: Ich habe dich gern.
native_language_example: I like you / I’m fond of you.

meaning: to like doing (something); to do (something) gladly.
additional_notes: "gern" means "gladly/with pleasure" and is commonly used with a verb to say you enjoy doing something. Usually you put "gern" after the verb: "Ich mache das gern." If you name the activity, use a verb phrase: "Ich mache gern Sport" (I like doing sports), or "Ich mache das gern" (I like doing that). For offers/requests you often use "gern" to mean "with pleasure": "Gern!" / "Das mache ich gern."
target_language_example: Ich mache das gern.
native_language_example: I like doing that.

meaning: to like speaking; to enjoy talking.
additional_notes: Used to say you enjoy talking or are happy to talk. In conversation, you’ll more often see it in forms like “Ich spreche gern (Deutsch).” (I like speaking (German).) You can also use “gern” with other verbs in the same way (e.g., „gern lesen“ = like reading).
target_language_example: Ich spreche gern Deutsch, aber ich spreche nicht so gut.
native_language_example: I like speaking German, but I don’t speak that well.

additional_notes: Used to say you enjoy drinking a particular beverage or drink in general. Very common with an object: „Ich trinke gern Kaffee.“ You can also put „gern“ at the end: „Ich trinke Kaffee gern.“ For preferences, „gern“ often corresponds to “gladly / with pleasure.”
target_language_example: Ich trinke gern Kaffee.
native_language_example: I like drinking coffee.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened during the night before today. In everyday German, people often say “letzte Nacht” for “last night”; “gestern Nacht” is also common, especially in speech. “Nacht” is a noun and is always capitalized.
target_language_example: Gestern Nacht habe ich schlecht geschlafen.
native_language_example: Last night I slept badly.

additional_notes: Used to mean practical, reasonable thinking based on everyday experience. Often appears with verbs like „haben“ (to have) or „benutzen“ (to use): „Er hat gesunden Menschenverstand.“ It’s a neutral, standard expression (not slang).
target_language_example: Das ist doch nur gesunder Menschenverstand.
native_language_example: That’s just common sense.

additional_notes: Used as an adjective or adverb. Common in phrases like „getrennt sein“ (to be separated), „getrennt leben“ (to live separately; often used for couples who are separated), and „getrennt schlafen“ (to sleep separately). Also used for doing something separately: „Wir bezahlen getrennt.“ (We pay separately / split the bill).
target_language_example: Wir bezahlen getrennt.
native_language_example: We’ll pay separately (split the bill).

additional_notes: Common as an adverb meaning “usually” (often with "(ganz) gewöhnlich" = “quite/just usually”). As an adjective it means “ordinary/normal” and can contrast with "besonders" (special) or "ungewöhnlich" (unusual).
target_language_example: Ich gehe gewöhnlich um sieben Uhr zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: I usually go to work at seven o’clock.

meaning: just around the corner; very nearby.
additional_notes: Used to say something is very close by (often a shop, stop, or place). Common in giving directions. It can also be used more generally for “coming up soon” in time, but most often it’s about location.
target_language_example: Der Supermarkt ist gleich um die Ecke.
native_language_example: The supermarket is just around the corner.

meaning: to bring (someone) luck; to be lucky.
additional_notes: Used when something is believed to cause good luck. Often with a dative person: „jemandem Glück bringen“ (to bring someone luck). You can also use it without a person, meaning something is lucky for you: „Das bringt Glück.“
target_language_example: Der Glücksbringer soll dir Glück bringen.
native_language_example: The lucky charm is supposed to bring you luck.

meaning: to be lucky; to have luck.
additional_notes: Used to say someone has good luck in a situation. Often with a person as subject: „Ich habe Glück.“ / „Du hast Glück.“ You can also add „dass …“: „Ich habe Glück, dass …“ The opposite is „Pech haben“ (to have bad luck).
target_language_example: Du hast Glück, dass der Bus noch kommt.
native_language_example: You're lucky that the bus is still coming.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase. "glücklich" = happy, "machen" = to make/do. Typically used with an object (a person): "Du machst mich glücklich" (You make me happy). Can also be used for things/situations that bring happiness: "Das macht mich glücklich" (That makes me happy).
target_language_example: Du machst mich wirklich glücklich.
native_language_example: You really make me happy.

additional_notes: Used to express relief that something bad didn’t happen or that a situation turned out well. Very common in spoken German; often also written as "Gott sei Dank". Similar to "zum Glück" (luckily).
target_language_example: Gott sei Dank ist niemand verletzt worden.
native_language_example: Thank God nobody was hurt.

additional_notes: Used to say something is unknown or uncertain, often with a sigh or emphasis (similar to “God knows” or “who knows” in English). You’ll also often see it as part of a longer phrase, e.g. “Gott weiß, warum …” (“God knows why …”) or “Gott weiß wie/wo/wann …” (“God knows how/where/when …”). Usually written “Gott weiß” with a capital G.
target_language_example: Gott weiß, wann der Zug endlich kommt.
native_language_example: God knows when the train will finally come.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male sibling who is older than you. It can also be used more generally to mean a protective/authoritative “big brother” figure (and in political contexts can allude to “Big Brother” surveillance). Often appears with a possessive: „mein großer Bruder“, „ihr großer Bruder“.
target_language_example: Mein großer Bruder wohnt in Berlin.
native_language_example: My older brother lives in Berlin.

additional_notes: Usually said about a person/body part after an impact: „jemanden grün und blau schlagen“ = to beat someone black and blue. Can also be used more generally for being badly bruised after an accident or fall. Not typically used for colors in this exact fixed phrase; for literal colors you’d normally just list them as adjectives (e.g., „ein grün-blaues Kleid“ = a green-blue dress).
target_language_example: Nach dem Sturz war mein Arm ganz grün und blau.
native_language_example: After the fall, my arm was completely black and blue.

meaning: to send (someone) greetings; to say hi to someone via another person.
additional_notes: Used when you ask someone to pass on your greetings to a third person. Common patterns: „Grüß ihn/sie bitte von mir.“ and „Lass (deine Eltern) von mir grüßen.“ Often said when saying goodbye or when someone mentions they’ll see another person soon.
target_language_example: Wenn du deine Schwester siehst, grüß sie bitte von mir.
native_language_example: If you see your sister, please say hi to her from me.

additional_notes: Most commonly said as **„Gute Nacht!“** (with **-e** ending and capital **Nacht**). Used as a farewell in the evening/at bedtime (not as a greeting when arriving).
target_language_example: Gute Nacht! Schlaf gut.
native_language_example: Good night! Sleep well.

meaning: to be (doing) well; to be fine.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "gehen" to talk about how someone is feeling or how things are going. Very common in: "Wie geht es dir/Ihnen?" → "Mir geht es gut." You can also use it for situations/things: "Es geht gut" (It’s going well). In sentences, "gut" often comes at the end: "Mir geht es gut."
target_language_example: Danke, mir geht es gut.
native_language_example: Thanks, I’m doing well.

additional_notes: Used to praise someone for doing something well. Often said to a person directly (especially to kids, students, colleagues). You can also use it with an object: “Gut gemacht!” (Well done!) or “Gut gemacht, Maria!” (Well done, Maria!).
target_language_example: Gut gemacht! Das hast du wirklich super gemacht.
native_language_example: Well done! You did that really great.

additional_notes: Used to agree with or praise what someone just said (often as a short comment by itself). Similar to “That’s well put.” You can also use it with “Das ist gut gesagt.”
target_language_example: Gut gesagt! Genau so sehe ich das auch.
native_language_example: Well said! That’s exactly how I see it too.

meaning: "good night" (said as a goodbye in the evening or before sleep).
additional_notes: Used when someone is going to bed or when ending a conversation late in the day. Often said as "Gute Nacht!"; you can also say "Gute Nacht, [Name]". As a greeting when arriving, Germans usually say "Guten Abend" instead (not "Gute Nacht").
target_language_example: Ich bin müde. Gute Nacht!
native_language_example: I'm tired. Good night!

additional_notes: A common greeting used from the late afternoon/early evening onward. You can use it when arriving (and sometimes when leaving) in more neutral or polite situations; with friends you might also hear/use “Hallo”. Often capitalized as “Guten Abend” at the start of a sentence or in writing.
target_language_example: Guten Abend, wie geht’s Ihnen?
native_language_example: Good evening, how are you?

additional_notes: A standard greeting used in the morning until around late morning/noon. Often written and said with a capital M in Morgen. You can also shorten it to "Morgen!" in casual speech.
target_language_example: Guten Morgen, wie geht es Ihnen?
native_language_example: Good morning, how are you?

additional_notes: Common, polite greeting in many situations (shops, workplaces, with strangers). Usually capitalized in writing: „Guten Tag“. Often used as both a greeting and (more formally) a goodbye, though „Auf Wiedersehen“ is more typical for goodbye.
target_language_example: Guten Tag, wie kann ich Ihnen helfen?
native_language_example: Good day, how can I help you?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „sein“ and „bleiben“ to say someone is feeling cheerful/hopeful, often about what will happen next. Common patterns: „Ich bin guter Dinge, dass …“ = “I’m optimistic that …”; „guter Dinge bleiben“ = “to stay optimistic.”
target_language_example: Ich bin guter Dinge, dass wir den Test bestehen.
native_language_example: I’m optimistic that we’ll pass the test.

meaning: to be able to have; can have (have the possibility/permission to have).
additional_notes: Combination of the verbs "haben" (to have) + modal verb "können" (can/to be able to). Used to talk about possibility, ability, or permission to possess something. Common in questions and polite requests (often with "ich" or "wir"): "Kann ich ... haben?" In a main clause, the conjugated modal comes in position 2 and the other verb goes to the end in infinitive form: "Ich kann ... haben."
target_language_example: Kann ich bitte ein Glas Wasser haben?
native_language_example: Can I please have a glass of water?

meaning: 'to be supposed to have' / 'is said to have' (done something).
additional_notes: Used with a past participle to talk about something in the past that someone was expected to do (obligation) or that is only reported/claimed (hearsay). Common pattern: "sollen" + perfect infinitive: "Er soll das gemacht haben." Meaning depends on context: obligation ("was supposed to") vs report ("is said to").
target_language_example: Er soll gestern angerufen haben, aber ich habe nichts gehört.
native_language_example: He is said to have called yesterday, but I didn’t hear anything.

meaning: hand in hand; closely together / in cooperation.
additional_notes: Used to say that people, groups, or things work closely together or happen together. Can be literal (walking hand in hand) or figurative (working hand in hand). Often used with verbs like „gehen“, „arbeiten“, or „Hand in Hand gehen“ (= to go hand in hand).
target_language_example: Wir arbeiten hand in Hand, um das Projekt fertigzustellen.
native_language_example: We work hand in hand to finish the project.

meaning: (in: „Das hat Hand und Fuß.“) It makes sense; it’s solid and well thought out.
additional_notes: Used mainly in the fixed phrase „etwas hat Hand und Fuß“ to say an idea/plan/explanation is sensible, practical, and reliable (not random or poorly prepared). Often said about arguments, plans, or concepts.
target_language_example: Dein Plan hat Hand und Fuß.
native_language_example: Your plan makes sense / is solid.

meaning: a happy ending (especially in a film, book, or story).
additional_notes: Common in everyday German, often when talking about movies/books: „Der Film hat ein happy End.“ Written as two words in German; the noun is „das End(e)“ here, so you’ll often see it with an article: „ein happy End“, „kein happy End“. Sometimes also said with the more German adjective: „ein glückliches Ende“.
target_language_example: Der Film hat zum Glück ein happy End.
native_language_example: Luckily, the movie has a happy ending.

additional_notes: Common verb phrase for schoolwork you need to complete at home. Also used as "Hausaufgaben machen für + subject" (e.g., für Mathe) or "Hausaufgaben machen in + subject" (less common). You can also say "Hausaufgaben erledigen" (to get homework done).
target_language_example: Ich muss heute Abend noch Hausaufgaben machen.
native_language_example: I still have to do homework tonight.

meaning: “Hail Hitler” — a Nazi salute/chant expressing allegiance to Adolf Hitler.
additional_notes: This is a historical Nazi slogan associated with extremist ideology and hate. It is highly offensive, and using it can be illegal in Germany and Austria except in clearly educational, historical, or anti-Nazi contexts (e.g., quoting a document or discussing history). Learners should not use this as a greeting.
target_language_example: Im Unterricht sprachen wir darüber, warum der Gruß „Heil Hitler“ in Deutschland verboten ist.
native_language_example: In class we talked about why the salute “Heil Hitler” is banned in Germany.

additional_notes: Common café/drink order. Capitalize the noun: Schokolade. You may also hear "Kakao" (especially for the drink); in many places "heiße Schokolade" implies a richer drink made with real chocolate.
target_language_example: Ich hätte gern eine heiße Schokolade, bitte.
native_language_example: I’d like a hot chocolate, please.

additional_notes: Uses the modal verb "wollen" (to want) with the infinitive "helfen" (to help). Often said as "Ich will helfen" (I want to help) or politely as a question: "Wollen Sie helfen?" / "Willst du helfen?". With a specific person, "helfen" takes the dative: "Ich will dir/Ihnen helfen" (I want to help you).
target_language_example: Ich will dir helfen.
native_language_example: I want to help you.

meaning: to come here; (often) to be from / to come from (an origin).
additional_notes: Often used to ask about someone’s origin: „Woher kommst du?“ = “Where are you from?” In the conjugated form, the prefix is typically separated: „Ich komme aus Berlin her“ (less common) / much more common: „Ich komme aus Berlin.“ In questions and answers about origin, you’ll usually see „woher“ + „kommen“ rather than the full verb „herkommen“.
target_language_example: Woher kommst du?
native_language_example: Where are you from?

meaning: “For God’s sake!” / “For heaven’s sake!” (an exclamation of annoyance or impatience).
additional_notes: Used as a standalone exclamation or at the start of a sentence when you’re frustrated, surprised, or impatient. It’s fairly common in spoken German and is stronger than neutral phrases like „Ach, Mann!“; in polite/formal situations it can sound rude. Often written/spoken as „Herrgott nochmal!“ or „Herrgott, noch mal!“
target_language_example: Herrgott noch mal, beeil dich doch!
native_language_example: For heaven’s sake, hurry up!

additional_notes: Used to congratulate someone (for a birthday, passing an exam, a wedding, a new job, etc.). Often said as: „Herzlichen Glückwunsch!“ or „Herzlichen Glückwunsch zum Geburtstag/zur Hochzeit/zur Beförderung.“ You can also use it in writing (cards, messages).
target_language_example: Herzlichen Glückwunsch zum Geburtstag!
native_language_example: Happy birthday! / Many happy returns!

additional_notes: Used to talk about plans or events happening later today in the evening. Often interchangeable with "heute Nacht" only in the sense of "tonight" in English, but "heute Nacht" specifically means at night (late hours), while "heute Abend" is the evening period. In speech you may also hear "heut Abend" (shortened).
target_language_example: Hast du heute Abend Zeit?
native_language_example: Do you have time this evening?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the coming/ current night after today. In German, "heute Nacht" refers specifically to the night-time hours (not the whole evening). For "this evening," use "heute Abend." You can also say "in der Nacht" for "at night" in general.
target_language_example: Ich kann heute Nacht nicht schlafen.
native_language_example: I can’t sleep tonight.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a location above the speaker or at a higher level/floor, often relative to where the speaker currently is. Common with verbs of location/movement like „sein“ (to be), „stehen“ (to stand), „sitzen“ (to sit), or „kommen“ (to come). For emphasis or clarity, you may also hear „hier oben im/in der …“ (up here in/on the …).
target_language_example: Ich bin hier oben im zweiten Stock.
native_language_example: I’m up here on the second floor.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a location below the speaker’s position or lower down on something nearby (e.g., on a page/screen, on a shelf). Often contrasted with "da oben" (up there). "Hier" = here, "unten" = down/below, so it’s straightforward and common in everyday directions.
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte hier unten unterschreiben?
native_language_example: Can you please sign down here?

meaning: to here (toward the speaker / this place).
additional_notes: Used for movement in the direction of where the speaker is (or where “here” is). Often with verbs like „kommen“ (to come), „bringen“ (to bring), „gehen“ (to go). Contrast: „dorthin / dahin“ = to there; „hier“ = here (location, not movement). In everyday speech, people also say „hierhin“; „hierher“ can feel a bit more directional (“over to here”).
target_language_example: Komm bitte hierher!
native_language_example: Please come here!

additional_notes: Used for movement in two directions (physically or in conversation). Also common as an adjective/adverb phrase: "das Hin und Her" = "the back-and-forth"; "hin und her gehen" = "to pace"; "hin und her überlegen" = "to go back and forth / be undecided." Often written "Hin und Her" when used as a noun.
target_language_example: Wir sind den ganzen Nachmittag hin und her gelaufen.
native_language_example: We walked back and forth all afternoon.

meaning: back and forth; to and fro.
additional_notes: Used for movement in two directions (e.g., walking or swinging), and also figuratively for discussions, arguments, or indecision ("das Hin und Her" = all the back-and-forth). Often appears with verbs like "gehen", "laufen", "pendeln", "schicken" (send back and forth), or phrases like "hin und her überlegen" (go back and forth in your mind).
target_language_example: Wir haben lange hin und her diskutiert, bevor wir entschieden haben.
native_language_example: We discussed back and forth for a long time before we decided.

meaning: now and then; from time to time.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens occasionally, but not regularly. It’s neutral and common in everyday speech and writing. Similar to "ab und zu" and "manchmal" (but "hin und wieder" often sounds a bit more like "every so often").
target_language_example: Ich gehe hin und wieder ins Kino.
native_language_example: I go to the cinema now and then.

meaning: 'to go there' (to go to a place).
additional_notes: Common separable verb: hingehen → ich gehe hin, du gehst hin, er/sie geht hin. Used for going to a specific place or event that’s understood from context. With an event, English often says “go” or “go to”: Ich gehe zur Party hin (often just: Ich gehe zur Party).
target_language_example: Gehst du heute Abend hin?
native_language_example: Are you going there tonight?

additional_notes: Commonly said as **hinter Gittern** (plural): it means someone is in jail/prison. Used both literally and figuratively (e.g., someone could end up there because of a crime). The preposition **hinter** takes the dative here (location), so **Gittern** is a fixed form in the idiom.
target_language_example: Nach dem Urteil musste er hinter Gittern.
native_language_example: After the verdict, he had to go behind bars.

additional_notes: Common as an adverb meaning either (1) time: “afterwards/later” (often in spoken German), or (2) direction/movement: “after, behind” (following someone/something). Often used with verbs like „laufen/fahren/rennen“ (to go after) or with „sein/kommen“: „Ich komme hinterher“ = “I’ll come after you / I’ll catch up.”
target_language_example: Geh schon mal los, ich komme gleich hinterher.
native_language_example: Go ahead, I’ll come right after you.

additional_notes: Formed from hin (“to there”) + wollen (“to want”). In real sentences it’s usually split: „Ich will da hin.“ / „Wir wollen morgen hin.“ The adverb „hin“ often appears as „da hin“ (there), „hier hin“ (to here), or „wohin“ (to where).
target_language_example: Ich will da hin, aber ich habe keine Zeit.
native_language_example: I want to go there, but I don’t have time.

additional_notes: Often used with a person in the dative: „jemandem Hoffnung geben“ = to give someone hope. You can also say what gives hope with „(etwas) gibt (mir/uns) Hoffnung“ (“something gives me/us hope”).
target_language_example: Der Arzt wollte ihr Hoffnung geben.
native_language_example: The doctor wanted to give her hope.

additional_notes: Used to describe a situation or person where there seems to be no chance of improvement or success. Often sounds quite strong/negative. Related forms: „die Hoffnung“ = hope; „-los“ = -less (e.g., „arbeitslos“ = unemployed).
target_language_example: Es sieht hoffnungslos aus, aber wir geben nicht auf.
native_language_example: It looks hopeless, but we’re not giving up.

additional_notes: Used as an exclamation to praise someone’s achievement or performance. Often said alone (“Hut ab!”) or with “vor” + dative to specify who/what you admire: “Hut ab vor dir!” = “Hats off to you!” More common in spoken/colloquial German.
target_language_example: Hut ab vor deiner Leistung!
native_language_example: Hats off to your performance!

additional_notes: A command used by police or in a robbery scenario to tell someone to raise their hands. In everyday contexts it can also be used jokingly (e.g., “hands up if you agree”). Often appears with an exclamation mark: „Hände hoch!“
