target_language_example: Polizist: „Hände hoch! Keine Bewegung!“
native_language_example: Police officer: “Hands up! Don’t move!”

additional_notes: Used when greeting or saying goodbye in a formal or polite way. You can also use it in the phrase „jemandem die Hand schütteln“ (“to shake someone’s hand”).
target_language_example: Bei der Begrüßung haben wir uns die Hände geschüttelt.
native_language_example: When greeting each other, we shook hands.

additional_notes: A strong warning or command telling someone to stop touching something or to keep away. Often said as an exclamation: “Hände weg!” You can also specify what to stay away from with “Hände weg von …” (hands off …).
target_language_example: Hände weg! Das ist zerbrechlich.
native_language_example: Hands off! That’s fragile.

meaning: ups and downs; good and bad times.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the positive and negative experiences in life, a relationship, a job, etc. Common patterns: „die Höhen und Tiefen (des Lebens)“, „mit allen Höhen und Tiefen“, „Höhen und Tiefen erleben“.
target_language_example: Jede Beziehung hat ihre Höhen und Tiefen.
native_language_example: Every relationship has its ups and downs.

meaning: to listen and talk (to practice listening and speaking).
additional_notes: Often used (especially in a class/learning context) to name the skills you practice: *Hören* = listening/understanding what you hear; *reden* = speaking/talking. In a sentence you’ll usually see it as **hören und reden** ("listen and talk") or in a list like **hören, reden, lesen, schreiben**.
target_language_example: Im Deutschkurs üben wir hören und reden.
native_language_example: In the German course we practice listening and speaking.

additional_notes: Mostly used in writing as an abbreviation for **im Ganzen**. It summarizes a general impression (similar to “overall” or “all in all”). Note: in business contexts, **i. G.** can also mean **in Gründung** (“in formation”, e.g., a company not yet fully established), but the everyday meaning is usually **im Ganzen**.
target_language_example: I. G. war der Urlaub sehr schön.
native_language_example: Overall, the vacation was very nice.

meaning: “in liquidation” (a company is being wound up/closed).
additional_notes: Business/legal abbreviation used after a company name (often written as “i.L.” or “i. L.”). It indicates the company is in the process of dissolving and settling its affairs. You’ll typically see it in official documents, invoices, or the commercial register, not in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: Die Muster GmbH i. L. wird aus dem Handelsregister gelöscht.
native_language_example: The Muster GmbH (in liquidation) will be removed from the commercial register.

meaning: abbr. for „im Sinne“: “in the sense of” / “within the meaning of.”
additional_notes: Used mainly in formal or legal/administrative writing to clarify how a word/phrase should be understood (often followed by a law, regulation, or definition). In running text you’ll often also see the full form „im Sinne (von) …“.
target_language_example: Kinder i. S. des Gesetzes sind Personen unter 18 Jahren.
native_language_example: Children within the meaning of the law are persons under 18.

meaning: “as a rule; usually” (short for „in der Regel“).
additional_notes: Common written abbreviation in German (emails, notices, manuals). Means something happens in most cases, but not always. In speech, people usually say the full phrase „in der Regel“.
target_language_example: Die Lieferung dauert i. d. R. 2–3 Werktage.
native_language_example: Delivery usually takes 2–3 business days.

additional_notes: Used to agree with someone by saying you feel/do the same thing. Often follows a statement like “Ich mag …” (“I like …”). In full sentences it’s “Ich auch.” or “Ich auch nicht.” (“Me neither.”). Word-by-word it’s “I also,” so it can also mean “I as well” in slightly more formal contexts.
target_language_example: Ich bin müde. – Ich auch.
native_language_example: I’m tired. – Me too.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re participating or agreeing to join an activity/plan. Common in spoken German when someone invites you along. Literally “I am (there) with it,” but in English it’s usually “I’m in” or “Count me in.”
target_language_example: Geht ihr heute Abend ins Kino? Ich bin dabei!
native_language_example: Are you going to the movies tonight? I’m in!

meaning: It’s my turn / I’m next (it’s my go).
additional_notes: Used when taking turns in a game, a queue, or a group activity. "dran" is short for "dran sein" (= to be up/next). You can swap the subject: "Du bist dran" (it’s your turn).
target_language_example: Okay, ich bin dran – ich würfle jetzt.
native_language_example: Okay, it’s my turn—I’ll roll the dice now.

additional_notes: Common, informal way to say you’ve finished something or you can’t go on because you’re tired/stressed. Often used after a task or intense situation: "Nach der Arbeit/Prüfung bin ich durch." It can also mean you’re done with a topic or person ("Mit dem Thema bin ich durch" = I’m done with this topic).
target_language_example: Nach der Prüfung bin ich durch.
native_language_example: After the exam, I’m done (and exhausted).

additional_notes: Often used to say you have completed a task (homework, work, eating). In some contexts it can also mean “I’m ready” (e.g., to leave), but “fertig” can sound like “done/exhausted” depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Ich bin fertig mit meinen Hausaufgaben.
native_language_example: I’m done with my homework.

additional_notes: Used to express strong confidence about a fact or opinion. Literally “I am sure (to myself)”: *mir* is dative reflexive (referring back to “ich”). Often followed by a clause with *dass*: *Ich bin mir sicher, dass …*
target_language_example: Ich bin mir sicher, dass wir den richtigen Weg nehmen.
native_language_example: I’m sure we’re taking the right way.

additional_notes: A common everyday sentence to say you feel tired or sleepy. Use it as a full reply to “Wie geht’s?” or to explain why you want to rest or go to bed. You can intensify it with “sehr”: “Ich bin sehr müde.”
target_language_example: Ich bin müde, ich gehe ins Bett.
native_language_example: I’m tired, I’m going to bed.

meaning: I think so / I believe so.
additional_notes: Used to confirm something in a slightly unsure or polite way (less direct than "ja"). "schon" here means roughly "yes, probably" or "I guess so". Common in conversation as a short answer; you can also add emphasis: "Ich glaube schon!" (I do think so!).
target_language_example: Kommst du morgen? – Ich glaube schon.
native_language_example: Are you coming tomorrow? – I think so.

additional_notes: A very common way to say you’re scared or anxious. You can add what you’re afraid of with "vor" + dative: "Ich habe Angst vor Hunden." Also common: "Ich habe Angst, dass ..." (I’m afraid that ...) and "Ich habe Angst zu ..." (I’m afraid to ...). More informal/shorter: "Ich hab Angst."
target_language_example: Ich habe Angst vor der Prüfung.
native_language_example: I’m afraid of the exam.

additional_notes: A common, neutral way to say you are hungry. Literally “I have hunger,” using the verb *haben* (“to have”) + the noun *Hunger*. You can also say *Ich habe großen Hunger* (“I’m very hungry”).
target_language_example: Ich habe Hunger. Können wir etwas essen?
native_language_example: I’m hungry. Can we eat something?

meaning: I feel like it / I’m in the mood (to do something).
additional_notes: Used to say you want to do something right now. Very commonly followed by “auf + accusative” for nouns (“Ich habe Lust auf Pizza.” = I feel like pizza) or by “zu + infinitive” for verbs (“Ich habe Lust, ins Kino zu gehen.” = I feel like going to the movies). You can also say “Keine Lust!” for “I don’t feel like it.”
target_language_example: Ich habe Lust, heute Abend etwas zu essen.
native_language_example: I feel like eating something tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say you are correct or that your opinion/statement is correct. Often said in disagreements or when confirming a point. You can also hear it as “Ich habe recht.” (often not capitalized in informal writing), but the noun is technically “Recht” (rights/being right).
target_language_example: Ich habe Recht – das Restaurant ist heute geschlossen.
native_language_example: I’m right—the restaurant is closed today.

additional_notes: Common way to say you’re available, often as an answer to a question like „Hast du Zeit?“ (“Do you have time?”). You can add details: „Ich habe Zeit für ein Treffen.“ (“I have time for a meeting.”). To say the opposite: „Ich habe keine Zeit.“ (“I don’t have time.”).
target_language_example: Heute Nachmittag habe ich Zeit.
native_language_example: This afternoon I have time.

additional_notes: Polite, common phrase to get someone’s attention before asking something. Often followed by a question starting with a question word (e.g., „Wo…?“, „Wie…?“, „Was…?“). In more formal situations you can also say „Ich hätte eine Frage“ (“I would have a question”).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich habe eine Frage: Wo ist der Bahnhof?
native_language_example: Excuse me, I have a question: where is the train station?

additional_notes: Used to say you’ve reached your limit (with a situation, behavior, noise, waiting, etc.). Often followed by “von” + dative to name what you’re fed up with: “Ich habe genug von dem Lärm.” You may also hear the shorter “Genug!” (“Enough!”). In some contexts it can also mean you have enough of something (e.g., food): “Ich habe genug gegessen.”
target_language_example: Ich habe genug von diesem Streit.
native_language_example: I’ve had enough of this argument.

additional_notes: A very common way to say you don’t have money. Use “kein” (not “nicht”) with nouns: “kein Geld” = “no money.” You can also say “Ich habe kein Geld dabei.” (I don’t have any money on me.)
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, ich habe kein Geld.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have no money.

meaning: I don’t feel like it / I’m not in the mood (to).
additional_notes: Used to say you don’t want to do something. Often followed by “auf + accusative” (Ich habe keine Lust auf Pizza. = I don’t feel like pizza.) or by “zu + infinitive” (Ich habe keine Lust, zu gehen. = I don’t feel like going.) Also common in the shorter form “Keine Lust!” = “Not in the mood!”.
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Lust, heute Abend auszugehen.
native_language_example: I don’t feel like going out tonight.

additional_notes: Common, polite way to say you’re busy or can’t do something right now. You can add a reason or a time: „Ich habe keine Zeit, ich muss arbeiten.“ / „…heute“ (today) / „…gerade“ (right now). Often used with „für“ + accusative: „Ich habe keine Zeit für dich.“ (I don’t have time for you.)
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, ich habe keine Zeit.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have time.

additional_notes: Used to say you have the intention or plan to do something. Usually followed by an infinitive with "zu": "Ich habe vor, heute zu lernen." (In speech, the comma is often not noticeable.) You can also use it with a noun: "Ich habe vor, einen Ausflug zu machen."
target_language_example: Ich habe vor, nächstes Jahr nach Deutschland zu reisen.
native_language_example: I’m planning to travel to Germany next year.

additional_notes: A very strong, harsh sentence used to express intense anger or dislike. In everyday situations, Germans often use softer phrases like “Ich mag dich nicht” (I don’t like you) or “Ich kann dich nicht ausstehen” (I can’t stand you). Word order: subject “ich” + verb “hasse” + object “dich” (informal “you”). For polite “you,” use “Ich hasse Sie,” but this is rare and extremely rude.
target_language_example: Ich hasse dich! Lass mich in Ruhe.
native_language_example: I hate you! Leave me alone.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your name. It’s the 1st-person singular of "heißen" (to be called). Typically followed by your name: "Ich heiße Anna." In questions you’ll often hear: "Wie heißt du?" (What’s your name?).
target_language_example: Hallo, ich heiße Tom.
native_language_example: Hi, my name is Tom.

meaning: "I can't anymore" / "I can't go on" (I'm exhausted or at my limit).
additional_notes: Common way to say you’ve reached your limit physically, mentally, or emotionally. Often implies being too tired, overwhelmed, or unable to continue doing something. You can add what you can’t do anymore with an infinitive clause: "Ich kann nicht mehr arbeiten."
target_language_example: Ich kann nicht mehr, ich brauche eine Pause.
native_language_example: I can't go on, I need a break.

additional_notes: Used to say where you are from (country, city, region). Commonly followed by a place name: "Ich komme aus Deutschland." You can also add "und" + another place if needed. For asking someone: "Woher kommst du?"
target_language_example: Ich komme aus den USA, aber ich wohne jetzt in Berlin.
native_language_example: I’m from the USA, but I live in Berlin now.

additional_notes: A direct way to express romantic love. In German it can feel strong/serious, so friends more often say “Ich hab(e) dich lieb” (affectionate, not necessarily romantic). “dich” is the informal singular “you” (used with du).
target_language_example: Ich liebe dich.
native_language_example: I love you.

additional_notes: A common, straightforward way to say you like someone (friendly or romantic). It’s generally less strong than „Ich liebe dich“ (I love you). In casual speech you may also hear: „Mag ich!“ (I like it!) or „Ich mag dich gern.“ (I like you / I’m fond of you).
target_language_example: Ich mag dich wirklich.
native_language_example: I really like you.

additional_notes: Common, encouraging phrase meaning you’re able to handle a task or situation. It can also mean you’ll make it on time (“I’ll make it”). Uses the verb “schaffen” in the sense of “to manage/achieve” (not “to create”). Often said to motivate yourself or reassure someone: “Du schaffst das!” = “You can do it!”
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich schaffe das schon.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll manage.

additional_notes: Common phrase to say you don’t understand what someone said. Often used with an object or clause: “Ich verstehe das nicht.” (I don’t understand that.) / “Ich verstehe nicht, was du meinst.” (I don’t understand what you mean.) You can also use it as a polite clarification request, especially with “Entschuldigung”: “Entschuldigung, ich verstehe nicht.”
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich verstehe nicht. Können Sie das bitte wiederholen?
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t understand. Could you please repeat that?

meaning: I don’t know anymore / I can’t remember anymore.
additional_notes: Used to say you no longer know or remember something, often after thinking about it. Common in conversation; you can add what you don’t remember: “Ich weiß nicht mehr, wie er heißt.” Note: “nicht mehr” means “no longer / anymore” (different from “noch nicht” = “not yet”).
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht mehr, wo ich meine Schlüssel hingelegt habe.
native_language_example: I can’t remember anymore where I put my keys.

meaning: “I’d like to know” / “I’d be interested to know.”
additional_notes: Polite way to ask for information, using the subjunctive II of "wissen" ("wüsste"). Often followed by an indirect question with "ob" (whether/if) or a question word like "wie", "wann", "wo", "was". Common in emails and formal requests: "Ich wüsste gern, ob …" or "Ich wüsste gern, wann …".
target_language_example: Ich wüsste gern, ob Sie morgen Zeit haben.
native_language_example: I’d like to know whether you have time tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement (not about a specific case). Often placed at the beginning of a sentence (Im Allgemeinen …) or after the verb (… ist im Allgemeinen …).
target_language_example: Im Allgemeinen ist das Wetter hier mild.
native_language_example: In general, the weather here is mild.

meaning: to keep an eye on; to monitor.
additional_notes: Used when you want to watch something/someone carefully and not lose track of it (often plans, deadlines, costs, or a situation). Common in everyday and work contexts. Grammar: usually with an object in the accusative: „Ich behalte X im Auge.“ Related: „im Blick behalten“ (very similar).
target_language_example: Ich behalte die Kosten im Auge.
native_language_example: I’m keeping an eye on the costs.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what is happening in the present time. Common in both speech and writing. Similar in meaning to "gerade" and "momentan". Often appears with the present tense (e.g., "Ich habe im Augenblick keine Zeit.").
target_language_example: Ich kann im Augenblick nicht telefonieren.
native_language_example: I can’t talk on the phone at the moment.

meaning: broken; ruined; messed up (not working / gone wrong).
additional_notes: Very common colloquial phrase meaning something is “gone down the drain.” Often used with verbs like „sein“ (to be) or „gehen“ (to go): „Das ist/war im Eimer“ = “That’s messed up/ruined,” „Mein Handy ist im Eimer“ = “My phone is broken.” Also used about situations or plans: „Der Urlaub ist im Eimer“ = “The vacation is ruined.” Not literal “in the bucket.”
target_language_example: Mein Laptop ist im Eimer, ich kann nicht arbeiten.
native_language_example: My laptop is broken, I can’t work.

meaning: in accordance with; in harmony with.
additional_notes: Used to say something matches, agrees with, or follows something (a rule, plan, values, nature, etc.). Common in more formal writing and speech (e.g., laws, policies, guidelines), but also usable in everyday contexts. Grammar: it’s followed by the dative case (mit + dative).
target_language_example: Das ist im Einklang mit unseren Regeln.
native_language_example: That is in accordance with our rules.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you mean something sincerely or that something is not a joke. Often appears in questions to express surprise: “Im Ernst?” = “Seriously?” Similar in meaning to “ernsthaft” in many contexts. Commonly used in spoken German and informal writing.
target_language_example: Im Ernst, ich habe keine Zeit dafür.
native_language_example: Seriously, I don’t have time for that.

meaning: “in case (of)” / “in the event (that)” (also: “in the case of”).
additional_notes: Most often used in the fixed expression **im Fall(e)** + **Genitive** or with a clause: **im Fall(e), dass ...** (“in case that ...”). In everyday speech, **im Fall, dass ...** is common. Also appears in phrases like **im Fall von ...** (“in the event of ...”).
target_language_example: Im Fall(e), dass du später kommst, ruf mich bitte an.
native_language_example: In case you come later, please call me.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens outside, not inside a building. Often used with verbs like sein (to be), schlafen (to sleep), essen (to eat), trainieren (to train), or feiern (to celebrate). It contrasts with drinnen/innen (inside).
target_language_example: Im Sommer essen wir oft im Freien.
native_language_example: In summer we often eat outdoors.

additional_notes: Usually used with "zu": "im Gegensatz zu" + dative noun/pronoun (e.g., "im Gegensatz zu mir"). It can also appear in patterns like "Im Gegensatz dazu" (in contrast to that) or "Im Gegensatz hierzu" (in contrast to this). Common in comparisons and written/spoken formal contexts.
target_language_example: Im Gegensatz zu gestern ist es heute warm.
native_language_example: In contrast to yesterday, it’s warm today.

meaning: in contrast to; as opposed to.
additional_notes: Used to compare two things and highlight a difference. It is followed by a noun or pronoun in the dative case: im Gegensatz zu mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen; im Gegensatz zu diesem Plan. Often used in more formal or written German, but common and neutral.
target_language_example: Im Gegensatz zu gestern ist es heute warm.
native_language_example: In contrast to yesterday, it’s warm today.

additional_notes: Used to express a reciprocal action: someone does something, and you do something back as compensation or exchange. Often followed by a clause with what the other person will do: “..., und im Gegenzug ...” or “..., im Gegenzug für ...” (in exchange for ...). Common in both everyday and formal contexts.
target_language_example: Ich helfe dir beim Umzug, und im Gegenzug hilfst du mir nächste Woche.
native_language_example: I’ll help you with the move, and in return you’ll help me next week.

additional_notes: Used as a sentence adverb to soften or summarize what you’re saying (similar to “basically” or “in principle”). Often followed by a comma: “Im Grunde, …”. Also common in the longer phrase “im Grunde genommen” (“basically / when all is said and done”).
target_language_example: Im Grunde habe ich nichts dagegen, aber ich habe heute keine Zeit.
native_language_example: Basically, I don’t have anything against it, but I don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Often used to talk about feelings, what someone truly believes, or what matters most to them. You’ll see it with a possessive pronoun: „in meinem/deinem/seinem/ihrem Herzen“. It can be literal (the physical heart) in medical contexts, but most commonly it’s figurative.
target_language_example: Im Herzen wusste ich, dass es die richtige Entscheidung war.
native_language_example: Deep down, I knew it was the right decision.

meaning: at the moment; right now (for now).
additional_notes: Very common time phrase meaning something is true now or temporarily. Used to answer questions about current situations: "Im Moment habe ich keine Zeit." It can also soften statements (similar to “currently”): "Im Moment ist es schwierig." Often interchangeable with "gerade" or "jetzt," but "im Moment" can feel a bit more neutral/formal.
target_language_example: Im Moment kann ich nicht telefonieren.
native_language_example: At the moment I can’t talk on the phone.

additional_notes: Used to say you are acting with someone’s authority or representing them: im Namen + genitive (formal) or often dative in everyday speech. Common in formal contexts (letters, announcements, legal language): „im Namen der Firma“, „im Namen des Teams“, „im Namen von …“.
target_language_example: Ich unterschreibe im Namen der Firma.
native_language_example: I’m signing on behalf of the company.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens very fast. It’s fairly common in spoken German. Often used with future or past actions: „Das ist im Nu erledigt.“ / „Ich war im Nu da.“
target_language_example: Ich bin im Nu zurück.
native_language_example: I’ll be right back in no time.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an average or typical value (often with numbers, time, costs, etc.). Very common in statistics and everyday speech. Often used with verbs like „kosten“, „dauern“, „verdienen“: „Im Schnitt kostet/dauert/verdient …“
target_language_example: Im Schnitt dauert die Fahrt zur Arbeit 30 Minuten.
native_language_example: On average, the trip to work takes 30 minutes.

meaning: let down; abandoned (when you needed help).
additional_notes: Usually used with "jemanden im Stich lassen" (= to let someone down/abandon them) or "im Stich gelassen werden" (= to be let down). It means someone didn’t support you or didn’t show up when it mattered.
target_language_example: Du hast mich im Stich gelassen, als ich dich gebraucht habe.
native_language_example: You let me down when I needed you.

meaning: to let someone down; to abandon someone when they need you.
additional_notes: Used when someone doesn’t help or support you in an important situation. Common patterns: „jemanden im Stich lassen“ (to let someone down) and „nicht im Stich lassen“ (to not abandon/let someone down). Often used about friends, family, or colleagues when help was expected.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir helfen? Lass mich bitte nicht im Stich.
native_language_example: Can you help me? Please don’t let me down.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things. It’s a fixed prepositional phrase and is followed by the dative case (zu + dative): im Vergleich zu dem/der/den … Often used in neutral, formal, or written contexts; in everyday speech you may also hear „verglichen mit“.
target_language_example: Im Vergleich zu letztem Jahr sind die Preise höher.
native_language_example: Compared to last year, prices are higher.

additional_notes: Used to talk about doing something earlier than the main event (e.g., paying, booking, planning). Very common with verbs like "bezahlen" (pay), "buchen" (book), or "planen" (plan), and also in the polite phrase "Danke im Voraus" (thanks in advance).
target_language_example: Ich muss das Hotel im Voraus bezahlen.
native_language_example: I have to pay for the hotel in advance.

meaning: to be in the way; to block something.
additional_notes: Used when a person or thing is obstructing movement or progress. Often said as a request in the imperative: „Steh/Stehen Sie nicht im Weg!“ You can also use it figuratively for obstacles: „Etwas steht im Weg“ = something is preventing something from happening. Related: „jemandem im Weg stehen“ = to be in someone’s way.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, du stehst im Weg.
native_language_example: Sorry, you’re in the way.

additional_notes: Used to summarize the main point and leave out details. Common in formal and neutral speech/writing. Often followed by a whole clause: "Im Wesentlichen bedeutet das ..." or "Im Wesentlichen ist es ...".
target_language_example: Im Wesentlichen ist der Plan gut, aber wir müssen noch über die Kosten sprechen.
native_language_example: Essentially, the plan is good, but we still need to talk about the costs.

meaning: in the course of; as part of (something).
additional_notes: Used with a following genitive noun phrase (often written as one chunk in speech: im Zuge der/des …). Common in formal contexts (news, administration, work emails) to mean “during the process of” or “as a result/part of” a larger action or development. Similar in meaning to „während“ (during) or „im Rahmen“ (within the framework of), depending on context.
target_language_example: Im Zuge der Renovierung wurde die Straße gesperrt.
native_language_example: As part of the renovation, the street was closed.

additional_notes: Common in both speech and writing to introduce a general statement or overall tendency. Often followed by a main clause, e.g., "Im Allgemeinen ist/ sind ...". Also written lowercase as "im allgemeinen" in informal contexts, but the standard spelling is capitalized (because "Allgemeinen" is a noun here).
target_language_example: Im Allgemeinen ist das Wetter hier mild.
native_language_example: In general, the weather here is mild.

meaning: getting better and better; improving more and more.
additional_notes: Used to describe continuous improvement over time. Often used with verbs like „werden“ (to become): „Es wird immer besser.“ It can also be used about someone’s ability, mood, health, or a situation in general.
target_language_example: Mein Deutsch wird immer besser.
native_language_example: My German is getting better and better.

additional_notes: Used to show a gradual increase over time or as a trend. Often goes with verbs like „werden“ (to become) or „zunehmen“ (to increase): „Es wird immer mehr.“ = “It’s getting more and more.” You can also use it with nouns to mean “an increasing number/amount”: „Immer mehr Menschen …“ = “More and more people …”.
target_language_example: Immer mehr Menschen arbeiten von zu Hause.
native_language_example: More and more people work from home.

additional_notes: Commonly used to say a situation continues: „Ich bin immer noch müde.“ = I’m still tired. It can also express surprise/annoyance that something hasn’t changed yet: „Bist du immer noch nicht fertig?“ = Are you still not finished? Word order: it usually sits in the middle of the sentence (after the verb in yes/no questions, after the subject in statements). Not the same as „noch“ alone, which often means “(one) more” or “another” (e.g., „noch ein Kaffee“ = another coffee).
target_language_example: Ich warte immer noch auf den Bus.
native_language_example: I’m still waiting for the bus.

additional_notes: Used to say a situation is continuously deteriorating. Often comes after „Es wird …“ (“It’s getting …”) or „Das wird …“ (“That’s getting …”).
target_language_example: Es wird immer schlimmer, je länger wir warten.
native_language_example: It’s getting worse and worse the longer we wait.

meaning: less and less; fewer and fewer.
additional_notes: Used to show a continuing decrease over time. Use "immer weniger" with uncountable quantities (less) and also commonly with countable nouns in everyday speech; more formally you may see "immer weniger" (less and less) vs. "immer weniger" + plural noun for "fewer and fewer." Often contrasts with "immer mehr" (more and more).
target_language_example: Ich habe immer weniger Zeit für Sport.
native_language_example: I have less and less time for sports.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens repeatedly each time a certain situation occurs. It introduces a dependent clause (usually with the verb at the end): „Immer wenn ich Zeit habe, …“. Often interchangeable with „jedes Mal, wenn …“.
target_language_example: Immer wenn ich Kaffee trinke, kann ich nachts nicht schlafen.
native_language_example: Whenever I drink coffee, I can’t sleep at night.

meaning: again and again; repeatedly; time and time again.
additional_notes: Often used to describe something that happens repeatedly over time (not necessarily continuously). It can express annoyance (“always again”), emphasis (“over and over”), or simply that something occurs regularly. Common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Ich vergesse immer wieder meinen Schlüssel.
native_language_example: I keep forgetting my key.

additional_notes: Used to complain that something (money, time, food, salary, etc.) is insufficient. Often said about quantity or amount: "Das Geld ist immer zu wenig" (The money is always too little). You can also use it with "Es ist..." or "... ist...".
target_language_example: Die Zeit ist immer zu wenig.
native_language_example: There’s never enough time.

meaning: to make use of; to take advantage of (a service/offer).
additional_notes: Common with services, rights, help, offers, or time: "einen Service / Hilfe / Beratung / eine Leistung / Urlaub" in Anspruch nehmen. In formal contexts it can also mean "to claim" (e.g., insurance): "eine Versicherung in Anspruch nehmen". Word order: the separable verb is "nehmen"; in main clauses it splits ("Ich nehme … in Anspruch"), and in subordinate clauses it stays together at the end ("…, weil ich … in Anspruch nehmen möchte").
target_language_example: Ich möchte die Beratung in Anspruch nehmen.
native_language_example: I’d like to make use of the consultation.

meaning: to consider (an option); to take into consideration.
additional_notes: Common in more formal or written German when talking about possible options or plans. Often used with an object (e.g., „etwas in Betracht ziehen“) and frequently with „ziehen“ in the infinitive in structures like „Ich ziehe in Betracht, …“ or „Wir ziehen X in Betracht.“
target_language_example: Wir ziehen in Betracht, nächstes Jahr nach Berlin zu ziehen.
native_language_example: We’re considering moving to Berlin next year.

meaning: to set in motion; to get something moving (literally or figuratively).
additional_notes: Used when you cause something to start moving or start happening. Can be literal (a machine, a vehicle, your body) or figurative (a process, changes, developments). Common with objects like „eine Maschine / einen Motor / einen Stein / einen Prozess / etwas“.
target_language_example: Mit diesem Knopf setzt du die Maschine in Bewegung.
native_language_example: With this button, you set the machine in motion.

additional_notes: Used in more formal speech and writing to specify what something refers to. It’s often followed by a noun/pronoun: „in Bezug auf den Vertrag“ (regarding the contract). Common alternative: „bezüglich“ (also formal).
target_language_example: In Bezug auf Ihre Anfrage melde ich mich morgen.
native_language_example: Regarding your inquiry, I’ll get back to you tomorrow.

meaning: to come true; to be fulfilled (e.g., a wish, dream, prophecy).
additional_notes: Used mainly for wishes, dreams, hopes, promises, or prophecies becoming reality. Common pattern: „ein Wunsch/Traum geht in Erfüllung“ (a wish/dream comes true). The verb is „gehen“ with the fixed phrase „in Erfüllung“; in the past: „ist in Erfüllung gegangen“.
target_language_example: Mein größter Traum ist endlich in Erfüllung gegangen.
native_language_example: My biggest dream finally came true.

meaning: to be an option; to be possible/eligible.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is a possible choice or is eligible/acceptable in a given situation. Common in questions/negations like "Kommt X in Frage?" (Is X an option?) and "X kommt nicht in Frage." (X is out of the question / not an option). Note: "in Frage" here is part of the fixed expression; it doesn’t mean literally that something is coming "into a question" in English.
target_language_example: Für mich kommt nur der frühe Zug in Frage.
native_language_example: For me, only the early train is an option.

meaning: to question; to challenge; to call into question.
additional_notes: Used when you doubt something’s correctness, truth, or legitimacy (e.g., a decision, a claim, someone’s authority). Common pattern: „etwas (Akk.) in Frage stellen“ = to question something. Often a bit formal in tone and used in discussions, work, news, and academic contexts.
target_language_example: Niemand stellt seine Entscheidung in Frage.
native_language_example: No one questions his decision.

additional_notes: Used to say someone lives or can live without conflict or worry, and also in phrases like "Ruhe in Frieden" (Rest in peace) in condolences. Often paired with verbs like "leben" (to live) or "sterben" (to die).
target_language_example: Ich möchte einfach in Frieden leben.
native_language_example: I just want to live in peace.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is thinking deeply and not paying attention to what’s happening around them. Often appears with verbs like „sein“ or „versinken“ (to be/lost in thought), or to describe doing something automatically while thinking about something else.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich war gerade in Gedanken.
native_language_example: Sorry, I was just lost in thought.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "sein" (to be): "in Gefahr sein" = to be in danger. Often refers to people, animals, or things that are threatened (e.g., by an accident, fire, financial problems). You can also use it with "bringen" (to put in danger) and "geraten" (to get into danger).
target_language_example: Das Kind ist in Gefahr.
native_language_example: The child is in danger.

additional_notes: Used mainly in legal/official language to say a law, rule, contract, or regulation is currently valid. Common patterns: „in Kraft treten“ = to come into force; „in Kraft sein“ = to be in force; „außer Kraft setzen“ = to repeal/void.
target_language_example: Das neue Gesetz tritt am 1. Januar in Kraft.
native_language_example: The new law comes into force on January 1st.

additional_notes: Used after a noun (often with "sein") to say something is currently trendy: "X ist (wieder) in Mode". Also used with clothing/styles (e.g., "lange Röcke sind in Mode"). Opposite: "aus der Mode" = out of fashion.
target_language_example: Gerade sind weiße Sneaker wieder in Mode.
native_language_example: Right now, white sneakers are back in style.

meaning: to come into fashion; to become trendy.
additional_notes: Used to say that a style, item, or activity is becoming popular again. Often refers to trends (clothes, hairstyles, foods, tech, etc.). Similar: „in Mode sein“ = to be in fashion. Opposite idea: „aus der Mode kommen“ = to go out of fashion.
target_language_example: Schlaghosen kommen wieder in Mode.
native_language_example: Bell-bottoms are coming back into fashion.

additional_notes: Used to say something is fine/correct ("Alles ist in Ordnung."), to accept/agree ("In Ordnung." = "OK."), or to check if someone is okay ("Alles in Ordnung?" = "Is everything okay?"). Also common for things working properly ("Der Computer ist wieder in Ordnung." = "The computer is fine/working again.").
target_language_example: Ist alles in Ordnung?
native_language_example: Is everything okay?

additional_notes: Used to mean doing something without stress, noise, or interruption. Common in phrases like „in Ruhe lassen“ (to leave someone alone) and „in Ruhe arbeiten/essen“ (to work/eat quietly). Often implies “take your time” or “calmly,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich möchte in Ruhe essen.
native_language_example: I want to eat in peace.

meaning: to leave (someone/something) alone; to let (someone) be.
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase meaning you don’t want to be bothered or interfered with. Often used as an imperative: „Lass mich in Ruhe!“ = “Leave me alone!” You can also use it more politely: „Bitte lassen Sie mich in Ruhe.“ It can refer to people or things: „Lass das in Ruhe.“ = “Leave that alone.”
target_language_example: Lass mich bitte in Ruhe, ich muss arbeiten.
native_language_example: Please leave me alone; I have to work.

additional_notes: Used to say something can be seen or is within view (literally), and also figuratively for something approaching/soon to happen (e.g., a goal, the end of a trip). Common patterns: „in Sicht sein“ (to be in sight), „in Sicht kommen“ (to come into view).
target_language_example: Das Ziel ist schon in Sicht.
native_language_example: The goal is already in sight.

additional_notes: Used to contrast words with actions (often in phrases like „in Worten und in Taten“ = “in words and deeds”). It’s a literal prepositional phrase: „in“ + dative plural „Taten“ (deeds/actions). Note: Don’t confuse with „in der Tat“, which means “indeed / in fact.”
target_language_example: Er hilft nicht nur mit Worten, sondern auch in Taten.
native_language_example: He doesn’t help only with words, but also through actions.

additional_notes: Used to contrast an assumption/appearance with what is really true. Common in everyday speech and writing; often placed early in the sentence for emphasis (e.g., „In Wirklichkeit …“). Similar to „eigentlich“, but „in Wirklichkeit“ is a bit more explicit: “in actual fact.”
target_language_example: Ich dachte, er ist krank, aber in Wirklichkeit ist er im Urlaub.
native_language_example: I thought he was sick, but in reality he’s on vacation.

additional_notes: Used when you want someone to spell out an amount or answer using words instead of digits, especially for money, dates, or official forms. Often appears as a note on documents (e.g., "Betrag in Zahlen / in Worten"). You may also hear "in Worten:" followed by the spelled-out amount.
target_language_example: Bitte geben Sie den Betrag in Zahlen und in Worten an.
native_language_example: Please state the amount in digits and in words.

meaning: in the future; from now on.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the future in general or to say something will change going forward. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis. Contrast: „in der Zukunft“ = in the (more distant/abstract) future.
target_language_example: In Zukunft möchte ich mehr Sport machen.
native_language_example: In the future, I want to do more exercise.

meaning: (used for emphasis) “in the world / on earth” (often in questions: “where/why/how on earth…?”).
additional_notes: A fixed phrase used to express surprise, confusion, or annoyance—very common in questions and exclamations. It usually follows a question word: „Wo/Was/Wie/Wer in aller Welt …?“ Register is neutral (not slang). Literally “in all the world,” but the natural English equivalent is often “on earth” or “in the world.”
target_language_example: Wo in aller Welt hast du meinen Schlüssel hingelegt?
native_language_example: Where on earth did you put my key?

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a specific situation just mentioned (often as a consequence or next step). Very common in conversation. Often shortened to “in dem Fall” after someone explains something: “Ah, in dem Fall …”. Also appears with the relative pronoun “wo” in speech: “In dem Fall, wo …” (= “in the case where …”).
target_language_example: Ich kann heute nicht kommen. – Okay, in dem Fall treffen wir uns morgen.
native_language_example: I can’t come today. – Okay, in that case we’ll meet tomorrow.

meaning: in the eyes (of); in someone’s view/opinion.
additional_notes: Used to express how someone is seen or judged from a particular person’s perspective. Often appears as “in den Augen von + Dative” (in the eyes of …) or with a possessive: “in meinen/deinen/seinen Augen” (in my/your/his eyes). Common with verbs like “sein” and “gelten” (to be/considered).
target_language_example: In den Augen vieler Menschen ist sie eine Heldin.
native_language_example: In the eyes of many people, she is a hero.

meaning: to come to mind; to occur to someone.
additional_notes: Used when an idea, memory, or thought suddenly appears in your mind. Often with a dative pronoun/noun for the person: „Mir/Dir/Ihm … kommt (etwas) in den Sinn.“ Similar to „einfallen“ and more formal/neutral than slang.
target_language_example: Mir kommt gerade ein guter Name für die Katze in den Sinn.
native_language_example: A good name for the cat just came to mind.

additional_notes: Used mostly as “in der Lage sein, … zu …” to say you are able/able to manage to do something. Often paired with “nicht” (nicht in der Lage sein = not able to). More formal than “können” and common in written German and official contexts.
target_language_example: Ich bin nicht in der Lage, heute zu kommen.
native_language_example: I’m not able to come today.

additional_notes: Used to say something is close to a place or person. Often with "von" + dative: "in der Nähe von + [place]" = "near [place]". You can also use it on its own to mean "nearby": "Ist hier ein Café in der Nähe?".
target_language_example: Gibt es hier in der Nähe eine Apotheke?
native_language_example: Is there a pharmacy nearby?

additional_notes: A common, fairly formal phrase used to talk about what normally happens. Often appears at the start of a sentence, but it can also be placed mid-sentence. Close in meaning to "normalerweise" or "meistens".
target_language_example: In der Regel dauert die Lieferung drei bis fünf Tage.
native_language_example: As a rule, delivery takes three to five days.

additional_notes: Used to confirm or emphasize that something is true. Often sounds a bit formal or written. Common positions: after the verb (“Das ist in der Tat so.”) or at the start for emphasis (“In der Tat, …”).
target_language_example: Das ist in der Tat ein großes Problem.
native_language_example: That is indeed a big problem.

meaning: in the past; in former times.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a time before now, often when contrasting past vs. present. Common in more formal or neutral contexts (news, writing, explanations). Similar everyday alternatives: „früher“ (earlier/used to) and „damals“ (back then).
target_language_example: In der Vergangenheit habe ich in Berlin gewohnt, aber jetzt lebe ich in Hamburg.
native_language_example: In the past I lived in Berlin, but now I live in Hamburg.

additional_notes: Used to talk about future time in general. Often paired with verbs like „werden“ (will) or phrases like „in der Zukunft möchte ich …“ (in the future I’d like to …). For a specific point later on, German also commonly uses „in Zukunft“ (from now on) or „in ein paar Tagen/Wochen“ (in a few days/weeks).
target_language_example: In der Zukunft möchte ich in Deutschland arbeiten.
native_language_example: In the future, I’d like to work in Germany.

meaning: into the distance; far away (figuratively: to a far-off place).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of looking or moving to express direction toward a distant place (e.g., schauen/blicken/starren in die Ferne, reisen/ziehen in die Ferne). Often implies "far away" rather than a specific destination.
target_language_example: Sie blickte lange in die Ferne.
native_language_example: She looked into the distance for a long time.

meaning: up; upward; into the air; to a higher level.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement or change to express a direction upward (literally or figuratively), e.g. „steigen“, „heben“, „werfen“, „schnellen“. Common in phrases like „in die Höhe steigen“ (rise), „in die Höhe heben“ (lift up), „in die Höhe schnellen“ (shoot up).
target_language_example: Die Preise sind in die Höhe gestiegen.
native_language_example: Prices have risen (gone up).

additional_notes: Used with verbs of motion (especially **gehen/fahren/kommen**) to mean going to school. It contrasts with **in der Schule**, which means “at school” (location). Most commonly you’ll say **in die Schule gehen** (“to go to school”).
target_language_example: Meine Tochter geht jeden Morgen in die Schule.
native_language_example: My daughter goes to school every morning.

meaning: to put into practice; to carry out (a plan/idea).
additional_notes: Used when you stop just talking or planning and actually do something, especially an idea, plan, decision, or project. Often appears with "einen Plan / eine Idee / ein Projekt" (accusative): "einen Plan in die Tat umsetzen". Slightly formal and common in writing and business contexts.
target_language_example: Wir müssen den Plan endlich in die Tat umsetzen.
native_language_example: We have to finally put the plan into practice.

additional_notes: A common prepositional phrase used with verbs of movement/time direction (e.g., "reisen", "zurückgehen", "blicken") to mean going/traveling back to earlier times or looking back in time. Often appears with "zurück" ("back"): "in die Vergangenheit zurück".
target_language_example: Manchmal wünsche ich mir, ich könnte in die Vergangenheit reisen.
native_language_example: Sometimes I wish I could travel into the past.

meaning: in this case; if so; then.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a particular situation or condition that applies. Common in explanations and decisions. Often paired with a condition: „Wenn …, dann in diesem Fall …“ or used to respond to new information: „Ah, in diesem Fall …“.
target_language_example: Wenn du keine Zeit hast, können wir uns in diesem Fall morgen treffen.
native_language_example: If you don’t have time, then in that case we can meet tomorrow.

meaning: in these cases; in such situations.
additional_notes: Used to refer back to specific situations just mentioned or understood from context. It’s common in instructions, rules, or explanations. Grammar: "in" + dative plural → "diesen Fällen" (from "der Fall" = case/situation). Often followed by a comma and a main clause: "In diesen Fällen, ..."
target_language_example: In diesen Fällen müssen Sie das Formular online ausfüllen.
native_language_example: In these cases you have to fill out the form online.

meaning: in three days; three days from now.
additional_notes: Used with the dative after "in" to express a point in the future ("in three days" = three days from now). To express duration (how long something takes), German often uses "drei Tage lang" or "für drei Tage" instead. The noun stays plural: "drei Tagen" (dative plural).
target_language_example: In drei Tagen fliegen wir nach Berlin.
native_language_example: In three days we’re flying to Berlin.

additional_notes: Used to give an approximate number, time, or description (often like “about” in English). Common with quantities and durations: “in etwa zehn Minuten” (in about ten minutes). Can also mean “more or less / roughly like that” when summarizing or agreeing: “Ja, in etwa.”
target_language_example: Es dauert in etwa zehn Minuten.
native_language_example: It takes about ten minutes.

meaning: in a way; in some sense.
additional_notes: Used to soften or qualify a statement ("sort of", "to a certain extent"). Often followed by a contrasting point, e.g. "..., aber ...". More formal/neutral than "irgendwie".
target_language_example: In gewisser Weise hast du recht, aber es ist komplizierter.
native_language_example: In a way, you're right, but it's more complicated.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize how much something is true or how intense something is. It’s more formal/written than everyday options like „sehr“ or „total“. Often appears with adjectives or with verbs like „beeindrucken“, „interessieren“, „bewundern“ (e.g., „Das beeindruckt mich in höchstem Maße.“).
target_language_example: Ich bin in höchstem Maße zufrieden mit dem Ergebnis.
native_language_example: I am extremely satisfied with the result.

additional_notes: Common time expression meaning “in the past few days/weeks/months.” Often used to talk about changes or what has been happening recently. You can also say “In letzter Zeit…” at the start of a sentence, or place it in the middle: “Ich habe in letzter Zeit…”
target_language_example: In letzter Zeit habe ich viel gearbeitet.
native_language_example: Lately, I’ve been working a lot.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something expected to happen soon, but usually not immediately (often within the next days/weeks/months). Common in both spoken and written German, including plans, predictions, and announcements.
target_language_example: In naher Zukunft werde ich nach Berlin ziehen.
native_language_example: In the near future, I will move to Berlin.

additional_notes: Common with verbs like "gehen" or "sein": "in sich gehen" = to reflect / look inward; "in sich sein" = to be absorbed in one’s thoughts. Also used to mean "in itself" when evaluating something: "Das ist in sich logisch" = that is internally consistent.
target_language_example: Nach dem Streit musste ich erst mal in mich gehen.
native_language_example: After the argument, I first had to reflect / look inward.

additional_notes: Used to link two statements in a cause → effect relationship. It’s fairly formal/written; in everyday speech you’ll often hear alternatives like „deshalb“, „darum“, or „deswegen“. „Infolge“ means “as a consequence of,” and „dessen“ refers back to the previous situation/fact (“of that”). Often set off by commas in longer sentences.
target_language_example: Es hat stark geschneit; infolge dessen sind viele Straßen gesperrt.
native_language_example: It snowed heavily; as a result, many roads are closed.

meaning: to repair; to fix up; to restore to working order.
additional_notes: Often used for repairs of buildings, machines, cars, or equipment. It’s a separable verb: present tense splits ("Ich setze es instand"), while the infinitive stays together ("etwas instand setzen"). Common related nouns: "die Instandsetzung" (repair/restoration), "die Instandhaltung" (maintenance).
target_language_example: Wir lassen das Dach instand setzen.
native_language_example: We’re having the roof repaired.

additional_notes: Common structure: „Interesse an + dative“ (an dem → am; an der). You can also say what you’re interested in with a noun: „Ich habe Interesse an Musik.“ For people, use the same pattern: „Sie hat Interesse an ihm/ihr.“ In everyday speech, „sich für etwas interessieren“ is very common too.
target_language_example: Ich habe Interesse an Deutsch.
native_language_example: I’m interested in German.

additional_notes: Common in polite conversation, work, and dating. Usually used with “an” + dative: „Interesse an etwas/jemandem zeigen“ (e.g., „an dem Kurs“, „an dir“). Also used as a polite request/complaint: „Bitte zeigen Sie mehr Interesse.“
target_language_example: Er zeigt großes Interesse an dem Kurs.
native_language_example: He shows great interest in the course.

meaning: “meanwhile / in the meantime”; also “by now / in the meantime (since then)”.
additional_notes: Common time adverb used to say that something happens while something else is going on (“meanwhile”), or that a situation has changed up to the present point (“by now”). Often used with the present perfect or present tense to show a change over time: „Inzwischen habe ich verstanden …“ = “By now I’ve understood …”.
target_language_example: Ich koche, und du kannst inzwischen den Tisch decken.
native_language_example: I’m cooking, and meanwhile you can set the table.

additional_notes: Used when you don’t know or don’t want to specify what it is. Often in questions/negatives it means “anything” (Hast du irgend etwas gesehen? = Did you see anything?), and in statements it often means “something” (Ich brauche irgend etwas zu essen. = I need something to eat). Also commonly written as one word: „irgendetwas“.
target_language_example: Hast du irgend etwas Zeit?
native_language_example: Do you have any time (at all)?

additional_notes: Used when the person is unknown, unspecified, or doesn’t matter. Often written as one word: "irgendjemand" (especially after the 1996 spelling reform), but "irgend jemand" may still appear. In questions and negatives it often matches English "anybody" (e.g., "Ist hier irgendjemand?" = "Is anybody here?").
target_language_example: Kann mir irgendjemand helfen?
native_language_example: Can someone help me?

additional_notes: Used to say a different (unspecified) place. Common in everyday speech; often used with verbs like sein (to be), hingehen (to go), or wohnen (to live). Similar options: „woanders“ (shorter, same meaning) and „irgendwohin“ (somewhere to).
target_language_example: Ich möchte irgendwo anders sitzen.
native_language_example: I’d like to sit somewhere else.

additional_notes: Used for an unspecified destination with a verb of motion (e.g., gehen, fahren, fliegen). It answers the question "Wohin?" (where to?). Often contrasts with "irgendwo" (somewhere/anywhere in a place, answering "Wo?").
target_language_example: Lass uns heute Abend irgendwohin gehen.
native_language_example: Let’s go somewhere tonight.

additional_notes: Literally “is clear.” Used as a short response meaning you understand or agree. With a neutral tone it’s like “OK, got it.” With a sharp/ironic tone it can mean “Yeah, right” or “Of course” (annoyed). Often appears as “Alles klar.” or “Na klar.”; you can also say “Ist klar!” on its own in conversation.
target_language_example: Okay, ich bringe die Unterlagen morgen vorbei. – Ist klar.
native_language_example: OK, I’ll bring the documents by tomorrow. – Got it.

additional_notes: Used in comparative correlative sentences to show that one thing changes along with another: “Je + comparative, desto/umso + comparative.” Example: “Je länger ich warte, desto ungeduldiger werde ich.” On its own, “je länger” usually sounds incomplete because it expects a second part with “desto/umso.”
target_language_example: Je länger ich warte, desto ungeduldiger werde ich.
native_language_example: The longer I wait, the more impatient I get.

meaning: "the more" (used in comparisons: the more…, the more…).
additional_notes: Used in the correlative comparative pattern: "Je mehr …, desto/umso …" = "The more …, the …". "Je" here is not "you"—it’s a special comparative marker. Often paired with "desto" or "umso" in the second clause; both are common and mean the same.
target_language_example: Je mehr ich lerne, desto besser verstehe ich Deutsch.
native_language_example: The more I learn, the better I understand German.

meaning: 'the less ...' (used in the pattern 'je weniger ..., desto/umso ...').
additional_notes: Used in correlative comparisons: **Je weniger** + clause, **desto/umso** + clause = “the less …, the …”. Both parts typically use normal German word order for a clause (verb in 2nd position), e.g. *Je weniger du arbeitest, desto weniger verdienst du.*
target_language_example: Je weniger du lernst, desto schwieriger wird die Prüfung.
native_language_example: The less you study, the harder the exam becomes.

meaning: a lot of; lots of; plenty of.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize a large quantity of something (often with a noun), similar to “lots of” in English. It’s common in spoken and written German. Grammar note: it’s usually followed by a noun in the plural or an uncountable noun (e.g., „jede Menge Leute“, „jede Menge Zeit“).
target_language_example: Ich habe jede Menge Arbeit heute.
native_language_example: I have lots of work today.

meaning: any moment; at any moment; any second (very soon).
additional_notes: Used to say something can happen very soon/at any time, often with a feeling of expectation or urgency. Common with verbs like „kann“ (can) and in phrases like „jeden Augenblick kommen/ankommen“ (arrive any moment). Literally means “every moment,” but in English it’s usually “any moment.”
target_language_example: Der Bus kann jeden Augenblick kommen.
native_language_example: The bus could come any moment.

meaning: “any moment” / “at any moment”; also “one moment” (please wait briefly).
additional_notes: Often used to mean something will happen very soon: „Er kann jeden Moment kommen.“ In conversation it can also function like “Just a moment / One moment, please” to ask someone to wait: „Jeden Moment!“ Similar to „einen Moment“ and „einen Augenblick“.
target_language_example: Warte bitte, ich bin jeden Moment fertig.
native_language_example: Please wait, I’ll be done any moment now.

additional_notes: Common time expression meaning something happens daily. Literally “each day” (accusative: jeden + Tag). Often used with the present tense for routines: „Ich arbeite jeden Tag.“ You can also say „Tag für Tag“ (day after day) but that’s a bit more emphatic.
target_language_example: Ich gehe jeden Tag zu Fuß zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: I walk to work every day.

meaning: of any kind; of all kinds.
additional_notes:
Means “of whatever kind/type.” It’s most often used after a noun in the genitive: 
- "Probleme jeder Art" = problems of any kind
- "Hilfe jeder Art" = help of all kinds
Note: "Art" here means “kind/type,” not “art” (painting, music).
target_language_example: Wir bieten Unterstützung jeder Art an.
native_language_example: We offer support of any kind.

additional_notes: Used to mean “every person” in a general sense, often in formal or written German (e.g., rules, laws, announcements). Similar in meaning to „jeder“ / „alle“, but „jedermann“ sounds more official. Not gender-specific despite containing „Mann“.
target_language_example: Der Eintritt ist für jedermann kostenlos.
native_language_example: Admission is free for everyone.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens on every occasion when a situation repeats. Very common in everyday speech. Often followed by a clause with wenn (“whenever/if”), but it can also stand alone.
target_language_example: Jedes Mal, wenn ich ihn sehe, muss ich lachen.
native_language_example: Every time I see him, I have to laugh.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to mean that something happens in an alternating pattern (1st, 3rd, 5th, etc.) or at a frequency of 50%. It’s the neuter form of the pattern "jeder/jede/jedes + ordinal number" (e.g., "jeden zweiten Tag" = every other day; "jede zweite Woche" = every second week). The ending changes with gender/case: "jeder zweite" (masc.), "jede zweite" (fem.), "jedes zweite" (neut.).
target_language_example: Ich nehme jedes zweite Wochenende den Zug.
native_language_example: I take the train every other weekend.

additional_notes: Common in writing and more formal speech than "aber". It can come after a comma and often sits in the middle of the sentence: "..., jedoch ..." or "..., ich kann jedoch nicht ...". It can also mean "though" at the end of a clause: "Er ist nett, jedoch."
target_language_example: Ich möchte kommen, ich kann jedoch nicht.
native_language_example: I’d like to come, but I can’t.

additional_notes: Used to refer to another person, not the one you just mentioned (or not you). Often used with prepositions like "mit" or "von": "mit jemand anders" (with someone else), "von jemand anders" (from someone else). In careful writing you may also see "jemand anderes" (neuter ending), but "jemand anders" is very common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ich will mit jemand anders sprechen.
native_language_example: I want to speak with someone else.

additional_notes: A proper name used in Christianity. In everyday speech it can also be used as a strong exclamation of surprise or shock (often considered rude or offensive, especially in religious contexts).
target_language_example: Für viele Christen ist Jesus Christus der Sohn Gottes.
native_language_example: For many Christians, Jesus Christ is the Son of God.

additional_notes: Used to say there is very little of something. Often appears after a verb: "Ich habe kaum etwas gegessen" (= I ate almost nothing). "Kaum" can also mean "hardly" with other words (e.g., "kaum Zeit" = hardly any time).
target_language_example: Ich habe heute kaum etwas gemacht.
native_language_example: I hardly did anything today.

meaning: to have no money; to be broke.
additional_notes: Used to say you don’t have any money (often at the moment). Common in everyday situations like not being able to pay, go out, or buy something. You can specify what for: „Ich habe kein Geld für …“.
target_language_example: Ich kann heute nicht mitkommen, ich habe kein Geld.
native_language_example: I can't come along today; I have no money.

additional_notes: Used to say you’ve run out of money. Often appears with verbs like „haben“ (to have) or „brauchen“ (to need): „Ich habe kein Geld mehr.“ / „Ich brauche Geld, ich habe kein Geld mehr.“ Also common with „für“ + noun to say you can’t afford something: „Ich habe kein Geld mehr für ein Ticket.“
target_language_example: Ich habe kein Geld mehr, ich kann heute nicht ausgehen.
native_language_example: I have no money left, I can’t go out today.

additional_notes: Colloquial way to say you don’t know or haven’t decided. Often used as a short reply on its own ("Kein Plan.") or with a clause like "kein Plan, wie/was/wo …". More neutral/formal alternatives: "Keine Ahnung." or "Ich weiß nicht."
target_language_example: Kein Plan, wann der Bus kommt.
native_language_example: No idea when the bus is coming.

additional_notes: Common, friendly reply meaning something is not an issue—used after thanks (similar to “you’re welcome”), when accepting a small request, or to reassure someone after an apology. Also appears as “Kein Problem!” or shortened to “Kein Prob.”
target_language_example: Danke fürs Helfen! – Kein Problem.
native_language_example: Thanks for helping! – No problem.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is understandable or unsurprising given the situation. Often stands alone as a comment ("Kein Wunder!") or introduces an explanation with „dass“ ("Kein Wunder, dass …").
target_language_example: Kein Wunder, dass du müde bist – du hast kaum geschlafen.
native_language_example: No wonder you’re tired — you barely slept.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened intentionally or for a reason (often implying a pattern or meaning): Es ist kein Zufall, dass ... = It’s no coincidence that .... Also common: Das ist kein Zufall. Note: Zufall = chance/coincidence; kein is the negation ("no/not a").
target_language_example: Es ist kein Zufall, dass er immer zur richtigen Zeit anruft.
native_language_example: It’s no coincidence that he always calls at the right time.

additional_notes: Very common way to say you don’t know something. Used as a short standalone reply (“Keine Ahnung.”) or with a clause (“Keine Ahnung, wo er ist.”). More neutral/colloquial than formal; for extra politeness you can add: “Ich habe leider keine Ahnung.”
target_language_example: Keine Ahnung, wann der Bus kommt.
native_language_example: No idea when the bus is coming.

meaning: to have no idea; to not know.
additional_notes: Very common everyday phrase. Often used as a complete answer: "Keine Ahnung." or "Ich habe keine Ahnung." You can also add "von" + dative to specify the topic: "Ich habe keine Ahnung von Mathe."
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, ich habe keine Ahnung, wie das funktioniert.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have no idea how that works.

additional_notes: Used to strongly agree or confirm something, similar to “for sure,” “absolutely,” or “no doubt.” Often said as a short standalone reply. Literally “no question,” and it can also mean “there’s no question about it.”
target_language_example: Kommst du morgen mit? – Keine Frage!
native_language_example: Are you coming along tomorrow? – Definitely!

meaning: to not matter; to be irrelevant.
additional_notes: Used to say something is unimportant for a decision or situation. Often followed by "für" (for) or used with "ob" (whether): "Das spielt keine Rolle" = "That doesn’t matter." Also common in questions: "Spielt das eine Rolle?" = "Does that matter?"
target_language_example: Es spielt keine Rolle, ob du heute oder morgen kommst.
native_language_example: It doesn’t matter whether you come today or tomorrow.

meaning: to have no time; to be too busy.
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase for saying you’re busy or don’t have time for something. Often used with an infinitive clause: „Ich habe keine Zeit, dir zu helfen.“ You can also specify what you have no time for with „für“ + accusative: „Ich habe keine Zeit für Sport.“ (Conjugate „haben“: ich habe, du hast, er/sie/es hat, wir haben, ihr habt, sie/Sie haben.)
target_language_example: Sorry, ich habe gerade keine Zeit.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have time right now.

meaning: to get to know; to meet (and get acquainted).
additional_notes: Used when you become acquainted with a person, place, or thing (not just knowing facts). Often written as one word: "kennenlernen" (especially after a modal verb or in infinitive form), but it can appear separated in some sentence structures. Common patterns: "jemanden kennen lernen" (to get to know someone), "sich kennen lernen" (to meet each other), "etwas/einen Ort kennen lernen" (to get to know/experience something/a place).
target_language_example: Ich möchte dich gern kennenlernen.
native_language_example: I’d like to get to know you.

additional_notes: Literally “small finger.” Common in everyday talk about hands, injuries, sizes (e.g., rings), and gestures. In German it’s typically said as “der kleine Finger” (nominative) or “den kleinen Finger” (accusative).
target_language_example: Ich habe mir den kleinen Finger verletzt.
native_language_example: I hurt my pinky.

additional_notes: Means water that is at (or very near) the boiling point. In standard German you’ll most often see it with an adjective ending: **kochendes Wasser** (nominative/accusative neuter). Common in cooking and safety instructions (e.g., don’t pour boiling water on something).
target_language_example: Vorsicht: Das ist kochendes Wasser!
native_language_example: Careful: That’s boiling water!

additional_notes: You’ll usually see this idea expressed as **"zu Besuch kommen"** (to come for a visit) or **"kommen, um … zu besuchen"** (to come in order to visit …). **"besuchen"** takes a direct object (the person/place you visit): *Ich besuche meine Freundin.* (I’m visiting my friend.)
target_language_example: Morgen kommen meine Eltern zu Besuch.
native_language_example: My parents are coming to visit tomorrow.

additional_notes: An encouraging phrase used to comfort someone who is sad, worried, or discouraged. Often said as a short standalone comment, or with “! ”. Common additions: “Kopf hoch, das wird schon.”
target_language_example: Kopf hoch! Morgen sieht die Welt schon anders aus.
native_language_example: Chin up! Tomorrow things will look different.

meaning: “no matter what it costs” / “whatever the cost.”
additional_notes: Fixed idiom meaning you will do something regardless of the price, effort, or negative consequences. Often used for determination or urgency. Grammatically, it uses the subjunctive I (koste, wolle) and is typically set off by commas.
target_language_example: Ich werde dir helfen, koste es, was es wolle.
native_language_example: I will help you, no matter what it costs.

additional_notes: Used when you report that you are not coming because you are ill. Most commonly heard in the reflexive form "sich krank machen" (e.g., "Ich mache mich krank") meaning "I’m calling in sick." It can also literally mean "to make someone/something sick" depending on context ("Das Essen macht mich krank").
target_language_example: Ich mache mich heute krank und komme nicht zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: I’m calling in sick today and I’m not coming to work.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "sein" (to be) to describe someone’s health. Common in everyday speech for feeling unwell (e.g., a cold). In German you often say you are "sick" rather than saying you "have" a sickness. You can also specify the illness: "Ich bin erkältet" (I have a cold).
target_language_example: Ich bin heute krank.
native_language_example: I’m sick today.

meaning: to get sick; to become ill.
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase for becoming ill (often in contrast to being ill: „krank sein“). Conjugate „werden“: ich werde, du wirst, er/sie/es wird, wir werden, ihr werdet, sie werden. Past: „ich bin krank geworden“ (uses „sein“ as the helping verb).
target_language_example: Ich glaube, ich werde krank.
native_language_example: I think I’m getting sick.

additional_notes: Used to say that a second event happened a short time after a previously mentioned event. It often refers back to something in the same story or conversation (darauf = “on that/after that”). Common in narration and everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn angerufen, und kurz darauf hat er zurückgerufen.
native_language_example: I called him, and shortly after that he called back.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens very soon before a point in time or event, or that someone is on the verge of doing something. Often appears with "sein" + infinitive ("kurz davor sein, etwas zu tun" = to be just about to do something) or with a time/event reference ("kurz davor" meaning "shortly before then").
target_language_example: Ich war kurz davor, dir zu schreiben, als du angerufen hast.
native_language_example: I was just about to text you when you called.

additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happens a short time after another event or time point. Common with times/dates and events: „kurz nach sechs“, „kurz nach dem Essen“, „kurz nach ihrer Ankunft“. Often followed by a dative noun phrase when „nach“ means “after” (e.g., „nach dem Essen“).
target_language_example: Kurz nach dem Essen gehen wir spazieren.
native_language_example: Shortly after eating, we go for a walk.

additional_notes: Used with a time point/event to say something happens soon before it (temporal), or that someone/something is on the verge of doing something. Often followed by a noun in the dative or by an infinitive clause with „zu“ (e.g., „kurz davor, … zu …“). Common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Ich bin kurz vor dem Einschlafen.
native_language_example: I’m just about to fall asleep.

additional_notes: A common formal term for computer systems that can perform tasks that seem intelligent (e.g., recognizing speech, writing text, analyzing data). Often shortened to "KI" in German (pronounced like the letters K and I). Used in tech, news, school, and work contexts.
target_language_example: Viele Firmen nutzen künstliche Intelligenz, um Daten schneller zu analysieren.
native_language_example: Many companies use artificial intelligence to analyze data faster.

meaning: a long time ago; long since.
additional_notes: Used to say that something happened far in the past. Often appears in phrases like "Das ist lange her" (That was a long time ago) or with "schon": "Das ist schon lange her" (That was a long time ago / It’s been a long time). "Her" here means "ago" (time), not "here" (place).
target_language_example: Das ist schon lange her, dass wir uns gesehen haben.
native_language_example: It was a long time ago that we last saw each other.

meaning: to have something done (by someone else).
additional_notes: Used when you arrange for someone else to do a task for you (often a service). It’s typically used with an object in between: "etwas machen lassen" (e.g., "die Haare schneiden lassen" = to get your hair cut). In everyday speech, it can also imply "leave it and let someone handle it."
target_language_example: Ich lasse mein Auto morgen in der Werkstatt reparieren.
native_language_example: I’m having my car repaired at the garage tomorrow.

additional_notes: Usually appears as part of a larger sentence, e.g. with a subject: **Sie lassen uns ...** = “They let us ...”. For making suggestions in everyday speech, German typically uses **lass uns ...** (singular informal “let’s ...”) or **lasst uns ...** (plural informal “let’s ...”), not **lassen uns** by itself.
target_language_example: Sie lassen uns nicht rein.
native_language_example: They won’t let us in.

additional_notes: Used to suggest leaving or starting to go somewhere. In correct everyday German, you usually say **„Lass uns gehen.“** (informal, to one person) or **„Lasst uns gehen.“** (to a group). **„Lassen Sie uns gehen.“** is more formal/polite.
target_language_example: Es ist spät. Lass uns gehen.
native_language_example: It’s late. Let’s go.

meaning: to let (something) run; to leave (something) running/on.
additional_notes: Often used when you don’t stop something that is running (a tap, engine, program, music). It’s a separable verb phrase: present/imperative like „Lass es laufen!“; in a normal sentence „Ich lasse das Wasser laufen.“ In the past you’ll often see „hat … laufen lassen“ (e.g., „Ich habe den Motor laufen lassen.“). It can also mean “to just let it go / let it happen” (e.g., „Lass es einfach laufen.“).
target_language_example: Kannst du das Wasser kurz laufen lassen?
native_language_example: Can you let the water run for a moment?

meaning: “farewell” / “goodbye (for good)”, said to more than one person.
additional_notes: An old-fashioned, solemn farewell used when parting for a long time or permanently. It’s the plural imperative of „leben“ + „wohl“ (“live well”), addressed to a group (ihr). For one person you can say „Leb wohl“ (also written „Leb’ wohl“). In everyday situations people more often say „Tschüss“, „Auf Wiedersehen“, or „Mach’s gut“.
target_language_example: Lebt wohl, meine Freunde – wir sehen uns vielleicht nie wieder.
native_language_example: Farewell, my friends—we may never see each other again.

meaning: to be sorry (to regret); to feel bad for someone.
additional_notes: Used to express regret or an apology ("Es tut mir leid" = "I'm sorry") and also to express sympathy ("Das tut mir leid" = "I'm sorry to hear that"). It’s usually used with "tun" in fixed phrases like "Es tut mir leid" or "Das tut mir leid"; the literal word order is different from English (literally “it does me sorrow”).
target_language_example: Es tut mir leid, ich komme zu spät.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, I'm late.

additional_notes: A common phrase for learning the skill of reading (often used for children, but also for adult learners). It’s built from the verb "lesen" (to read) + "lernen" (to learn). You can also say "Ich lerne lesen" (I’m learning to read), but "lesen lernen" is very common when talking about the goal/skill. In past tense: "Ich habe lesen gelernt" (I learned to read).
target_language_example: Mein Sohn will lesen lernen.
native_language_example: My son wants to learn to read.

additional_notes: Used to sum up or state the final result/conclusion after considering everything. Often appears as an adverbial phrase at the beginning or in the middle of a sentence. Common synonym: „letztendlich“.
target_language_example: Letzten Endes ist es deine Entscheidung.
native_language_example: In the end, it’s your decision.

additional_notes: Used to sum up or give the final conclusion/decision after considering other points. Often appears at the start of a sentence or clause (e.g., "Letztendlich ..."). Similar in meaning to "am Ende" or "schlussendlich".
target_language_example: Letztendlich habe ich mich für das günstigere Angebot entschieden.
native_language_example: Ultimately, I decided on the cheaper offer.

meaning: recently; the other day (a little while ago).
additional_notes: Colloquial word meaning something happened not long ago. Often interchangeable with "neulich" or "kürzlich". Many speakers consider "letztens" informal/non-standard; in more formal German, use "neulich", "kürzlich", or "vor Kurzem" instead.
target_language_example: Letztens war ich mit Freunden im Kino.
native_language_example: The other day I went to the movies with friends.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the previous calendar year (or the year immediately before now). Often used with past tense: "Letztes Jahr war ich in Berlin." You can also say "im letzten Jahr" (= in the last year / over the past year), which can emphasize the time period rather than the specific year.
target_language_example: Letztes Jahr habe ich Deutsch gelernt.
native_language_example: Last year I learned German.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the most recent past occasion when something happened. Often appears with past tense: “Letztes Mal war ich …” (Last time I was …). Also common in reminders/contrast: “Letztes Mal hast du gesagt …” (Last time you said …). Capitalization: “Mal” is a noun, so it’s always capitalized. Don’t confuse with “das letzte Mal” (“the last time,” often meaning the final time) vs. “letztes Mal” (“last time,” meaning the previous time).
target_language_example: Letztes Mal habe ich die Schlüssel zu Hause vergessen.
native_language_example: Last time I forgot the keys at home.

meaning: ultimately; in the end; when all is said and done.
additional_notes: Used to sum up what the final result, real reason, or decisive point is. Common in spoken and written German, often to express a conclusion after considering different options (similar to “ultimately” or “at the end of the day”). Note: It can be confused with English “lately,” but it does NOT mean “recently” (that’s "in letzter Zeit" or "neulich").
target_language_example: Letztlich müssen wir selbst entscheiden, was wir wollen.
native_language_example: Ultimately, we have to decide for ourselves what we want.

meaning: to love (someone/ something); to be fond of.
additional_notes: Often used for affectionate, warm feelings that can be less intense or less formal than „lieben“ (e.g., for family members, kids, pets, or things you’re fond of). It’s used like a verb phrase: „Ich habe dich lieb.“ Word order in questions/negation works with „haben“ (e.g., „Hast du mich lieb?“, „Ich habe ihn nicht lieb.“). Note: „Ich liebe dich“ is typically stronger and more romantic than „Ich hab(e) dich lieb.“
target_language_example: Ich hab dich lieb.
native_language_example: I love you (in an affectionate, non-romantic way).

meaning: to be due to; to be because of.
additional_notes: Used to say what the cause/reason is. Often with a pronoun: „Es liegt an …“ = “It’s due to … / It’s because of …”. Takes the dative after „an“: an mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen, or „an dem“/„an der“ (often contracted to „am“). Common in explanations and excuses.
target_language_example: Es liegt an dem Wetter, dass wir zu Hause bleiben.
