native_language_example: It’s because of the weather that we’re staying at home.

meaning: to leave (something) lying; to leave (something) where it is.
additional_notes: Used when you don’t move or take something and just leave it in its place. Common with objects: "Lass das Buch liegen" (don’t pick it up). Can also be used figuratively, meaning to drop/ignore a task or issue for now: "Ich lasse das erst mal liegen" (I’ll leave that for now).
target_language_example: Lass die Tasche bitte hier liegen.
native_language_example: Please leave the bag here.

additional_notes: Used as an adjective ("a logical"), but very often as a short reply meaning “of course” or “obviously” to confirm something. Tone can sound a bit blunt depending on context. Related: "Logisch!" = “Of course!”
target_language_example: Kommst du morgen? – Logisch!
native_language_example: Are you coming tomorrow? – Of course!

meaning: Los Angeles (a city in California, USA).
additional_notes: A proper name (city). In German it’s usually written the same as in English. You can use it with location phrases like „in Los Angeles“, „nach Los Angeles“ (to Los Angeles), and „aus Los Angeles“ (from Los Angeles).
target_language_example: Ich fliege nächste Woche nach Los Angeles.
native_language_example: I'm flying to Los Angeles next week.

meaning: to be going on; to be happening (also: to be rid of).
additional_notes: Most commonly used as "Was ist los?" meaning "What's going on? / What's wrong?" You can also use it to say what’s happening: "Hier ist viel los" = "There’s a lot going on here." In another common meaning, "etwas/jemanden los sein" means "to be rid of something/someone" (often with "endlich" = "finally").
target_language_example: Was ist los? Du siehst traurig aus.
native_language_example: What’s wrong? You look sad.

additional_notes: Commonly used when you want to remove, sell, throw away, or otherwise stop having something: *etwas loswerden* (get rid of something). It can also be used with people: *jemanden loswerden* (get rid of someone). Verb: *loswerden* is usually used with an object (*Ich will das loswerden*). In the present tense it often appears split: *Ich werde es los.*
target_language_example: Ich will diese alten Sachen loswerden.
native_language_example: I want to get rid of these old things.

target_language_multi_word_term: lustig machen (sich lustig machen über + Akk.)
meaning: to make fun of; to mock.
additional_notes: Most often used reflexively as „sich lustig machen über …“ (to make fun of someone/something). The thing/person you mock comes after „über“ and is in the accusative: „über ihn / über die Idee“. You can also say „jemanden auslachen“ for “to laugh at someone” (often more direct/mean).
target_language_example: Mach dich nicht über ihn lustig!
native_language_example: Don’t make fun of him!

additional_notes: A common, friendly farewell in spoken German. It’s short for “Mach es gut” (“do it well”), meaning “take care.” Often used with friends, family, or colleagues; can be paired with “Tschüss!” or “Bis bald!” The apostrophe replaces the omitted “e” in “mach(e)s.”
target_language_example: Okay, ich muss los—mach's gut!
native_language_example: Okay, I have to go—take care!

additional_notes: Used to say something is not important or to politely respond to an apology (“Sorry!” — “Macht nichts.”). Common in everyday speech; also similar to “kein Problem” and “nicht so schlimm.” Literally “makes nothing,” but it means “it doesn’t matter.”
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, ich bin zu spät. – Macht nichts.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m late. – No problem.

meaning: "we’ll see" / "let’s see" (i.e., wait and find out).
additional_notes: Very common in everyday German. Used when you’re unsure or don’t want to commit yet ("We’ll see"), or when you’re about to check or try something ("Let’s see"). "Mal" here is a softener meaning roughly "just/a moment" and makes it sound casual. Often used as a stand-alone reply: "Mal sehen."
target_language_example: Kommst du morgen mit? – Mal sehen, ich weiß es noch nicht.
native_language_example: Are you coming along tomorrow? – We’ll see, I don’t know yet.

additional_notes: Common, neutral phrase used to say something is uncertain or unpredictable. It often appears on its own as a comment, or followed by a reason/possibility (e.g., "Man weiß nie, was passiert."). Similar in meaning to "Wer weiß?" (= who knows?).
target_language_example: Nimm lieber einen Regenschirm mit – man weiß nie.
native_language_example: Better take an umbrella— you never know.

additional_notes: Common adverb for frequency. Often placed in the middle of the sentence (after the verb in simple statements): "Ich gehe manchmal..." It can also start a sentence for emphasis: "Manchmal gehe ich..." Similar options: "oft" (often), "selten" (rarely), "nie" (never).
target_language_example: Manchmal trinke ich morgens Kaffee.
native_language_example: Sometimes I drink coffee in the morning.

meaning: to take measures; to take action (steps).
additional_notes: Common formal phrase used in news, work, politics, and official contexts for doing something to solve a problem or improve a situation. Often used with an issue introduced by "gegen" (against) or "zur" (for/toward): "Maßnahmen gegen die Inflation ergreifen" / "Maßnahmen zur Verbesserung der Sicherheit ergreifen".
target_language_example: Die Regierung will Maßnahmen gegen die steigenden Preise ergreifen.
native_language_example: The government wants to take measures against rising prices.

additional_notes: Used to say you have an excess of something or that something is sufficient to the point of being too much. Often used with “haben” (to have) or to emphasize that no more is needed: “Ich habe mehr als genug.” / “Das ist mehr als genug.” Can also express being fed up: “Ich habe mehr als genug von …” (“I’ve had more than enough of …”).
target_language_example: Danke, ich habe mehr als genug gegessen.
native_language_example: Thanks, I’ve eaten more than enough.

meaning: more or less; roughly; kind of.
additional_notes: Used to say something is approximately true or only partly true. Common in everyday speech to soften a statement ("more or less finished") or to mean "approximately" ("around").
target_language_example: Ich bin mehr oder weniger fertig.
native_language_example: I’m more or less finished.

additional_notes: An adverb meaning something happens more than once. Common in everyday speech and writing. Often used with verbs like „anrufen“ (to call), „versuchen“ (to try), „passieren“ (to happen). Similar to „mehrere Male“ (more formal/explicit) and „wiederholt“ (more formal).
target_language_example: Ich habe es mehrmals versucht, aber es hat nicht geklappt.
native_language_example: I tried several times, but it didn’t work.

meaning: “my God!” (an exclamation of surprise, shock, frustration, etc.).
additional_notes: Used as a standalone exclamation (often with an exclamation mark) in both spoken and written German. Tone depends on context: it can be mild (“Oh my gosh”) or stronger (“Oh my God”). You may also hear it stretched out: “Mein Gooott…”.
target_language_example: Mein Gott! Hast du dich erschreckt?
native_language_example: Oh my God! Did you get scared?

meaning: “oh my goodness!” / “good grief!” (an exclamation of surprise, shock, annoyance, etc.).
additional_notes: Used as a mild exclamation (less strong than swearing). Often said on its own, or at the start of a sentence. You may also hear it shortened to “Güte!” or in the variant “Meine Güte!” with stronger emphasis. Literally “my goodness.”
target_language_example: Meine Güte, ist das kalt hier!
native_language_example: Oh my goodness, it’s so cold in here!

additional_notes: Used to strongly agree with someone and confirm that you’ve been thinking the same thing. Often said as a short standalone response in conversation (similar to “Tell me about it” or “You said it”). Literally “my speech,” but it’s idiomatic in this meaning.
target_language_example: „Das ist viel zu teuer.“ – „Meine Rede!“
native_language_example: “That’s way too expensive.” – “Exactly!”

additional_notes: A common way to give your view or judgment. Used in both spoken and written German and works in formal and informal contexts. It often comes at the start of a sentence, but can also be placed mid-sentence. The verb usually comes right after it when it starts the sentence (verb-second word order): „Meiner Meinung nach ist …“.
target_language_example: Meiner Meinung nach ist das eine gute Idee.
native_language_example: In my opinion, that’s a good idea.

meaning: “as far as I know” / “to my knowledge”.
additional_notes: Used to qualify a statement and show you’re not 100% certain. It’s fairly neutral and common in spoken and written German. Grammatically it’s in the genitive (“of my knowledge”), often used at the start of a sentence; you can also say “meines Wissens nach” (a bit longer, same idea).
target_language_example: Meines Wissens gibt es hier keinen Geldautomaten.
native_language_example: As far as I know, there’s no ATM here.

additional_notes: Used when something suddenly comes to mind. Literally "(it) falls into me," but in natural English you say "I just remembered" or "it occurs to me." Often followed by a clause with "dass" (that) or a question word: "Mir fällt ein, dass ..." / "Mir fällt ein, wo ...".
target_language_example: Mir fällt ein, dass ich noch Milch kaufen muss.
native_language_example: I just remembered that I still need to buy milk.

additional_notes: Used with things/activities (subject = the thing you like). Structure: "Mir gefällt + singular noun" (e.g., Der Film gefällt mir.) and "Mir gefallen + plural nouns" (e.g., Die Schuhe gefallen mir.). With a verb, use: "Mir gefällt es, … zu + infinitive" (e.g., Mir gefällt es, hier zu sein.). Word order often: "Das gefällt mir" = "I like that."
target_language_example: Mir gefällt dieser Film sehr.
native_language_example: I like this movie a lot.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t like something. German often expresses “to like” with gefallen: the thing you like is the grammatical subject, and the person is in the dative (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen). Typical pattern: „X gefällt mir (nicht).“ For plural things, use „gefallen“: „Die Schuhe gefallen mir nicht.“
target_language_example: Der Film gefällt mir nicht.
native_language_example: I don’t like the movie.

additional_notes: A very common reply to “Wie geht’s?” (“How are you?”). Literally means “It goes well for me.” You can also say “Mir geht’s gut” in casual speech. Similar patterns: “mir geht es schlecht” (I’m doing badly), “mir geht es so la la” (so-so).
target_language_example: Danke, mir geht es gut. Und dir?
native_language_example: Thanks, I’m doing well. And you?

meaning: "I don't care" / "it's all the same to me."
additional_notes: Common way to say you have no preference or that something doesn’t matter to you. Often followed by a clause starting with „ob“ (whether): „Mir ist egal, ob …“. Word order can vary for emphasis: „Egal ist mir das nicht“ means "I do care" (the opposite). You can also specify alternatives: „Mir ist egal, ob wir Pizza oder Pasta essen.“
target_language_example: Mir ist egal, was wir heute Abend machen.
native_language_example: I don't care what we do tonight.

additional_notes: A very common way to talk about how you feel temperature-wise. Literally “to me it is cold,” so German often uses the dative pronoun (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen) + „ist“ + adjective: „Mir ist warm“ (I’m warm), „Mir ist heiß“ (I’m hot), „Mir ist schlecht“ (I feel sick). For emphasis you can add „sehr“: „Mir ist sehr kalt.“
target_language_example: Mach bitte das Fenster zu, mir ist kalt.
native_language_example: Please close the window, I’m cold.

additional_notes: Used to say something was done intentionally (not by accident). Common in everyday speech. Often contrasts with "aus Versehen" (by mistake).
target_language_example: Ich habe das nicht mit Absicht gemacht.
native_language_example: I didn’t do that on purpose.

meaning: by far; with a clear margin (the most).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is clearly more than the others (often with superlatives): „mit Abstand der/die/das beste/schlechteste …“. Also used in comparisons to mean there is a noticeable gap or difference (e.g., in points, time, distance). Literally “with distance,” but idiomatically “by far.”
target_language_example: Das ist mit Abstand das beste Restaurant in der Stadt.
native_language_example: That is by far the best restaurant in the city.

additional_notes: Usually appears as part of longer phrases, especially: „mit eigenen Augen (sehen)“ = “to see with your own eyes” (i.e., to witness something yourself). Also common: „etwas mit anderen Augen sehen“ = “to see something in a different way.” On its own, „mit Augen“ can sound incomplete without the rest of the expression.
target_language_example: Ich habe es mit eigenen Augen gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw it with my own eyes.

meaning: in view of; with regard to.
additional_notes: A formal-ish prepositional phrase used to introduce the topic or consideration something is based on (similar to “regarding” or “considering”). Often used in news, writing, and meetings. It takes the accusative case: mit Blick auf + Akkusativ (e.g., mit Blick auf den Termin / die Kosten / das Wetter).
target_language_example: Mit Blick auf das Wetter verschieben wir das Picknick auf morgen.
native_language_example: In view of the weather, we’re postponing the picnic until tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something with genuine feeling and dedication (often about work, helping others, or a hobby). Common in phrases like „mit Herz und Seele“ (“with heart and soul”).
target_language_example: Sie arbeitet mit Herz und hilft den Kunden gern.
native_language_example: She works wholeheartedly and likes helping the customers.

meaning: with the help of; using (something) as help.
additional_notes: Commonly used as a prepositional phrase. Often appears as "mit Hilfe von + dative" ("with the help of ..."): "mit Hilfe von Freunden", "mit Hilfe eines Wörterbuchs". You can also use it without "von" to mean "using" a tool or method: "mit Hilfe eines Computers".
target_language_example: Ich habe mit Hilfe von Freunden eine Wohnung gefunden.
native_language_example: I found an apartment with the help of friends.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is justified in thinking/feeling/doing something (“and they’re right to”). Often appears with verbs like sagen/behaupten (“to say/claim”), kritisieren (“to criticize”), erwarten (“to expect”), and with phrases like „Du hast mit Recht …“ (“You’re right to …”). Not the same as „recht haben“ (“to be right”), though the idea is similar.
target_language_example: Du bist mit Recht stolz auf dich.
native_language_example: You’re rightly proud of yourself.

additional_notes: Used with the dative: "mit" + dative. It can mean (1) including everything (no exclusions) or (2) together with everything that comes with something (details/extras). Often appears in phrases like "mit allem Drum und Dran" (= with all the extras) or in negative sentences: "Ich bin mit allem fertig" (= I’m done with everything).
target_language_example: Ich nehme den Salat mit allem, bitte.
native_language_example: I’ll take the salad with everything, please.

additional_notes: Used when something can be seen without a tool like binoculars, a microscope, or a telescope. Often appears with verbs like „sehen“, „erkennen“, or „sichtbar“: „mit bloßem Auge sehen/erkennen“ or „mit bloßem Auge sichtbar“.
target_language_example: Den Stern kann man mit bloßem Auge sehen.
native_language_example: You can see the star with the naked eye.

additional_notes: Used to express someone’s purpose or goal. Commonly followed by “zu” + infinitive ("mit der Absicht, ... zu ...") or by a clause introduced with “dass” ("mit der Absicht, dass ..."). Similar in meaning to “mit dem Ziel” (with the goal) and “in der Absicht” (with the intention).
target_language_example: Er kam mit der Absicht, sich zu entschuldigen.
native_language_example: He came with the intention of apologizing.

additional_notes: Used to say you do something manually (not with a machine) or using your hand. Often appears with verbs like „machen“, „schreiben“, „waschen“, „rühren“, „halten“. For tools/instruments you may also hear „von Hand“ (“by hand”).
target_language_example: Ich schreibe das Formular mit der Hand.
native_language_example: I fill out the form by hand.

meaning: over time; in time; with time.
additional_notes: Means that something happens gradually or after some time has passed. Commonly used with changes, learning, or getting used to something (e.g., "Mit der Zeit wird es leichter"). Often interchangeable with "im Laufe der Zeit" (more formal: "in the course of time").
target_language_example: Mit der Zeit habe ich mich an die neue Arbeit gewöhnt.
native_language_example: Over time, I got used to the new job.

additional_notes: Used literally (eyes physically closed) and also figuratively to mean doing something automatically or easily, without needing to look or think much. Often paired with verbs like „machen“, „können“, „erkennen“, „finden“ (e.g., „Das kann ich mit geschlossenen Augen.“).
target_language_example: Ich kann den Weg nach Hause mit geschlossenen Augen finden.
native_language_example: I can find the way home with my eyes closed.

additional_notes: Common, neutral way to say you’re having a conversation with a person. "mit" takes the dative case: mit mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen. You can also use it for phone calls or meetings: "Ich muss mit dir sprechen" often implies something important needs to be discussed.
target_language_example: Ich möchte kurz mit dir sprechen.
native_language_example: I’d like to talk to you briefly.

additional_notes: "Mit sich" is a fixed combination of "mit" + reflexive pronoun (mich/dich/sich/uns/euch/sich) used in several very common expressions. Most frequent meanings: (1) carrying something along: "Ich habe meinen Ausweis mit (mir)." (2) being by oneself/alone: "Ich bin gern mit mir." (3) automatically/inevitably: "Das ergibt sich (von selbst)." (4) in the sense of 'to accept/cope': "Damit kann ich leben / Ich komme damit klar" is often more natural than "Ich bin damit mit mir". In dictionaries you’ll often see it as part of set verbs like "mit sich bringen" (to bring about), "mit sich nehmen" (to take with you), "etwas mit sich machen/ausmachen" (to do something with it / to make something of it).
target_language_example: Nimm deinen Pass mit dir, wenn du reist.
native_language_example: Take your passport with you when you travel.

meaning: to entail; to bring along (as a consequence).
additional_notes: Used when something has a consequence or results in something else (often challenges, costs, risks, responsibilities). Common in formal or neutral contexts: “Das bringt Kosten/Risiken/Probleme mit sich.” The verb is separable in many tenses: “Es bringt … mit sich.” / “Das hat … mit sich gebracht.”
target_language_example: Die Entscheidung bringt große Verantwortung mit sich.
native_language_example: The decision entails great responsibility.

additional_notes: Used to say people do something jointly or have a relationship/interaction with each other. Common with verbs like sprechen (talk), arbeiten (work), spielen (play), umgehen (deal/treat), or zusammen sein (be together). Often contrasts with "gegeneinander" (against each other).
target_language_example: Wir müssen miteinander reden.
native_language_example: We need to talk to each other.

meaning: by now; in the meantime; meanwhile.
additional_notes: Used to say that something has changed over time up to the present ("by now"), or that something happens during the time between two events ("in the meantime/meanwhile"). Often appears with present tense to describe a current state resulting from earlier changes: "Mittlerweile wohne ich in Berlin."
target_language_example: Mittlerweile habe ich das schon verstanden.
native_language_example: By now I’ve already understood that.

meaning: to encourage; to give someone courage.
additional_notes: Usually used with an object and often with a dative person: „jemandem Mut machen“ = encourage someone (literally: make courage for someone). Common in supportive contexts, e.g., before an exam, a difficult talk, or a challenge.
target_language_example: Meine Freunde machen mir Mut vor der Prüfung.
native_language_example: My friends encourage me before the exam.

meaning: “would like” (polite way to say you want something).
additional_notes: Very common in polite requests, especially when ordering or asking for help. Often used with a verb in the infinitive: “Ich möchte gern …” + infinitive (e.g., “bezahlen”), or with a noun: “Ich möchte gern einen Kaffee.” It’s slightly softer/more polite than just “ich möchte …”.
target_language_example: Ich möchte gern einen Kaffee, bitte.
native_language_example: I’d like a coffee, please.

additional_notes: Used with a modal verb + perfect infinitive (gesehen haben) to express a strong assumption or logical conclusion about the past (what you think happened), not an obligation. Often used like: „Er muss das gesehen haben.“ = “He must have seen that.”
target_language_example: Sie muss den Unfall gesehen haben.
native_language_example: She must have seen the accident.

meaning: to have to go / to have to leave (now).
additional_notes: Usually used as part of a full sentence with a subject and conjugated verb: „Ich muss los.“ / „Wir müssen los.“ It often implies urgency or that it’s time to head out. „los“ here means ‘off/away’ (as in ‘to set off’).
target_language_example: Sorry, wir müssen los.
native_language_example: Sorry, we have to go.

additional_notes: Common in spoken German to react to something with uncertainty or reservations (like English “well…”). It can also mean “not really / only okay” when answering how something is ("Na ja, es geht."). Tone depends on context: it can sound neutral, hesitant, or slightly skeptical.
target_language_example: Na ja, ich weiß nicht, ob das eine gute Idee ist.
native_language_example: Well, I don’t know if that’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Common, casual way to agree or confirm something (often with a friendly or slightly obvious tone: “well, of course”). Can be used as a short standalone reply. Similar to “klar!” or “na ja” (but “na ja” is more hesitant).
target_language_example: Kommst du morgen mit? – Na klar!
native_language_example: Are you coming along tomorrow? – Sure!

additional_notes: Used in speech to brush off what someone just said, show indifference, or challenge them to continue (similar to “and?”). Tone is often blunt or slightly confrontational; not a neutral connector like English “and.”
target_language_example: Na und? Das ist doch kein Problem.
native_language_example: So what? That’s not a problem.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement to show direction (going/coming home): „gehen/kommen/fahren/rennen nach Hause“. Contrast: „zu Hause“ means “at home” (location, not movement). Note that „Hause“ is an older form of „Haus“ used in this fixed expression; you don’t normally say *„nach Haus“* in standard German.
target_language_example: Ich gehe jetzt nach Hause.
native_language_example: I’m going home now.

additional_notes: Polite phrase used to let someone go before you (e.g., through a door, into an elevator, or ahead in a line). Often said with a gesture. Can also appear after phrases like „Bitte“ or „Gern“ (e.g., „Bitte, nach Ihnen.“). Uses the dative form „Ihnen“ (formal “you”). For friends/family, you’d usually say „nach dir“ (singular) or „nach euch“ (plural).
target_language_example: Bitte, nach Ihnen.
native_language_example: After you, please.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement to show direction outward (e.g., gehen, laufen, bringen): going from inside to outside. Common alternatives are "raus" (informal) and "nach draußen" is a bit more explicit. For location (being outside), you often use "draußen" without "nach".
target_language_example: Wir gehen nach draußen.
native_language_example: We're going outside.

additional_notes: Often used with movement verbs (gehen, treten, rücken, setzen) to indicate direction toward the back (e.g., toward the rear of a room) or movement backward. With "nach" it’s about direction (where to), while "hinten" alone often describes a location (where something is). Common in everyday instructions like "Ein Stück nach hinten" (a bit further back).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte ein Stück nach hinten gehen?
native_language_example: Can you please step back a bit?

meaning: to backfire; to have the opposite effect than intended.
additional_notes: Used when a plan, comment, or action turns out badly and causes problems for the person who did it. Often said about strategies, jokes, or attempts to help that end up making things worse. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Der Witz sollte die Stimmung auflockern, aber er ist nach hinten losgegangen.
native_language_example: The joke was supposed to lighten the mood, but it backfired.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or movement. Common in giving directions (e.g., when driving or walking). Often used with verbs like „gehen“ (to go), „fahren“ (to drive), and „abbiegen“ (to turn). Opposite: „nach rechts“ (to the right).
target_language_example: Biegen Sie an der nächsten Kreuzung nach links ab.
native_language_example: Turn left at the next intersection.

additional_notes: Used to describe movement/direction upward (often with verbs like gehen, fahren, schauen, ziehen). Can also mean “up” in interfaces/instructions (e.g., scroll or move up). Literally “to/toward above.”
target_language_example: Geh bitte nach oben in den dritten Stock.
native_language_example: Please go upstairs to the third floor.

additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or direction (not location). Common in giving directions: „Biegen Sie nach rechts ab“ (Turn right). For location you more often use „rechts“ or „auf der rechten Seite“ (e.g., „Das ist rechts“ = That’s on the right).
target_language_example: Gehen Sie nach rechts und dann geradeaus.
native_language_example: Go to the right and then straight ahead.

meaning: gradually; little by little; step by step.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens slowly over time, in small stages. Common with verbs like „werden“, „sich verbessern“, „lernen“, „entstehen“, or „wachsen“. Often interchangeable with „allmählich“ in meaning, but „nach und nach“ feels very everyday and conversational.
target_language_example: Nach und nach wird mein Deutsch besser.
native_language_example: Little by little, my German is getting better.

additional_notes: Commonly used to describe movement or direction toward a lower place (often with verbs like gehen, schauen, fallen: „nach unten gehen/schauen/fallen“). It contrasts with „nach oben“ (up/upwards). It can also be used for position in simple instructions: „nach unten“ = down (e.g., on a screen/page or stairs).
target_language_example: Schau bitte nach unten.
native_language_example: Please look down.

additional_notes: Used with motion or direction (often with verbs like gehen, kommen, rücken, beugen) to indicate movement/position toward the front. Also common in instructions: „Bitte nach vorne!“ = “Please come/move to the front!”
target_language_example: Bitte kommen Sie nach vorne.
native_language_example: Please come to the front.

additional_notes: Used to say something continues to be true or hasn’t changed over time. Common in both spoken and written German. Often placed near the verb or after the subject: "Ich bin nach wie vor hier." / "Nach wie vor ist es schwierig."
target_language_example: Ich warte nach wie vor auf deine Antwort.
native_language_example: I’m still waiting for your reply.

additional_notes: Common everyday time adverb. Often used on its own to mean “later” (e.g., as an answer to “When?”), or with a time frame like “nachher” = later today / later on. You’ll also see the clearer but slightly more formal equivalent “nachher” ↔ “später” (later) and “danach” (after that, following an event).
target_language_example: Ich rufe dich nachher an.
native_language_example: I’ll call you later.

meaning: the Middle East (literally: the Near East).
additional_notes: A geographic/political region term. Usually written capitalized in German: „Naher Osten“. Often used in news, history, and politics. In everyday conversation, people also say „der Nahe Osten“.
target_language_example: Viele Nachrichten berichten über Konflikte im Nahen Osten.
native_language_example: Many news reports cover conflicts in the Middle East.

additional_notes: Most commonly used in conversation to mean “of course” (agreeing, confirming, reassuring): “Natürlich!” You can also use it as an adverb meaning “naturally” (“Er spricht natürlich Deutsch.”) or as an adjective meaning “natural” (“natürliches Licht” = natural light).
target_language_example: Natürlich kann ich dir helfen.
native_language_example: Of course I can help you.

meaning: next to each other; side by side.
additional_notes: Used to describe two or more people/things being positioned directly beside one another. Often with verbs like „stehen“ (stand), „sitzen“ (sit), „liegen“ (lie), or „gehen“ (walk). Can also be used more generally for things happening in parallel (alongside each other).
target_language_example: Die beiden Häuser stehen nebeneinander.
native_language_example: The two houses are next to each other.

meaning: New York (the city or the U.S. state).
additional_notes: In German, proper names usually keep their original spelling. Context determines whether it means the city (often said as "New York City" / "NYC") or the state ("der Staat New York"). Typical prepositions: "in New York" (in New York), "nach New York" (to New York).
target_language_example: Ich fliege nächste Woche nach New York.
native_language_example: I’m flying to New York next week.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something does not happen or is not true in the smallest/weakest case ("not even X"). With time/frequency it can mean "not once" (e.g., not even a single time). Often placed before the word/phrase it emphasizes: „nicht einmal + noun/pronoun/number“.
target_language_example: Er hat nicht einmal Hallo gesagt.
native_language_example: He didn’t even say hello.

additional_notes: Used to say that an amount/quantity/effort is insufficient. Often followed by a noun: „nicht genug Zeit/Geld/Platz“ (“not enough time/money/space”). Also common before an infinitive with „zu“: „nicht genug … zu …“ (“not enough to …”), e.g. „nicht genug Geld, um das zu kaufen“ (“not enough money to buy that”).
target_language_example: Ich habe nicht genug Zeit.
native_language_example: I don’t have enough time.

meaning: not OK; not all right; unacceptable.
additional_notes: Used to say something is wrong, not acceptable, or not functioning properly. Common in everyday speech: "Das ist nicht in Ordnung" = "That’s not OK." Also used about health or condition: "Mir ist nicht in Ordnung" is less idiomatic; more common is "Mir geht’s nicht gut" (I’m not well) or "Mit mir ist etwas nicht in Ordnung" (Something is wrong with me).
target_language_example: Es ist nicht in Ordnung, so spät ohne Bescheid zu kommen.
native_language_example: It’s not OK to come that late without letting (me/us) know.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something does not happen or is not true to a surprising degree. Very common in spoken German. Often placed before the word it emphasizes: “nicht mal 5 Minuten” = “not even 5 minutes.” Can also mean “not once” with actions/time: “Er hat nicht mal angerufen” = “He didn’t even call / didn’t call once.”
target_language_example: Ich habe nicht mal fünf Euro dabei.
native_language_example: I don’t even have five euros on me.

additional_notes: Used to say that something that was true before is now no longer true (a change over time). Common with the present tense (Ich rauche nicht mehr.) or past (Er war nicht mehr da.). Often contrasts with "noch" (“still / yet”). Word order: it usually sits near what it negates (often after the verb in simple tenses).
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Zeit mehr; ich arbeite nicht mehr hier.
native_language_example: I don’t have any time anymore; I don’t work here anymore.

additional_notes: Used at the end of a statement to ask for agreement or confirmation, similar to English “right?” or “isn’t it?”. It can sound a bit formal or old-fashioned compared to casual “oder?” in everyday speech. Literally it means “not true,” but as a fixed phrase it functions like a tag question.
target_language_example: Du kommst morgen, nicht wahr?
native_language_example: You’re coming tomorrow, right?

additional_notes: Used to say something is nearby or at a short distance. Often appears with "von" + dative ("nicht weit von hier" = not far from here) or with "weg" ("nicht weit weg" = not far away).
target_language_example: Der Bahnhof ist nicht weit von hier.
native_language_example: The train station isn’t far from here.

meaning: not far away; not far from here.
additional_notes: Used to say something is close by, often about a place or location. You can also use it with a reference point: „nicht weit entfernt von …“ (not far from …). Common in giving directions or describing where something is.
target_language_example: Der Bahnhof ist nicht weit entfernt.
native_language_example: The train station isn’t far away.

meaning: “not to go too far” (to overstep a limit).
additional_notes: Used to warn someone not to overdo something or cross a boundary (behavior, jokes, criticism, demands). Common as an infinitive phrase after verbs like „du solltest…“ or „bitte…“, and also as „Geh nicht zu weit!“ as a direct warning.
target_language_example: Pass auf, dass du mit deinen Witzen nicht zu weit gehst.
native_language_example: Be careful not to go too far with your jokes.

additional_notes: Used to say something is intentional or meaningful (there’s a reason behind it). Often appears in statements like "Es ist nicht zufällig, dass …" (“It’s not a coincidence that …”). You can also use it about a person’s actions: "Er hat das nicht zufällig gesagt" (“He didn’t say that by accident”).
target_language_example: Es ist nicht zufällig, dass sie heute so früh da ist.
native_language_example: It’s not a coincidence that she’s here so early today.

meaning: 'nothing but' / 'nothing other than' (used to emphasize exclusivity).
additional_notes: Used before a noun, pronoun, or infinitive clause to stress that something is only that one thing—often as criticism or strong emphasis. Common patterns: "nichts als + noun" (nichts als Probleme = nothing but problems), "nichts als + Infinitiv" (nichts als warten = nothing but wait).
target_language_example: Das ist nichts als eine Ausrede.
native_language_example: That’s nothing but an excuse.

additional_notes: Used to say that there is no other thing/option, or to emphasize that something is simply (and only) that. Often appears with "als" ("nichts anderes als ..." = "nothing other than ..." / "nothing but ...") or as a short answer: "Nichts anderes."
target_language_example: Das ist nichts anderes als eine Ausrede.
native_language_example: That’s nothing but an excuse.

meaning: to not be at fault; to not be able to help it.
additional_notes: Used to say someone isn’t responsible for a situation. Commonly with a person as the subject: "Ich kann nichts dafür" (It’s not my fault / I can’t help it) or "Er kann nichts dafür" (It’s not his fault). "dafür" refers to the problem/thing being discussed. Often used to reassure someone: "Du kannst nichts dafür."
target_language_example: Es tut mir leid, aber ich kann nichts dafür.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but it’s not my fault / I can’t help it.

meaning: “never been there” / “never existed (like it never happened)”
additional_notes: Literally “never there been.” Used to say something didn’t exist or happen, or to deny something completely. Often appears with “als wäre … nie da gewesen” (“as if … had never been there”) or “so tun, als wäre … nie da gewesen” (“to act as if … had never happened”).
target_language_example: Nach dem Streit tat er so, als wäre alles nie da gewesen.
native_language_example: After the argument, he acted as if nothing had happened.

additional_notes: Used for strong emphasis, often as an emphatic refusal or denial. It can be a dramatic, emotional way to say you will never do something or that something is impossible (similar to “never ever” or “no way” in English). Tone depends on context; it can sound quite blunt.
target_language_example: Nie im Leben mache ich das!
native_language_example: No way am I doing that! / I’m never doing that!

additional_notes: Used to say that something will not happen again in the future. Common in promises, strong decisions, or regrets. Similar in meaning to "nie wieder" (often interchangeable). Word order is flexible; it often comes near the end of the clause for emphasis.
target_language_example: Ich mache das nie mehr.
native_language_example: I’ll never do that again.

additional_notes: "Nie" means "never" and is used with a verb to say you don’t do something at any time. In "nie sagen", the verb is "sagen" (to say). Often used with an object: "nie sagen, dass …" (to never say that …) or "nie sagen, was …" (to never say what …). Word order: "nie" usually comes before the verb in the final position in subordinate clauses ("…, dass er es nie sagt").
target_language_example: Er sagt nie, dass er Hilfe braucht.
native_language_example: He never says that he needs help.

additional_notes: Used to say something will not happen anymore, often after a bad experience or as a strong promise. Common in statements like „Das mache ich nie wieder.“ You can also use it for emphasis with the future: „Nie wieder werde ich …“.
target_language_example: Das mache ich nie wieder.
native_language_example: I’ll never do that again.

additional_notes: A fixed phrase meaning you shouldn’t rule something out completely, because circumstances can change. Used in everyday speech, often as advice or a reminder (sometimes with a slightly humorous tone).
target_language_example: Ich weiß, du willst das nie machen, aber: Niemals nie sagen.
native_language_example: I know you never want to do that, but: never say never.

additional_notes: Used to improve a suggestion or add a stronger alternative: “X …, or even better, Y.” It can also emphasize that something is an improvement compared to before. Literally “still/yet better” (noch = still/yet, besser = better).
target_language_example: Wir können morgen ins Kino gehen – noch besser, wir gehen gleich heute.
native_language_example: We can go to the movies tomorrow—or better yet, let’s go today.

additional_notes: Used to add extra information that strengthens what you just said—often something unexpected, annoying, or impressive. It usually refers back to the previous point (like “and what’s more…”). Commonly placed after the added item or clause: “..., noch dazu.”
target_language_example: Es ist schon spät, und es regnet noch dazu.
native_language_example: It’s already late, and on top of that it’s raining.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to repeat something or to say you want to do something another time. Very common in spoken German. Often used as a polite request: "Noch einmal, bitte" = "Again, please" / "Could you say that again?". Similar options: "noch mal" (more casual) and "noch einmal" (a bit more formal/clear).
target_language_example: Kannst du das bitte noch einmal sagen?
native_language_example: Can you please say that again?

additional_notes: Often used when offering more help or adding one more item. As a question (Noch etwas?) it’s common in shops, cafés, or at the end of a request, meaning “Anything else?”. As a statement (noch etwas + noun/verb) it means “one more” or “something else,” e.g., noch etwas Wasser = “some more water.”
target_language_example: Kann ich Ihnen sonst noch etwas helfen?
native_language_example: Can I help you with anything else?

additional_notes: Used when you’re asking if there is another person in addition to those already mentioned, or when checking if anyone else needs/wants something. Often appears in questions like “Noch jemand?” (e.g., in a café) or “Möchte noch jemand …?” / “Will noch jemand …?”. The word order can vary depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Möchte noch jemand Kaffee?
native_language_example: Would anyone else like coffee?

meaning: “for a long time yet” / “still for a long time.”
additional_notes: Used to say something will continue for quite a while into the future. Often appears with verbs like bleiben (to stay), dauern (to last), warten (to wait), or brauchen (to need). Not the same as „lange nicht“ (“not for a long time”).
target_language_example: Das dauert noch lange.
native_language_example: That will take a long time yet.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken German to ask for repetition or to do something again. Also written as one word: „nochmal“ (often in informal writing). Typical with imperatives: „Sag das noch mal!“ (Say that again!). Can also mean “another” in the sense of “one more”: „Noch mal Kaffee?“ (Another coffee?).
target_language_example: Kannst du das bitte noch mal sagen?
native_language_example: Can you please say that again?

additional_notes: Used to say you want an additional amount beyond what you already have/know/expect. Common in everyday requests and comparisons. Similar to "mehr" (more), but "noch" adds the sense of "in addition / on top of that".
target_language_example: Kann ich noch mehr Wasser haben?
native_language_example: Can I have even more water?

additional_notes: Used to say something hasn’t happened up to now, but may happen later. Often answers questions like „Bist du fertig?“ (Are you finished?) → „Noch nicht.“ You can also use it inside a sentence: „Ich habe noch nicht gegessen.“ (I haven’t eaten yet.)
target_language_example: Ich bin noch nicht fertig.
native_language_example: I’m not finished yet.

additional_notes: Used to say that up to now something has never happened. Very common with the present perfect (Perfekt): “Ich habe das noch nie gemacht.” It can also be used with the simple past in narratives. Word order: “noch nie” usually goes before the past participle or toward the middle of the sentence. Contrast: “nie” = never (at any time), “noch nicht” = not yet (but expected to happen).
target_language_example: Ich habe das noch nie gegessen.
native_language_example: I’ve never eaten that before.

additional_notes: Used to intensify a negative situation or to add a worse point: "It’s bad—and even worse…" Often followed by a clause introduced by "ist" or "wird" (e.g., "Noch schlimmer ist, dass…"). Also common as a short reaction: "Noch schlimmer!"
target_language_example: Es regnet, und noch schlimmer: Ich habe meinen Regenschirm vergessen.
native_language_example: It’s raining, and even worse: I forgot my umbrella.

additional_notes: Common in everyday speech as a shorter form of „noch einmal“. Used to ask someone to repeat something (e.g., a question or instruction), to do something another time, or to add an extra item (“another”). Often used as „Noch mal, bitte.“ In writing you may also see „noch mal“ as two words.
target_language_example: Kannst du das nochmal sagen, bitte?
native_language_example: Can you say that again, please?

additional_notes: Common adjective meaning something is not special or unusual: "ein normaler Tag" (a normal day). It can also be used adverbially in everyday speech to mean "normally/just in the usual way": "Mach das bitte normal." (Do that normally / the usual way). For "normally" in the sense of "usually," German often uses "normalerweise."
target_language_example: Heute ist ein ganz normaler Tag.
native_language_example: Today is a completely normal day.

additional_notes: Used as a filler when you pause to think, or to signal mild doubt, uncertainty, or reluctant acceptance (often similar to "well, I guess" or "so, anyway"). Tone depends on context and can sound slightly noncommittal or skeptical.
target_language_example: Nun ja, ich weiß nicht, ob das eine gute Idee ist.
native_language_example: Well, I don’t know if that’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Common adjective for something that doesn’t help or has no use. Often used with “sein” (to be): “Das ist nutzlos.” The related noun is “der Nutzen” (benefit/use), and “-los” means “-less” (without).
target_language_example: Ohne Internet ist die App für mich nutzlos.
native_language_example: Without internet, the app is useless for me.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the week after the current one. Common for making plans and appointments. Often used with a day: „nächste Woche am Montag …“ (next Monday) or simply „nächste Woche“ (sometime next week).
target_language_example: Ich habe nächste Woche einen Termin beim Arzt.
native_language_example: I have a doctor’s appointment next week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a future occasion: either the next time something happens in general, or the next time you meet/see someone. Often used with "bis" (until): "Bis nächstes Mal!" You can also say "das nächste Mal" when it functions as a time expression in a sentence (e.g., "Das nächste Mal komme ich früher.").
target_language_example: Bis nächstes Mal!
native_language_example: See you next time!

additional_notes: Used at the end of a statement to ask for confirmation, similar to English “right?” or “isn’t it?”. Often said with rising intonation. Can also be used literally in questions meaning “or not?”.
target_language_example: Du kommst morgen, oder nicht?
native_language_example: You’re coming tomorrow, right?

additional_notes: Used at the end of a phrase to make it less exact or to show you’re not sure (similar to “or something” in English). Very common in casual speech; in more formal contexts you might prefer “oder ähnliches” (“or something similar”).
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns um acht oder so.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at eight or so.

meaning: "or what?" (used to challenge/confirm what someone said).
additional_notes: Used at the end of a sentence to question, challenge, or demand confirmation—often with an impatient, skeptical, or confrontational tone (similar to “right?” or “or what?”). Can sound rude depending on intonation and context; in friendly contexts it can be teasing.
target_language_example: Du kommst morgen, oder was?
native_language_example: You’re coming tomorrow, or what?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a direct or candid opinion, often before something critical or surprising. Common at the start of a sentence: “Offen gesagt, …”. Slightly more neutral/formal than “ehrlich gesagt,” but both are common. Literally “openly said.”
target_language_example: Offen gesagt, gefällt mir der Film nicht.
native_language_example: Frankly, I don’t like the movie.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a rule or statement applies to every single case. Often appears with words like „immer“ (always) or in formal rules/announcements. Literally „without exception“.
target_language_example: In diesem Gebäude gilt ohne Ausnahme Rauchverbot.
native_language_example: In this building, smoking is forbidden without exception.

additional_notes: Used to say that an attempt did not work or had no result. Common after verbs like „versuchen“ (to try), „suchen“ (to look for), or „anrufen“ (to call): „Ich habe es ohne Erfolg versucht.“ / „Wir suchten ohne Erfolg.“
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn ohne Erfolg angerufen.
native_language_example: I called him, but without success.

meaning: without a reason; for no reason.
additional_notes:
Used to say something happens with no clear cause or justification. Often appears as an adverbial phrase in a sentence: 
- "ohne Grund" = without a reason
- "ohne jeden Grund" = without any reason at all
- "ohne Grund (zu ...)" can also mean "for no reason (to ...)" depending on context.
target_language_example: Er hat mich ohne Grund angeschrien.
native_language_example: He yelled at me for no reason.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens with no difficulties or complications. Common after verbs like gehen, funktionieren, laufen, klappen (e.g., „Es hat ohne Probleme geklappt.“). Also used as a short answer meaning “no problem / sure” (though „kein Problem“ is even more common).
target_language_example: Die Anmeldung hat ohne Probleme funktioniert.
native_language_example: The registration worked without any problems.

additional_notes: Used to say something is easy to do or happens easily. Often used with verbs like „gehen“ (to work/go), „schaffen“ (to manage), or „bewältigen“ (to cope). Similar in meaning to „ohne Probleme“ or „problemlos“.
target_language_example: Ich habe die Prüfung ohne Schwierigkeit bestanden.
native_language_example: I passed the exam without difficulty.

meaning: "speechless" / "no words" (I’m so surprised/shocked I can’t speak).
additional_notes: Used as a reaction to something very surprising, shocking, or unbelievable—often with a negative tone (disbelief, disappointment), but it can also be used positively (amazed). Common as a short standalone comment: "Ohne Worte." Literally "without words."
target_language_example: Was er gestern gesagt hat, hat mich echt sprachlos gemacht – ohne Worte.
native_language_example: What he said yesterday really left me speechless—no words.

additional_notes: Used to express strong certainty in statements (“definitely”). Often placed before the verb or after the subject: “Er ist ohne Zweifel …” or “Ohne Zweifel ist er …”. Can also be used as a short reply meaning “Absolutely.”
target_language_example: Ohne Zweifel ist das die beste Lösung.
native_language_example: Without a doubt, that’s the best solution.

meaning: without thinking; without a second thought.
additional_notes: Often used to say someone reacts immediately or does something automatically/impulsively. It can describe a quick decision (sometimes careless) or simply something done instinctively. Commonly used with verbs like „machen“, „sagen“, „antworten“, „helfen“.
target_language_example: Er hat ohne nachzudenken Ja gesagt.
native_language_example: He said yes without thinking.

meaning: “without (oneself)” — used in the pattern “ohne sich zu + infinitive” = “without (doing something)”.
additional_notes: Most commonly appears in an infinitive clause with *zu*: **ohne sich zu + Verb**. It refers back to the subject and is often used with reflexive verbs (e.g., *sich verabschieden* = to say goodbye, *sich entschuldigen* = to apologize). In English you usually translate it as “without + -ing” rather than literally “without oneself.”
target_language_example: Er ging, ohne sich zu verabschieden.
native_language_example: He left without saying goodbye.

additional_notes: Commonly used with the definite article: „die Olympischen Spiele“ (capitalized as a proper name). You can also specify the season: „die Olympischen Sommerspiele“ (Summer Olympics) / „die Olympischen Winterspiele“ (Winter Olympics).
target_language_example: Dieses Jahr werden die Olympischen Spiele in Paris ausgetragen.
native_language_example: This year the Olympic Games are being held in Paris.

meaning: tidy; proper/decent; (also: really/quite a lot, as an intensifier).
additional_notes: Common as an adjective: "ein ordentliches Zimmer" = a tidy room; "ein ordentlicher Mensch" = a respectable/proper person. Also used adverbially to mean "properly": "Mach das ordentlich!" = Do that properly! In everyday speech it can act as an intensifier meaning "really/quite a lot": "ordentlich Spaß haben" = to have a lot of fun; "ordentlich kalt" = really cold. The meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: Mach bitte dein Zimmer ordentlich.
native_language_example: Please tidy your room.

additional_notes: An adjective often used to say something is the right choice for a situation (“Das ist passend.”). It can also mean that something fits (e.g., clothes) or matches something else. Common pattern: **passend zu + dative** = “matching/appropriate for” (e.g., „passend zu deinem Kleid“).
target_language_example: Ich finde, das ist passend für den Anlass.
native_language_example: I think that’s appropriate for the occasion.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase. Use it to say someone is unlucky in a situation: „Ich habe (heute) Pech.“ You can also say „Pech gehabt!“ meaning “Too bad!” / “Bad luck!” (often when something didn’t work out).
target_language_example: Ich habe Pech gehabt – der Zug ist mir vor der Nase weggefahren.
native_language_example: I had bad luck—the train left right in front of my nose.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive + „zu“ to express an intention or plan. Pattern: „Ich plane, + zu + Infinitiv“ (often with a comma in writing) or „Ich plane zu + Infinitiv“ in simpler sentences. Similar to „vorhaben, … zu …“.
target_language_example: Ich plane, nächstes Jahr nach Berlin zu ziehen.
native_language_example: I’m planning to move to Berlin next year.

meaning: to have space; to fit (have room).
additional_notes: Used to say there is enough room for someone/something. Often with a subject like "das" or "es" (e.g., "Das hat Platz." / "Da ist noch Platz.") and with a destination: "in" + dative ("im Koffer", "im Auto"). In everyday speech you also hear "reinpassen" for "fit".
target_language_example: Der Kofferraum ist klein, aber der Kinderwagen hat noch Platz.
native_language_example: The trunk is small, but the stroller still fits.

meaning: to make room; to move aside.
additional_notes: Often used as an instruction/request when someone is in the way: „Mach bitte Platz!“ (common in everyday situations like buses, queues, doorways). As a verb phrase it’s usually used with the separable verb „Platz machen“: „Ich mache Platz.“ / „Wir machen Platz.“ It can also mean “to clear space” (e.g., on a table).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, können Sie bitte Platz machen?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could you please make room?

meaning: to take a seat; to sit down (polite/formal).
additional_notes: Common polite phrase used by staff or hosts (e.g., in restaurants, waiting rooms): "Bitte nehmen Sie Platz." You can also say "Nehmen Sie bitte Platz." Literally means "take a place/seat."
target_language_example: Bitte nehmen Sie Platz.
native_language_example: Please take a seat.

meaning: to ride a bike; to cycle.
additional_notes: Common everyday verb phrase. Often written as one word in infinitive form: „Radfahren“ (as a noun: „das Radfahren“ = cycling). In a sentence, the verb part is conjugated: „Ich fahre Rad.“ Past: „Ich bin Rad gefahren.“
target_language_example: Ich fahre jeden Tag mit dem Fahrrad zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: I ride my bike to work every day.

meaning: to agree with someone; to say someone is right.
additional_notes: Used with a person in the dative (jemandem): „Ich gebe dir/Ihnen recht.“ Often appears in the structure „Du hast recht“ (you’re right) / „Ich habe recht“ (I’m right). You can also say „Da gebe ich dir recht“ (“I agree with you on that”).
target_language_example: Da muss ich dir recht geben.
native_language_example: I have to agree with you on that.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone’s opinion or statement is correct. Conjugate only the verb "haben" (ich habe recht, du hast recht, er/sie hat recht). The noun "Recht" stays the same. Common phrases: "Du hast recht." (You’re right.), "Ich habe recht." (I’m right.), "Er hatte recht." (He was right.).
target_language_example: Du hast recht, das ist eine gute Idee.
native_language_example: You’re right, that’s a good idea.

meaning: right hand; (figuratively) a trusted assistant / right-hand person.
additional_notes: Often used literally for the physical right hand (e.g., in instructions), and figuratively in the phrase „die rechte Hand (von jemandem)“ meaning someone’s most trusted helper. Capitalization varies: „die rechte Hand“ (right hand) vs. „die Rechte“ (rights/the political right) — different meanings.
target_language_example: Er ist meine rechte Hand im Büro.
native_language_example: He is my right-hand man at the office.

additional_notes: "Reden über" is a common verb + preposition combination. It takes the topic in the accusative case: reden über + Akkusativ (e.g., über das Wetter, über dich, über den Film). Similar options: "sprechen über" (slightly more neutral/formal) and "über etwas reden" (same meaning, different word order).
target_language_example: Können wir über das Problem reden?
native_language_example: Can we talk about the problem?

additional_notes: Used as an adverb ("regularly") or adjective ("regular"). Common with time/frequency phrases like „regelmäßig Sport machen“ (exercise regularly) or „regelmäßige Termine“ (regular appointments).
target_language_example: Ich gehe regelmäßig ins Fitnessstudio.
native_language_example: I go to the gym regularly.

meaning: a Romance language (e.g., French, Spanish, Italian).
additional_notes: Used in linguistics/everyday talk to refer to languages that developed from Latin. Often appears in singular/plural: „eine romanische Sprache“ / „romanische Sprachen“. Don’t confuse with „Roman“ (novel) or „römisch“ (Roman, from Rome).
target_language_example: Spanisch ist eine romanische Sprache.
native_language_example: Spanish is a Romance language.

additional_notes: Commonly used for blushing from embarrassment, shyness, or sometimes anger. It’s an adjective + verb phrase: "rot" (red) + "werden" (to become/turn). In the past tense, "werden" changes to "wurde" ("Er wurde rot").
target_language_example: Als sie das Kompliment hörte, wurde sie rot.
native_language_example: When she heard the compliment, she blushed.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens continuously, day and night (e.g., services, care, work, availability). Often used with verbs like „arbeiten“, „geöffnet sein“, or „erreichbar sein“: „Wir sind rund um die Uhr erreichbar.“
target_language_example: Die Notaufnahme ist rund um die Uhr geöffnet.
native_language_example: The emergency room is open around the clock.

additional_notes: Used as an adverb, often with movement verbs: „rückwärts gehen/fahren/laufen“ (to walk/drive/run backwards). Also common in set phrases like „rückwärts zählen“ (to count backwards) and „rückwärts einparken“ (to reverse park).
target_language_example: Kannst du ein Stück rückwärts fahren?
native_language_example: Can you drive backwards a bit?

meaning: abbr. for „siehe dort“ (“see there”; a written cross-reference).
additional_notes: Used in formal written German (books, academic texts, manuals) to point the reader to another place in the same document, similar to “see there / see above / see below”. Not used in everyday conversation. Often appears in footnotes, indexes, or references.
target_language_example: Weitere Details finden Sie in Kapitel 2; s. d.
native_language_example: You can find further details in chapter 2; see there.

additional_notes: "schon" adds emphasis to "sagen". In an imperative, "Sag schon!" means "Come on, say it already!" (often impatient; informal when using "du"). In statements, it often means "indeed/definitely": "Das kann man schon sagen" = "You can definitely say that."
target_language_example: Das kann man schon sagen.
native_language_example: You can definitely say that.

meaning: to mean; to want to say.
additional_notes: Used when you’re expressing intended meaning or clarifying what someone meant. Often appears in questions like "Was willst du damit sagen?" (What do you mean by that?) or statements like "Ich will sagen, dass …" (What I mean is that …).
target_language_example: Was willst du damit sagen?
native_language_example: What do you mean by that?

meaning: San Francisco (a city in California, USA).
additional_notes: A proper noun (city name). In German it’s usually written the same as in English and used with the preposition "in" (in San Francisco).
target_language_example: Ich war letztes Jahr in San Francisco.
native_language_example: I was in San Francisco last year.

additional_notes: Colloquial spoken form of **schaffe ich** (from **schaffen**). Often used to say you’re able to do something or will succeed/finish it: **Das schaff ich!** = “I can do it!” In careful/formal speech or writing, use **schaffe ich**.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, das schaff ich bis morgen.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll manage it by tomorrow.

meaning: I can’t do it / I won’t manage.
additional_notes: Colloquial spoken phrasing of "Das schaffe ich nicht" (from "schaffen" = to manage). Used to say you can’t do something because it’s too hard, you don’t have time, or you’re not able to. Often followed by what you can’t manage: "Schaff ich heute nicht" (I won’t manage today).
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, ich bin total müde — schaff ich nicht.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m really tired — I can’t do it.

additional_notes: Used to say that something appears to be true (based on what you see/know), without stating it as a certain fact. It’s the verb "scheinen" + "zu" + infinitive (here: "sein"). You can use it with other verbs too (e.g., "scheint zu kommen" = seems to be coming). Common in statements like "Es scheint, dass …" / "Er scheint … zu sein".
target_language_example: Er scheint müde zu sein.
native_language_example: He seems to be tired.

meaning: to go to sleep; to go to bed (to sleep).
additional_notes: Used when you mean you’re going to bed with the intention of sleeping. Very common in everyday speech. Often used with a time: „Ich gehe um 23 Uhr schlafen.“ In separable usage, the verb changes: „Ich gehe schlafen“, „Gehst du schon schlafen?“. You can also say „ins Bett gehen“ for “to go to bed,” sometimes without emphasizing sleeping.
target_language_example: Ich gehe jetzt schlafen.
native_language_example: I’m going to sleep now.

additional_notes: Describes someone’s mood (often temporary). Used with forms of "sein" (to be): "Ich bin schlecht gelaunt" / "Er ist schlecht gelaunt." It can also be used attributively before a noun: "ein schlecht gelaunter Chef" (a bad-tempered boss).
target_language_example: Ich bin heute schlecht gelaunt, weil ich schlecht geschlafen habe.
native_language_example: I’m in a bad mood today because I slept badly.

additional_notes: Used when you feel bad because you did something (or didn’t do something) and think it was wrong. Very common with verbs like „haben“ (to have) and „machen“ (to cause): „Ich habe ein schlechtes Gewissen.“ / „Du machst mir ein schlechtes Gewissen.“
target_language_example: Ich habe ein schlechtes Gewissen, weil ich nicht geholfen habe.
native_language_example: I feel guilty because I didn’t help.

meaning: finally; in the end; after all.
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens at the end of a process ("finally/in the end"), or to justify a point with the sense of “after all” (often when giving a reason or emphasizing what should be obvious). Common in both spoken and written German. Often appears in the middle of a sentence: “Ich habe schließlich keine Zeit.”
target_language_example: Schließlich haben wir ein Taxi gefunden.
native_language_example: In the end, we found a taxi.

meaning: to break up (end a relationship); also: to stop/quit something.
additional_notes: Most commonly used for ending a romantic relationship: „mit jemandem Schluss machen“ = to break up with someone. It can also mean to put an end to an activity or habit: „Schluss machen mit + dative“ (e.g., with smoking). In spoken German you also hear the shorter „Schluss!“ meaning “Stop!” or “That’s enough!”
target_language_example: Ich mache mit ihm Schluss.
native_language_example: I’m breaking up with him.

meaning: to hurry up; to do something quickly.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to be quicker or to do something faster. In everyday speech, it often appears as an imperative: „Mach schnell!“ (Hurry up!). It can also describe doing a task quickly: „Ich muss das schnell machen.“.
target_language_example: Mach schnell, wir müssen los!
native_language_example: Hurry up, we have to go!

additional_notes: Common, very everyday response to calm someone down, accept an apology, or stop a discussion. Tone depends on context: it can sound reassuring (“It’s okay”) or slightly annoyed/dismissive (“Fine, fine”). Often used alone as a short reply.
target_language_example: Schon gut, kein Problem.
native_language_example: It’s okay, no problem.

meaning: for as long as I can remember; always (up to now).
additional_notes: Used to say something has been true since a very long time ago and continues to be true now. Often used with the present tense ("Ich wollte schon immer ...") or perfect ("Ich habe das schon immer gemacht"). It’s stronger/more specific than just "immer" because it emphasizes continuity from the past until now.
target_language_example: Ich wollte schon immer nach Berlin reisen.
native_language_example: I’ve always wanted to travel to Berlin.

additional_notes: Used to say something has been true/going on for a long time up to now. Often appears with the present perfect or present tense: "Ich war schon lange nicht mehr dort" (I haven’t been there in a long time), "Ich kenne ihn schon lange" (I’ve known him for a long time). "schon" adds the idea of "already" or emphasis.
target_language_example: Ich wollte dich schon lange anrufen.
native_language_example: I’ve been meaning to call you for a long time.

meaning: (have) already for a long time; long ago (by now).
additional_notes: Used to say something happened long ago or has been true for a long time already. Often appears with the present perfect or simple past ("Ich habe das schon längst gemacht"), or with "seit"-type ideas to stress that it’s overdue/should be known by now. Word order is flexible: "Das weiß ich schon längst" / "Ich weiß das schon längst."
target_language_example: Ich habe dir das schon längst gesagt.
native_language_example: I told you that a long time ago (already).

additional_notes: Very common in spoken German. Used to ask whether someone has had an experience at least once: "Hast du schon mal ...?" = "Have you ever ...?" It can also mean "before" in statements: "Ich war schon mal in Berlin" = "I've been to Berlin before." Often written as two words ("schon mal"), but you may also see "schonmal" informally.
target_language_example: Hast du schon mal Sushi gegessen?
native_language_example: Have you ever eaten sushi?

meaning: “again” / “once again” (often: “already again,” expressing annoyance or surprise).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken German. Used when something happens repeatedly, sometimes sooner than expected. Often carries an emotional tone (complaint, impatience, surprise): *Schon wieder Regen!* = “Rain again (already)!” Can stand alone as an exclamation or be used in a full sentence.
target_language_example: Schon wieder hast du deinen Schlüssel vergessen.
native_language_example: You forgot your key again.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is responsible for a mistake or problem. Common patterns: „jemandem die Schuld geben“ (to blame someone) and „die Schuld auf jemanden schieben“ (to shift the blame onto someone). Often used with „an“ to say what you blame something on: „Ich gebe dir nicht die Schuld an allem.“
target_language_example: Gib mir nicht die Schuld!
native_language_example: Don’t blame me!

meaning: to be (at) fault; to be to blame.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is responsible for a mistake/problem. Very common with the pattern „an etwas schuld sein“ (= to be to blame for something): „Ich bin schuld an dem Fehler.“ Also common in questions/denials: „Wer ist schuld?“ / „Ich bin nicht schuld.“ Note: „die Schuld“ = guilt/fault; „Schulden“ (plural) = debts (different word).
target_language_example: Ich bin nicht schuld an dem Unfall.
native_language_example: It wasn’t my fault in the accident.

meaning: to owe (money); to be guilty (of something).
additional_notes: "Schuldig sein" has two common uses: (1) owing money: "Ich bin dir 10 Euro schuldig" = I owe you 10 euros; (2) being guilty: "Er ist schuldig" or "Er ist an dem Unfall schuldig" = He is guilty / at fault. For a specific crime, German often uses "schuldig an" + dative: "schuldig an einem Verbrechen". Note: "schuld sein" (without -ig) usually means "to be to blame/at fault" rather than "to owe."
target_language_example: Ich bin dir noch 20 Euro schuldig.
native_language_example: I still owe you 20 euros.

meaning: black hole (in space); also: a place where things disappear (figurative).
additional_notes: Literally “black hole.” Most often used for the astronomy concept (ein schwarzes Loch). In everyday speech it can be used figuratively for something that “swallows” money, time, or items (e.g., paperwork, a messy room).
target_language_example: Meine Socke ist wie in einem schwarzen Loch verschwunden.
native_language_example: My sock disappeared as if into a black hole.

meaning: to be lucky; to have good luck.
additional_notes: Colloquial idiom used when someone has a stroke of luck (often unexpectedly). You can say it about yourself or someone else: „Du hast (aber) Schwein gehabt!“ = “You got lucky!” Past form is very common: „Schwein gehabt“.
target_language_example: Du hast Schwein gehabt, dass du den letzten Zug noch erwischt hast.
native_language_example: You were lucky that you still caught the last train.

additional_notes: Common way to talk about the activity of swimming (as a plan or hobby). Uses "gehen" (to go) + the infinitive "schwimmen". In the perfect tense, use "sein": "Ich bin schwimmen gegangen."
target_language_example: Wir gehen morgen im See schwimmen.
native_language_example: We’re going swimming in the lake tomorrow.

meaning: to be able to swim; can swim.
additional_notes: Uses the modal verb "können" (can/to be able to) with the infinitive "schwimmen" (to swim). It often answers the question "Kannst du schwimmen?" (Can you swim?). In the negative: "nicht schwimmen können" = "can’t swim" / "not be able to swim."
target_language_example: Ich kann nicht schwimmen.
native_language_example: I can’t swim.

additional_notes: Used to praise something or say it’s going well. Often said by teachers, cashiers, or in everyday conversation. Can also be used as a quick, enthusiastic response (similar to “Great!”).
target_language_example: Das schmeckt sehr gut!
native_language_example: That tastes very good!

meaning: “be it …” / “whether it’s …” (introduces an example or alternative).
additional_notes: Used to name one or more possibilities, often in lists. Common patterns: **„sei es X“** (“be it X”) and **„sei es X oder Y“** (“be it X or Y”). It’s the Konjunktiv form of **sein** + **es**, and is especially common in written/formal German.
target_language_example: Wir helfen dir gerne, sei es bei der Wohnungssuche oder beim Umzug.
native_language_example: We’re happy to help you, whether it’s with apartment hunting or with the move.

additional_notes: Common way to say you do what you said you would. The verb is "(ein) Versprechen halten" (to keep a promise). Change "sein" to match the person: "mein/dein/sein/ihr/unser/euer/Ihr Versprechen halten". You can also say: "Er hält sein Versprechen nicht" (He isn’t keeping his promise).
target_language_example: Du hast gesagt, du kommst — kannst du dein Versprechen halten?
native_language_example: You said you’d come—can you keep your promise?

meaning: to break one’s word (not keep a promise).
additional_notes: Used when someone doesn’t do what they promised or agreed to do. Often refers to a promise, an agreement, or giving someone your word (“jemandem sein Wort geben”). Common in everyday speech and in more formal contexts too.
target_language_example: Er hat sein Wort gebrochen und ist nicht gekommen.
native_language_example: He broke his word and didn’t come.

meaning: to stop it; to leave it alone; to not do it.
additional_notes: Commonly used as an imperative: „Lass es sein!“ = “Stop it!” / “Don’t do that!” It can also mean “to refrain from” in more general statements: „Ich lasse das lieber sein.“ = “I’d better not (do that).” Often appears with a pronoun (es/das) referring to an action or idea: „Lass das!“ / „Lass es!“
target_language_example: Ich lasse das lieber sein.
native_language_example: I’d better not do that.

meaning: for (the past) a week; since a week ago.
additional_notes: Used with the present tense in German to describe an action or state that started one week ago and is still continuing now. Often answers the question „Seit wann?“ (Since when?). Compare: „vor einer Woche“ = a week ago (completed past point in time).
target_language_example: Ich bin seit einer Woche krank.
native_language_example: I’ve been sick for a week.

meaning: for some time (now); for a while.
additional_notes: Used with the present tense to say something started in the past and is still true now. Often answers “since when?” (Seit wann?). Similar to “seit einiger Zeit schon …” (= for quite some time already).
target_language_example: Ich wohne seit einiger Zeit in Berlin.
native_language_example: I’ve been living in Berlin for a while now.

additional_notes: Used with the present tense in German to say something started yesterday and is still true/ongoing now. For completed actions, German often uses "gestern" alone or a different structure. Related patterns: "seit + time point" (seit Montag, seit 2020) and "seitdem" (since then).
target_language_example: Ich bin seit gestern krank.
native_language_example: I’ve been sick since yesterday.

additional_notes: Used with the present tense to say something started today and is still true now. Often answers “Since when?” (Seit wann?). You can add a time of day if needed: „seit heute Morgen“ = since this morning.
target_language_example: Ich bin seit heute in Berlin.
native_language_example: I’ve been in Berlin since today (starting today).

meaning: for a long time; for a long while.
additional_notes: Used with the present tense to say something started in the past and is still true now (duration up to the present). It often answers “Wie lange?” (How long?) and is similar to “seit langer Zeit”.
target_language_example: Ich wohne seit langem in Berlin.
native_language_example: I’ve been living in Berlin for a long time.

meaning: “since when?” (asking from what point in time something has been true).
additional_notes: Used to ask when something started: Seit wann wohnst du hier? It often shows surprise or doubt, similar to “Since when…?” in English. Typical word order: Seit wann + verb + subject …?
target_language_example: Seit wann arbeitest du hier?
native_language_example: Since when have you worked here?

meaning: to think for yourself; to form your own opinion.
additional_notes: Often used to encourage independence in thinking, or to criticize someone for just repeating what others say. Also commonly said as an imperative: "Denk selbst!" (= Think for yourself!).
target_language_example: Du solltest selbst denken und nicht alles glauben, was du online liest.
native_language_example: You should think for yourself and not believe everything you read online.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is obvious or goes without saying, often to reassure or confirm politely. Common as a standalone answer: “Selbstverständlich!” It can also be used in sentences like an adverb: “Das ist selbstverständlich.” / “Selbstverständlich helfe ich dir.”
target_language_example: Selbstverständlich kann ich dir helfen.
native_language_example: Of course I can help you.

additional_notes: Direct, explicit wording. In more polite/formal contexts people often avoid it or use softer phrasing (e.g., "miteinander schlafen" = to sleep with each other).
target_language_example: Sie hatten Sex.
native_language_example: They had sex.

meaning: to make an effort; to try hard.
additional_notes: A very common phrase to say you’re putting effort into something. Use it with a reflexive pronoun that matches the subject: ich gebe mir Mühe, du gibst dir Mühe, er/sie gibt sich Mühe, wir geben uns Mühe, ihr gebt euch Mühe, sie/Sie geben sich Mühe. Often followed by an infinitive with „zu“: „Ich gebe mir Mühe, pünktlich zu sein.“
target_language_example: Ich gebe mir Mühe, Deutsch zu lernen.
native_language_example: I’m making an effort to learn German.

additional_notes: Very common everyday phrase. Used with a reflexive pronoun that matches the subject (ich mache mir…, du machst dir…, er/sie/es macht sich…, wir machen uns…, ihr macht euch…, sie machen sich…). It usually takes "um" + accusative for what you worry about: "sich Sorgen um + Akk." You can also say "Mach dir keine Sorgen!" = “Don’t worry!”
target_language_example: Ich mache mir Sorgen um meine Schwester.
native_language_example: I’m worried about my sister.

meaning: to take your time; not to hurry.
additional_notes: Reflexive phrase (with dative): "Ich lasse mir Zeit" = “I’m taking my time.” Often used to say you don’t want to rush, or to tell someone to slow down. Variations: "Lass dir Zeit!" (Take your time!), "Wir lassen uns Zeit." (We’re taking our time.).
target_language_example: Du kannst dir Zeit lassen, ich warte hier.
native_language_example: You can take your time; I’ll wait here.

meaning: to set off; to start going (to a place).
additional_notes: A common reflexive phrase used when you are leaving and beginning a trip or journey. It often implies you’re starting out now or soon. Typical patterns: „Ich mache mich auf den Weg.“ (I’m setting off.) / „Wir machen uns auf den Weg nach Berlin.“ (We’re setting off for Berlin.)
target_language_example: Ich mache mich jetzt auf den Weg nach Hause.
native_language_example: I'm setting off for home now.

meaning: to not feel well (to feel unwell).
additional_notes: Used to say you’re unwell or not feeling good physically (and sometimes emotionally). The verb is reflexive: ich fühle mich nicht wohl, du fühlst dich nicht wohl, etc. Common in everyday conversation; more formal alternatives include „sich unwohl fühlen“ or „sich nicht gut fühlen“.
target_language_example: Ich fühle mich heute nicht wohl.
native_language_example: I don’t feel well today.

additional_notes: Reflexive phrase: "sich" changes to match the person (ich fühle mich schuldig, du fühlst dich schuldig, er/sie fühlt sich schuldig, wir fühlen uns schuldig, ihr fühlt euch schuldig, sie/Sie fühlen sich schuldig). Often used with "wegen" + Genitive/Dative or "für" + Accusative to say what you feel guilty about (e.g., "wegen meines Fehlers", "für meinen Fehler").
target_language_example: Ich fühle mich schuldig wegen meines Fehlers.
native_language_example: I feel guilty because of my mistake.

additional_notes: Reflexive verb used when two people will meet/see one another. Very common in the phrase “Wir sehen uns” as a casual way to say “See you” or “We’ll see each other.” The reflexive pronoun changes with the subject (ich sehe mich, du siehst dich, wir sehen uns, ihr seht euch).
target_language_example: Wir sehen uns morgen.
native_language_example: See you tomorrow. / We’ll see each other tomorrow.

additional_notes: Reflexive phrase used to emphasize that the subject and object are the same person (often meaning "personally" or "by oneself"). It changes with the person: ich → mich selbst; du → dich selbst; er/sie/es → sich selbst; wir → uns selbst; ihr → euch selbst; sie/Sie → sich selbst.
target_language_example: Du musst dich selbst darum kümmern.
native_language_example: You have to take care of it yourself.
