additional_notes: Often used with a clause introduced by „dass“ (I’m sure that...) or with „ob“ for uncertainty in questions. Common patterns: „Ich bin mir sicher, dass …“ (I’m sure that …), „Bist du sicher?“ (Are you sure?), „Ich bin nicht sicher.“ (I’m not sure.) You can also use it with „über“ + accusative to mean “sure about” something: „Ich bin sicher über den Termin“ (more natural: „Ich bin mir sicher wegen des Termins“ / „Ich bin mir über den Termin sicher“).
target_language_example: Bist du sicher, dass du morgen Zeit hast?
native_language_example: Are you sure that you have time tomorrow?

additional_notes: Common in written German (books, manuals, websites, Wikipedia) to point you to another related section, entry, or link. Also used in messages or emails when you want someone to check an extra file or note. Formal/neutral and mostly used in writing.
target_language_example: Siehe auch Kapitel 3 für weitere Informationen.
native_language_example: See also Chapter 3 for more information.

meaning: “there you go” / “well, look at that” (used to point something out, often with mild surprise).
additional_notes: Used as an interjection when you notice or reveal something (“Look!”). It can be friendly or slightly ironic depending on tone. Often appears when something turns out as expected: “Siehe da, es klappt!” Sometimes also written with an exclamation mark: “Siehe da!”
target_language_example: Siehe da, jetzt funktioniert der Drucker wieder.
native_language_example: Well, look at that—now the printer works again.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is logical/understandable. Very common with questions or negatives: „Ergibt das Sinn?“ (Does that make sense?) / „Das ergibt keinen Sinn.“ (That doesn’t make any sense.). You’ll also see it as „Sinn machen“ in everyday speech, but „Sinn ergeben“ is often considered more standard.
target_language_example: Das ergibt keinen Sinn.
native_language_example: That doesn’t make any sense.

additional_notes: Used to say something is logical or understandable. Very common in spoken German; in formal writing you may also see "Sinn ergeben". Often used in questions and negatives: "Macht das Sinn?" / "Das macht keinen Sinn."
target_language_example: Das macht keinen Sinn.
native_language_example: That doesn't make any sense.

additional_notes: Used to say something has no purpose or makes no sense (an action, plan, discussion, etc.). Often used in phrases like „Das ist sinnlos.“ (“That’s pointless.”) or „Es ist sinnlos, …“ (“It’s pointless to …”).
target_language_example: Es ist sinnlos, darüber zu streiten.
native_language_example: It’s pointless to argue about it.

additional_notes: Used to express urgency in a polite, neutral way in emails, messages, and spoken German. Often shortened in writing to „s. b. w. m.“ or replaced by the more formal „so schnell wie möglich“. You can also hear „so bald wie’s geht“ in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Bitte antworten Sie so bald wie möglich.
native_language_example: Please reply as soon as possible.

additional_notes: Used before a singular noun (masculine/neuter) to point out or emphasize the kind/degree of something: So ein Auto! (“Such a car!”). Often expresses surprise/admiration/annoyance. For feminine nouns use “so eine”, and for plural use “so welche/solche” (or simply “solche”). Can also appear with an adjective: “so ein schönes Wetter” (“such nice weather”).
target_language_example: So ein blöder Fehler!
native_language_example: Such a stupid mistake!

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified thing or situation, often something already mentioned or obvious from context. Very common in everyday speech. Can also express surprise or disapproval ("So etwas!" = "Such a thing!" / "I can't believe that!"). Often followed by a relative clause: "so etwas, das …" or "so etwas wie …" ("something like …").
target_language_example: So etwas habe ich noch nie gesehen.
native_language_example: I've never seen anything like that before.

meaning: meant (it) that way; intended (it) like that.
additional_notes: Usually used after „(nicht)“ to clarify intention, often as an apology or correction: „Das war nicht so gedacht“ = “I didn’t mean it like that.” You’ll also see it with „sein“: „Das ist so gedacht“ / „Das war so gedacht“ = “That’s how it’s meant/intended (to be).”
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, das war nicht so gedacht.
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t mean it like that.

meaning: to be so kind (as to…); a polite way to ask someone to do something.
additional_notes: Used mainly in requests, often in the imperative: „Seien Sie so gut und …“ (formal) / „Sei so gut und …“ (informal singular). It can also appear with „bitte“ and is similar in tone to “please” or “would you be so kind as to…”.
target_language_example: Seien Sie so gut und schließen Sie die Tür.
native_language_example: Would you be so kind as to close the door?

additional_notes: Used to say something is nearly true or nearly complete. Often placed right before what it modifies: "so gut wie fertig" (almost finished), "so gut wie nie" (almost never). Literally "so good as" → "as good as" → "practically."
target_language_example: Ich bin so gut wie fertig.
native_language_example: I’m almost finished.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens very rarely (close to “never,” but not absolutely). Common in spoken and written German. Often placed near the verb: “Ich gehe so gut wie nie …”.
target_language_example: Ich esse so gut wie nie Fast Food.
native_language_example: I almost never eat fast food.

additional_notes: Used to express acceptance or resignation when something unfortunate, unfair, or unexpected happens—similar to “oh well” or “that’s just how it is.” Often said after a setback or disappointment. Can be said neutrally or with a sigh; in some contexts it can sound a bit dismissive.
target_language_example: Der Zug ist weg – na ja, so ist das Leben.
native_language_example: The train is gone—oh well, that’s life.

meaning: "so long" / "as long as"; also "for so long" (duration).
additional_notes: Often used to talk about a condition or limit: **so lange + clause** = “as long as …” (e.g., *So lange du hier bist, ...*). It can also refer to duration: **so lange** = “for so long” (e.g., *Ich warte schon so lange.*). Spelling: usually two words; before a clause it’s often written **solange** as a conjunction.
target_language_example: So lange du mir hilfst, helfe ich dir auch.
native_language_example: As long as you help me, I’ll help you too.

meaning: “as long as” (for duration), or “as long as / provided that” (condition).
additional_notes:
Used in comparisons and clauses. 
• Duration: means something continues for the same amount of time. Often paired with a clause: „… so lange wie …“. 
• Condition: similar to „solange“ = “as long as / provided that” (something is true). 
Word order: after „wie“ you typically have a normal clause (verb goes to the end if it’s a subordinate clause).
target_language_example: Ich bleibe hier, so lange wie du mich brauchst.
native_language_example: I’ll stay here as long as you need me.

meaning: either way; one way or another; anyway.
additional_notes: Used to say that the result/conclusion is the same regardless of which option happens. Common in everyday speech to wrap up a discussion or decision. Often followed by a comma in writing: „So oder so, …“.
target_language_example: So oder so müssen wir morgen früh los.
native_language_example: Either way, we have to leave early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express urgency: you want something done at the earliest possible time. Often shortened in writing to "s. s. w. m." or simply replaced with "ASAP" in informal contexts. Common in emails and everyday speech: "Bitte antworten Sie so schnell wie möglich."
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte so schnell wie möglich zurückrufen?
native_language_example: Can you please call me back as soon as possible?

meaning: “So be it.” / “Let it be that way.”
additional_notes: Used to accept something (often reluctantly) and move on: “fine, then” in a resigned, formal-ish tone. It’s somewhat old-fashioned/literary; in everyday speech you’ll more often hear “Dann ist das eben so.” or “Na gut.” The form “sei” is the subjunctive of “sein” (to be), giving it a declarative/accepting feel.
target_language_example: Wenn du nicht mitkommen willst, so sei es.
native_language_example: If you don’t want to come along, so be it.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is acting like something is true when it isn’t (or may not be). Often followed by a clause in the subjunctive (Konjunktiv II) for unreal situations: „Er tut so, als ob er krank wäre.“ In everyday speech you may also hear indicative: „… als ob er krank ist.“
target_language_example: Er tut so, als ob er mich nicht kennen würde.
native_language_example: He pretends as if he doesn’t know me.

meaning: something like that; such a thing.
additional_notes: Common in spoken German. Used to refer to an unspecified thing/idea or to point to an example: "so was" = "something like that". Often appears with a negative or surprised reaction ("So was mache ich nicht." = "I don’t do that kind of thing."). In casual speech you’ll also see it written as one word: "sowas".
target_language_example: So was habe ich noch nie gesehen.
native_language_example: I’ve never seen anything like that.

additional_notes:
Commonly used to talk about progress or extent. 
- "so weit" = "so far" in time/progress: "So weit ist alles gut." (So far everything is fine.)
- With comparisons/limits: "so weit wie" = "as far as" / "as much as": "Ich helfe dir, so weit ich kann." (I’ll help you as much/as far as I can.)
- In questions: "Wie weit?" (How far?), but "so weit" answers it: "So weit." (That far.)
target_language_example: So weit habe ich alles verstanden.
native_language_example: So far I’ve understood everything.

meaning: as far as the eye can see.
additional_notes: A fixed idiomatic phrase used to emphasize that something extends very far in every direction (often about landscapes, crowds, fields, water, etc.). Commonly used with verbs like „sehen“ and „(sich) erstrecken“ or in descriptions: „… so weit das Auge reicht.“
target_language_example: Überall waren Felder, so weit das Auge reicht.
native_language_example: Everywhere there were fields, as far as the eye can see.

meaning: to be ready; to be at the point/stage (of something).
additional_notes: Often used to say you’re ready to start or that you’ve progressed to a certain stage. Common on its own: “Ich bin so weit.” = “I’m ready.” Also used with a clause: “so weit sein, dass …” = “to be at the point where …”.
target_language_example: Ich bin so weit, wir können jetzt losgehen.
native_language_example: I’m ready; we can leave now.

meaning: as soon as; once (immediately when something happens).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a time clause: *sobald* + subject + verb (verb goes to the end in the *sobald*-clause). Often paired with a main clause describing what will happen next: *Sobald ich Zeit habe, ...* You can also use it without a second clause when the rest is clear: *Sobald wie möglich.*
target_language_example: Sobald ich fertig bin, rufe ich dich an.
native_language_example: As soon as I’m finished, I’ll call you.

additional_notes: Used to express a condition or time limit: something is true/possible only for the duration that another situation is true. Common patterns: „solange + verb…“ (e.g., „Solange es regnet, …“) and „solange …, bis …“ (“as long as …, until …”).
target_language_example: Du kannst bleiben, solange du möchtest.
native_language_example: You can stay as long as you want.

meaning: “are said to …” / “apparently …” (reported information or a guess).
additional_notes: Used to distance yourself from the information: you’re reporting what you heard or making an assumption, not stating a fact. Very common in news and everyday speech. It often corresponds to English “supposedly” or “is/are said to”. Grammar note: this is usually the modal verb "sollen" (often in present tense) + the particle "wohl" + an infinitive, e.g., "Er soll wohl krank sein."
target_language_example: Er soll wohl krank sein.
native_language_example: He’s apparently (said to be) sick.

additional_notes: Often used to say there is nothing more, or to ask if someone wants/needs anything else. In a shop or at a restaurant you might hear: „Sonst noch etwas?“ (“Anything else?”). As an answer, „Sonst nichts.“ means “Nothing else.”
target_language_example: Ich nehme einen Kaffee, sonst nichts.
native_language_example: I’ll have a coffee, nothing else.

additional_notes: Used to exclude everyone other than the person(s) already mentioned. Often appears in short answers or with verbs like „kommt“, „weiß“, „war“: „Sonst niemand.“ / „Sonst niemand kommt.“ Literally „otherwise nobody“ (sonst = otherwise/else; niemand = nobody).
target_language_example: Kommt sonst niemand zur Party?
native_language_example: Isn’t anyone else coming to the party?

additional_notes: Used very often at the end of a conversation or transaction to check if there’s more the other person wants (e.g., in shops, restaurants, at the doctor’s). Can be a standalone question: “Sonst noch?” or expanded: “Haben Sie sonst noch etwas?” / “Möchtest du sonst noch was?”.
target_language_example: Sonst noch etwas?
native_language_example: Anything else?

meaning: to take care of; to ensure; to provide for.
additional_notes: Common verb + preposition used with an accusative object: für + Akk. Meanings vary by context: (1) care/provide: für jemanden/etwas sorgen (take care of someone/something; provide for). (2) ensure/cause: für etwas sorgen (make sure something happens; see to it). Often used in everyday situations about responsibilities, safety, food, childcare, etc.
target_language_example: Ich sorge für die Kinder, während du einkaufst.
native_language_example: I’ll take care of the kids while you shop.

additional_notes: Most often used reflexively: „sich Sorgen machen“ = to worry. Common patterns: „Ich mache mir Sorgen.“ (I’m worried.) / „Mach dir keine Sorgen!“ (Don’t worry!) / „sich Sorgen um + accusative“ (to worry about someone/something): „Ich mache mir Sorgen um dich.“ You can also say „Sorgen machen“ without „sich“ to mean “to cause worries”: „Das macht mir Sorgen.“
target_language_example: Ich mache mir Sorgen um meine Mutter.
native_language_example: I’m worried about my mother.

meaning: so much; so many; as much as (in fixed expressions).
additional_notes: Most commonly written as two words: **so viel** (e.g., *so viel Geld* = “so much money”, *so viele Leute* = “so many people”). The one-word spelling **soviel** is mainly seen in set phrases meaning “as much as / as far as”: **soviel ich weiß** (“as far as I know”), **soviel ich mich erinnere** (“as far as I remember”).
target_language_example: Soviel ich weiß, kommt er morgen.
native_language_example: As far as I know, he’s coming tomorrow.

meaning: 'as far as' / 'insofar as' (also: 'as long as', depending on context).
additional_notes:
Often used to limit a statement to what you know or to a certain condition.

Common patterns:
- „soweit ich weiß …“ = “as far as I know …”
- „soweit möglich“ = “as far as possible”
- „soweit …, (dann) …“ can mean “as long as …, (then) …” when it introduces a condition.
target_language_example: Soweit ich weiß, kommt der Zug um 18 Uhr.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the train arrives at 6 p.m.

meaning: "as far as I know" / "to the best of my knowledge."
additional_notes: Used to show that you’re not 100% sure and are sharing what you currently believe is true. Common in answers or when giving information politely. Often followed by a full statement: "Soweit ich weiß, ..."
target_language_example: Soweit ich weiß, fährt der Zug um 18 Uhr ab.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the train leaves at 6 p.m.

meaning: to be ready; to be at that stage / that far (along).
additional_notes: Used to say you’ve reached a certain point in a process, plan, or development. Often with "noch nicht" (not yet): "Ich bin noch nicht so weit." You’ll also hear it as "soweit sein" in writing, but it’s typically spoken/written as two words: "so weit".
target_language_example: Wir sind jetzt so weit, dass wir anfangen können.
native_language_example: We’re ready now; we can start.

additional_notes: Used to say that up to now everything is going well, often with an implied “but we’ll see what happens next.” Common in conversation and in written updates. Can also introduce a problem or next step: “Soweit so gut, aber …”
target_language_example: Soweit so gut, aber wir müssen noch auf die Antwort warten.
native_language_example: So far, so good, but we still have to wait for the reply.

additional_notes: Common in written and formal German to link two items or add information. It often connects nouns or short phrases: "X sowie Y" = "X as well as Y." It can also link clauses meaning "as well as/and also" (similar to "außerdem"), but it’s less common in casual speech than "und".
target_language_example: Wir brauchen Brot sowie Milch.
native_language_example: We need bread as well as milk.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a single social media platform or channel (e.g., Instagram, TikTok). The plural is often used for the general concept: „soziale Medien“ = social media. You may also see „Social Media“ used in German, but „soziale Medien“ is the more common German phrasing.
target_language_example: Instagram ist ein soziales Medium, das viele Leute täglich nutzen.
native_language_example: Instagram is a social media platform that many people use every day.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone can speak Spanish, or to ask if they do. In the present tense: „Ich spreche Spanisch.“ / „Sprichst du Spanisch?“ You can replace „Spanisch“ with other languages (e.g., „Deutsch sprechen“, „Englisch sprechen“).
target_language_example: Sprichst du Spanisch?
native_language_example: Do you speak Spanish?

meaning: to go for a walk (for pleasure).
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase for taking a leisurely walk (often shorter and more relaxed than "wandern" = to hike). In the present tense it’s often split: "Ich gehe spazieren." Past: "Ich bin spazieren gegangen." You can add where/with whom: "im Park", "mit dem Hund".
target_language_example: Wir gehen nach dem Essen im Park spazieren.
native_language_example: After the meal, we go for a walk in the park.

meaning: to have fun; to enjoy yourself.
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase. Use it for enjoying an activity/event: "Wir haben Spaß" (We’re having fun). You can also say "Spaß an + dative" to mean “to enjoy/take pleasure in” something (e.g., "Spaß an Musik haben"). Often used in the imperative: "Hab Spaß!" (Have fun!).
target_language_example: Wir hatten gestern auf der Party viel Spaß.
native_language_example: We had a lot of fun at the party yesterday.

meaning: to be fun; to be enjoyable (literally: “to make fun”).
additional_notes: Used to say an activity is fun or that someone is enjoying it. Common patterns: „Das macht Spaß.“ = “That’s fun.” / „Es macht (mir) Spaß, …“ = “I enjoy … / It’s fun (for me) to …”. Not to be confused with „Spaß machen“ meaning “to joke around / kid” in some contexts (then you’ll often hear „nur Spaß“ = “just kidding”).
target_language_example: Es macht Spaß, Deutsch zu lernen.
native_language_example: It’s fun to learn German.

additional_notes: Uses the formal “Sie” form, appropriate with strangers, in shops, or in professional situations. Often used as a question: “Sprechen Sie Deutsch?” You can add “?” in writing and raise intonation when speaking. Informal version to one person: “Sprichst du Deutsch?”
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, sprechen Sie Deutsch?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you speak German?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask one person (a stranger, service staff, someone you don’t know well) whether they speak English. "Sie" is the formal 'you' in German, so the verb is "sprechen". In a full question you’ll often hear: "Sprechen Sie Englisch?" (with a question mark and rising intonation). For friends/peers you’d use informal: "Sprichst du Englisch?".
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, sprechen Sie Englisch?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you speak English?

additional_notes: Common verb + preposition combo: **über** means “about.” Use it when the topic is a thing, idea, or situation. Structure: **über + accusative** (e.g., *über das Wetter*, *über ihn*, *über meine Pläne*). For talking about a person, you can also use **über jemanden sprechen** (can sometimes sound like “talking about someone behind their back,” depending on context).
target_language_example: Wir sprechen über das Wetter.
native_language_example: We’re talking about the weather.

additional_notes: Common way to ask someone if they can speak English. Use with a question mark and rising intonation: „Sprichst du Englisch?“ This uses informal „du“ (for friends, peers, kids). For a more formal/polite version, say: „Sprechen Sie Englisch?“ You can also add „(ein bisschen)“: „Sprichst du (ein bisschen) Englisch?“
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, sprichst du Englisch?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you speak English?

meaning: to stand up for; to advocate for (also: to encourage/embolden someone).
additional_notes: Often used as reflexive: "sich stark machen für + Akk." = to campaign/advocate for something (show strong support). With a person as object: "jemanden stark machen" can mean to encourage/embolden someone (make them feel confident).
target_language_example: Ich mache mich für mehr Klimaschutz stark.
native_language_example: I’m advocating for more climate protection.

meaning: to stop (moving) and remain standing; to come to a standstill.
additional_notes: Common with people, vehicles, and machines. With a person it often means to stop walking and not move: „Bleib stehen!“ = “Stop!” / “Stay where you are!” With transport it means to stop running: „Der Zug bleibt stehen.“ = “The train comes to a standstill.” In the perfect tense: „ist stehen geblieben“.
target_language_example: Ich bin stehen geblieben, weil die Ampel rot war.
native_language_example: I stopped because the traffic light was red.

additional_notes: Basic verb meaning “to die” (a person/animal stops living). It’s fairly direct; in sensitive contexts people may choose softer alternatives like „versterben“ (more formal) or „einschlafen“ (literally “fall asleep,” used euphemistically, especially about pets/children). Conjugation: ich sterbe, du stirbst, er/sie/es stirbt; Präteritum: starb; Perfekt: ist gestorben (uses „sein“).
target_language_example: Sein Großvater ist letztes Jahr gestorben.
native_language_example: His grandfather died last year.

additional_notes: Common spoken tag question used to ask for confirmation or agreement. Very informal contraction of “stimmt es?”; in writing you’ll also see “Stimmt’s?” as a standalone question, or at the end of a sentence like “..., stimmt’s?”.
target_language_example: Du kommst morgen, stimmt's?
native_language_example: You’re coming tomorrow, right?

additional_notes: Used with „auf“ + accusative to say what you’re proud of: „Ich bin stolz auf dich.“ You can also be proud of something you did: „Ich bin stolz auf meine Arbeit.“ Note: „stolz“ is an adjective and „sein“ is the verb (often conjugated: „ich bin“, „du bist“, „er/sie ist“).
target_language_example: Ich bin stolz auf dich.
native_language_example: I’m proud of you.

additional_notes: Means something happens repeatedly over many days, often with a sense of routine or monotony. Commonly used with verbs like „passieren“, „machen“, „wiederholen“ (e.g., „Tag für Tag das Gleiche“ = the same thing day after day).
target_language_example: Tag für Tag steht er früh auf und geht zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: Day after day, he gets up early and goes to work.

meaning: day and night; around the clock (continuously).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens all the time or without stopping. Often with verbs like arbeiten (to work), lernen (to study), regnen (to rain), or denken an (to think about). Also common in the phrase „Tag und Nacht“ = “24/7.”
target_language_example: Sie arbeitet Tag und Nacht an dem Projekt.
native_language_example: She works on the project day and night.

additional_notes: Common verb phrase with "spielen" (to play). You can say: "Ich spiele Tennis" (I play tennis) or "Spielst du Tennis?" (Do you play tennis?). For an invitation: "Willst du Tennis spielen?" (Do you want to play tennis?).
target_language_example: Am Samstag spiele ich mit meiner Freundin Tennis.
native_language_example: On Saturday I’m playing tennis with my friend.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true even though there were problems, bad news, or reasons against it. Often introduces a contrast: "Es war schwierig, aber trotz allem ..." You can also hear the very similar "trotzdem" ("nevertheless"), which is slightly more common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Es hat den ganzen Tag geregnet, aber trotz allem hatten wir Spaß.
native_language_example: It rained all day, but we still had fun.

additional_notes: Used to contrast with what was just said: something happens even though there’s a reason it might not. It can stand at the start of a sentence (Trotzdem gehe ich …) or after the verb (Ich gehe trotzdem …). Often equivalent to “despite that” or “even so.”
target_language_example: Es regnet, aber ich gehe trotzdem spazieren.
native_language_example: It’s raining, but I’m going for a walk anyway.

additional_notes: Abbreviation for **unter Umständen**. Common in written German (emails, notes, reports) to mean that something may happen depending on the circumstances; in speech people usually say **unter Umständen** or **möglicherweise**. Often used to soften a statement or express uncertainty.
target_language_example: Das kann u. U. zu Verzögerungen führen.
native_language_example: That could possibly lead to delays.

additional_notes: Common in written German (emails, articles, lists). It signals that the list is not complete. „u. a.“ = among other things; „u. a. m.“ = among other things (and more). In speech, people usually say „unter anderem“ instead of the abbreviation.
target_language_example: Wir verkaufen u. a. Bücher, Spiele und Elektronik.
native_language_example: We sell, among other things, books, games, and electronics.

meaning: (for a clock/watch) to run / work; to keep time.
additional_notes: Used mainly with a subject: "Die Uhr geht." = the clock/watch is running (not stopped). Very often you add an adverb to say whether it’s fast or slow: "Die Uhr geht vor" (it’s fast) / "Die Uhr geht nach" (it’s slow). Also common: "Meine Uhr geht nicht." (My watch doesn’t work / is stopped).
target_language_example: Meine Uhr geht fünf Minuten vor.
native_language_example: My watch is five minutes fast.

additional_notes: Common polite phrase. Often used with a person you’re asking: „jemanden um Hilfe bitten“ (to ask someone for help). Similar alternatives: „um Hilfe fragen“ (also common) and the direct request „Kannst du/Können Sie mir helfen?“ (Can you help me?).
target_language_example: Ich muss dich um Hilfe bitten.
native_language_example: I have to ask you for help.

additional_notes: Used when you ask someone for guidance or an opinion. Common patterns: „jemanden um Rat fragen“ (to ask someone for advice) and „jemanden um einen Rat bitten“ (slightly more formal). The noun „Rat“ is usually uncountable in this phrase, but you can also say „einen Rat“ when referring to one specific piece of advice.
target_language_example: Ich werde meine Mutter um Rat fragen.
native_language_example: I will ask my mother for advice.

meaning: “for the life of me / in the world” (used to express strong surprise, confusion, or emphasis).
additional_notes: Used in questions or exclamations to intensify emotion, like “Why on earth…?” or “How in the world…?”. Often paired with question words: "Warum um alles in der Welt…?", "Wie um alles in der Welt…?". It’s strong emphasis but not slang; it can sound dramatic/annoyed depending on tone.
target_language_example: Warum um alles in der Welt hast du das gemacht?
native_language_example: Why on earth did you do that?

additional_notes: Commonly used to say something is very close by, often a short walk away (e.g., a shop, café, or station). You can use it with verbs like „sein“ (to be) or „liegen“ (to be located): „Der Supermarkt ist um die Ecke.“ It can also be used more literally to mean turning a corner: „Geh um die Ecke und dann links.“
target_language_example: Der Bäcker ist gleich um die Ecke.
native_language_example: The bakery is just around the corner.

meaning: around (someone’s) ears; often used in phrases meaning 'to throw/hit (something) at/around someone’s head.'
additional_notes: Commonly appears in fixed expressions like **jemandem etwas um die Ohren hauen/werfen/schlagen** (to smack/throw something at someone; also figuratively: to confront someone harshly with facts or accusations). Less commonly, **etwas um die Ohren fliegen** means something 'goes flying around your ears' (i.e., explodes or breaks violently nearby). On its own it’s not usually used as a complete phrase; it’s typically part of these verb phrases.
target_language_example: Er hat mir die Wahrheit um die Ohren gehauen.
native_language_example: He threw the truth in my face.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an honest opinion or a (sometimes slightly uncomfortable) truth. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence; also commonly appears as the shorter variant "um ehrlich zu sein" (to be honest).
target_language_example: Um die Wahrheit zu sagen, habe ich keine Lust heute auszugehen.
native_language_example: To tell the truth, I don’t feel like going out today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an approximate point in time in the past or future. Common with past tense ("um die Zeit war ich ...") or when recalling events ("Um die Zeit fing es an zu regnen"). For approximate clock times, German more often uses "gegen" (e.g., "gegen drei Uhr" = around 3 o’clock).
target_language_example: Um die Zeit war ich noch in der Schule.
native_language_example: Around that time, I was still in school.

meaning: around this time (of day/year); at about this time.
additional_notes: Used to refer to an approximate time, often with a sense of “roughly now” (today) or “roughly then” (in the past/future). Common with past or habitual statements: "Um diese Zeit war ich schon zu Hause" (around this time I was already home). Not to be confused with "zu dieser Zeit", which is closer to “at that time” (less emphasis on approximation).
target_language_example: Um diese Zeit ist es hier normalerweise sehr voll.
native_language_example: Around this time, it’s usually very crowded here.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a frank opinion or confession, often softening what follows. Very common in spoken and informal written German. Often followed by a main clause: "Um ehrlich zu sein, ..." Variants: "ehrlich gesagt" (honestly, frankly).
target_language_example: Um ehrlich zu sein, habe ich keine Lust heute auszugehen.
native_language_example: To be honest, I don’t feel like going out today.

additional_notes: Used to say the exact time when something happens. "um" + time (clock time) = "at" (a specific time). Often used without "Uhr" when it’s clear you mean a time (e.g., "um fünf"); with minutes you can say "um 5:15" or "um fünf Uhr fünfzehn".
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns um fünf Uhr.
native_language_example: We’re meeting at five o’clock.

meaning: at any cost; no matter what.
additional_notes: Means you are determined to do something even if it has negative consequences or requires big sacrifices. Often used to criticize someone’s attitude ("not at any price" = "um keinen Preis").
target_language_example: Er will um jeden Preis gewinnen.
native_language_example: He wants to win at any cost.

additional_notes: Used with reflexive pronoun „sich“ to mean the area around a person/thing, often in set phrases like „um sich sehen“ (look around), „um sich greifen“ (spread / take hold), „um sich schlagen“ (hit out, flail), or „(etwas) um sich werfen“ (throw something around).
target_language_example: Sie sah sich um und suchte ihren Schlüssel.
native_language_example: She looked around and searched for her key.

additional_notes: Used to ask for a specific clock time. Often used with meetings, appointments, departures, etc. Common alternatives: "Um wie viel Uhr?" (more common in everyday speech) and "Zu welcher Zeit?" (more formal/less common). Word order often continues with the verb: "Um welche Zeit fängt es an?"
target_language_example: Um welche Zeit beginnt der Unterricht?
native_language_example: At what time does the class start?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the size of a difference or change (increase/decrease). Often appears with comparatives or change verbs like „steigen“ (to rise), „sinken“ (to fall), or „sich erhöhen/verringern“ (to increase/decrease): „Um wie viel ist X teurer?“ / „Um wie viel steigt der Preis?“ Also used with amounts/units: „Um wie viel Uhr…?“ is a different phrase (time) and not the same as „um wie viel“ (difference).
target_language_example: Um wie viel ist das Ticket teurer als gestern?
native_language_example: By how much is the ticket more expensive than yesterday?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a specific clock time, often when arranging plans. Common word order: “Um wie viel Uhr …?” or “Um wie viel Uhr ist/sind …?” (e.g., “Um wie viel Uhr geht der Zug?”). Often interchangeable with “Wann …?” but “um wie viel Uhr” is more precise (expects a time like 7:30).
target_language_example: Um wie viel Uhr fängt der Film an?
native_language_example: What time does the movie start?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a specific clock time (hours/minutes). Common in questions about schedules and appointments. Often followed by a verb: “Um wieviel Uhr fängt es an?” You can also say “Um wieviel Uhr ist …?” or, more commonly in everyday speech, “Um wieviel Uhr …?” / “Wann …?”
target_language_example: Um wieviel Uhr beginnt der Film?
native_language_example: At what time does the movie start?

meaning: to die (often in an accident/disaster); to perish.
additional_notes: Used for deaths in accidents, disasters, or violent events: "Bei dem Unfall sind drei Menschen umgekommen." Also used in the pattern "umkommen vor + Dativ" meaning "to be overwhelmed/swamped" (literally "to perish from"), e.g. "Ich komme in Arbeit um" = "I’m swamped with work" (more colloquial).
target_language_example: Bei dem Brand sind zwei Menschen umgekommen.
native_language_example: Two people died in the fire.

meaning: to be killed; to lose one’s life (often in an accident or disaster).
additional_notes: A fixed expression meaning someone dies as a result of an external event (accident, war, catastrophe). It’s used in news and serious contexts; the focus is often on the circumstances rather than on the person’s action. Grammar: comes with "sein" (ist ums Leben gekommen) and commonly appears in the past (Präteritum/Perfekt). It is not the same as "um sein Leben kommen" (to lose one’s life) in the sense of dying naturally; it typically implies an incident.
target_language_example: Bei dem Unfall sind zwei Menschen ums Leben gekommen.
native_language_example: Two people were killed in the accident.

meaning: for free; or: in vain (for nothing).
additional_notes: "Umsonst" has two common meanings. (1) "for free" (no cost): "Der Eintritt ist umsonst." (2) "in vain" / "for nothing" (effort without success): "Die Arbeit war umsonst." Context usually makes it clear which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Der Eintritt ist heute umsonst, aber wir sind umsonst hingefahren, weil das Museum zu war.
native_language_example: Admission is free today, but we drove there for nothing because the museum was closed.

additional_notes: Used as an adjective: *ein unbekannter Mann* (an unknown man), *mir ist das unbekannt* (I’m not familiar with that / that’s unknown to me). You’ll also see it as a label meaning “Unknown,” e.g., on caller ID (*Unbekannt*). Often contrasts with *bekannt* (known, famous).
target_language_example: Die Nummer ist mir unbekannt.
native_language_example: The number is unknown to me (I don’t recognize the number).

additional_notes: Used as an emphatic confirmation, often as a standalone answer to a yes/no question. It can also introduce a strong statement (“und ob ich …!” = “of course I …!”). More informal and punchy than “ja, natürlich”.
target_language_example: Kommst du morgen? – Und ob!
native_language_example: Are you coming tomorrow? – You bet!

meaning: “and so on; etc.” (and sometimes: “and stuff like that”).
additional_notes: Used to indicate an incomplete list or to avoid listing everything. Often follows examples: “Ich habe Obst gekauft: Äpfel, Bananen und so.” In casual speech it can also soften or trail off a thought (similar to “and all that”), but in writing it’s usually the straightforward “etc.”.
target_language_example: Wir können Pizza, Pasta und so bestellen.
native_language_example: We can order pizza, pasta, and so on.

additional_notes: Used to indicate that a list could continue (like English “etc.”). Often shortened to “usw.” in writing. Common after examples: “Ich brauche Milch, Brot und so weiter.”
target_language_example: Wir müssen noch einkaufen: Obst, Gemüse und so weiter.
native_language_example: We still have to shop: fruit, vegetables, and so on.

additional_notes: Often used as a short, emphatic reply to confirm something strongly. Frequently appears as “Und wie!” with an exclamation mark. Literally it looks like “and how,” but in this idiomatic use it means a very strong “yes” or “definitely,” not a real question.
target_language_example: Kommst du morgen? – Und wie!
native_language_example: Are you coming tomorrow? — You bet!

additional_notes: Used to introduce a more precise detail, clarification, or exact information about what was just said. Very common in spoken and written German. Often followed by the specific item, number, time, or explanation (similar to “namely,” “to be precise,” “I mean:”).
target_language_example: Ich brauche zwei Tickets, und zwar für morgen Abend.
native_language_example: I need two tickets—namely for tomorrow evening.

additional_notes: An adjective used to describe something that is not normal or typical. Often used with "sein" (to be): "Das ist ungewöhnlich." Opposite: "gewöhnlich" (usual/normal). Comparative/superlative: "ungewöhnlicher", "am ungewöhnlichsten".
target_language_example: Das ist ein ungewöhnlicher Name.
native_language_example: That’s an unusual name.

meaning: to be wrong (to not be right).
additional_notes: Used to say someone’s opinion or statement is incorrect. Often appears as "Du hast unrecht" (informal) or "Sie haben unrecht" (formal). Note: It’s usually written as two words: "Unrecht haben" (noun + verb). The opposite is "recht haben" (“to be right”).
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, aber da hast du Unrecht.
native_language_example: Sorry, but you’re wrong about that.

additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like „haben“ (to have) and „bekommen“ (to get): „Ich habe es unter Kontrolle“ = “I have it under control.” Also used to describe a situation that is managed or not chaotic: „Die Lage ist unter Kontrolle“ = “The situation is under control.”
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich habe alles unter Kontrolle.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I have everything under control.

additional_notes: Means “maybe/it depends,” often used to show something is not certain. Commonly followed by a conditional clause (often with „wenn …“), e.g., „Unter Umständen komme ich später“ (= I might come later). More formal/neutral than „vielleicht“ in many contexts.
target_language_example: Unter Umständen kann ich morgen früher kommen, wenn das Meeting ausfällt.
native_language_example: I might be able to come earlier tomorrow if the meeting is canceled.

meaning: under all circumstances; no matter what.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something must happen (or must not happen) in every situation. Common with verbs like „müssen“ (must) or in warnings/advice: „Das darf unter keinen Umständen passieren.“ Note: „unter allen Umständen“ = in any/every case; „unter keinen Umständen“ = under no circumstances.
target_language_example: Du musst unter allen Umständen pünktlich sein.
native_language_example: You must be on time under all circumstances.

additional_notes: Used to mention one or more examples without listing everything. Very common in both spoken and written German. It can refer to things ("among other things") or people ("among others"). Often placed after the verb or before the item(s) being highlighted: "Wir haben unter anderem ..." / "Unter anderem haben wir ...".
target_language_example: Wir haben unter anderem Berlin und München besucht.
native_language_example: We visited Berlin and Munich, among other places.

additional_notes: Used to mention one or more examples from a larger group (often like “among other things/people”). It typically follows what it refers to: „Ich habe unter anderen Anna eingeladen.“ = “I invited Anna, among others.” Common variants: „unter anderem“ (singular) = “among other things / for example,” and „unter anderem“ is more common than „unter anderen“ in everyday German.
target_language_example: Ich habe unter anderem in Berlin und Hamburg gewohnt.
native_language_example: I have lived in Berlin and Hamburg, among other places.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens outside, not inside a building. Common with activities like sleeping, camping, concerts, markets, or events held outside. Often appears with verbs like schlafen (to sleep), campen (to camp), übernachten (to stay overnight), feiern (to celebrate), or stattfinden (to take place).
target_language_example: Wir haben unter freiem Himmel geschlafen.
native_language_example: We slept outdoors (under the open sky).

additional_notes: Used to signal that something should stay private or not be shared with others. Common in phrases like "Unter uns gesagt, …" (“Between us, … / Just between us, …”). It can also describe a relaxed, informal atmosphere among friends: "Wir sind hier unter uns" (“It’s just us here”).
target_language_example: Unter uns gesagt: Ich mag meinen Job nicht.
native_language_example: Just between us: I don’t like my job.

meaning: in private; one-on-one (just the two of us).
additional_notes: Used when you want to speak without other people listening. Often follows verbs like „sprechen“, „reden“, or „besprechen“: „Können wir unter vier Augen sprechen?“ Literally “under four eyes,” meaning two people (each with two eyes).
target_language_example: Können wir kurz unter vier Augen sprechen?
native_language_example: Can we talk privately for a moment?

meaning: among each other; between one another.
additional_notes: Used when several people or things interact within the group (not with outsiders). Common with verbs like sprechen/reden (talk), sich verstehen (get along), teilen (share), tauschen (exchange), vergleichen (compare), and with "sich" (reflexive) for mutual actions: "Sie helfen sich untereinander." Also used with "und" to mean “with/among each other”: "Die Kinder spielen untereinander."
target_language_example: Wir sollten das untereinander klären.
native_language_example: We should sort that out among ourselves.

meaning: to go down (set), to sink; to perish/go under.
additional_notes: Most common with the sun: „Die Sonne geht unter.“ = “The sun sets.” In the present tense it splits: „(sie) geht unter“, „(wir) gehen unter“. Also used literally for sinking (boats) and figuratively for failing/perishing (e.g., a business). Not the same as English “to undergo” (false friend).
target_language_example: Die Sonne geht heute um 18 Uhr unter.
native_language_example: The sun sets today at 6 p.m.

meaning: to find a place to stay; to be accommodated/put up (somewhere).
additional_notes: Often used when you need lodging, especially short-term: *Wo kann ich unterkommen?* = “Where can I stay?” It can also mean being placed somewhere by someone else: *Er ist bei Freunden untergekommen.* In the perfect tense it usually takes **sein**: *Ich bin bei meiner Schwester untergekommen.*
target_language_example: Können wir heute Nacht irgendwo unterkommen?
native_language_example: Can we find somewhere to stay tonight?

meaning: to be on the way; to be out and about (travelling).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is currently traveling somewhere or not at home (e.g., out running errands). Often with a destination: „Ich bin nach Berlin unterwegs.“ Also common without a destination: „Ich bin gerade unterwegs“ (= I’m on my way / I’m out right now).
target_language_example: Sorry, ich bin gerade unterwegs und kann nicht telefonieren.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m on my way / out right now and can’t talk on the phone.

additional_notes: Often used with **mit + dative**: *mit etwas verbunden* = connected to/linked with something. Also common: *miteinander verbunden* (connected with each other) and *sich (jemandem) verbunden fühlen* (to feel connected/indebted to someone).
target_language_example: Mein Handy ist mit dem WLAN verbunden.
native_language_example: My phone is connected to the Wi‑Fi.

additional_notes: Usually appears as **die Vereinigten Staaten** (plural) and is often shortened to **die USA**. In formal contexts you may also see **die Vereinigten Staaten von Amerika**. Because it’s plural, use plural grammar: **die Vereinigten Staaten sind ...**
target_language_example: Die Vereinigten Staaten sind ein großes Land.
native_language_example: The United States is a big country.

additional_notes: Used for products, appointments, rooms, tickets, information, or people’s time. Common in shops and online (e.g., "nicht verfügbar" = "not available"). Often used with "sein": "Ist das noch verfügbar?"
target_language_example: Ist dieses Zimmer heute Abend noch verfügbar?
native_language_example: Is this room still available tonight?

additional_notes: Used to say that an effort had no success. Often appears with verbs like „versuchen“ (to try), „warten“ (to wait), or „suchen“ (to search): „vergebens warten/suchen/versuchen“. Similar to „umsonst“, but „umsonst“ can also mean “free (no cost)”, while „vergebens“ only means “in vain”.
target_language_example: Ich habe vergebens versucht, dich anzurufen.
native_language_example: I tried to call you, but it was in vain.

meaning: in vain; unsuccessfully (without achieving the desired result).
additional_notes: Used to say that an effort didn’t work out or was pointless because it didn’t lead to success. Common with verbs like „versuchen“ (to try), „suchen“ (to search), „warten“ (to wait), and phrases like „vergeblich hoffen“ (to hope in vain).
target_language_example: Ich habe vergeblich versucht, ihn anzurufen.
native_language_example: I tried to call him in vain.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a comparison between two things. It’s the past participle of "vergleichen" (to compare) plus "mit" (with), and it’s often followed by a noun/pronoun: "Verglichen mit letztem Jahr..." You may also see the synonym "im Vergleich zu" (in comparison to).
target_language_example: Verglichen mit letztem Jahr ist es heute viel wärmer.
native_language_example: Compared with last year, it’s much warmer today.

meaning: the wrong way around; upside down/backwards.
additional_notes: Used to say something is oriented incorrectly (e.g., reversed, inside out, upside down). Often describes how you put on clothes or how an object is placed. Common variants: „falsch herum“ (wrong way around), „andersherum“ (the other way around).
target_language_example: Du hast das T-Shirt verkehrt herum an.
native_language_example: You’re wearing the T-shirt the wrong way around.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “familiar/known well” (a situation, place, face, voice, etc.). Often used with **sein**: **Mir ist das vertraut.** (“That’s familiar to me.”) You’ll also see **mit + Dativ**: **mit etwas vertraut sein** = “to be familiar with something.” In other contexts it can mean “trusted/confidential” (e.g., **ein vertrauter Freund** = “a trusted friend”).
target_language_example: Ich bin mit dem Programm schon vertraut.
native_language_example: I’m already familiar with the program.

additional_notes: Most often used to say someone is related to someone else: „mit jemandem verwandt sein“ or „verwandt mit …“. It can mean family-related (e.g., cousins) and also more generally “related” in meaning or type (e.g., related words/ideas).
target_language_example: Ich bin mit ihr verwandt.
native_language_example: I’m related to her.

additional_notes: A common wish said to someone before an exam, job interview, performance, trip, etc. Often used on its own as an exclamation: “Viel Glück!” You can also use it with “bei” + dative: “Viel Glück bei der Prüfung!” or with “für” + accusative: “Viel Glück für morgen!”
target_language_example: Viel Glück bei der Prüfung!
native_language_example: Good luck on the exam!

additional_notes: Common friendly wish said before someone does an activity (a trip, a party, watching a show, etc.). Often used with verbs: „Viel Spaß beim Lernen!“ (have fun learning) or „Viel Spaß auf der Party!“ (have fun at the party).
target_language_example: Viel Spaß beim Konzert!
native_language_example: Have fun at the concert!

meaning: far too much; way too much.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that an amount is excessive (more than acceptable/needed). Often said about quantity, money, time, food, etc. You can also use it with adjectives/adverbs: "viel zu teuer" (far too expensive), "viel zu spät" (way too late).
target_language_example: Das ist viel zu viel Zucker im Kaffee.
native_language_example: That is way too much sugar in the coffee.

meaning: far too little; way too few.
additional_notes: Used to say that an amount or number is not enough, and it’s not even close. Common in complaints or emphasis. With uncountable nouns (money, time) it means “too little”; with countable plurals (people, chairs) it means “too few.” Often placed before the noun phrase: “viel zu wenig Zeit / viel zu wenige Leute.”
target_language_example: Ich habe viel zu wenig Zeit für diese Aufgabe.
native_language_example: I have far too little time for this task.

additional_notes: A common, polite way to express strong thanks. Used in both spoken and written German (e.g., emails). Often followed by "für ..." to say what you’re thanking someone for: "Vielen Dank für Ihre Hilfe." You can reply with "Gern geschehen" or "Bitte (schön)".
target_language_example: Vielen Dank für Ihre Hilfe!
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your help!

meaning: four-leaf clover (a symbol of good luck).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the rare four-leaf version of a clover, often as a lucky charm. You may also see the phrasing "ein vierblättriges Kleeblatt". Common in wishes and sayings about luck (e.g., finding one).
target_language_example: Ich habe ein vierblättriges Kleeblatt gefunden – das bringt Glück!
native_language_example: I found a four-leaf clover — that brings good luck!

meaning: from the beginning (right from the start).
additional_notes: Used to say something was true or happened starting at the very beginning and continuing from there. Often pairs with verbs like sein (to be), wissen (to know), klar sein (to be clear), or funktionieren (to work). Word order is flexible: you’ll often see it early in the sentence for emphasis (e.g., „Von Anfang an war …“), but it can also appear later.
target_language_example: Von Anfang an war mir klar, dass das nicht klappt.
native_language_example: From the beginning, it was clear to me that this wouldn’t work.

meaning: from scratch; from the ground up.
additional_notes: Means starting completely anew and building something in a thorough, fundamental way (not just making small changes). Often used with verbs like "aufbauen" (build), "neu machen" (do anew), "lernen" (learn), or "verstehen" (understand).
target_language_example: Ich habe Deutsch von Grund auf gelernt.
native_language_example: I learned German from scratch.

additional_notes: Used to say something is someone’s natural trait or default situation, not the result of training or change. Often with adjectives like „schüchtern“, „ruhig“, „optimistisch“ or with states like „(nicht) religiös“. It can also mean “originally” in the sense of where someone is based/from (especially in Austria/Southern German): „Ich bin von Haus aus Wienerin.“
target_language_example: Ich bin von Haus aus eher schüchtern, aber bei Freunden rede ich viel.
native_language_example: By nature I’m rather shy, but with friends I talk a lot.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize genuine, heartfelt feelings—often with thanks, congratulations, or good wishes. Common in phrases like „Danke von Herzen“ (thank you from the bottom of my heart) or „Alles Gute von Herzen“ (heartfelt best wishes).
target_language_example: Danke von Herzen für deine Hilfe.
native_language_example: Thank you from the bottom of my heart for your help.

meaning: from year to year; year by year.
additional_notes: Used to describe something that changes gradually over time when comparing one year with the next (often trends like prices, numbers, or growth). It can also mean that something varies and isn’t stable from one year to the next. Often used with verbs like „steigen“ (rise), „sinken“ (fall), „wachsen“ (grow), or „sich ändern“ (change).
target_language_example: Die Mieten steigen von Jahr zu Jahr.
native_language_example: Rents rise year by year.

additional_notes: Used to say a trait or tendency is innate (not learned). Often placed after the adjective or description: „Er ist von Natur aus ruhig.“ Can also describe something being naturally the case: „Das Material ist von Natur aus wasserabweisend.“
target_language_example: Ich bin von Natur aus eher schüchtern.
native_language_example: I’m naturally rather shy.

meaning: from day to day; day by day.
additional_notes: Used to describe something changing gradually over time or happening on a daily basis. Often used with verbs like „werden“ (to become) or „sich verändern“ (to change), e.g., getting better/worse day by day.
target_language_example: Es wird von Tag zu Tag kälter.
native_language_example: It’s getting colder day by day.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens sometimes but not regularly. Often placed at the beginning or end of a sentence. Similar to: „manchmal“ (sometimes) or „ab und zu“ (now and then).
target_language_example: Ich gehe von Zeit zu Zeit ins Kino.
native_language_example: I go to the cinema from time to time.

meaning: by itself; on its own (without help).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens automatically or without anyone doing anything. Common with verbs like „gehen“ (to work/run), „passieren“ (to happen), „kommen“ (to come), or „sich lösen/erledigen“ (to resolve itself / get done). Also appears as „ganz von allein“ = “all by itself.”
target_language_example: Das geht von allein.
native_language_example: That works by itself.

meaning: by itself; on its own (without help).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens automatically or without anyone doing anything: "Das geht von alleine" = "It works by itself." Also used to describe doing something independently: "Er macht das von alleine" = "He does that on his own." Common variants you may also hear: "von allein" (same meaning) and "ganz von alleine" (all by itself).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, das Problem löst sich von alleine.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, the problem will solve itself.

meaning: from all sides; from every direction.
additional_notes: Used to say something comes/acts from every direction or that someone is under pressure/criticism from everyone. Often used with verbs like „kommen“, „umgeben“, „angreifen“, „kritisieren“.
target_language_example: Er wurde von allen Seiten kritisiert.
native_language_example: He was criticized from all sides.

additional_notes: Used to describe something seen, affected, or coming from outside (a place, object, or situation). Often contrasts with "von innen" (from the inside). Common with verbs like "aussehen" (to look), "kommen" (to come), "öffnen" (to open), or in descriptions like "von außen zugänglich" (accessible from outside).
target_language_example: Von außen sieht das Haus klein aus, aber innen ist es sehr groß.
native_language_example: From the outside the house looks small, but inside it’s very big.

additional_notes: Old-fashioned/poetic expression, often used with verbs of leaving or going away (e.g., „ziehen/gehen/reiten von dannen“). In modern everyday German you’d usually say „weg“, „fort“, „von dort“ or „davon“.
target_language_example: Er zog von dannen, ohne ein Wort zu sagen.
native_language_example: He went away without saying a word.

additional_notes: Literally “from the work,” but in everyday German it usually means “from work” in the sense of returning from your job or workplace. Often used with verbs like kommen (“to come”) or zurückkommen (“to come back”): „Ich komme von der Arbeit.“ You can also use „von der Arbeit nach Hause“ (“from work to home”).
target_language_example: Ich komme gerade von der Arbeit.
native_language_example: I’m just coming from work.

additional_notes: "von" + dative means "from" or "coming from" a place. "der Schule" is dative feminine singular of "die Schule". Very common with verbs of coming/returning (kommen, zurückkommen) or with "sein" to describe where someone is coming from: "Ich komme von der Schule." It can also mean "from the school" in the sense of originating from that institution (less common for beginners).
target_language_example: Ich komme gerade von der Schule.
native_language_example: I’m just coming from school.

additional_notes: Used for a physical direction/angle (e.g., looking at something from the side, a photo taken from the side). It can also describe an indirect approach (e.g., asking a question “from the side” instead of directly), but the most common beginner use is the literal, spatial meaning.
target_language_example: Ich habe das Auto von der Seite fotografiert.
native_language_example: I photographed the car from the side.

additional_notes: Used with certain expressions to mean “in the world” (e.g., *die/der/das ... von der Welt* = “the ... in the world”). Also common in phrases like *nicht von dieser Welt* (“not of this world”) and *von der Welt sein* (“to be in the world / alive/existing,” often in the negative: *nicht mehr von der Welt sein* = “to be no longer alive”).
target_language_example: Das ist das Beste von der Welt!
native_language_example: That’s the best in the world!

additional_notes: Used to talk about movement or origin starting at a specific place that was mentioned or is clear from context. Often answers the question "Woher?" (From where?). Common with verbs like kommen (to come), gehen (to go), fahren (to travel/drive), abholen (to pick up), and schicken (to send).
target_language_example: Ich komme von dort.
native_language_example: I come from there.

additional_notes: Used to express very sincere feelings—especially gratitude, congratulations, apologies, or good wishes. Often appears with verbs like „danken“ (to thank), „gratulieren“ (to congratulate), „wünschen“ (to wish), or „leidtun“ (to be sorry): „Ich danke dir von ganzem Herzen.“
target_language_example: Ich danke dir von ganzem Herzen für deine Hilfe.
native_language_example: I thank you with all my heart for your help.

additional_notes: Usually used as a casual, slightly critical way to say something (an idea, style, technology, or a person’s attitude) is behind the times. Often used with "sein" (to be): "Das ist total von gestern."
target_language_example: Diese Meinung ist echt von gestern.
native_language_example: That opinion is really outdated.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the starting point/location of movement, distance, or travel (often with directions). Common in phrases like „von hier aus“ (= from here / starting from here). Contrast: „hier“ = here; „nach hier“ = to here; „bis hier“ = up to here.
target_language_example: Von hier aus sind es zehn Minuten zu Fuß zum Bahnhof.
native_language_example: From here, it’s a ten-minute walk to the train station.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a location or point in time as the starting point. Common with movement/direction (“Von hier aus gehen wir …”) and with giving directions (“Von hier aus ist es nicht weit”). Can also refer to next steps (“Von hier aus machen wir weiter”). Often interchangeable with “von hier” or “ab hier,” but “von hier aus” sounds especially like “starting from here.”
target_language_example: Von hier aus kannst du den Bahnhof schon sehen.
native_language_example: From here you can already see the train station.

additional_notes: Used to describe direction or position (approaching, coming, or seeing something from the rear side). Common with verbs like kommen (to come), anfahren (to hit/drive into), überholen (to overtake), and aussehen (to look like) in contexts like “from the back.” Often contrasts with von vorn/vorne (“from the front”).
target_language_example: Vorsicht, da kommt ein Fahrrad von hinten!
native_language_example: Watch out, a bicycle is coming from behind!

meaning: from the inside; on the inside (from within).
additional_notes: Used to describe something seen, done, or coming from the interior of something (a room, building, container, body, organization). Often contrasts with "von außen" (from the outside). Also common with verbs like "sehen" (to see), "öffnen" (to open), "streichen" (to paint), or to describe perspective: "von innen betrachtet" (seen from the inside).
target_language_example: Man kann die Tür nur von innen öffnen.
native_language_example: You can only open the door from the inside.

additional_notes: Used to mark a change starting at the present moment and continuing into the future. Often paired with future plans, rules, or new habits. You can also hear/see the equivalent phrasing "ab jetzt" in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Von jetzt an trinke ich jeden Tag mehr Wasser.
native_language_example: From now on, I drink more water every day.

additional_notes: Used to mark a change that begins at the present moment and continues into the future. Common in rules, decisions, or announcements. Often followed by a present tense statement about what will be true going forward (German present can refer to future). Similar alternatives: „ab jetzt“ (more informal/colloquial), „von jetzt an“.
target_language_example: Von nun an bin ich jeden Tag um acht Uhr im Büro.
native_language_example: From now on, I’m in the office every day at eight o’clock.

additional_notes: Used to describe where something comes from or the direction something is moving/seen (often with verbs like kommen, fallen, sehen). Also common for viewpoints: "von oben sehen" = to see from above / from a top-down view. Often contrasts with "von unten" (from below).
target_language_example: Von oben sieht die Stadt ganz anders aus.
native_language_example: From above, the city looks completely different.

meaning: by itself; on its own (without help).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens automatically/naturally without anyone doing anything, or that someone/something can do something independently. Common with verbs like „gehen“ (to go/work), „passieren“ (to happen), „kommen“ (to come), „sich ergeben“ (to turn out). Often appears as „ganz von selbst“ = “all by itself.”
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, das Problem löst sich von selbst.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, the problem will solve itself.

additional_notes: Most commonly used with reflexive verbs and set phrases. With verbs like „sich erinnern“ it means the memory comes “from yourself” (you recall it): „Ich erinnere mich von sich aus“ is uncommon, but you’ll often see „sich (an etwas) erinnern“ with related phrasing like „aus dem Kopf“ etc. Very common in the fixed expression „von sich aus“ = “on one’s own / by oneself / without being prompted.” Also used in phrases like „von sich reden“ (talk about oneself) or „von sich geben“ (utter/say, sometimes “let out” a sound).
target_language_example: Er hat das von sich aus gemacht.
native_language_example: He did that on his own.

meaning: from the beginning; again from the start.
additional_notes: Used to say you need to restart something. Often appears with verbs like „anfangen“ (start), „beginnen“ (begin), „machen“ (do), or „noch mal“ (again). Common longer forms are „von vorn anfangen“ and „von vorn beginnen“.
target_language_example: Wir müssen von vorn anfangen.
native_language_example: We have to start again from the beginning.

meaning: from the beginning; again from the start.
additional_notes: Used when you want to restart or repeat something from the beginning (e.g., an explanation, a task, a song). Often heard in phrases like „Nochmal von vorne!“ (“Again from the beginning!”) or „Fangen wir von vorne an.“ (“Let’s start from the beginning.”).
target_language_example: Ich habe es nicht verstanden — kannst du bitte von vorne anfangen?
native_language_example: I didn’t understand it — can you please start again from the beginning?

meaning: from a distance; from far away.
additional_notes: Used to describe something you can see, notice, or recognize without being close. Often with verbs like „sehen“ (to see), „erkennen“ (to recognize), „hören“ (to hear), or „wirken“ (to seem). Similar to „aus der Ferne“.
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn schon von weitem erkannt.
native_language_example: I recognized him from a distance.

additional_notes: Used to say you do something while staying at home, especially in phrases like „von zu Hause arbeiten“ (work from home) or „von zu Hause aus lernen“ (study from home). Note: It refers to your location while doing the activity; „nach Hause“ means “(go) home,” and „zu Hause“ means “at home.”
target_language_example: Ich arbeite heute von zu Hause.
native_language_example: I’m working from home today.

additional_notes: Used to express separation, difference, or learning/receiving something mutually between people or things. Common with verbs like „lernen“ (learn), „unterscheiden“ (distinguish), „abhängen“ (depend), and phrases like „weit voneinander entfernt“ (far apart from each other). Often contrasts with „miteinander“ (with each other/together).
target_language_example: Wir können viel voneinander lernen.
native_language_example: We can learn a lot from each other.

meaning: on site; at the place (in person).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is physically at the location, not online or elsewhere. Common in announcements and services (e.g., support, inspections, appointments). Often with verbs like „sein“ (to be) or „besichtigen“ (to inspect/visit).
target_language_example: Ein Techniker ist vor Ort und hilft Ihnen weiter.
native_language_example: A technician is on site and will help you.

additional_notes: Used to highlight the most important point in a list or situation. Very common in both speech and writing. Often followed by a noun or phrase (e.g., „vor allem Kaffee“ / „vor allem am Wochenende“). You can also use it sentence-initially to emphasize what matters most.
target_language_example: Ich mag viele Sportarten, aber vor allem Schwimmen.
native_language_example: I like many sports, but especially swimming.

meaning: right in front of your nose; right in front of you.
additional_notes: Used for something very close or directly in your view. Often appears with verbs like „stehen/liegen/hängen“ (to be standing/lying/hanging) or „weglaufen“ (to run away) and can also mean someone does something very close to you (e.g., an opportunity you missed was „vor deiner Nase“). Can sound a bit annoyed in context: „Es war die ganze Zeit vor deiner Nase!“
target_language_example: Der Schlüssel liegt direkt vor deiner Nase.
native_language_example: The key is right in front of your nose.

meaning: to be standing in front of the door; to be at the door.
additional_notes: Used literally for someone physically waiting outside a door. Often also used figuratively to mean something is about to happen very soon ("just around the corner"). You can specify who/what is at the door with "jemand/etwas steht vor der Tür".
target_language_example: Ich stehe vor der Tür — kannst du bitte aufmachen?
native_language_example: I’m at the door—can you please open up?

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened not long ago. It often goes with the past tense (Perfekt/Präteritum) and can appear at the beginning of the sentence or later as a time expression.
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn vor kurzem in Berlin gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw him in Berlin recently.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened far in the past. Common in storytelling (like “Once upon a time…”) and in everyday speech. It often comes at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis, but it can also appear later.
target_language_example: Vor langer Zeit habe ich in Berlin gewohnt.
native_language_example: A long time ago, I lived in Berlin.

meaning: (to do something) quietly/aimlessly to oneself, without much energy or purpose.
additional_notes: Used with many verbs to mean something happens in a subdued, ongoing way, often without clear direction or attention from others. Common patterns: "vor sich hin + verb" (e.g., "vor sich hin starren" = to stare blankly; "vor sich hin murmeln" = to mumble to oneself; "vor sich hin träumen" = to daydream; "vor sich hin arbeiten" = to work away quietly). Often implies low intensity, boredom, or being absorbed in one’s own thoughts.
target_language_example: Er starrte eine Weile vor sich hin.
native_language_example: He stared blankly for a while.

meaning: pros and cons; advantages and disadvantages.
additional_notes: Used when weighing options or discussing the positive and negative sides of something. Often appears as „die Vor- und Nachteile (von + dative)“ or in questions like „Was sind die Vor- und Nachteile?“
target_language_example: Wir sollten die Vor- und Nachteile dieser Entscheidung besprechen.
native_language_example: We should discuss the pros and cons of this decision.

meaning: for now; for the time being (temporarily).
additional_notes: Used to say something is the case only temporarily and may change later. Often used with decisions or plans: "Vorerst machen wir ..." / "Das bleibt vorerst so." Similar to "zunächst" (at first), but "vorerst" emphasizes “until further notice.”
target_language_example: Vorerst bleiben wir zu Hause.
native_language_example: For now, we’re staying at home.

meaning: to plan / to intend (to do something).
additional_notes: Often used with the structure „vorhaben, … zu + Infinitiv“ (to intend to do …): „Ich habe vor, morgen zu kommen.“ In the present tense it commonly appears as „ich habe vor“ (separable in this form). Related noun: „das Vorhaben“ = a plan/project/undertaking.
target_language_example: Ich habe vor, nächstes Jahr nach Berlin zu ziehen.
native_language_example: I’m planning/intending to move to Berlin next year.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive clause: **vorhaben, zu + Infinitiv**. It expresses an intention or plan (often fairly concrete). Conjugate **vorhaben** and put the other verb at the end with **zu**: *Ich habe vor, morgen zu kommen.* In spoken German you may also hear **vorhaben, … zu** without **vor** explicitly separated in the sentence.
target_language_example: Ich habe vor, nächstes Jahr nach Berlin zu ziehen.
native_language_example: I plan/intend to move to Berlin next year.

additional_notes: Common adverb for time. Often used with a reference point: before something else happens (vorher = earlier than that). Typical patterns: „Vorher …, dann …“ (Before that…, then…); „schon vorher“ (already beforehand); „kurz vorher“ (shortly before). With a clause you often use „bevor“ instead: „Bevor wir gehen, …“ (Before we go, …).
target_language_example: Ich muss vorher noch einkaufen.
native_language_example: I still have to go shopping beforehand.

meaning: earlier (a short while ago; usually today).
additional_notes: Used to refer to something that happened a short time before now, often within the same day: *Vorhin war ich im Supermarkt.* It’s common in spoken German. Contrast: *vorher* = earlier/before (more general, not necessarily recent); *vor kurzem* = a short time ago (also common, slightly less tied to ‘earlier today’).
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn vorhin gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw him earlier (a little while ago).

additional_notes: Used as an adverb for physical movement (walking/driving) or for making progress. Common in short commands: "Vorwärts!" = "Forward!" / "Move forward!" Also appears with verbs like "gehen" (to go), "fahren" (to drive), and "kommen" (to come): "Geh vorwärts" (go forward).
target_language_example: Geh bitte zwei Schritte vorwärts.
native_language_example: Please go two steps forward.

meaning: to come true; to become reality.
additional_notes: Used for hopes, wishes, dreams, predictions, or fears that become reality. Often used with a subject like "ein Traum" (a dream) or "ein Wunsch" (a wish): "Mein Traum wird wahr." In the present tense, German uses "werden" (wird/wirst/wird ...); in the past, commonly "ist wahr geworden" (has come true).
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass dein Wunsch wahr wird.
native_language_example: I hope your wish comes true.

additional_notes: Used to mean “at any time” or “no matter when,” often to show flexibility or that the exact time doesn’t matter. It can introduce a clause (“Wann auch immer du Zeit hast, …”) or be used on its own (“Wann auch immer.”).
target_language_example: Ruf mich an, wann auch immer du Zeit hast.
native_language_example: Call me whenever you have time.

additional_notes: "warten" takes the preposition "auf" + accusative for the person/thing you are waiting for. Ask: "Worauf wartest du?" (What are you waiting for?) / "Auf wen wartest du?" (Who are you waiting for?) Common time phrase: "Ich warte seit ..." (I’ve been waiting since/for ...).
target_language_example: Ich warte auf den Bus.
native_language_example: I’m waiting for the bus.

meaning: to make (someone) wait; to keep (someone) waiting.
additional_notes: Used when one person or situation causes another person to wait longer than expected. The person who has to wait is usually in the accusative: „Ich lasse dich warten.“ Often appears with time words: „lass mich nicht lange warten“ (don’t keep me waiting long).
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, ich wollte dich nicht warten lassen.
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t mean to keep you waiting.

additional_notes: Used in the construction **sehen + infinitive** to say you saw someone doing something. Typically you put the person/object in the accusative: **Ich habe ihn warten sehen.** = “I saw him waiting.” In the past, it’s common to use **haben** + past participle + infinitive: **Ich habe sie warten sehen.**
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn vor dem Kino warten sehen.
native_language_example: I saw him waiting in front of the movie theater.

additional_notes: Used to mean “whatever” in a neutral or sometimes dismissive way, depending on tone. It can stand alone as a short reply (“Whatever.”) or introduce an unknown/irrelevant thing (“whatever you want/need/say”). Often followed by a clause: “was auch immer du willst/brauchst/sagst …”.
target_language_example: Nimm dir, was auch immer du brauchst.
native_language_example: Take whatever you need.

additional_notes: Used to express determination or reassurance that something will be true regardless of the outcome. Often paired with a main clause: "Was auch passiert, ich …". Similar in meaning to "egal, was passiert". Word order: the main clause usually comes after it, separated by a comma.
target_language_example: Was auch passiert, ich bin für dich da.
native_language_example: Whatever happens, I’m here for you.

meaning: 'what (then)?' / 'what do you mean?' (often expressing surprise or impatience).
additional_notes: Used in questions, usually reacting to something someone just said or did: "Was denn?" = "What is it?/What do you mean?" It can sound a bit impatient, annoyed, or surprised depending on tone. Often appears as "Was denn?" on its own, or in longer questions like "Was denn genau?" (What exactly?) or "Was denn los?" (What’s going on?).
target_language_example: Was denn? Was meinst du damit?
native_language_example: What (then)? What do you mean by that?

additional_notes: Used before a noun to ask about the type or category: "Was für ein Buch?" = "What kind of book?" In exclamations it expresses surprise/admiration: "Was für ein schöner Tag!" = "What a beautiful day!" Often followed by the correct article/case (e.g., "was für ein/eine/einen …").
target_language_example: Was für ein Kaffee möchtest du?
native_language_example: What kind of coffee would you like?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the type or category of something ("What kind of ...?") or as an exclamation showing surprise/opinion ("What a ...!"). The form changes with gender, case, and number: was für ein Mann? (masc.), was für eine Frau? (fem.), was für ein Kind? (neut.), and plural: was für (keine ending): was für Leute? Often followed by a noun; in questions you’ll also see it without a noun when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Was für ein Film ist das?
native_language_example: What kind of movie is that?

additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun to ask about the type of something (“What kind of a …?”) or to exclaim/say you’re surprised (“What a …!”). For masculine/neuter use “was für ein”, and for plural use “was für”. Often in questions: “Was für eine Tasche ist das?” and in exclamations: “Was für eine tolle Idee!”
target_language_example: Was für eine schöne Wohnung!
native_language_example: What a beautiful apartment!

additional_notes: Very common informal greeting among friends (similar to “What’s up?”). Often used on its own, or with “Na,” (Na, was geht?) and can also mean “What’s happening/going on (here)?” depending on context. A typical reply is “Nicht viel.” / “Alles gut.”
target_language_example: Hey, was geht?
native_language_example: Hey, what’s up?

meaning: “what’s there?” / “what do you have?” / “what’s up?” (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literally “what is there.” Common in shops or restaurants to ask what’s available: “Was gibt es?” = “What do you have/What’s available?” Also used more casually as a greeting or opener like “Was gibt’s?” (= shortened) meaning “What’s up?/What’s going on?” In conversation it can also mean “What’s new?”
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, was gibt es heute zu essen?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what’s there to eat today?

additional_notes: Common, very natural question to ask what the problem is or what is happening. Often used when someone seems upset or when you notice something unusual. Can also be used as a greeting meaning 'What’s up?', but in many contexts it sounds more like 'What’s the matter?' than casual small talk.
target_language_example: Du siehst traurig aus—was ist los?
native_language_example: You look sad—what’s wrong?

meaning: “What’s wrong with you?” / “What’s going on with you?”
