additional_notes: Used to ask what the problem is or why someone is acting strangely. Tone depends on context: it can be caring (“Are you okay?”) or accusatory/annoyed (“What’s your problem?”). Often said as an exclamation: “Was ist denn mit dir?!”
target_language_example: Hey, was ist mit dir? Du bist heute so still.
native_language_example: Hey, what’s up with you? You’re so quiet today.

additional_notes: Common question to ask after something unexpected (a noise, an accident, surprising news). Uses Perfekt: “ist passiert” (happened/has happened). You can also say “Was ist denn passiert?” to sound a bit more concerned/curious, or “Was ist passiert?” on its own as a neutral question.
target_language_example: Was ist passiert? Geht es dir gut?
native_language_example: What happened? Are you okay?

meaning: “What’s that supposed to mean?” / “What is this?” (often: “What the heck is this?”).
additional_notes: Used to express annoyance, criticism, or disbelief about what someone said or did. Tone depends on context: it can be mildly questioning, but very often it’s confrontational (“What are you doing?/What’s your problem?”). Literally “what should that (be)”, but idiomatically it means “what’s the point/meaning of that?”
target_language_example: Was soll das? Warum hast du einfach die Tür zugemacht?
native_language_example: What’s that supposed to mean? Why did you just close the door?

meaning: “what do I know?” / “I have no idea.”
additional_notes: Used to express that you don’t know (or don’t care) about the details. Often sounds a bit dismissive or impatient depending on tone. Commonly appears in the longer phrase “was weiß ich (schon)” (“what do I know (anyway)?”).
target_language_example: Er kommt um acht, neun, was weiß ich.
native_language_example: He’s coming at eight, nine—who knows.

additional_notes: An exclamation used to show surprise, confusion, or annoyance. Stronger than plain “was?” but milder/less vulgar than “was zum Teufel?” or “was zum Fick?”. Often used in spoken German; can sound rude depending on tone and situation.
target_language_example: Was zum Henker machst du da?
native_language_example: What the heck are you doing there?

meaning: 'what the hell' / 'what the devil' (strong surprise or annoyance).
additional_notes: Used as an exclamation or at the start of a question when you’re shocked, confused, or irritated (similar strength to “what the hell”). It’s colloquial and can sound rude, so avoid it in formal situations or with strangers. Often appears as: „Was zum Teufel machst du?“
target_language_example: Was zum Teufel machst du da?
native_language_example: What the hell are you doing there?

meaning: to be gone; to be away; (also) to be out of it/absent-minded.
additional_notes: "Weg sein" literally means "to be away/gone" and is used very often in everyday German. It can describe (1) someone/something not being there anymore ("Der Schlüssel ist weg" = the key is gone), (2) someone being away from a place ("Ich bin morgen weg" = I’m away tomorrow), or (3) someone not paying attention / mentally absent ("Er ist gerade total weg").
target_language_example: Mein Handy ist weg.
native_language_example: My phone is gone.

meaning: to want to leave; to want to go away.
additional_notes: Uses the adverb "weg" (away/gone) with "wollen" (to want). Common when someone wants to leave a place or stop being somewhere. Often used with a subject like "Ich will weg" (I want to get away). In full sentences, conjugate "wollen" and keep "weg" together with it: "Ich will weg", "Wir wollen weg", "Er will weg". Can also be used with a destination: "Ich will weg nach Hause" (I want to go away/home).
target_language_example: Ich will weg, es ist schon spät.
native_language_example: I want to leave; it’s already late.

meaning: to leave by vehicle; to drive off; to go away (by car/train/etc.).
additional_notes: Separable verb: in the present tense and simple past, the prefix splits off: „Ich fahre weg.“ / „Ich fuhr weg.“ In the perfect tense it stays together with ge- in the middle: „Ich bin/ habe weggefahren.“ (often „bin weggefahren“ when it’s about leaving/going away). Common with time expressions: „morgen/früh/später wegfahren“.
target_language_example: Wir fahren morgen früh weg.
native_language_example: We’re leaving tomorrow early.

meaning: to go away; to leave (a place).
additional_notes: A separable verb: in the present tense, it often splits ("Ich gehe weg."). It’s used for leaving a location, going away from someone, or leaving an event. In the past, it’s usually "ist weggegangen" ("Er ist weggegangen.").
target_language_example: Ich muss jetzt weggehen.
native_language_example: I have to go now.

meaning: to take away; to remove (from someone).
additional_notes:
Commonly used when someone takes something away from you or removes something from a place. Often takes a direct object: 
- jemandem etwas wegnehmen = to take something away from someone (dative + accusative)
Example pattern: „Nimm mir das nicht weg!“ (Don’t take that away from me!).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte den Teller wegnehmen?
native_language_example: Can you please take the plate away?

additional_notes: Most commonly used as the separable verb phrase „wehtun“: „Es tut weh“ = “It hurts.” With a person/object: „Das tut mir weh“ (that hurts me) or „Das tut weh“ (that hurts). Past: „Es tat weh“ / „Es hat wehgetan“. You’ll often hear it about body parts or injuries.
target_language_example: Mein Kopf tut weh.
native_language_example: My head hurts.

additional_notes: Literally “white house.” Most commonly refers to the official residence and workplace of the U.S. president. Spelling note: “weiß” can also be written “weiss” (Swiss spelling, or when ß isn’t available), so you may also see “Weisses Haus.”
target_language_example: Der Präsident hielt eine Rede im Weißen Haus.
native_language_example: The president gave a speech at the White House.

meaning: far away; a long way off.
additional_notes: Used to say something is at a large distance, both literally (a place) and figuratively (an idea/goal). Often used with “von” (far from): „weit entfernt von …“. Similar to „weit weg“.
target_language_example: Das Hotel ist weit entfernt vom Bahnhof.
native_language_example: The hotel is far from the train station.

meaning: far away; a long distance away.
additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is at a great distance, either physically (a place) or figuratively (someone feels distant). Common with verbs like sein/wohnen/fahren: „Es ist weit weg.” / „Ich wohne weit weg.” Often with „von”: „weit weg von hier” (far from here).
target_language_example: Das Hotel ist weit weg von hier.
native_language_example: The hotel is far away from here.

meaning: Keep it up! / Carry on like that!
additional_notes: Used to encourage someone to continue doing what they’re doing (often because they’re doing well). Common in workplaces, sports, and everyday praise. Can be said as a short cheer (“Weiter so!”) or as part of a sentence (“Mach weiter so!”).
target_language_example: Das hast du super gemacht – weiter so!
native_language_example: You did that really well—keep it up!

meaning: to go on; to continue; to move on.
additional_notes: Used for continuing an action or process (Es geht weiter.) and also literally for walking on (Wir gehen weiter.). Can describe events continuing (Wie geht es weiter?) or that something is “still happening” (Es geht noch weiter.).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich muss jetzt weitergehen.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go now / I have to move on now.

meaning: white house; (also) the White House (U.S. president’s residence).
additional_notes: Literally an adjective + noun: *weiß* (white) + *Haus* (house). In German, adjectives change endings: with no article you often see *weißes Haus* (neuter). When referring to the U.S. White House, it’s usually written with capitals and an article: *das Weiße Haus*.
target_language_example: Der Präsident spricht heute im Weißen Haus.
native_language_example: The president is speaking at the White House today.

additional_notes: Used to add a polite condition or preference: you’d like something to happen, but only if it can be done. Common in requests and suggestions. Often paired with polite forms like „bitte“ or used at the end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Könnten Sie mir bitte morgen antworten, wenn möglich?
native_language_example: Could you please reply to me tomorrow, if possible?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition where something is not true: “Wenn nicht, …” = “If not, … / Otherwise, …”. Often follows a question, request, or assumption (e.g., asking if something will happen, and what to do if it doesn’t).
target_language_example: Kommst du morgen? Wenn nicht, ruf mich bitte an.
native_language_example: Are you coming tomorrow? If not, please call me.

additional_notes: Used to say something is uncertain or only true in the best-case scenario, and it might not happen or apply at all. Often adds a slightly skeptical tone. Common with words like „jemals“ (ever) or „noch“ (still) and in comparisons: „weniger …, wenn überhaupt“.
target_language_example: Er kommt heute spät — wenn überhaupt.
native_language_example: He’ll come late today—if he comes at all.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unknown or unimportant person, or to express that it doesn’t matter which person it is. Often appears in relative clauses or as a standalone phrase: „Wer auch immer das war …“ = “Whoever that was …”. Similar forms: „was auch immer“ (whatever), „wo auch immer“ (wherever).
target_language_example: Wer auch immer angerufen hat, hat keine Nachricht hinterlassen.
native_language_example: Whoever called didn’t leave a message.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or that something is unknown. Often stands alone as a short reply, and can also be used in a longer sentence (e.g., “Wer weiß, ob …”). It’s neutral and common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Wer weiß, vielleicht klappt es morgen.
native_language_example: Who knows, maybe it’ll work tomorrow.

additional_notes: Common question used to ask someone’s age. Informal (uses “du”); for formal situations use “Wie alt sind Sie?”. Typical answer pattern: “Ich bin … Jahre alt.”
target_language_example: Wie alt bist du?
native_language_example: How old are you?

additional_notes: Used to say something doesn’t matter or you don’t care about the details: "Whatever." It can also mean "anyway" to move the conversation on. Depending on tone, it can sound neutral, dismissive, or slightly annoyed. As a connector it can introduce a clause meaning "no matter how/whatever the case": "Wie auch immer du es machst …"
target_language_example: Wie auch immer, ich muss jetzt los.
native_language_example: Anyway, I have to go now.

additional_notes: Common greeting, often used as the start of the full question: "Wie geht es dir?" (informal, to one person) or "Wie geht es Ihnen?" (formal). You’ll also hear it shortened to "Wie geht’s?" In replies, Germans often use: "Gut, danke. Und dir/Ihnen?"
target_language_example: Hallo! Wie geht es dir?
native_language_example: Hi! How are you?

additional_notes: A polite, formal way to ask someone how they are. Use it with people you address as "Sie" (e.g., strangers, customers, older people, officials). Common replies: "Danke, gut." / "Sehr gut, danke." / "Es geht so." / "Nicht so gut." You can add "Und Ihnen?" (= And you?) to ask back.
target_language_example: Guten Tag! Wie geht es Ihnen?
native_language_example: Good day! How are you?

meaning: How are you? (informal; to one person).
additional_notes: Common greeting using the verb "gehen" (to go) to ask how someone is doing. "dir" is the informal dative form of "du" (you). For a formal or polite version, say "Wie geht es Ihnen?" You can answer with "Gut, danke." (Good, thanks.), "Es geht." (So-so.), or "Nicht so gut." (Not so good.).
target_language_example: Hallo! Wie geht es dir?
native_language_example: Hi! How are you?

additional_notes: Used to ask how a group of people is doing (friends, family, classmates). "euch" is the informal plural dative pronoun (“to you all”). For one person: "Wie geht es dir?" (informal). For a formal group: "Wie geht es Ihnen?" A common reply: "Gut, danke!" / "Es geht so."
target_language_example: Hallo zusammen! Wie geht es euch?
native_language_example: Hi everyone! How are you all?

additional_notes: Common informal greeting. Short for “Wie geht es (dir/Ihnen)?” You can answer with “Gut, danke.” (Good, thanks.), “Es geht.” (I’m okay / so-so), or “Nicht so gut.” (Not so good). Often followed by “Und dir?” / “Und Ihnen?” (And you?).
target_language_example: Hallo! Wie geht's?
native_language_example: Hi! How’s it going?

additional_notes: Common greeting. In standard spelling you’ll usually see "Wie geht’s?" (short for "Wie geht es?"). Often followed by "Und dir?" (to one person) or "Und euch/Ihnen?" (to a group / formal). Typical answers: "Gut, danke." / "Es geht." (so-so) / "Nicht so gut."
target_language_example: Hallo! Wie geht’s dir?
native_language_example: Hi! How are you?

additional_notes: A polite, formal way to ask someone’s name. Use **Sie** with strangers, customers, older people, or in professional settings. The verb **heißen** literally means “to be called.” A common reply is: **Ich heiße ...** (“My name is ...”).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, wie heißen Sie?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what is your name?

additional_notes: Common way to ask someone’s name when speaking to one person you address with du (friends, family, kids, many peers). Literally “how are you called,” but in English you usually say “What’s your name?” For a formal/polite version use: Wie heißen Sie?
target_language_example: Hallo! Wie heißt du?
native_language_example: Hi! What’s your name?

additional_notes: Very informal, spoken contraction of "wie ist es?" (often said as "wie is' es?"). Used as a casual greeting or to ask how things are (situation, day, life). Not appropriate for formal settings; use "Wie geht es Ihnen?" or "Wie geht's?" instead.
target_language_example: Hey, wie isses bei dir?
native_language_example: Hey, how’s it going with you?

additional_notes: A common question to ask about current weather conditions (often followed by a location or time). You’ll also hear: “Wie ist das Wetter heute?” (today) or “Wie ist das Wetter in Berlin?” (in Berlin). Answer patterns: “Es ist sonnig/kalt/warm/windig.” (It’s sunny/cold/warm/windy.)
target_language_example: Wie ist das Wetter heute in München?
native_language_example: What’s the weather like today in Munich?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the state or condition of something (often with more context): “Wie ist es in Berlin?” (“What’s it like in Berlin?”) or “Wie ist es heute?” (“How is it today?”). It can also introduce follow-up questions, e.g. “Wie ist es mit …?” (“What about …?”). In everyday speech you’ll often hear it as part of the longer question “Wie ist es?” or “Wie ist es denn?”.
target_language_example: Wie ist es in deiner neuen Wohnung?
native_language_example: What is it like in your new apartment?

meaning: “How do I get …?” / “How can I get …?” (starting a directions question).
additional_notes: Used to ask for directions when you’re about to mention a destination. Most often you’ll hear it with the pattern “Wie komme ich zu + dative?” (to a place/building) or “Wie komme ich nach + place?” (to a city/country). You can also say “Wie komme ich zum/zur …?” (= zu dem/zu der).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, wie komme ich zum Bahnhof?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how do I get to the train station?

additional_notes: Used to ask about duration (time length), not clock time. Common in questions like "Wie lange dauert das?" (How long does that take?) and with the present perfect or present tense to ask how long something has been happening: "Wie lange bist du schon hier?" (How long have you been here?). Often answered with a time expression (zwei Stunden, drei Tage, seit gestern).
target_language_example: Wie lange dauert der Film?
native_language_example: How long is the movie?

additional_notes: Used to ask how much time has passed since something happened. It’s often used in questions like “Wie lange ist das her?” (“How long ago was that?”). You can also attach it to an event: “Wie lange ist der Unfall her?” (“How long ago was the accident?”).
target_language_example: Wie lange ist das her?
native_language_example: How long ago was that?

meaning: “what do you mean?” / “how do you mean?” (asking for clarification).
additional_notes: Used when you didn’t understand something or want the other person to explain. Very commonly used as a question: “Wie meinst du das?” (= “What do you mean by that?”). It can also appear in indirect speech: “Ich weiß nicht, wie er das meint.” (= “I don’t know what he means by that.”).
target_language_example: Wie meinst du das?
native_language_example: What do you mean (by that)?

additional_notes: Used to ask about frequency (how many times / how regularly something happens). Often answered with adverbs like „oft“ (often), „selten“ (rarely), „manchmal“ (sometimes), or time expressions like „einmal pro Woche“ (once a week), „zweimal im Monat“ (twice a month). You can also use it with the present tense for routines: „Wie oft gehst du ins Fitnessstudio?“
target_language_example: Wie oft fährst du mit dem Bus zur Arbeit?
native_language_example: How often do you take the bus to work?

additional_notes: Used to ask the current time. Often appears as the question "Wie spät ist es?" (“What time is it?”) or more politely "Wie spät ist es, bitte?". You can also use it in indirect questions: "Ich weiß nicht, wie spät es ist." (“I don’t know what time it is.”).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, wie spät ist es?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what time is it?

additional_notes: A common, neutral way to ask for the current time. You can answer with: „Es ist … Uhr.“ (It’s … o’clock) or „Es ist …“ (It’s …). Also common: „Wie viel Uhr ist es?“
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, wie spät ist es?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what time is it?

additional_notes: Used to ask about an amount or quantity. Most common: without a noun (Wie viel kostet das? = How much does that cost?) or with uncountable nouns (Wie viel Wasser? = How much water?). With countable plural nouns, you usually use **wie viele**: Wie viele Leute kommen? = How many people are coming?
target_language_example: Wie viel kostet das?
native_language_example: How much does that cost?

additional_notes: Used to ask about a number/quantity you can count. It changes with gender and case: **wie viele** (plural), **wie viel** (uncountable: “how much”), and **wie viele/r/s** for singular (“how many” of a specific noun, e.g. *wie viele Stunden* / *wie viel Zeit*). Often followed by a noun: *Wie viele Personen …?*
target_language_example: Wie viele Geschwister hast du?
native_language_example: How many siblings do you have?

additional_notes: Used in questions about distance (often with “ist es …?” or “ist es bis …?”) and about the extent of progress (“Wie weit bist du?” = how far are you / how far along are you). Can also be used more abstractly: “Wie weit sind wir?” (Where are we at?).
target_language_example: Wie weit ist es bis zum Bahnhof?
native_language_example: How far is it to the train station?

additional_notes: Used to make a suggestion or propose an option, often followed by “mit” + noun (“Wie wäre es mit einem Kaffee?”) or by a subordinate clause (“Wie wäre es, wenn wir morgen gehen?”). Literally it’s “how would it be,” but in everyday English it’s usually “how about.”
target_language_example: Wie wäre es mit einem Spaziergang nach dem Essen?
native_language_example: How about a walk after dinner?

additional_notes: Used to make a friendly suggestion or propose an idea. It’s commonly followed by a noun or by an infinitive with „zu“ (e.g., „wie wäre es mit einem Kaffee?“ / „wie wäre es, wenn wir …?“). Often used in casual conversation and also polite enough in most situations.
target_language_example: Wie wäre es mit einem Kaffee nach der Arbeit?
native_language_example: How about a coffee after work?

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something has returned and is here again. Often said when someone comes back from a trip, a break, or steps out briefly. It can be used on its own as a short statement ("Wieder da!") or in a full sentence ("Ich bin wieder da."). Related phrases: "wieder hier" (back here), "wieder zurück" (back again/returned).
target_language_example: Ich bin wieder da.
native_language_example: I’m back.

additional_notes: Common verb for returning to a place or coming again later. Often used with a time expression: „Ich komme morgen wieder.“ In conversation you’ll also hear the split form with „wieder“ later in the sentence: „Ich komme wieder.“
target_language_example: Ich komme später wieder.
native_language_example: I’ll come back later.

additional_notes: A motivating phrase used to express confidence that a task or challenge can be handled. Uses "schaffen" in the sense of “to manage/achieve,” not just “to create.” It can sound like a slogan (famously used in German politics).
target_language_example: Es ist viel Arbeit, aber wir schaffen das.
native_language_example: It’s a lot of work, but we can do it.

meaning: “will it rain?” / “is it going to rain?”
additional_notes: Used to ask about the weather in the near future. It’s the future tense with **werden** + infinitive (**regnen**). Often appears in a full question like **Wird es (heute/morgen/später) regnen?** The **es** is a dummy subject (like English “it”) used with weather verbs.
target_language_example: Wird es morgen regnen?
native_language_example: Will it rain tomorrow?

meaning: to become reality; to come true.
additional_notes: Used for plans, hopes, dreams, or predictions that actually happen. Often appears with a subject like „ein Traum/Plan“: „Mein Traum wird Wirklichkeit.“
target_language_example: Mein Traum wird endlich Wirklichkeit.
native_language_example: My dream is finally coming true.

meaning: to know about; to be aware of.
additional_notes: Used with a direct object to say you have knowledge/awareness of something (often facts, plans, secrets). Commonly in negatives: „Ich weiß nichts von …“ = “I don’t know anything about …”. More formal/literary than „von etwas wissen“ is „Kenntnis von etwas haben“.
target_language_example: Ich weiß nichts von einem Termin morgen.
native_language_example: I don’t know anything about an appointment tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express curiosity or the wish to get information. Often appears as "ich will ... wissen" or in questions like "Willst du wissen, ...?" It takes a direct object (e.g., "das", "es", or a whole clause): "Ich will wissen, warum ...".
target_language_example: Ich will wissen, wann der Zug abfährt.
native_language_example: I want to know when the train leaves.

meaning: to know about; to have knowledge about.
additional_notes: "Wissen über" is used with a noun to express knowledge on a topic/person/thing: "Wissen über Geschichte" (knowledge about history). It’s common in more formal contexts and often appears with "viel/wenig" (a lot/little) or "kein" (no) and with the verb "haben": "Ich habe viel Wissen über …". In everyday speech, Germans also often say "etwas über … wissen" (to know something about …).
target_language_example: Ich habe viel Wissen über deutsche Geschichte.
native_language_example: I have a lot of knowledge about German history.

additional_notes: Used to ask one person (du) about their place of residence. Very common in introductions and small talk. For a more formal/polite version, use “Wo wohnen Sie?”. Answer patterns: “Ich wohne in …” (I live in …) or “Ich wohne bei …” (I live with …).
target_language_example: Hallo! Wo wohnst du?
native_language_example: Hi! Where do you live?

meaning: “to come from” (to ask or say where someone/something is from).
additional_notes: Used in questions and answers about origin. In questions, it often appears as: “Woher kommst du?” (informal) or “Woher kommen Sie?” (formal). In statements, you can answer with “Ich komme aus …” (I’m from …) or “Das kommt aus …” (That comes from …). Note: “woher” = “from where,” and “kommen” = “to come.”
target_language_example: Woher kommst du?
native_language_example: Where are you from?

additional_notes: Used to ask about a destination or direction, especially with verbs of motion (gehen, fahren, fliegen, laufen). Contrast: **wo?** asks where someone/something is (location), while **wohin?** asks where someone/something is going (destination). Often answered with a place expression in the accusative (e.g., **in die Stadt**, **nach Berlin**, **zu meiner Freundin**).
target_language_example: Wohin gehst du nach der Arbeit?
native_language_example: Where are you going after work?

additional_notes: Used to ask about a destination or direction. "Wohin?" is used with movement verbs like gehen/fahren/fliegen (to where?), while "wo?" asks about location (where?). Often appears in questions like "Wohin gehst du?" or with a place: "Ich gehe wohin?" → "Ich gehe nach Hause."
target_language_example: Wohin gehst du heute Abend?
native_language_example: Where are you going this evening?

meaning: probably rather; more likely (in contrast to what was said/expected).
additional_notes: Used to soften a correction or to express that something is more likely the case than another option. Often appears when disagreeing politely or revising an assumption: "Das ist wohl eher ..." / "Er kommt wohl eher später." Note: "wohl" adds uncertainty/politeness ("probably"), and "eher" means "rather / sooner / more likely" depending on context.
target_language_example: Das ist wohl eher keine gute Idee.
native_language_example: That’s probably not such a good idea (more likely not a good idea).

meaning: for better or worse; whether you like it or not.
additional_notes: Used to say something must be accepted or will happen regardless of preference. Often used with verbs like „müssen“ or „sein“ (e.g., „Wir müssen es wohl oder übel akzeptieren.“). Spelling note: often also written as „wohl oder übel“ in running text; it’s a fixed expression.
target_language_example: Wir müssen das wohl oder übel akzeptieren.
native_language_example: We have to accept it, for better or worse / whether we like it or not.

meaning: to live with (someone), usually in their home.
additional_notes: Used with a person or household (not a place name) to say you live with them, often implying you are staying in their place (e.g., with parents, friends, host family). Grammar: wohnen + bei + dative (bei meinem Vater / bei meinen Eltern). For locations you usually use „in“ (in Berlin wohnen).
target_language_example: Ich wohne bei meinen Eltern.
native_language_example: I live with my parents.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone’s home is directly next to another person/place. In a full sentence you usually add an object after it: „neben + dative“ (e.g., „neben meinem Bruder“, „neben der Schule“). Often appears as „nebenan wohnen“ (= to live next door).
target_language_example: Ich wohne neben der Schule.
native_language_example: I live next to the school.

meaning: to be busy with / to deal with (something).
additional_notes: Usually used as **sich mit etwas beschäftigen** (“to occupy oneself with / to work on / to deal with something”). **Womit** is the question form meaning **“with what?”**. Common in questions like **Womit beschäftigst du dich?** (“What are you working on / occupied with?”). In everyday speech, it can mean anything from studying a topic to handling a task or problem.
target_language_example: Womit beschäftigst du dich gerade?
native_language_example: What are you working on right now?

additional_notes: Used with the preposition-like form "woran" (= "an was" / "an welche Sache"), especially when referring back to an unspecified thing or asking about it. Often appears in questions like "Woran denkst du?" or with a clause: "Ich denke daran, dass ..." For a specific noun, you usually say "an + Akkusativ" (e.g., "an meinen Urlaub denken").
target_language_example: Woran denkst du gerade?
native_language_example: What are you thinking about right now?

meaning: 'to wait for what' / 'what are you waiting for?'
additional_notes: "Worauf" = "what for" (literally "whereon"). Used to ask what someone is waiting for or what the delay is. Often appears as a question: "Worauf wartest du?" (What are you waiting for?) or as a prompt: "Worauf wartest du noch?" (What are you still waiting for?). In statements, German more commonly uses "auf (etwas/jemanden) warten" (to wait for something/someone).
target_language_example: Worauf wartest du noch?
native_language_example: What are you still waiting for?

meaning: to keep one’s word; to do what you promised.
additional_notes: Used when someone follows through on a promise or commitment. Common patterns: „Ich halte mein Wort.“ (I’ll keep my word.) / „Kannst du dein Wort halten?“ (Can you keep your word?) / „Er hat sein Wort gehalten.“ (He kept his word.) Often appears with possessive pronouns: mein/dein/sein/ihr Wort.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich halte mein Wort.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll keep my word.

additional_notes: Used to ask for the topic or main point of a conversation, text, meeting, problem, etc. Very common as a standalone question: “Worum geht’s?” (shorter, more spoken). Often followed by “in” + dative for a specific area: “Worum geht es in dem Film?” (What is the movie about?).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, worum geht es hier?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what is this about?

additional_notes: Used to ask what the topic of a conversation is. "worüber" is a question word meaning "about what" and is used with verbs that take "über" (to talk about, think about, etc.). In indirect questions, it becomes "worüber" as well: "Ich weiß nicht, worüber sie sprechen."
target_language_example: Worüber sprecht ihr gerade?
native_language_example: What are you talking about right now?

meaning: to talk/speak about (something); in questions: “what are you talking about?”
additional_notes: Used with “von” to indicate the topic: “von + Dativ” (e.g., „von dem Film“). In questions, „Wovon…?“ asks what the topic is: „Wovon sprichst du?“ / „Wovon sprechen wir?“ Often interchangeable with „worüber sprechen“ (“talk about what/which?”), especially in conversation.
target_language_example: Wovon sprichst du gerade?
native_language_example: What are you talking about right now?

additional_notes: Most commonly used as (1) a preposition with genitive: während des Urlaubs = during the vacation; in everyday German you’ll often also hear dative: während dem Urlaub. (2) a conjunction: während ich koche, liest du = while I’m cooking, you’re reading. In this conjunction use, the verb goes to the end of the clause (subordinate clause word order).
target_language_example: Während ich arbeite, hört er Musik.
native_language_example: While I’m working, he listens to music.

additional_notes: Common abbreviation of “zum Beispiel.” Used in writing and formal/informal contexts to introduce an example. In speech, people usually say the full phrase “zum Beispiel.” It’s typically followed by a comma: “z. B., …”.
target_language_example: Du kannst z. B. Kaffee oder Tee bestellen.
native_language_example: You can order, for example, coffee or tea.

additional_notes: Used almost only in writing as an abbreviation. It means the same as the much more common „z. B.“ (= „zum Beispiel“). In everyday German, prefer „z. B.“.
target_language_example: Viele Obstsorten enthalten viel Vitamin C, z. E. Orangen und Kiwis.
native_language_example: Many types of fruit contain a lot of vitamin C, for example oranges and kiwis.

meaning: “zum Teil” = partly; in part; to some extent.
additional_notes: Common abbreviation in writing (notes, reports, forms). It’s the shortened form of “zum Teil” and means that something is only true for part of a group/situation. In full sentences you usually say “zum Teil” or “teilweise” rather than writing “z. T.”.
target_language_example: Die Ergebnisse sind z. T. noch unklar.
native_language_example: The results are still partly unclear.

meaning: to need time; to take time.
additional_notes: Used to say that something requires time or that a process will take a certain amount of time. Common patterns: „Ich brauche Zeit.“ (I need time.) / „Das braucht Zeit.“ (That takes time.) / with a time amount: „Das braucht zwei Stunden.“ (That takes two hours.) / with an infinitive: „Ich brauche Zeit, um … zu …“ (I need time to …).
target_language_example: Das braucht noch Zeit.
native_language_example: That still takes time.

meaning: to give (someone/yourself) time; to allow time.
additional_notes: Used when you don’t want to rush and want patience (either for a person or a process). Often appears with a dative object (jemandem Zeit geben = to give someone time) or reflexively (sich Zeit geben = to take your time / not rush yourself). Common in advice or reassuring situations.
target_language_example: Gib mir bitte Zeit, darüber nachzudenken.
native_language_example: Please give me time to think about it.

meaning: to have time; to be free (available).
additional_notes: Used to say you have time for something or are available. Often used with "für" + accusative: "Ich habe Zeit für dich." You can also negate it: "Ich habe keine Zeit." Common questions: "Hast du (kurz) Zeit?"
target_language_example: Hast du heute Abend Zeit?
native_language_example: Do you have time this evening?

meaning: to take your time; to not hurry.
additional_notes: Usually said as the reflexive verb phrase **sich Zeit lassen** (“to take one’s time”). Common in polite situations to tell someone there’s no rush: **Lass dir Zeit** (informal singular), **Lasst euch Zeit** (informal plural), **Lassen Sie sich Zeit** (formal). You can also say **Wir lassen uns Zeit** (“We’re taking our time”).
target_language_example: Lassen Sie sich Zeit, ich warte hier.
native_language_example: Take your time, I’ll wait here.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase. Often used with "ich/du/wir" etc. (e.g., "Ich spare Zeit") or with "damit/um ... zu" to say you do something in order to save time: "Ich mache das online, um Zeit zu sparen."
target_language_example: Ich mache das online, um Zeit zu sparen.
native_language_example: I do that online to save time.

meaning: to kill time; to pass the time doing something (often while waiting).
additional_notes: Usually used as „die Zeit totschlagen“ (with the article): „Wir schlagen die Zeit tot, bis …“. Common in everyday speech and often implies you’re doing something just to fill time, not because it’s important. Related: „sich die Zeit vertreiben“ (to pass the time).
target_language_example: Wir schlagen die Zeit tot, bis der Zug kommt.
native_language_example: We’re killing time until the train arrives.

meaning: to spend time (doing something / with someone).
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase. Often used with "mit" + dative (mit Freunden, mit der Familie) or with "bei" for places/people you stay with (bei meinen Eltern). You can add an activity with "mit" + noun (mit Lesen) or more naturally use a verb phrase like: "Ich verbringe Zeit damit, ...".
target_language_example: Am Wochenende verbringe ich Zeit mit meiner Familie.
native_language_example: On the weekend I spend time with my family.

meaning: to waste time; to lose time.
additional_notes: Used when something takes unnecessary time or causes delays. Common with "nicht" (don’t waste time) and with "mit" to say what you’re wasting time on ("Zeit mit etwas verlieren"). Also used for missing a deadline or getting delayed ("Wir haben Zeit verloren").
target_language_example: Wir dürfen keine Zeit verlieren!
native_language_example: We mustn’t waste any time!

additional_notes: Common verb phrase used when you think something is unproductive. Conjugate "verschwenden" (ich verschwende, du verschwendest, er/sie/es verschwendet) and place the object "Zeit" after the verb. Often used with "nicht" to say you don’t want to waste time: "Ich will keine Zeit verschwenden."
target_language_example: Wir sollten keine Zeit verschwenden und jetzt anfangen.
native_language_example: We shouldn’t waste any time and start now.

meaning: to eat dinner; to have an evening meal.
additional_notes: Commonly appears as "zu Abend essen" (separable verb) or "Abend essen". Often used with a time or with "bei" to say where/with whom you eat: "Wir essen um sieben zu Abend." / "Wir essen bei Freunden zu Abend." Also very common: "zu Abend essen gehen" = "to go out for dinner."
target_language_example: Wir essen heute um sieben zu Abend.
native_language_example: We’re having dinner today at seven.

meaning: to bed (i.e., to go to bed).
additional_notes: Most commonly used with a verb, especially **zu Bett gehen** (= to go to bed). You’ll also hear **jemanden zu Bett bringen** (= to put someone to bed). It describes the action of going to bed; for being in bed already, German often uses **im Bett** (= in bed).
target_language_example: Ich gehe jetzt zu Bett.
native_language_example: I’m going to bed now.

meaning: (to be) finished; (to come) to an end.
additional_notes: Often used with verbs like „sein“ (to be) and „gehen“ (to go) to say something is over: „Der Film ist zu Ende.“ / „Die Ferien gehen zu Ende.“ You can also use it with „bringen“ to mean to finish something: „Ich bringe die Arbeit zu Ende.“ Related: „am Ende“ = at the end (position/time), while „zu Ende“ = finished/over.
target_language_example: Der Kurs ist jetzt zu Ende.
native_language_example: The course is finished now.

meaning: to finish; to bring to completion.
additional_notes: Used for completing a task, project, or activity. Often implies you keep going until it’s done (not just “stop”). Common with objects like Arbeit, Projekt, Ausbildung, Aufgabe. Separable verb: bringe … zu Ende, brachte … zu Ende, hat … zu Ende gebracht.
target_language_example: Ich muss die Arbeit heute zu Ende bringen.
native_language_example: I have to finish the work today.

meaning: to finish; to bring (something) to a conclusion.
additional_notes: Used for completing a task, project, or process, often emphasizing that you carry it through until the end. Common with an object (e.g., ein Projekt / eine Aufgabe) and can sound slightly formal compared to einfach „fertig machen“ or „beenden“. Conjugates as a separable verb: „Ich führe das Projekt zu Ende.“ / „Wir haben es zu Ende geführt.“
target_language_example: Wir müssen das Projekt bis Freitag zu Ende führen.
native_language_example: We have to finish the project by Friday.

meaning: to come to an end; to be over.
additional_notes: Used for events, periods of time, TV shows, meetings, etc. It’s a common neutral phrase meaning something finishes (often by itself), similar to “end” or “be finished.” For people, you’d usually use other verbs (e.g., „sterben“ for “to die”). Also common: „zu Ende sein“ = “to be over/finished.”
target_language_example: Der Film geht gleich zu Ende.
native_language_example: The movie is about to end.

additional_notes: Used to say you go somewhere by walking (not by car/bus/bike). Often follows a verb of movement like gehen/kommen or is used with a form of sein: „Ich gehe zu Fuß.“ / „Ich bin zu Fuß unterwegs.“
target_language_example: Ich gehe zu Fuß zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: I walk to work (I go to work on foot).

meaning: to walk; to go on foot.
additional_notes: Used to say you travel somewhere by walking (not by car/bus/bike). Often answers the question "Wie kommst du dahin?" (How do you get there?). You can also use it with a destination: "Ich gehe zu Fuß zur Arbeit."
target_language_example: Ich gehe jeden Tag zu Fuß zur Schule.
native_language_example: I walk to school every day.

meaning: at the feet of; at someone’s feet (lying/sitting close by).
additional_notes: Used with a dative noun/pronoun to show location right by someone’s feet (often with verbs like liegen/stehen/sitzen). Common in phrases like „jemandem zu Füßen liegen“ (to lie at someone’s feet; also figuratively: to adore someone). As a prepositional phrase it contrasts with „an den Füßen“ (at/on the feet as a body part).
target_language_example: Der Hund liegt mir zu Füßen.
native_language_example: The dog is lying at my feet.

additional_notes: Means being at home (location/state), often used with verbs like „sein“, „bleiben“, „arbeiten“: „Ich bin zu Haus.“ The more common spelling is „zu Hause“. Don’t confuse with „nach Hause“ (= (to) go home, direction).
target_language_example: Heute bleibe ich zu Hause.
native_language_example: Today I’m staying at home.

additional_notes: Means being at your home (location/state), not motion. Often used with verbs like „sein“ (to be) or „bleiben“ (to stay): „Ich bin zu Hause.“ In everyday speech it’s also common to say „Zuhause“ as one word with the same meaning. For motion to home, German usually uses „nach Hause“ (to go home).
target_language_example: Ich bin heute Abend zu Hause.
native_language_example: I’m at home this evening.

meaning: to take (something) to heart; to take (something) seriously.
additional_notes: Most commonly used in the phrase "sich etwas zu Herzen nehmen" (to take something to heart). It means you accept advice/criticism and let it affect you emotionally or you really try to follow it. Grammar: "sich" is a reflexive pronoun (ich nehme mir … zu Herzen, du nimmst dir … zu Herzen, etc.), and the thing you take to heart is usually in the accusative: "Ich nehme mir deinen Rat zu Herzen."
target_language_example: Ich nehme mir deine Kritik zu Herzen.
native_language_example: I take your criticism to heart.

meaning: 'for the attention of' (addressed to a specific person).
additional_notes: Formal phrase used in letters, emails, and on envelopes/packages to indicate the intended recipient within an organization or household. Often abbreviated as „z. Hd.“ and followed by the person’s name: „z. Hd. Frau Müller“. Typically appears in the address block or subject line.
target_language_example: Bitte senden Sie die Unterlagen zu Händen von Herrn Becker.
native_language_example: Please send the documents for the attention of Mr. Becker.

meaning: to eat lunch; to have lunch.
additional_notes: Used to talk about eating the midday meal. Often appears with a time or place: „Ich esse um 12 Uhr zu Mittag.“ / „Wir essen in der Kantine zu Mittag.“ You can also use it with „gehen“: „Wir gehen zu Mittag essen“ = “We’re going to get lunch.” Common related noun: „das Mittagessen“ (lunch).
target_language_example: Wir gehen heute zu Mittag essen.
native_language_example: We’re going to have lunch today.

additional_notes: Used to say something is correct or justified (often in opinions, criticism, or praise). Common with verbs like „haben“ and „sein“: „Du hast zu Recht gesagt …“ / „Er wurde zu Recht kritisiert.“ As an adverbial phrase it’s often written separately: „zu Recht“.
target_language_example: Du hast zu Recht gesagt, dass das keine gute Idee ist.
native_language_example: You were right to say that that’s not a good idea.

meaning: to get harmed; to suffer damage/injury.
additional_notes: Used to say that a person (or sometimes an object) is harmed, injured, or damaged, often in accidents or dangerous situations. Common with negation: „Niemand ist zu Schaden gekommen.“ The verb „kommen“ is used idiomatically here; the phrase is not as simple as “to come to damage.”
target_language_example: Bei dem Unfall ist zum Glück niemand zu Schaden gekommen.
native_language_example: Fortunately, no one was harmed in the accident.

meaning: to light; into view (i.e., becoming known or visible).
additional_notes: Most commonly used with verbs like "kommen" or "treten" to say that facts, problems, or details become known: "(etwas) kommt/tritt zu Tage" = "(something) comes to light". Often written as "zutage" in modern spelling, especially in fixed expressions. Slightly formal/literary compared with everyday "bekannt werden" (to become known).
target_language_example: Bei der Untersuchung kamen neue Details zu Tage.
native_language_example: During the investigation, new details came to light.

additional_notes: Used with verbs to mean something happens so much or so severely that it results in death (e.g., "schlagen" = beat, "hungern" = starve, "arbeiten" = work). Very common in fixed phrases like "jemanden zu Tode schlagen" (beat someone to death) or "sich zu Tode arbeiten" (work oneself to death). Not usually used as a standalone phrase; it typically follows the verb.
target_language_example: Er hat sich zu Tode gearbeitet.
native_language_example: He worked himself to death.

meaning: first of all; first and foremost.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the very first point in a list, plan, or explanation. It’s a bit more emphatic than "zuerst" and often comes at the beginning of a sentence. It can also be followed by commas when listing steps (e.g., "Zu allererst, ...").
target_language_example: Zu allererst müssen wir ein Ticket kaufen.
native_language_example: First of all, we have to buy a ticket.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific time period that’s already known from context (often something in the past). It’s close to “damals” (“back then”) or “zu dieser Zeit” (“at this time/at that time,” depending on context). In speech, it’s often said as “zu der Zeit” or contracted to “zur Zeit” (which can also mean “currently/at the moment” depending on context).
target_language_example: Zu der Zeit habe ich in Berlin gewohnt.
native_language_example: At that time, I lived in Berlin.

meaning: at that time; at this time (then/around then).
additional_notes: A time expression meaning “during that period.” Often refers back to a specific time already mentioned (e.g., in a story or explanation). You’ll also see the very similar phrase “zu der Zeit” (“at the time / back then”).
target_language_example: Zu dieser Zeit habe ich in Berlin gewohnt.
native_language_example: At that time, I lived in Berlin.

additional_notes: Used when someone arrives earlier than planned or expected. Common with appointments and meetings. Word order: you can split the verb in the present tense (e.g., „Ich komme …“), but „zu früh“ stays together as the time expression.
target_language_example: Ich bin zu früh gekommen; mein Termin ist erst um zehn Uhr.
native_language_example: I arrived too early; my appointment isn’t until ten o’clock.

meaning: to be available; to be for sale ("available to buy").
additional_notes: Used with sein (usually: "ist/sind ... zu haben") to say something is available, often in shops/ads. Common patterns: "X ist hier zu haben" (you can get X here), "in verschiedenen Größen zu haben" (available in different sizes), "noch zu haben" (still available).
target_language_example: Die Tickets sind online zu haben.
native_language_example: The tickets are available online.

meaning: at that time; in those days.
additional_notes: Refers to a specific time in the past (or a previously mentioned time period). It’s more formal/literary than “damals” and typically used when talking about historical events or earlier phases of someone’s life. Often follows context that makes clear which time period is meant.
target_language_example: Zu jener Zeit gab es noch keine Smartphones.
native_language_example: In those days, there were no smartphones yet.

additional_notes: Used to say you appreciate something/someone, often in polite or formal contexts. Common patterns: „Ich weiß es zu schätzen, dass …“ (I appreciate that …) and „Ich weiß deine Hilfe zu schätzen.“ (I appreciate your help.) The verb is split: „wissen“ is conjugated, and „zu schätzen“ stays together at the end of the clause.
target_language_example: Ich weiß es sehr zu schätzen, dass du mir hilfst.
native_language_example: I really appreciate that you’re helping me.

meaning: to oneself; back to consciousness (come to).
additional_notes: Most commonly used with verbs like „kommen“ (to come) or „bringen“ (to bring): „zu sich kommen“ = to regain consciousness / come to; „jdn. zu sich bringen“ = to revive someone. It can also be a reflexive idea meaning “to oneself” in phrases like „zu sich (nach Hause) einladen“ = to invite someone to one’s place. Note that it’s different from „zu sich nehmen“ (to consume/take in) and from „bei sich“ (with oneself / on one’s person).
target_language_example: Nach dem Unfall kam er langsam wieder zu sich.
native_language_example: After the accident, he slowly came to.

meaning: to regain consciousness; to come to (come around).
additional_notes: Often used after someone has fainted or been unconscious: "Er ist wieder zu sich gekommen." It can also mean to recover mentally/emotionally or come back to your senses after shock or stress. Verb pattern: "kommen" + "zu" + dative reflexive pronoun (zu mir/dir/sich/uns/euch).
target_language_example: Nach der Ohnmacht ist sie nach ein paar Minuten wieder zu sich gekommen.
native_language_example: After fainting, she came to again after a few minutes.

additional_notes: Used to say someone arrives after the expected time (for work, school, an appointment, a meeting, etc.). You can also say how late: „Ich komme zehn Minuten zu spät.“ Often used with a warning or rule: „Komm nicht zu spät!“
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich bin zu spät gekommen.
native_language_example: Sorry, I arrived late.

meaning: to have to do with; to be related to.
additional_notes: Most often used as "mit etwas/jemandem zu tun haben" (= to have something to do with something/someone). The negative "nichts mit … zu tun haben" means "to have nothing to do with …" / "to be unrelated." Common in explanations and when clarifying responsibility or connections.
target_language_example: Das hat nichts mit dir zu tun.
native_language_example: That has nothing to do with you.

additional_notes: Used to say an amount is excessive. With uncountable nouns it means “too much” (zu viel Kaffee). With plural/countable nouns it means “too many” (zu viele Leute). Often used on its own as a reply: “Zu viel!” = “Too much!”
target_language_example: Ich habe zu viel gegessen.
native_language_example: I ate too much.

meaning: to go too far (cross a line).
additional_notes: Used when someone’s behavior, words, demands, or actions are unacceptable or excessive (morally, socially, or in an argument). Often refers to overstepping boundaries, not physical distance. You can also say it about your own actions: „Ich bin zu weit gegangen.“
target_language_example: Du bist zu weit gegangen — das war wirklich beleidigend.
native_language_example: You went too far — that was really insulting.

additional_notes: A fairly formal way to ask why someone is doing something, focusing on the goal or intended use. Often used in questions like “Zu welchem Zweck brauchen Sie das?” In everyday casual speech, “Wozu?” is a shorter alternative.
target_language_example: Zu welchem Zweck brauchen Sie diese Daten?
native_language_example: For what purpose do you need this data?

meaning: to/with each other; toward each other.
additional_notes: Used to describe a relationship, interaction, or movement between two or more people/things. Common with verbs like „sprechen“ (talk), „passen“ (fit/match), „gehören“ (belong), „finden“ (find), „stehen“ (stand), or „gehen“ (go). Often answers the question “in relation to each other?”
target_language_example: Wir müssen besser zueinander sein.
native_language_example: We need to be better to each other.

additional_notes: Commonly used to show sequence or order. Often paired with words like „dann“ (then) or „danach“ (after that): „Zuerst …, dann …“. It can mean either (1) the first step in a series (“first”) or (2) the initial situation (“at first”).
target_language_example: Zuerst machen wir die Hausaufgaben, dann spielen wir.
native_language_example: First we do the homework, then we play.

additional_notes: Usually used as an adverb meaning you are in your home (location), not a physical building. Often written as two words in more formal spelling: „zu Hause“. Common with verbs like „sein“ (to be), „bleiben“ (to stay), and „gehen/kommen“ (to go/come): „Ich bin zuhause“, „Ich bleibe zuhause“, „Ich gehe nach Hause“ (note: „nach Hause“ = (go) home, direction).
target_language_example: Ich bin heute zuhause.
native_language_example: I’m at home today.

meaning: for dinner; to dinner (as an occasion).
additional_notes: "Zum" = "zu dem" (to/for the). Used to say something is meant for dinner or happening at dinner time (often like “for dinner”). Common with verbs like "einladen" (invite), "gehen" (go), "kommen" (come), or "es gibt ..." (there is/are ...).
target_language_example: Ich lade dich zum Abendessen ein.
native_language_example: I’m inviting you to dinner.

additional_notes: Commonly used to introduce what happens first or what you’ll do first. Often appears as “Zum Anfang …” (“To start, …”) or “Zum Anfang machen wir …” (“To start, we do …”). Literally means “to the beginning” (zu + dem → zum + Anfang).
target_language_example: Zum Anfang machen wir eine kurze Pause.
native_language_example: To start, we’ll take a short break.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase for visiting a doctor (a medical appointment or check-up). "zum" is the contraction of "zu dem" (= to the). You can also say "zum Arzt" on its own when the verb is clear from context (e.g., "Ich muss zum Arzt.").
target_language_example: Ich muss morgen zum Arzt gehen.
native_language_example: I have to go to the doctor tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce one or more examples. Often shortened in writing as “z. B.”. It can appear at the start of a sentence or in the middle after the item being discussed.
target_language_example: Wir können zum Beispiel ins Kino gehen.
native_language_example: We can go to the cinema, for example.

meaning: to the end; towards the end.
additional_notes: Often used to indicate reaching a final point (literal or figurative) or moving toward the conclusion of something. Common with verbs of movement or progression like gehen/kommen/bringen. Also used in the pattern „zum Ende + Genitive“ (e.g., „zum Ende des Jahres“ = toward the end of the year).
target_language_example: Zum Ende des Films wird es richtig spannend.
native_language_example: Toward the end of the movie, it gets really exciting.

meaning: for example; as an example (rather formal/old-fashioned).
additional_notes: Used to introduce an example, similar to "zum Beispiel" but noticeably more formal or literary. You’ll most often see it in writing or speeches rather than everyday conversation.
target_language_example: Zum Exempel könnte man die Preise senken.
native_language_example: For example, one could lower the prices.

additional_notes: Used to express relief or that a situation turned out well. Often placed near the beginning of a sentence: “Zum Glück …”. Literally “to the luck,” so it’s not a word-for-word English phrase, but the meaning is straightforward.
target_language_example: Zum Glück habe ich den Zug noch erwischt.
native_language_example: Luckily, I still caught the train.

additional_notes: Literally "to the coffee" (zu + dem = zum). Used to say something is intended to be eaten/drunk with coffee (often cake/cookies), or to invite/meet someone for coffee. Common in phrases like "Kommst du zum Kaffee?" (Are you coming for coffee?) or "Was gibt es zum Kaffee?" (What’s there for coffee?).
target_language_example: Kommst du heute Nachmittag zum Kaffee vorbei?
native_language_example: Are you coming by for coffee this afternoon?

meaning: to make a fool of someone; to tease/trick someone.
additional_notes: Used when someone is being deceived, mocked, or not taken seriously (often repeatedly): „Er hält mich zum Narren.“ Literally „to hold someone as a fool“—it means treating someone like an idiot or stringing them along, not physically holding them.
target_language_example: Du hältst mich doch zum Narren!
native_language_example: You’re making a fool of me!

meaning: in the end; finally; at the end.
additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens at the end of something (a story, a process, a meeting, a list). Often used to introduce the final point: "Zum Schluss möchte ich sagen …" It can mean either (1) at the very end in time/order, or (2) as a conclusion/lastly in a sequence.
target_language_example: Zum Schluss möchte ich mich bei euch allen bedanken.
native_language_example: Finally, I’d like to thank all of you.

additional_notes: Used to say you do something for enjoyment, not seriously or not for a practical purpose. Often answers “Why?” (Warum?) or clarifies intent: “Ich sage das nur zum Spaß.” Literally “to/for the fun” (zu + dem → zum + Spaß).
target_language_example: Ich mache das nur zum Spaß.
native_language_example: I’m only doing this for fun.

meaning: partly; in part; to some extent.
additional_notes: Common in both spoken and written German to say something is only partially true or done. Often paired with contrast words like „aber“ (but): „Zum Teil stimmt das, aber …“. Can also mean “some of them” when talking about people/things in a group: „Zum Teil waren sie müde.“ (Some of them were tired.)
target_language_example: Zum Teil hat sie recht, aber nicht ganz.
native_language_example: She’s partly right, but not completely.

additional_notes: Used to add irritation or emphasis in questions: "Was/Wo/Wer/Wieso zum Teufel …?" = "What/Where/Who/Why the hell …?" Also used in commands like "Geh zum Teufel!" = "Go to hell!" It’s rude/strong language—avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Wo zum Teufel ist mein Handy?
native_language_example: Where the hell is my phone?

additional_notes: Used when raising glasses and drinking together. Literally means “to (your) well-being/health,” so it’s a common, polite toast (especially with alcohol). Often said as “Zum Wohl!” or “Zum Wohl, alle zusammen!”
target_language_example: Zum Wohl! Auf einen schönen Abend!
native_language_example: Cheers! To a lovely evening!

additional_notes: Used to talk about doing/experiencing something the first time. Very common with the perfect tense (past), but can also be used in the present/future (e.g., when something is happening/going to happen for the first time). Often placed near the verb or the part of the sentence it relates to.
target_language_example: Ich bin zum ersten Mal in Berlin.
native_language_example: I am in Berlin for the first time.

meaning: for the last time (one last time).
additional_notes: Used to say something is happening the final time, often with emphasis or impatience (like a warning): "Zum letzten Mal: Hör auf!" Also common in neutral contexts meaning "one final time" before something ends: "Ich bin zum letzten Mal hier."
target_language_example: Zum letzten Mal: Mach bitte die Tür zu!
native_language_example: For the last time: Please close the door!

meaning: first; initially; for now (to begin with).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the first step in a sequence, or what happens before something else. Common in instructions and explanations. Often pairs with later steps like „dann“ (then) or „später“ (later).
target_language_example: Zunächst müssen wir die Formulare ausfüllen, dann können wir gehen.
native_language_example: First we have to fill out the forms, then we can go.

meaning: to work (to your workplace); to/for work.
additional_notes: Contraction of "zu der Arbeit" ("to the work/job"). Commonly used with verbs of going/commuting (e.g., gehen, fahren) and also to express being at work/working in some contexts (e.g., "Ich muss zur Arbeit" = "I have to go to work"). Often contrasts with "nach Hause" (home).
target_language_example: Ich gehe jetzt zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: I’m going to work now.

meaning: at hand; nearby and ready to use.
additional_notes: Used to say something is close by and available when needed, often in phrases like „etwas zur Hand haben“ (to have something at hand). Common with objects/tools/documents: „Haben Sie Ihren Ausweis zur Hand?“ It’s a fixed expression with „zur“ (= zu der).
target_language_example: Hast du deinen Reisepass zur Hand?
native_language_example: Do you have your passport at hand?

meaning: to confront (someone), often to demand an explanation.
additional_notes: Used when you directly confront someone about something they did or said, often in a serious tone. Common with a person as the object: jemanden zur Rede stellen. Similar to "jemanden zur Rede bringen" or "jemanden zur Verantwortung ziehen" (more formal).
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn zur Rede gestellt, weil er mich angelogen hat.
native_language_example: I confronted him because he lied to me.

meaning: to the point; about the matter at hand.
additional_notes: Used to steer a conversation back to the main topic or to start discussing the real issue. Common in phrases like „Komm zur Sache!“ (“Get to the point!”) and „Zur Sache:“ as a transition meaning “Now, to the matter.” Often sounds a bit firm/direct, depending on tone.
target_language_example: Komm bitte zur Sache — was ist passiert?
native_language_example: Please get to the point—what happened?

meaning: to school; to go to school.
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs of motion, especially "gehen" (to go): "zur Schule gehen" = to go to school / attend school. "zur" is a contraction of "zu der" (to the) and is used because "Schule" is feminine (die Schule). Often implies being a student or going to classes, not just physically going to a school building.
target_language_example: Meine Tochter geht jeden Tag zur Schule.
native_language_example: My daughter goes to school every day.

additional_notes: Used when someone accompanies a child (or someone else) to school, often by car, bike, or on foot. Common pattern: jemanden zur Schule bringen (accusative person). For taking yourself to school you’d usually say: zur Schule gehen/fahren (go to school / travel to school).
target_language_example: Ich bringe meine Tochter morgens zur Schule.
native_language_example: I take my daughter to school in the mornings.

meaning: to go to school (as a student; attend school).
additional_notes: Uses the fixed combination "zur" (= zu der) with "Schule". Often means attending school in general (not just physically going there right now). For specifically going there at the moment, you can also say "in die Schule gehen". For university, use "zur Uni gehen"/"an die Uni gehen" instead.
target_language_example: Meine Tochter geht jeden Tag zur Schule.
native_language_example: My daughter goes to school every day.

additional_notes: Used with movement or positioning verbs to mean moving/placing something out of the way (e.g., gehen/treten = step aside, stellen/legen = put aside). Common in polite requests: „Bitte zur Seite!“ / „Gehen Sie bitte zur Seite.“ Note: „jemandem zur Seite stehen“ is a different phrase meaning “to support/help someone.”
target_language_example: Gehen Sie bitte zur Seite.
native_language_example: Please step aside.

meaning: to step aside; to move to the side.
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to move out of the way (literally: to the side). In a more formal/figurative context it can also mean "to step down" or "to resign" (e.g., from a position), but beginners will mostly meet it in the physical sense. Often used as an instruction/imperative: "Treten Sie zur Seite" (formal) or "Tritt zur Seite" (informal).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, könnten Sie bitte zur Seite treten?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could you please step aside?

meaning: to be available; to be at someone’s disposal.
additional_notes: Used to say that something (time, money, information, a room, a person’s help) is available to be used. Very common in formal and everyday contexts. Often appears with a dative person: „jdm. zur Verfügung stehen“ = “to be available to someone / at someone’s disposal.” Related useful phrase: „etw. zur Verfügung stellen“ = “to provide / make something available.”
target_language_example: Wenn Sie Fragen haben, stehe ich Ihnen gern zur Verfügung.
native_language_example: If you have questions, I’m happy to be available to you / at your disposal.

additional_notes: Used mainly for the mother as a more formal or neutral way to say someone gave birth. Often appears with a direct object (a baby/child): „Sie hat ein Kind zur Welt gebracht.“ In everyday speech, people also commonly say „ein Kind bekommen“ (to have a baby).
target_language_example: Sie hat gestern ein gesundes Baby zur Welt gebracht.
native_language_example: She gave birth to a healthy baby yesterday.

meaning: to be born (to come into the world).
additional_notes: Common, neutral expression for being born. Often used with time/place details (e.g., in 1995, in Berlin). For people it means “to be born”; in a broader sense it can also mean “to come into existence” (e.g., an idea, a project). Past tense: „ist zur Welt gekommen“.
target_language_example: Meine Schwester ist 2003 in Köln zur Welt gekommen.
native_language_example: My sister was born in Cologne in 2003.

additional_notes: Common time expression meaning “right now/these days.” Often used with present tense: „Zur Zeit arbeite ich viel.“ It can also mean “for the time being.” Don’t confuse with „rechtzeitig“ (on time) or „in der Zeit“ (during the time).
target_language_example: Zur Zeit habe ich keine Zeit.
native_language_example: At the moment I don’t have time.

additional_notes: Used to say two things happen at the same time. Often used with two clauses ("…, und zur gleichen Zeit …") or with "gleichzeitig" as a synonym. Literally "to the same time" (zur = zu der).
target_language_example: Ich koche, und zur gleichen Zeit höre ich Musik.
native_language_example: I cook, and at the same time I listen to music.

meaning: at the right time; at the right moment.
additional_notes: Means something happens or someone does something at an appropriate/ideal moment. Often used with verbs like kommen (to come), passieren (to happen), or sein (to be). Note: "recht" here means "right/correct" (not "right" as in the opposite of left).
target_language_example: Du bist genau zur rechten Zeit gekommen.
native_language_example: You came at exactly the right time.

meaning: to be back; to have returned.
additional_notes: Used to say someone has returned to a place (home, the office, a city, etc.). Common with time expressions like „schon“, „wieder“, or „bald“: „Ich bin schon zurück.“ / „Wir sind wieder zurück.“ In separable-verb style you’ll also see it as „zurück sein“ in statements and „zurück?“ in questions.
target_language_example: Ich bin um sechs Uhr wieder zurück.
native_language_example: I’ll be back again at six o’clock.

meaning: to go back; to return (on foot).
additional_notes: Often used for physically going back to a place: "Wir gehen zurück." In the present/past it usually splits: "ich gehe zurück", "wir sind zurückgegangen". It can also mean "to decrease" (e.g., prices/temperatures) or "to date back to" ("Das geht auf 1800 zurück"), but the basic beginner meaning is "go back/return".
target_language_example: Ich gehe schnell zurück zum Auto.
native_language_example: I’m quickly going back to the car.

additional_notes: A separable verb: in the present/past tense, the prefix often goes to the end ("Ich komme morgen zurück."). In the Perfekt, it stays together: "ist zurückgekommen". It can mean returning to a place/person, and also returning to a topic ("Darauf komme ich später zurück." = "I’ll come back to that later.").
target_language_example: Ich komme heute Abend nach Hause zurück.
native_language_example: I’m coming back home this evening.

additional_notes: A separable verb: in the present tense the prefix often goes to the end (Ich lasse mein Handy zu Hause zurück.). In the past participle it becomes one word: zurückgelassen (Ich habe mein Handy zu Hause zurückgelassen.). Used for forgetting something somewhere, or leaving a person/animal behind (sometimes with the sense of abandoning them).
target_language_example: Ich habe meinen Regenschirm im Bus zurückgelassen.
native_language_example: I left my umbrella behind on the bus.

additional_notes: Used as an adverb. It can describe people doing something jointly (Wir gehen zusammen.) or things being combined/assembled (Setz das zusammen.). Also common with verbs like "zusammenkommen" (to meet/come together), "zusammenarbeiten" (to work together), and in the phrase "zusammen sein" (to be together / to be a couple, depending on context).
target_language_example: Wollen wir heute Abend zusammen essen?
native_language_example: Do we want to eat together tonight?

meaning: to be together; (as a couple) to be in a relationship.
additional_notes: Often describes being physically together (spending time together) or being romantically together. In the relationship sense, it’s common with "mit" + dative: "Ich bin mit Anna zusammen" = "I’m together with Anna" (i.e., we’re dating). Also used with "wieder" (again) for getting back together: "Wir sind wieder zusammen."
target_language_example: Seid ihr zusammen oder nur gute Freunde?
native_language_example: Are you together (a couple) or just good friends?

additional_notes: Used when people or organizations cooperate on a task or project. Often with "mit" + dative ("mit jemandem zusammenarbeiten" = to work with someone). Common forms: "Wir arbeiten zusammen" (we work together), "Ich arbeite mit ihr zusammen" (I work with her).
target_language_example: Ich möchte mit dir an diesem Projekt zusammenarbeiten.
native_language_example: I would like to work with you on this project.

meaning: to happen / to come about; to be reached (agreement/deal).
additional_notes: Common with things like plans, agreements, deals, meetings, or results. Often used with “wie” or “ob” (how/whether something comes about): “Wie ist das zustande gekommen?” Literally “to come into being,” and often implies something became possible through circumstances or effort.
target_language_example: Der Vertrag ist zustande gekommen.
native_language_example: The contract was reached / came about.

additional_notes: Common in written and more formal speech to refer to something that happened earlier. Often used with past tense narration or instructions (e.g., "zuvor" = earlier than the event just mentioned). Similar to "vorher", but "zuvor" sounds a bit more formal.
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn zuvor noch nie gesehen.
native_language_example: I had never seen him before.

meaning: “indeed / it’s true (that) …” often introducing a contrast (“…, but …”).
additional_notes: Most often used in the pattern **zwar …, aber …** to mean **“although …, (still) … / it’s true that …, but …”**. In this use, **zwar** signals that the first statement is true, but a contrasting point follows. It can also appear without **aber** when the contrast is implied by context.
target_language_example: Ich habe zwar Zeit, aber ich habe keine Lust.
native_language_example: I do have time, but I don’t feel like it.

additional_notes: Used for fractions and proportions, especially in math, measurements, recipes, and statistics. In German, fractions are often formed as a number + ordinal in plural: ein Drittel (1/3), zwei Drittel (2/3), drei Viertel (3/4).
target_language_example: Zwei Drittel der Klasse sind heute da.
native_language_example: Two thirds of the class are here today.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens two times. Often answers questions like „Wie oft?“ (How often?) and can be placed flexibly in the sentence: „zweimal pro Woche“ (twice a week), „zweimal täglich“ (twice daily).
target_language_example: Ich gehe zweimal pro Woche ins Fitnessstudio.
native_language_example: I go to the gym twice a week.

meaning: to read between the lines (understand an implied meaning).
additional_notes: Used when the real message isn’t stated directly, but is hinted at. Common in conversations about emails, texts, and polite or indirect wording. Grammar tip: it’s a separable idea—often used with a modal verb (e.g., „Man muss … lesen“).
target_language_example: Du musst zwischen den Zeilen lesen – er sagt nicht direkt, dass er Nein meint.
native_language_example: You have to read between the lines—he isn’t directly saying that he means no.

additional_notes: Refers to what most people (or society at large) think about a topic. Common in news, politics, and social discussions. Often used with verbs like "beeinflussen" (to influence) or "vertreten" (to represent): "die öffentliche Meinung beeinflussen".
target_language_example: Die öffentliche Meinung zu diesem Thema hat sich in den letzten Jahren stark verändert.
native_language_example: Public opinion on this topic has changed a lot in recent years.

meaning: public transport (a public means of transportation).
additional_notes: Often used in the plural: „öffentliche Verkehrsmittel“ = public transportation in general (buses, trains, trams, subway). In everyday speech, people also say „die Öffis“ (informal). You’ll commonly see it with verbs like „benutzen/nutzen“ (to use) or „mit … fahren“ (to go by).
target_language_example: Ich fahre meistens mit öffentlichen Verkehrsmitteln zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: I usually go to work by public transport.

meaning: overnight; during the night (also: suddenly/very quickly).
additional_notes: Most literally means something happens or changes during the night: „über Nacht“. It’s also commonly used figuratively to mean ‘all of a sudden’ or ‘in a very short time,’ often in phrases like „(sich) über Nacht ändern“ (to change overnight) or „über Nacht berühmt werden“ (to become famous overnight).
target_language_example: Das Wetter hat sich über Nacht geändert.
native_language_example: The weather changed overnight.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that something matters the most (often with verbs like lieben, schätzen, stellen). Example pattern: „Ich liebe dich über alles“ = “I love you more than anything.” Note: The phrase „Deutschland über alles“ is historically loaded/controversial today and is best avoided in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ich liebe dich über alles.
native_language_example: I love you more than anything.

additional_notes: Most often used to say you have just enough money/resources to live, but not comfortably. It commonly appears with "gerade/kaum" (barely) and with money-related context (rent, bills, salary).
target_language_example: Mit meinem Nebenjob komme ich gerade so über die Runden.
native_language_example: With my part-time job, I can just about get by.

additional_notes: Used for discussing a topic. The thing you talk about is introduced with **über** and takes the **accusative** (e.g., über den Film, über die Arbeit). Often used with questions like **Worüber sprechen wir?** (“What are we talking about?”).
target_language_example: Können wir über das Problem sprechen?
native_language_example: Can we talk about the problem?

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize zero/none. It usually comes before a noun ("überhaupt kein Geld" = no money at all) or can stand alone when the noun is clear from context ("Überhaupt keine." = None at all.). Often used in replies or to contradict an assumption.
target_language_example: Ich habe überhaupt kein Geld dabei.
native_language_example: I don’t have any money with me at all.

additional_notes: Used to strongly negate something. Often answers a yes/no question or corrects an assumption. In speech, stress is typically on “überhaupt”: “ÜBERHAUPT nicht”. You can also use it inside a sentence to emphasize the negation (e.g., “Das stimmt überhaupt nicht.”).
target_language_example: Nein, das stimmt überhaupt nicht.
native_language_example: No, that’s not true at all.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that there is zero of something (no amount, no information, no interest, etc.). Often appears in negative sentences (with „nicht“/„kein“ implied by context) and in answers to questions: „Was hast du gemacht?“ – „Überhaupt nichts.“ You can also use it to contradict an assumption: „Ich habe überhaupt nichts gesagt.“
target_language_example: Ich habe überhaupt nichts verstanden.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand anything at all.

meaning: to trick someone; to rip someone off (to swindle).
additional_notes: Usually used with a direct object: „jemanden übers Ohr hauen“ = to deceive someone, often to get money or an advantage. It’s a common colloquial idiom; the literal words (“hit over the ear”) are not what it means.
target_language_example: Pass auf, sonst haut dich der Verkäufer übers Ohr.
native_language_example: Be careful, or the seller will rip you off.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is normal or generally done in a place, group, or situation. Common patterns: "Es ist üblich, ..." (It’s customary to ...), "Das ist (nicht) üblich." (That’s (not) usual.), and "etwas ist üblich" (something is common).
target_language_example: Es ist üblich, Trinkgeld zu geben.
native_language_example: It’s customary to leave a tip.
